Judaism and the Sins of Israel: On the Essential Nature of Religion
Israel, an "artificial state" established by Zionists, has brought immense catastrophe to Palestine and the Middle East, exerting a profound and unsettling impact on the global order while severely jeopardizing humanity's faith in justice. To enable a clearer discernment of the true nature of Judaism and the state of Israel, distinguish right from wrong, and offer humanity a glimmer of hope to rectify deviations and restore justice, this article systematically delineates their multiple transgressions.
1. Blaspheming God and Serving the Devil
Does God exist? It is a question to which no definitive empirical answer can be given. Yet, for any religion, the existence of God is an absolute certainty—a Supreme Being who created the universe and will ultimately deliver it. Since God created the world, the Divine must be inherently grand, righteous, and impeccable. God cannot behave like an earthly despot who blurs the line between right and wrong, harbors blind favoritism, or instigates conflict that leaves the earth devastated and drenched in blood. Any entity that perpetuates such horrors must be the devil, not God. God would deem it beneath Divine dignity to broker arbitrary covenants, grant exclusive real estate titles to specific mortals, demonstrate absolute partiality toward a selective few, or engage in physical wrestling matches with humans—much like a human would never engage in such absurdities with an ant, and would find it reviling to hear an ant boast of such a relationship. Therefore, what Judaism worships is the devil, not God; consequently, Judaism itself is the true object of divine retribution.
2. A Total Syndicate Snuffing Out the Beacon of Humanity
The ultimate purpose of religion is self-interest, utilizing individual benefit as a mechanism to attract adherents. This self-interest can be bifurcated into two categories: temporal self-interest in the material world, and transcendental self-interest in the afterlife. While the vast majority of religions pursue the latter, the modalities of religious dissemination can be categorized into three paradigms: self-interest, altruism, and self-abnegation.
· Righteous Religions: Expand their doctrines through structural altruism to attain both temporal and transcendental self-interest (modern Protestantism, to a qualified extent, approaches this paradigm).
· Neutral Religions: Enjoin strict self-abnegation to achieve transcendental self-interest (authentic Chinese Mahayana Buddhism emphasizes high self-abnegation and moderate altruism; Tibetan Buddhism, however, deviates from this).
· Malevolent Religions: Disseminate their faith via raw self-interest to maximize both temporal and transcendental gains (Judaism fits this mold).
· Criminal Syndicates: When a group systematically inflicts harm upon external populations to secure transcendental self-interest, it ceases to be a religion and becomes a criminal enterprise (such as ISIS).
True righteous religion is singular; it must rely on altruism as its proselytizing engine to fulfill its dual self-interest. Judged by this criterion, Islam must also be categorized as a cultish entity.
When a religion becomes pathologically insular yet fiercely unified for collective self-enrichment, it must perpetually extract illicit advantages from the external world to fulfill its internal theological promises and suppress external criticism or interference. This manifests through predatory usury, monopolistic syndicates, the systematic deprivation of opportunities for outsiders, the monopolization of media to strangle freedom of speech, the utilization of ill-gotten wealth to manipulate foreign governments, and the deployment of collective intimidation against dissenters. Judged by any objective metric, this exhibits the classic hallmarks of a mafia.
Consider the contemporary world: we witness the collective intimidation of protesting students at Harvard, where syndicates coerced the university administration to surrender blacklists and threatened a total hiring boycott against student dissidents. Even in my own experience, when attempting to publish a critique of Israel, editors at major media outlets felt compelled to cautiously warn me to "ensure my personal safety." These multi-faceted realities reveal a chilling truth: when confronting Israel, the constitutional right to free speech is immediately compromised by physical and professional security anxieties.
Look at the sheer absurdity of our global reality: within the United States—the very nation that birthed the United Nations and once stood as a beacon of civilization—the government stands in obstinate, isolated solidarity with Israel, defiantly opposing the overwhelming majority of the international community on Palestinian sovereignty. Nearly all mainstream political figures line up in lockstep behind Israel, even when the comment sections beneath their public statements are flooded with denunciation from the populace. Are we to believe that every single American politician is a fundamentally malicious actor? Facing the spilled blood of the Palestinian people and the living hell of their homeland, have these politicians truly been possessed by demons to consciously walk in alignment with evil? No matter how compromised these politicians may be, it is impossible that this reflects the genuine, uncoerced intent of all of them. This unveils a profoundly horrifying reality upon closer reflection: the United States is rapidly transforming into a hollowed-out zombie, its sovereign soul thoroughly extracted by Israel and Zionist interest groups.
3. Bloodlust Masked by Hypocritical Dogma
We must remain hyper-vigilant against a common tactic employed by certain theologians and scholars who attempt to sanitize Judaism by citing altruistic laws within its scriptures—such as the Decalogue, commands to "give alms to the poor," or prohibitions against "oppressing the stranger." However, any insular, predatory interest group must inevitably weave a cloak of righteous justice to survive within secular society and deflect external scrutiny. As the ancient proverb goes, "there is honor even among thieves"—the most ruthless cartels in history eagerly built bridges and paved roads for their local neighborhoods, and the most extreme cults frequently used charitable handouts to buy public compliance.
These manicured facades are by no means the essence of the system; they are merely moral ornaments designed to deceive the world. In practice, "giving alms to the poor" stands in irreconcilable, parasitic contradiction with "predatory usury and capital monopoly." Through usurious practices and financial blood-sucking, they drive millions of Gentile families into destitution and ruin; then, they turn inward to distribute welfare within their enclosed circle, placating their own kin and delivering on the material benefits promised upon initiation. This closed-loop mechanism of "extreme external predation coupled with internal distribution of spoils" precisely validates its absolute identity as a mafia syndicate. To evaluate an entity, one must look past its ornamental garments and examine whose fundamental right to survival it has stripped away. Any appeasement of this profound hypocrisy constitutes an outright betrayal of human justice.
4. Actions Divorced from Modern Civilization
The foundational premise of modern civilization dictating that the Earth is the shared home of all living things; even apex species possess no arbitrary right to violently displace or dispossess other creatures of their habitats. If humanity lacks the ethical authority to evict monkeys from a mountain to claim it for ourselves, who under heaven possesses the right to strip the Palestinian people of their sovereign right to exist and reside in Palestine?
Following the conclusion of World War II in 1945, Jewish populations no longer faced an existential threat to their survival; what, then, justified their subsequent threat to the very survival of the Palestinians? Apologists might argue that the Jewish community, having just endured the horrors of the Holocaust, was trapped in an extreme crisis of survival. Yet, this can never serve as a legitimate pretext for violent dispossession. Existential crises are not unique to the Jewish experience. According to the most basic threshold of fairness and justice in modern civilization, any localized catastrophe or crisis must be resolved at its historical source; it can never grant a right to displace the catastrophe onto innocent third parties by plundering their legitimate right to life. The bitter fruits of European anti-Semitism ought to have been borne by Europe itself. Forcing the native inhabitants of Palestine—who played absolutely no part in European crimes—to foot the bill for "moral reparations" of the Holocaust, and framing the so-called "two-state solution" as justice, represents one of the most hypocritical, shameless, and predatory acts of banditry in the history of modern international politics.
5. The Abuse of Violence to Perpetrate Genocide
For nearly eighty years, Zionist forces in Palestine have systematically displaced the indigenous population, brutally massacred and incarcerated Palestinians, and relentlessly expanded illegal settlements. This has triggered an endless exodus of refugees, resulted in innumerable casualties, and caused harrowing atrocities to play out on a daily basis—all driven by a calculated attempt to gradually liquidate the Palestinian people and completely usurp their land.
Thanks to the ubiquity of modern digital media, the tragic plight of the Palestinians is now laid bare before the collective conscience of humanity. Who, then, is the true terrorist? The moral framework governing the justifiable use of violence dictating that violence is righteous only when one's own survival or the survival of others is actively threatened. Consequently, the Palestinian people possess an absolute, legitimate right to employ violence against their Israeli oppressors. Their resistance is fundamentally just, whereas Israel constitutes the actual terrorist entity.
6. Constructing an Invisible Empire Parasitic Upon Modern States
By tightly binding religious identity to material self-interest, the Zionist cartel has engineered an invisible empire that effectively reigns supreme over sovereign nations. Leveraging their monopolized financial wealth and sprawling media conglomerates, they exert deep, manipulative control over Western political landscapes. This insular, self-serving apparatus utilizes aggressive financial lobbying to transmute the hard-earned tax dollars of foreign citizens into their own political leverage, ultimately hijacking the foreign policies of major global powers. This is a textbook case of a predatory interest group subverting, hollow out, and invisibly parasitizing modern democracy and sovereign civilization.
7. Ideological Thought Policing and the Destruction of Public Justice
To immunize themselves against external critique, these groups weaponize historical trauma, swiftly branding any discourse that interrogates their atrocities with the label of "anti-Semitism." This calculated form of ideological thought policing is brutally suffocating academic freedom and liberty of expression. As the world witnesses the blood-soaked purgatory inflicted upon the Palestinian people, Western politicians—paralyzed by the intimidation of powerful lobby groups—lapse into a collective, spineless silence, willfully aligning themselves with demonic forces. This absolute double standard has triggered a profound crisis of trust in modern morality, fundamentally dismantling humanity's self-evident faith in equity, justice, and universal law.

Despite the reality that certain factions within the Jewish populace remain bound by a nexus of religion and self-interest—forming an invisible, crushing force capable of flattening any individual resistance to suppress anti-Zionist critiques—there are still courageous Jewish individuals who actively resist Israeli policies and oppose draconian anti-Semitism legislation. Though born into the fold of Judaism, their conscience and commitment to justice have triumphed over institutional evil. They represent the true pride of the Jewish people and the sole beacon of hope for their eventual moral redemption.

Brian Stelter is upset that Politico wasn’t allowed on Air Force One on Monday. He shouldn’t be. A plane seat isn’t a right, and Politico spent years using that seat to promote one party.

The White House kept Politico off the plane for Trump’s trip to Nebraska. Politico was the assigned print pooler, the one reporter who files notes the rest of the print outlets share. Other outlets were offered the seat and declined it, so the trip had no primary print pooler. The Washington Post still flew as the secondary, and the TV pool was still on board.

Trump was right to start this fight. He pulled the White House passes of Politico, CNN, and MS NOW because those outlets spent years promoting one party. A judge ordered the building access restored. The administration says that order doesn’t cover the plane, and CNN has already been kept off it on its own pool days.

Biden never had to do this because the press pool was already on his side. The press buried the laptop story, falsely called Biden’s border secure, and kept his decline off the front page until a debate made it impossible.

Stelter isn’t actually mourning a missing reporter from Air Force One. He’s mourning a guaranteed seat for an outlet that spent years using it against one party and not the other.

I’m thankful that President Trump keeps calling out the activist media and reprimanding them. He’s doing all Americans a service with this, even those who don’t like him.

text:
🚀 Stock Study: Krishna Defence & Allied Industries Ltd (NSE: KRISHNADEF) ⚓🇮🇳

A niche, high-ROCE "picks & shovels" play on India's booming naval upcycle!

📊 Latest Snapshot (As of Oct 5, 2026):
• Share Price: ₹1,201.00
• Market Cap: ₹1,795 Cr
• P/E Ratio: 43.8x
• ROCE / ROE: 31.1% / 23.7%
• Debt-to-Equity: 0.01

🏢 The Business & Moat:
KDAIL is a Tier-1 metallurgical supplier to the Ministry of Defence, manufacturing critical shipbuilding steel sections (bulb bars), super alloy weld consumables, and T-90 tank chassis components. It operates as a monopoly or duopoly for several niche naval applications, protected by immense entry barriers including 10-year DRDO Tech Transfers and grueling 3-5 year naval quality approval cycles.

💰 Growth & Cash Flow Turnaround
FY26 was a fundamental breakout year. Net Profit (PAT) surged ~85% YoY to ₹38.12 Cr on revenues of ₹244.78 Cr. More importantly, the company historically suffered from long working capital cycles but successfully flipped this to generate a massive ₹86.05 Cr in Operating Cash Flow in FY26. The balance sheet remains highly unleveraged.

📈 Key Catalysts & Triggers

1️⃣ Unmanned Platforms: Currently constructing "Jalkapi," India's largest Extra-Large Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV), which could elevate the company to a prime defense platform integrator.

2️⃣ Order Execution: Secured direct MoD orders, successfully bypassing shipyard intermediaries for better payment visibility.

3️⃣ Margin Support: Formalized an MoU under the Ministry of Steel's PLI 1.2 Scheme, which offers direct cash incentives on incremental production.

4️⃣ Institutional Visibility: Successfully migrated from the NSE SME Emerge platform to the NSE Mainboard.

⚠️ Key Risks

• High Working Capital: Naval supply chains are notoriously slow, leading to heavily extended inventory holding days.

• Customer Concentration: Over 90% of revenue is tied directly to the sovereign defense sector and shipyards.

• Commodity Risks: Fixed-price MoD contracts lack automatic pass-through clauses, leaving margins vulnerable to sudden raw material (specialty steel) inflation.

⚖️ Valuation Verdict
While broader defense peers (systems integrators and space tech) are trading at frothy 80x to 100x+ multiples, KDAIL trades at a comparatively reasonable 43.8x P/E. Given its >80% profit CAGR and >30% ROCE, it stands out as a compelling Growth-at-a-Reasonable-Price (GARP) candidate for aggressive investors backing the 'Aatmanirbhar Bharat' defense theme.

For those unfamiliar with the story, here's the VERY basic version from Brent Friedman's (@BFree63 - BF) viewpoint. FYI, BF is the co-creator of "Dark Skies" with @BryceZabel).

~

In 1981, when BF was 18, his former neighbor, John Herrington (JH), who BF saw as a father figure, offered him some money and asked BF to drive his two cars, and the family dog from San Francisco to Virginia. JH was relocating to the DC area for work in the Reagan administration and would go on to become the Assistant Secretary of the Navy, and later, Secretary of Energy.

BF and his two friends made the cross-country trip and wound up at Herrington's house, with Friedman having a private conversation with his former neighbor.

JH told him he had been briefed in an underground facility for weeks for his new job, and cried himself to sleep every night. He also said, "aliens are real, they're here, and I've seen them." JH said the part of the briefing about aliens was on Day 3.

~From Sound, Light & Frequency~

Friedman: "I think that when people ask me, you know, 'You're a writer, how do we know that you didn't come up with this?' Well, it's laced with details I just could not have invented. It's beyond my capabilities. I'm just not that good of a writer. 

"Let me conclude how the whole story, essentially, ended. Which was, I said [to Herrington], 'My mind is reeling, and what I don't understand is you've told me all of this, and how do you know I'm not gonna go tell people myself about this?' And he said, 'Oh, I'm sure you will. But the question is, who's gonna believe you?'

"That kind of hit me in the solar plexus, like, wow, you're right [laughs]. Who is gonna believe an 18-year-old kid who's going off to UCLA to be a theater major? 

"Secondarily, he said, 'If you tell this story and you use my name, I'll just deny it, because that's how the cover-up works.'

"And so there I was with this incredible story, and already realizing there was no value to it, in terms of me telling anyone and being the whistleblower, right? If that was even crossing my mind. 

"But I have to say that, at 18 years old, I remember we'd stayed up late enough talking, and by the time I got downstairs where my friends were asleep down in the Rumpus room (a room usually in the basement of a home that is used for games, parties, and recreation), I remember laying there on my sleeping bag on the floor, looking up at this window and seeing the stars. And I thought, my whole world has just been turned upside down, and I don't think I fully understood how to process it. 

"But, I told that story to my family when I got back home, and I don't think I told it again until probably close to 30, when I was 30, because even my family had trouble believing it."

~

For the September 17th edition of @SchreckReports's "Signs of Life," he tracked down JH via email, spoke on the phone, and asked him about JF's claims. 

A summary...

Herrington: Brent who? I've never met him.

Schreckinger: Let me tell you his story and see if that refreshes your memory. 

Herrington: Oh yeah, I think he was a neighbor of mine. I DID pay for my car to be driven across the country but Friedman had nothing to do with that. It was my son-in-law who drove it. 

I didn't cry when briefed about UFOs and aliens, but I'm intrigued by those reports of Navy encounters with UAP. 

Friedman: I stand by my story. 

~

"And some people in the community have pointed out, 'Well, his daughters were in like, high school, middle school at this time.' So I interpret this as somebody who went on to be his son-in-law. I actually am looking into that a bit.

text: I shall tell a story to illustrate since intraconference play offers inconclusive results depending on timeframe measured, rankings at time of competition, and post season play including bowl games outside of the BCS. National championships in the BCS and CFP era tilt towards the SEC, but Alabama’s six chips loom large in that calculus. Remove Alabama and the results among remaining teams and conferences are comparable. The game day mythos surrounding Saturday football in the South builds a romanticized narrative that is hard to penetrate with facts. To argue with the diehard SEC fan is to accept the argument will eventually turn theological rather than a rational exploration of how we arrived at this moment of contention where the non SEC football world concurs in the bias shown to the SEC. Until expansion the SEC was generally understood to be dominated by a handful of teams rotating at the top and indistinguishable second tier teams.  Same with the B10, ACC and PAC 12. The Big12 only recently became something other than backyard offensive football with no defense. In the CFP era it became important to tout strength of schedule and quality losses as distinguishing criteria, devaluing conference championships. Saban was among the first to harp continuously about how hard SEC road games were regardless of the level of competition. At stake were limited playoff opportunities and huge paydays. Enter NIL and the upward pressure on player payments legitimizing the pay for play system long suspected to fuel top program success, particularly in the SEC. Players and coaches followed money which flows more free in the SEC than elsewhere because of rabid and desperate fan bases tired of being SEC doormats. Enter ESPN’s broadcast deal with both the SEC and the CFP which introduces the dynamic of conference preference and revenue driven match ups. Revenue driven match ups depend on relative rankings which rely heavily on preseason polling. Once competition begins there are significant barriers to movement into or out of the polls except in cases of egregious loss or unprecedented success.  This is called confirmation bias. Aided by a network incentivized to favorably promote the SEC, opinions are influenced towards its relative strength compared to conferences not subsidized in the same way. The last AP Top 25 stands as the most recent example of media created confirmation bias in action. At this point, with a 9 game schedule, the SEC is insulated from challenge except on the margins. Their remaining solution is to expand the CFP and allow for more intraconference match ups among the best teams in each P4 conference.

text:
The labor theory of value believes that value (which is what people pay for) is created by the labor done to produce the good or service on offer. It's preposterously easy to see how false it is. (What an embarrassment to Oren Cass!)est is:

"'Extra pay' is something you demand for doing work."

Okay, kids, that's called the "labor theory of value," and it's Marxist economic thinking. I recommend not listening to people who have used Marx's central conceptions as the foundations of their economic musings.

The labor theory of value believes that value (which is what people pay for) is created by the labor done to produce the good or service on offer. It's preposterously easy to see how false it is. (What an embarassment to Oren Cass!)

Here's an example!

One time, we needed a handyman to do some work for us, so we hired a guy we knew who needed the work. The thing is, the guy and his company had a quasi-mystical belief that work done without any power tools had a higher quality to it because it was done by hand instead of by machine. This probably would have been fine if he charged competitively by the job, but he didn't. He charged, in part, by the hour.

His work was insanely slower than it would have been with power tools and nail guns, so it turned out to be really expensive. It also wasn't done nearly as well as it might have been. The value created was lower, and the cost was higher, specifically because it took more labor. Labor ("extra work") did not create value here.

Here's another example!

Some people put a lot of labor into drawing useless pictures of anime fantasies or fan art or whatever. They're essentially worthless, but they take a lot of labor to produce between skills development and doing a good job. These things do not produce much value, though, even though they take considerable labor.

Labor is not the producer of value. Labor might be required to end up with value, but it isn't where value comes from. (In logic, we would call it a necessary but insufficient condition.)

Here's another example the other way!

It is entirely possible, if you live in the right place, to essentially dig a small hole in your yard taking less than ten minutes and find a diamond worth a million dollars (as was just found in Arkansas recently, apparently). Lots of value was produced with very little labor. You digging a little hole in your yard resulted in, but did not produce, a million dollars in value.

On the other hand, it's a lot more likely that you could go break your body digging in your yard for 15 hours a day until you're haggard and never find anything worth a dime. Lots of labor, same activity, no value.

The labor theory of value is stupid.

Actually, it's not just stupid; it's resentful.

The labor theory of value is the notion of a resentful person who thinks his work is intrinsically more valuable than it is and who resents that he isn't getting more for it than he is, either from the market or from an employer who is paying him to do things he probably couldn't do productively outside of that employment.

In my opinion, which isn't the opinion of a "Chief Economist" at a postliberal retard outlet, value is produced by solving problems for other people, which they are willing to pay for. Labor is a necessary condition to the production of that solution, but it isn't sufficient to determine the value produced because the value is determined otherwise: by how much solving a particular problem is worth to a person who needs it solved (because they can't solve it some other way, including through another service provider who does it more cheaply).

Anyway, Cass's failure to understand interest, by his own indication, seems to be a consequence of his having adopted Marx's resentful and wrong labor theory of value. To this I say, what a surprise!!

PS: Marx equipped his doctrine of the labor theory of value with a second crackpot belief that is relevant here too: the concept of "surplus value."

Marx believed the value in a product or service is produced by the labor which is only partially compensated for the value it produced. The owner (the capitalist) pockets the "surplus value" generated by the labor but not compensated by the wages he'll pay for that labor. Thus, the owner (capitalist) is exploiting the worker by extracting value from him that he doesn't pay. (Marx painted the picture for the worker more grimly than this, but we shan't digress.)

This is the same kind of idiotic bullshit reasoning that results in people like Cass not understanding that you are, in fact, paying for something when you pay interest. Owners own the capital; they carry the risk; they invest, at risk, to create the possibility to produce the thing their outfit produces, which would be far harder or impossible without that investment (which the average worker has no ability to match on their own). The owner also has to handle management since he's ultimately the one who deals with the responsibility of all other aspects of product development, delivery, and sale. He might pay people to do those things or to manage, but at the end of the day since he carries the risk, he has the responsibility to make sure it gets done, and it's mostly his reputation that's on the line.

That is, the owner earns that "surplus value" in a wide variety of ways, even if all he does is assume the risk. He isn't extracting it as an act of theft from the worker. Again, the logic is that labor is a necessary but insufficient condition, and the value Marx called "surplus" goes above the worker's wages by dealing with other necessary conditions until sufficiency is met.

Of course, "surplus value" is yet another resentment concept, aiming to make the worker feel robbed by his employer by systematically making sure he doesn't understand the condition he's in to begin with so he'll be mad not just about the situation but about parts of it he has no reasonable right to be upset about. That surplus anger gets channeled into idiotic pushes for revolution.

And, by the way, that's exactly what postliberal retards like Oren Cass are doing with the same kinds of misunderstanding, targeting largely the same kinds of people in order to get them worked up to achieving Cass's political ambitions for him, even at the threat of their own destruction.

U.S. stocks closed higher Monday, 10.05.26 led by large technology shares. https://t.co/jj0fb4Hh1Q via @YouTube 

U.S. stocks closed higher Monday, led by large technology shares. 

The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.1% to a record close of 27,477. The Samp;P 500 added 0.7% to 7,774, within about 0.3% of its summer high. The Dow gained 0.2% to 51,268. The Russell 2000 rose 0.5% to 2,847. 

That move sat next to a less friendly backdrop. The 10-year Treasury yield rose to 5.31%. Brent crude swung between about $100 and $103 and settled a little above $100. Deal news, including Schneider Electric’s roughly $22.6 billion bid for PTC, supported parts of the tape. Last Friday’s softer-than-expected September jobs report was still in the background. 

September ISM Services PMI printed 54.9, down from 55.4, a 27th straight month of expansion. The prices-paid index rose to 74.0, the highest since July 2022. Activity is still expanding. Services inflation is not cooling with it. 

The rest of the week is lighter on major data, ahead of bank earnings next week. 

Tuesday: the August trade report. Constellation Brands reports after the close. 

Wednesday: minutes of the September 15–16 FOMC meeting, 2:00 p.m. ET. At that meeting, the Committee raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75%–4.00%. 

Thursday: weekly jobless claims. PepsiCo reports before the open. 

Friday: preliminary University of Michigan consumer sentiment. Delta Air Lines reports before the open.

In 1996, a Libyan leader put one billion dollars on the table for Black America. Washington made sure it never reached them.
The offer came during Louis Farrakhan's visit to Tripoli in January 1996. Muammar Gaddafi pledged the money to the Nation of Islam for economic development—Black-owned banks, factories, housing, schools, hospitals. Not a loan.
Not charity with strings. A gift from an African head of state to the descendants of enslaved Africans.
Farrakhan did everything by the book. He applied to the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control for permission to accept the money. The Clinton administration denied it in August 1996. Libya was a state sponsor of terrorism. Sanctions barred the transaction. Case closed.
The Treasury also blocked a separate $250,000 award Gaddafi had given Farrakhan for organizing the Million Man March.
The Nation of Islam was chosen for a reason. Founded in Detroit in 1930, built by Elijah Muhammad, rebuilt by Farrakhan after 1975—it was the only Black American organization with the infrastructure to absorb that kind of capital. They had schools. Businesses. A newspaper. A security force. Hundreds of thousands of members.
Gaddafi saw organization where Washington saw a threat.
Farrakhan fought the decision. He called it a violation of religious freedom and legal rights. He said the money would create joint ventures with Black businesses. He threatened to mobilize across the country. It didn't matter. The Treasury Department had the final word.
Consider the context. The same government that blocked this gift was simultaneously funding death squads in Central America, propping up Mobutu in Zaire, and maintaining close ties with apartheid South Africa. Gaddafi was the enemy. Black economic development, funded by African money, was the threat.
The billion dollars never arrived. Black America never got to find out what it could have built.

@BernieSanders, or should I say @SenSanders , you put a teachers union shirt behind your microphone and asked California to trust it with healthcare.

I'm a teacher. I'll grade it for you.

That shirt says UTLA. United Teachers Los Angeles, the union that runs the show at LAUSD, the second biggest school district in the country. text:
When an injustice occurs, the journalists, historians and archivists document evidence and facts to establish a memory, with an underlying faith: that justice, action and wisdom will follow from it in time. But time in itself offers no such function on its own -- it all comes down to the individual will and effort to make wisdom and justice out of what has occurred. And what if the power imbalance is too great between the victim and the perpetrator? Accountability and enforcement of law require not only will, but also power. The realist in this situation would say: justice can come only if we accrue more power so we no longer remain victims in the future, and so we can enforce laws ourselves that all others have understood and accepted as cherished and supreme for sustained peace. (But power is a double-edged sword: the victim, if powerful and as one-sided as the perpetrator, when in a state of humiliation from the loss of dignity, is in a position with all reasons and emotions in agreement to unleash the very act that was unleashed upon it; after all, the nature of one-sidedness is such that justice for one is injustice for the other; the nature of power is such that it is vital for survival, but also carries in it temptation towards one-sidedness: for ugliness produces only ugliness, and by what justification can the perpetrator be denied the right to act in response from all the rage, hatred, vindictiveness and humiliation that the sight of ugliness has produced and has become all-consuming.)

Documentation of facts and production of history is as equally crucial as accrual of power, and both proceed from an injury; an injury precedes the act of seeking wisdom. Wisdom is earned, which we all hold to be a truism -- but what is actually earned? Injury through injustices from the imbalance of power. Which is to say: wisdom is earned through injustices. The path to wisdom, that is, more consciousness, is paved in blood from the sheer barbaric savagery, the author of which still lurks deep down in us all. Even when wisdom is earned, it is earned for a time, since it has to be earned again, which requires injuries. Where there is power, there can be no universal empathy, and where there is wisdom, there universal empathy can exist.

At least 20 men from Telangana are reported to have been caught in a recruitment network that allegedly took them to Russia after promising civilian jobs. While some have returned, others remain stranded and four are believed to have been deployed to fight for the Russian army against Ukraine.

How did the recruitment happen?

According to complaints from families, agents approached men seeking overseas employment and promised jobs such as cooks, cleaners, gardeners, mechanics, support staff and manual workers.

In one case, Megavath Prakash of Dammannapet in Dharpally mandal paid ₹2.4 lakh to Madhava Rao of Ramadugu for visa and travel expenses. Prakash travelled to Russia and worked for a private company for about four months before it shut down.

Madhava Rao allegedly then offered to arrange another job through Russia-based agents Odde Yellaiah and Telu Krishna, seeking another ₹50,000. Prakash was subsequently taken to Gourav Chaudhary, who allegedly facilitated his recruitment into the Russian Army.

What happened after they reached Russia?

Families said some men were made to undergo military training instead of doing the civilian jobs they had been promised. Accounts shared by returnees described prolonged physical training, inadequate food, insufficient sleep and poor accommodation.

Some men later circulated videos and messages seeking help. One returnee, Kasturi Thirupathi, said, "Because we needed to repay debts back home, we trusted the agents and got cheated."

The men identified include people from Nizamabad, Kamareddy and Sircilla districts. Three of the 16 men identified in a subsequent repatriation effort, Shekar of Banda Lingapur, Rajashekar of Keshapur and Thirupathi of Darpally, have returned home, while 13 were awaiting repatriation.

What action has followed?

Nizamabad police arrested Gourav Chaudhary, 34, a native of Karwar in Uttar Pradesh. Police said he claimed his bank accounts were used by a Russian Army recruitment agency and were verifying whether he acted in connivance with the agency.

Nizamabad MP Dharmapuri Arvind wrote to External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar seeking the repatriation of the 16 men. Arvind also thanked Jaishankar and the Indian embassy for assistance in securing the release of some men.

The Union government has advised Indians to exercise caution over Russian defence-related job offers, avoid unrecognised agents and verify recruitment credentials and employment contracts before travelling to Russia.

Uber Wait Times Rise 19% as Prices Climb 53%: Study | Alex Bitter, Business Insider

You might be waiting longer for your Uber ride to arrive — and paying more for it.

The time between when Uber matched a driver with a rider and when the car arrived grew 19% between the first quarter of 2023 and the same period this year, according to a new analysis by Len Sherman, an executive in residence and adjunct professor at Columbia Business School.

Over the same period, the price per mile that Uber charged rose 53% on average, per the analysis.

"You're charging more for less, for degrading the service," Sherman told Business Insider in an interview. Sherman released the wait-time and price findings on Wednesday in a new report.

"This analysis relies on a number of inaccuracies, which we've publicly refuted," an Uber spokesperson said. The spokesperson declined to comment specifically on Sherman's findings about wait time and per-mile cost.

The spokesperson referred Business Insider to a January blog post from the company, which said it was "false" that "the only reason Uber was able to become profitable was by raising prices while taking an ever larger share" of fares.

The data provide another example of how Uber has changed for riders over the last decade.

Once among startups that burned cash to acquire users, Uber has more recently used its upfront pricing strategy to become profitable. It is often done by charging riders more and paying drivers less, Sherman has previously contended.

Sherman examined 37,500 trips completed by drivers in six US cities, compiled using data from GigU, an app that shows drivers how much they will make per minute and per mile on a trip before they accept it. Wait times increased in five of the six cities, including Atlanta, Dallas, and Houston.

In the sixth city — Tampa, Florida — wait times declined slightly.

The data do not include the time that riders spent waiting for Uber to pair them with a driver, Sherman said, since he relied on data from drivers. Once a rider requests a ride, Uber sends the ride offer to nearby drivers, often at different payout rates.

That process can add minutes to rider wait times, Sherman said. "By definition, it's an underestimate," he said.

By increasing wait times and prices, Uber is risking its relationship with customers, Sherman said. The rise of AI agents means that riders are more easily able to compare prices with rival Lyft or local alternatives, he added.

Sherman's study also pointed to the 2026 Axios Harris Poll 100, which ranks major companies based on their reputation. This year's edition placed Uber 72nd on the list, lower than its position as 58th in 2025, with declines on metrics including trust, character, and ethics.

"This is a company that has acted in a way that clearly has lost the trust of their customers, riders, and drivers," Sherman said.

Sherman's report is his latest on Uber. His previous studies showed that Uber increased the share of each rider fare that it kept, known as the company's take rate, therefore reducing the pay that went to its gig-worker drivers.

Another study earlier this year showed that Uber's commercial insurance and operational charges varied significantly across seemingly identical trips.

text:
Inference's Next Competition Isn't Price. It's Verifiability.

Token prices have fallen roughly 600x since 2020. Enterprise inference spending has gone up, not down. That divergence is not a paradox of demand — it is a symptom of a market where the price signal has stopped carrying reliable information. OpenRouter processed over 200 trillion tokens last month, at a ~71% gross margin. Stripe acquired it for over $7 billion at roughly 50x revenue. What Stripe bought is the routing decision that sits in front of every AI request. What the market still cannot verify is whether the provider on the other side of that decision delivered what it claimed.

Three questions define the verifiability gap. Did you get the model you asked for? Did you pay for the tokens you actually burned across cache input, input, output, and tool calls? Is your data handled the way the retention policy says? Each has an evidence base. Each has a boundary between what is proven and what is asserted.

Start with pricing. Tarun Chitra's team published an experimental audit of OpenRouter's ranking algorithm and found a specific flaw: the algorithm aggregates cache rates across providers but does not penalize an individual provider whose cache hit rate declines. A provider can therefore under-report cache hits to look cheaper in price rankings, win traffic, then serve without cache and bill at a higher effective rate. Once under-reporting becomes a viable strategy for ranking, honest reporters are penalized — they either follow or lose traffic. Chitra's team estimated the mechanism extracts roughly $3.5 million annually across the platform. They also documented a related pattern: providers that repriced had sharply worse cache performance, some reporting almost no cache hits on a second identical prompt.

That is a pricing distortion, not fraud in the legal sense. It is a scoring-rule exploit. The distinction matters because the fix is governance, not enforcement.

Quantization is harder. UC Berkeley researchers described a covert substitution attack in which a provider serves a quantized model with probability p and the full-precision model with probability 1-p. As p approaches zero, the observed distribution converges on the nominal model, and sample-based detection degrades. A sophisticated provider can lower p when traffic looks like an audit and raise it on ordinary traffic. The detection problem is genuinely difficult. Identity prompting, the intuitive test, performs at roughly chance (50%) at distinguishing quantized from full-precision versions within the same model family. Llama3-70B at FP8 versus FP16 was not reliably distinguishable by BERT, T5, or GPT2 classifiers. The Berkeley work also flags a worse case: backdoors that are inert at FP32 and activate only after rounding to INT8 or FP4. Here the mechanism is verified in the lab. The scale of real-world deployment is not independently audited.

Model identity substitution has the hardest public evidence. In March 2026, CISPA Helmholtz conducted the first systematic audit of "shadow APIs" — third-party endpoints that resell access to frontier models. 45.83% of tested endpoints failed model fingerprint verification, with performance deviation up to 47.21%. The audit documented cases of wholesale backbone substitution, including GPT-5 served as GLM-4-9B. Those shadow APIs had been used in 187 academic papers; the most popular endpoint accumulated 5,966 citations. Follow-on work improved the tooling: KBF flags all 155 economically relevant substitutions across 16 production endpoints with no same-model false rejections, and AgentProv caught 100% of substitution pairs across 630 evaluation checkpoints with a 7% false-positive rate under system-prompt injection. OpenRouter's free-tier routing policy has been confirmed to allow nondeterministic model substitution within an active session; in one ~21-hour audit, nine different models from five providers served 143 requests.

Token inflation has the most developed academic base. A University of Tennessee paper formalized what it calls the trust paradox — every audit must trust some artifact, and current frameworks trust exactly the artifacts the provider is most incentivized to manipulate. Under the most permissive settings the authors tested, hidden reasoning usage could be inflated by an average of 1,469% without detection, turning a $100 honest bill into roughly $1,569. Even when the user can see the full reasoning string, tokenization ambiguity alone permits 50.85% over-reporting. The authors' conclusion is structural rather than technical: the problem is not any particular auditor, but that any evidence comes from the audited party. Maryland's CoIn framework, deployed as a trusted third-party auditor, detects token-count inflation with 94.7% success. The gap between the 1,469% inflation ceiling and the 94.7% detection rate is not a contradiction — it is the difference between laboratory bounds and deployed defenses. Neither is production-scale evidence.

Data monetization is the least well-evidenced category, and it is worth being precise about the boundary. OpenRouter states it has never shared, sold, or licensed underlying prompt data, and offers a Zero Data Retention option that can be enforced globally, per model group, or per request. It also discloses that some endpoints "do not train but retain data" for abuse scanning or legal reasons, and that ZDR applies only to eligible providers. Chinese media reporting has documented smaller relay stations selling user logs — buyers claiming to represent model vendors, requesting Claude 4-6+ sessions with 30+ turns of tool-calling dialogue, at roughly 0.1-0.2 RMB per conversation. There is no equivalent evidence of systematic user-data sales at the enterprise inference-provider tier. The monetization risk is real at the long tail. It is not the risk that justifies the premium pricing of the enterprise tier.

That distinction explains how the market is actually pricing verifiability. Fireworks raised $1.5 billion at a $17.5 billion valuation. Baseten raised roughly $1.5 billion at $13 billion. Together AI raised $800 million at $8.3 billion. Combined, nearly $4 billion in under four weeks. Their pitch is not "cheapest tokens." Fireworks says over 95% of its tokens come from customer-data-specialized models — fine-tunes, adapters, distillation, and customer training artifacts. What enterprises are buying is operational complexity solved: continuous batching, cache management, quantization, autoscaling, latency guarantees, observability, and billing that survives an audit. Research on confidential compute instances puts the premium for regulated environments at 20-30% over comparable standard instances, and characterizes it as a trust premium rather than a scarcity premium. Gartner projects $2.52 trillion in global AI spending in 2026, with $1.37 trillion to AI infrastructure, and enterprise attention shifting from "access to frontier models" to inference economics, data gravity, latency, and control.

The audit tooling exists, and it is not yet deployed at scale. Inference Receipts binds model identity, sampling configuration, and output tokens into a tamper-evident commitment chain at under 0.006% per-token overhead, with 100% tamper detection in 1,200 trials and zero false positives, dropping below 0.001% at 72B scale. But its trust model is honest-launcher: a malicious launcher can produce internally consistent receipts. GPU-level trusted execution environments would give a hardware-anchored alternative, but public side-channel audits of H100 confidential computing in multi-tenant settings are still thin. Behavioral fingerprinting has moved from academic prototypes to reusable tooling — single-token fingerprint verification covers 165 models at roughly 7% equal error rate — but it is a best-effort detector, not a proof.

The pattern across all five manipulation vectors is the same. The mechanism is verified. The scale is not. Audits produce evidence from the audited party. Cryptographic receipts require an honest launcher. TEEs require hardware the inference market does not yet widely expose. The result is that verifiability is not a technical problem waiting for a better algorithm. It is a market-structure problem waiting for someone with enough leverage to make disclosure the price of routing.

That is why Stripe paid 50x revenue for OpenRouter. The routing decision is the only point in the stack where a neutral party sees both what was requested and what was served. Whether OpenRouter converts that position into a verification layer — rather than a ranking layer that providers can game — is the variable to watch.

What to watch: whether OpenRouter begins distinguishing quantization levels in its routing and pricing display, rather than showing fp4, fp8, and bf16 endpoints under one model name at one price. Whether Inference Receipts or CoIn is integrated by any major inference platform, which would drop verification cost from academic-project levels to production levels. Whether the trust premium for confidential compute widens beyond 20-30%, which would confirm that verifiability is being priced as an asset class independent of compute. And whether Nvidia publishes multi-tenant side-channel audit results for H100 confidential computing — the missing hardware anchor for the entire verification stack.

text:
I’m posting this to help prevent anyone from losing money.
I want to warn people in the ranching community about a Facebook business page calling itself “Angus Calves Market.”
The page advertises $500–$750/head weaned Hereford and Black Angus bottle calves and appears to attract potential buyers through its posts. The administrator claims to be located in Texas, but there are some serious inconsistencies that I believe buyers should be aware of.
My girlfriend contacted the account first. During her conversation with the administrator, he told her he was in Odessa, Texas, and then blocked her when she asked about meeting and purchasing the cattle.
I later contacted him myself. After he had already claimed to be in Odessa, I told him that I was also in Odessa. However, when you look at the page’s public posts, they repeatedly state that the business is located in Dallas, Texas.
When I asked about purchasing the cattle, delivery was offered. When I said I would rather pick them up, I was told that pickup was a biosecurity issue and that they didn’t want anything brought onto the farm.
I then offered to pay upon delivery. I was told that payment had to be made in advance. That immediately raised a red flag for me. When I questioned why I couldn’t pay upon delivery, the account blocked me.
The same account had already blocked my girlfriend after she tried to arrange a meeting and purchase the cattle.
There are also concerning details in some of the photos associated with the page that appear inconsistent with the claimed Texas location. Some vehicle/identification details appear to be from outside the United States. I cannot independently verify where those images originated, but combined with the other inconsistencies, I believe potential buyers should proceed with extreme caution.
       PLEASE DO NOT SEND MONEY IN ADVANCE TO THIS ACCOUNT WITHOUT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFYING THE SELLER, THE CATTLE, AND THE LOCATION.
If someone is genuinely selling cattle, buyers should be able to independently verify who they are dealing with and where the cattle are located.
Before sending any money:
    Verify the seller’s identity and physical location.
     Ask to see the cattle in person or have someone you trust inspect them.
    Verify ownership and other relevant livestock documentation.
   Be extremely cautious about anyone demanding payment before delivery or refusing reasonable arrangements to verify the cattle.
    Report suspicious accounts to Facebook and share this warning with other cattle buyers.
I’m posting this because I would hate to see someone in the cattle community lose hundreds or thousands of dollars.
Please do your due diligence and don’t send money simply because a Facebook page has cattle listed for sale.   (Chris Caley)  credit  please share and Good luck

text:
I really appreciate you taking the time to write all of this out. I completely understand a lot of the concerns you’ve raised, agree that they need to be addressed, and genuinely apologize for the unacceptable behavior some from our culture have displayed.

At the same time, there are so many good Indian Americans who have made every effort to assimilate—and genuinely have—who still face hostility, like Bo French complaining about seeing too many Indians at the UT Austin game. Personally, I attended a military high school here and have lived in the US for over 15 years. I share my culture naturally, never force it on anyone, and have fully embraced everything the American way of life has to offer.
I feel equal outrage when Indians do bad things in the US; I’ve personally called out multiple people for acting like absolute idiots. But it feels like the X algorithm is designed to highlight the worst extremes on both sides to spark outrage.

I’ve tried having constructive dialogues about this, pointing out that Indian Americans have exceptionally low incarceration rates, high education levels, and a significant block of conservative voters who support an "America First" agenda. Yet that reality gets completely ignored. Out of the total Indian population in the country, the vast majority are law-abiding and contributing. I fully agree that bad actors should be held accountable and that strict policies should be enforced, but instead, all of us get lumped together. Whenever we try to assimilate or share our perspective, we just get harassed out of the conversation—you can see it right in the comments on my tweet, filled with keyboard warriors just hating.

What rarely gets brought up is the role of the middleman—the corporations—in setting everyday people against each other. American companies and their subsidiaries recruited Indian talent for these roles. People accepted those job offers, followed every legal process, and migrated seeking better career growth and stability—with zero intent to "take" an American's job. They simply responded to legitimate market opportunities and played by the rules. But now, after building lives here legally, people are told that shouldn't have been allowed and that everything they worked for should be uprooted.

Finally, it’s a massive double standard to judge an entire population by its worst elements. If we judged Americans solely by school shooters, white-collar crime, illegal lobbying, or fund smuggling, it would be recognized immediately as unfair and absurd. Entire groups shouldn't be vilified because of the actions of a few bad apples. 

Thank you for taking the time to read and critique it helps build constructive dialogue.

text:
Itinerary / recommendations

We spent six days in Tokyo, two in Hakone, and five in Kyoto. Given perfect foresight, we would have spent a day less in Tokyo. While Tokyo has some great museums and sightseeing, its biggest draws were the shopping and mind-boggling infrastructure. We easily could have spent another day in Kyoto either exploring here or taking a side trip.

Tokyo
Ginza is full of department stores, restaurants, and nightlife. The department stores are awesome. The basement levels of every floor have entire floors devoted to prepared foods. The restaurants here tend to be a bit spendy. The Imperial Palace nearby has beautiful grounds. Visiting the palace takes some planning; the hours are limited and tours fill up quickly.

The Tsukiji Outer Market is the biggest food market in Tokyo and has plenty of other random things for sale. Sushi for breakfast? Absolutely. A tourist trap I was happy to fall into.

TeamLab Planets is an immersive (literally, shin-deep in water at times) art exhibit. My wife and  had a blast here. I would book this a bit in advance; the better time slots tend to fill up.

The Miyzaki museum needs to be booked way, way in advance.

Akihabara is Japan's anime & pop culture hub and is absolutely worth a visit if you are at all into anime or just wants to see a very different neighborhood. Arcades are a huge deal here and can be a great place to kill some time. We found our favorite coffee shop in Tokyo here, Vault Coffee, which is run by a single (very) young man. Nearby is 2k540 Aki-Oka Artisan, a collection of shops selling handmade goods shoehorned in under a viaduct. Lots of neat stuff in here, in a really interesting space.

Shibuya is famous for the "Shibuya scramble", the world's busiest pedestrian crossing. The official stores of a number of gaming companies can be found here, including the only Nintendo store. The mall PARCO has the most insane collection of couture fashion I have ever seen; it was worth visiting this neighborhood just to see such wild clothing being sold (and worn!).

The Tokyo National Museum has an incredible collection. Thousand-year old katanas that look like they could be brand new, 1200 year old, somehow perfectly preserved wooden statues, and artwork spanning Japan's thousand-plus year history. Jonas will need to pick his spots unless he wants to spend a whole day here.

Hakone
The point of Hakone are the onsen (bathhouses) fed by the many hot springs in the area. There are some relatively inexpensive places to stay here. Great place to relax for a couple of days. Stayed in the Hotel Indigo, which I cannot recommend enough.

The town of Gora literally has steaming water bubbling out of driveways and flowing through spillways at all hours. The drive/train trip up is stunning. In Gora, there is a cable car and then a ropeway that goes up to the top of Owakudani with sulfurous gas pouring out of the mountainside. I think every person in the ropeway said "whoa!" out loud when we crested over the top and it came into view. This also gave us the best view of Mount Fuji on the trip.

Kyoto
Kyoto was Japan's capital for a thousand years, and, as such, has a wealth of incredible historical sites to visit.

The Otagi Nenbutsuji Temple has 1200 statues carved by people who made pilgrimages to learn how to carve (and thus were amateurs). This is one my favorite places to have ever visited. The statues are so unique and so expressive, and the entire temple was designed with such intent, that there is a certain magic captured here that has to be experienced. To get here, take a train to Arashiyama and then catch a taxi up to the temple. From there, it's an easy walk down into the town.

While in Arashiyama, we came across Cafe Dining Sera, which is a bit off the beaten path, and was one of the more unique places we dined in Kyoto. Lunch was fantastic and was still pretty cheap (~$10). This is near the Bamboo Forest, which is mostly a photo-op, and Daikuku-ji Temple. This temple has a statue of the Buddha from 932, the oldest man-made pond in Japan (~1150 years old!), and it's still a functioning place of worship. There were people transcribing the sutras and monks chanting when we visited. The statues at the entrance are absolutely frightening. Finally, also in Arashiyama is the Iwatayama Monkey Park. After a hike to the top of a mountain, with some of the best views in Kyoto, you enter a park with monkeys absolutely everywhere. Pretty fun experience.

We stayed in the Cross Hotel, which is excellent. If you don't stay here, look for something in this neighborhood - the location is perfect. It's right in the midst of restaurants, arcades, karaoke and other nightlife, and an incredible amount of thrift shopping. Big Time was my favorite thrift shop; that being said, there is something for every taste here.

The Fushimi Inari Taisha is a temple with over 10,000 gates that you walk under. This temple is home to the patron deity of business, and every last gate here is sponsored by a business. The gates follow a long trail to the top of a mountain, where you will see amazing views of the entire city. I recommend starting early; this is 2+ hours of walking.

The final set of temples and shrines we enjoyed were the Yasaka Shrine and the adjoining Chion-in Temple. It's worth walking there from the Pontocho area because the walk goes through Gion, a historic district of Kyoto famous for its geishas. The shine, which dates from 656 (!!!), is one of the most impressive we saw on the trip. The Chion-in temple is a short walk from the shrine. This temple is the headquarters of the Pure Land Sect and is a functioning religious site. The (rather imposing) main gate is the largest of its kind. The main hallway is one of the most beautiful holy sites I have ever had the fortune of visiting.

We had an absolute blast at a show named GEAR that is sort of like Cirque du Soleil in subminiature (5 performers in a very intimate theatre).

Finally, the Kyoto Railway Museum is the perfect place to geek out while viewing  many generations of Japanese trains, from the steam era all the way through the newest shinkansen. The museum has very thorough explanations of all of the technology their trains use. He will need Google Lens to translate.

Travel tips
Many places are cash only. 7-11s are ubiquitous here and have interoperable ATMs, so reloading cash is easy. No need to convert currency while still in the United States.

If you bring a large suitcase, I highly recommend using luggage forwarding (ta-q-bin) to send bags ahead to the next destination rather than haul large bags onto trains. Every hotel offers this. It costs less than $20 to overnight a bag from Tokyo to Kyoto.

It rains a lot in Japan. Rain gear is a must. No need to bring an umbrella, a large one is less than $5, and can even be had from vending machines.

I suspect you will be taking trains everywhere. If you have an iPhone (not Android!), you can pay for public transportation on his phone using Pasmo or Suica. This will spare the annoyance of buying many, many train tickets.

Many places (museums, restaurants, etc) do not have English signage. Google Lens solves this problem.

Even if your cellular plan has roaming, it's worth getting an esim to have access to more bandwidth for looking things up, traveling point to point, etc. I got a plan from Ubigi for $17 that covered our needs.

The one reversal is Israel. It was won the way Spain and Greece were won: by return, settlement, and war. Not by waiting.

The land was Jewish before it was Roman, Christian, or Muslim. Israel and Judah were kingdoms there. The Temple stood in Jerusalem. After the Roman destruction in 70 AD and the crushing of the Bar Kokhba revolt in 135, the Jews were reduced to a minority and scattered, but they were not erased. Communities remained in Galilee, Jerusalem, Hebron, and Safed through Byzantine, Arab, Crusader, and Ottoman rule. The liturgy kept the return to Zion as a daily prayer for close to two thousand years.

The modern return began before the state. In the late nineteenth century Jews bought land and built farms on it, under Ottoman and then British rule. By 1947 they were a third of the population west of the Jordan and a majority in the areas the United Nations assigned them. The partition plan of November 1947 offered two states. The Jews accepted it. The Arab states rejected it and invaded in May 1948. Israel held. About 850,000 Jews then left or were expelled from Arab countries, and most of them went there. A dispersed people reconstituted a majority on the land it had come from.

The parallel with Spain and Greece is the method. Spain was won back by centuries of reconquest. Greece survived Ottoman rule and was secured by the war of 1821. Israel was secured by the war of 1948, and again in 1967, when Jerusalem, Judea, and Samaria, lost to the legions and held by others for most of the centuries since, came back under Jewish control. None of the three was recovered by appealing to the legal order that had displaced them.

That is the warning. Where the shift ran its course, it was not undone by patience, petition, or demography running in reverse. The places that came back were won by war. The places that did not fight remained what conquest and subjugation had made them.

Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

text:
Here’s the full story, for those who aren’t that familiar with the history of medieval Balkans…

In May 1426, Despot Stefan Lazarević of Serbia and King Sigismund of Hungary agreed that, on Stefan’s death, the fortresses of Belgrade and Golubac (plus the region of Mačva) would return to Hungary. In exchange Sigismund would recognize Stefan’s nephew Đurađ Branković as the next despot and continue to protect Serbia.

Stefan died in July 1427. Belgrade and Mačva were handed over to Sigismund by the fall. However, the commander of Golubac, Duke Jeremiah (Vojvoda Jeremija) refused. He produced a document he said Stefan had given him promising 12,000 ducats and demanded payment before surrendering the fortress. (This amounts to roughly $5-6 million in raw gold today, or on the order of $20-50 million in broader purchasing power.) Sigismund rejected the claim and treated the document and seal as invalid or forged. Hungarian and Polish nobles advised him to pay, but he declined.

Around December 1427, Jeremiah sold Golubac to the Ottomans for the same sum of 12,000 ducats he claimed he was owed and joined them. The Ottomans immediately used the fortress as a base for raids into the Braničevo region and southern Hungary. Despot Đurađ Branković went to Golubac in person, offered Jeremija forgiveness, and tried to recover the fortress; Jeremiah refused and attacked his liege’s party at the gates.

Over the winter of 1427-28, Sigismund stayed on the Danube, gathered forces, and built a counter-fortress, Lászlóvára (Laslovar), on the opposite bank so he could control the river crossing.

In April-May 1428, he led a large army (estimates range from about 15k to 30k, including Hungarian troops, Wallachian archers under Dan II, Italian artillery, a river fleet, and a Polish contingent commanded by Zawisza the Black) and besieged Golubac from land and water. This was one of the first Hungarian campaigns to use substantial artillery.

In late May, an Ottoman relief force arrived (sources differ on whether Sultan Murad II was present in person or the army was led by the beylerbey Sinan Bey). Sigismund avoided open battle and negotiated a truce under which the Christians would lift the siege and withdraw unmolested while Golubac stayed in Ottoman hands.

Most of the army crossed the Danube under the truce. The Ottomans then broke the agreement and attacked the rearguard still on the Serbian bank. Many knights were killed or captured; Zawisza the Black refused a boat sent for him and was killed. Sigismund himself narrowly escaped (one account credits the noblewoman Cecília Rozgonyi with helping extract him).

The fortress remained Ottoman until the Peace of Szeged in 1444.

text:
Illinois parents in divorce or custody cases, your right to your child's school records is protected by statute, and the bar to take it away is high.

Under 750 ILCS 5/602.11(a), access to your child's records "shall not be denied to a parent for the reason that such parent has not been allocated parental responsibility."

The Illinois School Student Records Act backs it up. Under 105 ILCS 10/5, a parent "shall have the right to inspect and copy all school student permanent and temporary records," and the school must grant the request within 10 business days.

Both statutes name the same single exception. "No parent shall have access to the school records of a child if the parent is prohibited by an order of protection from inspecting or obtaining such records." That means an order of protection, issued on a finding of abuse, that specifically prohibits access.

Outside an order of protection, restricting a parent under 750 ILCS 5/603.10 takes a hearing and a finding, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the parent seriously endangered the child's mental, moral, or physical health, or significantly impaired the child's emotional development. Without that hearing and that finding on the record, there is no lawful restriction under 603.10.

Federal law says the same thing. Under 34 C.F.R. § 99.4, a school must give either parent full rights unless it is given a court order, statute, or legally binding document that "specifically revokes these rights"; the order has to revoke the right expressly. A custody order, a decision-making allocation, or a no-contact clause does not do that. In Illinois, the only basis the statutes name for cutting off school records is an order of protection.

None of the following takes away your right to your child's records.
Losing custody or decision-making.
Reserved, suspended, or supervised parenting time.
An order barring "contact" with a school.
A pending or court-ordered psychological evaluation.
A GAL recommendation.
Requesting the records.
Watch for this in court. A parent's records requests get recast as harassment, and the remedy offered is cutting off access. Asking for your child's records is diligence, not harassment.**

If opposing counsel moves to cut off your access, or drafts an order that does it, without an order of protection or a 603.10 finding, that order has no basis under 602.11 or 105 ILCS 10/5. Object on the record and cite both statutes.

Do not assume the attorneys or the court have checked these statutes. Bring them yourself.

A later judge relying on that order doesn't fix it. The finding still isn't there.

This isn't a substitute for co-parenting. You just shouldn't have to rely on anyone else's account of your own child's education and well-being. Requesting your child's records is part of being their parent.

text:
HONG KONG IS THE MARKET THAT MOVED. US FUTURES DID NOT:

The verdict: Hong Kong followed Monday's record. Tokyo did not add to its own surge. The hint for Tuesday can fade before regular trading starts at 9:30am ET.

Asia is in Tuesday's session. These readings are live.

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 70,082, +135 points / +0.19% so far in Tuesday's session, trading now.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 24,217, +177 points / +0.74% so far in Tuesday's session, trading now.

Mainland China is not open. The Shanghai Stock Exchange is shut from October 1 through October 7 for the National Day holiday. It reopens Thursday, October 8. The last print is Wednesday, September 30.

- Shanghai Composite: 3,842.20, +11.75 points / +0.31% in Wednesday's session, its latest. It has not traded since.

Hong Kong's first print was stronger than the live one.

- Hang Seng open, Xinhua: 24,279.63, +239.29 points / +1%.

Part of that opening jump is already gone. Technology shares and banks led. Mainland buyers are out until Thursday, so this is Hong Kong's first look at Monday in New York.

Tokyo is back above 70,000. Monday's close finished under that line, and it was the highest close since July 1. Chip and electronics shares led that Monday.

Monday's regular session is what Asia opened into.

- S&P 500: 7,773.95, +51.23 points / +0.66% on Monday.
- Dow Jones Industrial Average: 51,267.90, +90.94 points / +0.18% on Monday.
- Nasdaq composite: 27,477.31, +286.45 points / +1.05% on Monday.
- Russell 2000, smaller US companies: 2,847.14, +14.24 points / +0.50% on Monday.

The Nasdaq composite's close was a record. The S&P 500 finished within 0.3% of its own high, the Associated Press reported.

US stock futures are overnight contracts tied to the indexes, not the indexes themselves. Each change is since Monday's close.

- Dow futures: 51,651.00, +93.00 points / +0.18% since Monday's close.
- S&P 500 futures: 7,832.25, +6.00 points / +0.08% since Monday's close.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 31,334.75, +17.00 points / +0.05% since Monday's close.
- Russell 2000 futures: 2,867.50, -0.30 points / -0.01% since Monday's close.

Nasdaq-100 futures are up 0.05%. That is a fraction of Hong Kong's gain. The small-company contract is the only one lower.

Oil is the other support.

- Brent crude, the global oil price: little changed at $100 a barrel, after a 1.9% drop overnight.

More oil is leaving the Middle East, and the Group of Seven, the large rich economies, pledged to boost supplies. A cheaper barrel eases the fear that fuel costs light inflation again.

A 10-year yield is what a government pays to borrow for a decade. It feeds mortgage rates and company loans.

- US 10-year Treasury yield, in Asia: 5.3089%, steady, after touching 5.3493% overnight, the highest since 2002.

Stocks rose on Monday anyway.

Friday's jobs report cooled the case for a rate increase. It did not cool the bond market. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts jobs added across the country.

- September jobs added: 29,000, vs about 90,000 expected.
- Average monthly gain over the prior year: 45,000.
- Unemployment rate: 4.2%, up from 4.1% in August.

- Chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase at the October 27-28 meeting: about 23%, vs 71% a week earlier.

The services survey is why yields can stay high after that miss. The Institute for Supply Management asks purchasing managers at service firms, most of the economy, whether activity grew. Above 50 means growth.

- September services index: 54.9, vs 55.4 in August. A 27th straight month of growth.
- Prices paid, what those firms pay for inputs: 74.0, vs 72.6, the highest since July 2022.

Services are still growing. The bill for inputs is not cooling.

Japan's 10-year bond is the test that lands while Tokyo stocks are still open.

- Japan's 10-year yield: 3.116%, up 0.025 percentage point.

A small step. The Ministry of Finance posted the auction notice at 10:30am Tokyo time.

- Tuesday's 10-year sale: about 2.6 trillion yen. Coupon, the stated interest rate: 3.1%. Due September 20, 2036.

Investors have submitted their offers. The result is not out.

- Result: 12:35pm Tokyo time, 11:35pm ET, early in Tokyo's afternoon session.

A yield that lifts off 3.116% would say long-term government debt is getting harder to place. Washington runs the same test on Wednesday.

Europe is not live. These are Monday's finishes. Those markets next trade while the US is still dark.

- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,498, +35.99 points / +0.34% in Monday's session, now closed.
- DAX (Germany): 25,254, +23.01 points / +0.09% in Monday's session, now closed.
- CAC 40 (France): 7,834.10, -63.09 points / -0.80% in Monday's session, now closed.

Paris was the only decline. Investors charged France 1.37 extra percentage points over Germany to lend for 10 years, and that gap narrowed on Monday.

What would turn this into a weaker hint for Tuesday: Japan's auction pushing the 10-year yield above 3.116%, and S&P 500 futures back to unchanged before 9:30am ET. What would say Hong Kong's open was the right read: that index still higher at its own close, with S&P 500 futures still up at the US open.

The clock, Eastern time:

- 11:35pm tonight: Japan's 10-year auction result, with Tokyo's afternoon session under way.
- Tuesday, October 6, 1:00pm: the Treasury sells $58 billion of new 3-year notes.
- Wednesday, October 7, 1:00pm: $39 billion more of the 10-year note.
- Thursday, October 8: Shanghai reopens. At 1:00pm the Treasury sells $22 billion of 30-year bonds.
- October 27-28: the Fed's next rate decision.

Hong Kong's first look at the record has already given part of the jump back. US futures have not taken the rest. The auction can still change the night, and an overnight gain can be gone by the open.
