text:
Tucker’s Right About Hitler!

Bogdan Klich, chargé d'affaires ad interim of the Polish Embassy in Washington, sent Tucker Carlson a letter dated Oct. 5, 2026, demanding that he retract and apologize for statements in an interview with Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg. Klich calls him an apologist for Hitler and says he falsified the record. Klich is wrong. Carlson’s statement the letter quotes is true. The history Klich offers up is not.

Carlson said Hitler's case was that about 15 percent of Poland had once been Germany and was given to Poland by the Allies at Versailles after World War I. This was German territory with Germans in it. Interwar Poland covered 388,634 square kilometers. The land taken from Germany and assigned to Poland was about 46,300: most of Posen, most of West Prussia, the Polish share of Upper Silesia, and the Soldau district. That is just under 12 percent. Broader counts run to 13 or 14. Fifteen is a round number. Those provinces were German state territory, and they held a large German population — hundreds of thousands in the ceded provinces.

Danzig does not rescue Klich. The Free City's 1923 census put it at about 95 percent German-speaking. At Versailles, the Allies detached it from Germany. Germany asked for a plebiscite for Danzig; the Allies refused. Poland received the conduct of its foreign relations, a customs union, control of the railways and the port, and a munitions depot on the Westerplatte. That was the functional equivalent of a transfer. In tearing Germany apart to reconstruct Poland, the Allies ignored their own principle of self-determination.

Klich then writes as if September 1939 were a war for a democratic Poland. It was not. Poland in 1939 was an authoritarian state run by a military junta.

From that false picture he moves to a false account of Hitler's aims. He says Hitler's object was the physical extermination of the Polish population, then the conquest of the world and the destruction of every democratic state, and that Britain and France would have been attacked anyway. All false.

Hitler did not have, in September 1939, a plan or an intent to conquer the world. His program was continental: overturn Versailles, restore greater Germany, seize living space in the East, and keep Britain neutral.

He had no invasion of Britain or France prepared on Sept. 1. He wanted an accommodation with Britain and expected the Western powers to stay out of a Polish war. Britain and France turned it into a world war by declaring war on Germany on Sept. 3. On Oct. 6, with Poland defeated, Hitler offered a settlement: no further war aims against Britain or France, talks on arms and colonies, and acceptance of the new order in Poland. Chamberlain rejected it on Oct. 12. Hitler moved to knock France out only after the Western powers were in the war. After France fell, he issued the contingent order for the invasion of Britain on July 16, 1940, then made a second offer, the "appeal to reason," on July 19. Churchill, the greatest champion of the British Empire, rejected it.

London declared war because Germany invaded Poland, then did nothing to save the Polish nation-state. The British army sat in France. The air force dropped leaflets. Sixteen days later the Soviet Union invaded from the east and took more than half the country. Hitler and Stalin devoured Poland while the British stayed behind the Maginot Line. Stalin's NKVD deported hundreds of thousands of Poles and in the spring of 1940 shot about 22,000 officers and other prisoners at Katyn and at other sites.

In June 1941, after Hitler turned on Stalin, London allied with the Soviet Union, which had already conquered half of Poland. There goes the defense of the nation-state. Stalin's killing record already ran into the millions: collectivization, the famine in Ukraine, the Great Terror, the deportations, and Katyn. Hitler's did not yet. By sheer number of killings, Britain allied with the greater monster, then at Tehran and Yalta confirmed his half of Poland and a communist government for the rest. The nation Britain claimed it had gone to war to save was absorbed into the Soviet system, with British consent.

Sir Jacob, apparently completely detached from the historical record, insisted throughout the interview that Britain had a moral duty to fight to defend the nation-state. The claim is preposterous, and the irony is total. The power posing as the shield of the nation-state was the largest destroyer of nation-states on earth. In 1939 Britain was an empire built by conquest: Wales, Ireland, and Scotland; Egypt, the Sudan, Kenya, Uganda, Tanganyika, the Rhodesias, South Africa, Nigeria, and the Gold Coast; India, later broken into India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, plus Ceylon and Burma; Malaya, Singapore, Hong Kong, Palestine, Iraq, and the Gulf; and Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and the Caribbean.

Britain entered the war against Germany out of traditional balance of power politics, to contain Germany, not permit it to dominate the continent, and to protect its empire. The moral posturing from Sir Jacob is just that.
#TuckerCarlson #Versailles #AmericaFirst

This is “fat kid who can’t pass presidential fitness exam” logic but applied to books and I doubt it predates the 1960s.

The Founding Fathers were immigrant striver-pilled af
——————————————
Thomas Jefferson to his daughter Martha, March 28, 1787:

“Of all the cankers of human happiness, none corrodes it … as indolence.”
——————————————
Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758):

“Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labour wears; while the used key is always bright.”
——————————————
Letter from George Washington to George Steptoe Washington (Mar. 23, 1789):

“The first and great object with you at present is to acquire, by industry, and application, such knowledge as your situation enables you to obtain, as will be useful to you in life. In doing this two other important advantages will be gained besides the acquisition of knowledge: namely, a habit of industry, and a disrelish of that profusion of money and dissipation of time which are ever attendant upon idleness. I do not mean by a close application to your studies that you should never enter into those amusements which are suited to your age and station: they can be made to go hand in hand with each other, and, used in their proper seasons, will ever be found to be a mutual assistance to one another. But what amusements, and when they are to be taken, is the great matter to be attended to. Your own judgement, with the advice of yourreal friends who may have an opportunity of a personal intercourse with you, can point out the particular manner in which you may best spend your moments of relaxation, better than I can at a distance. One thing, however, I would strongly impress upon you, vizt. that when you have leisure to go into company that it should always be of the best kind that the place you are in will afford; by this means you will be constantly improving your manners and cultivating your mind while you are relaxing from your books; and good company will always be found much less expensive than bad. You cannot offer, as an excuse for not using it, that you cannot gain admission there; or that you have not a proper attention paid you in it: this is an apology made only by those whose manners are disgusting, or whose character is exceptionable; neither of which I hope will ever be said of you.”

text:
“You don’t study for the spelling bee” is a deep and important aspect of American culture. I was at a baseball game discussing some young players with a buddy one time and he said to me offhandedly, “hard work is fine, but nothing beats talent.” 

Americans have this sort of sense that there’s something a little off about working really hard to get good at something that you’re not naturally good at. You’re never really going to be on the same level as the guy who has a natural talent. We have room in our hearts for scrappy little guys who work hard, but we are by default suspicious of grinders and strivers.

If you were really meant to do it, then you’d be naturally good at it. You sign your kids up for little league, but you don’t take it too seriously unless they show remarkable early talent.

Yes, this sounds sort of ridiculous if you take it too literally. No, nobody is saying that there’s any kind of practical test for this or that anybody should be excluded because we found out that they secretly studied too hard.

But this is a part of American culture. And if you can’t understand it, then that just marks you out as foreign to that culture to an even greater degree.

text:
Tucker’s Right About Hitler!

Bogdan Klich, chargé d'affaires ad interim of the Polish Embassy in Washington, sent Tucker Carlson a letter dated Oct. 5, 2026, demanding that he retract and apologize for statements in an interview with Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg. Klich calls him an apologist for Hitler and says he falsified the record. Klich is wrong. Carlson’s statement the letter quotes is true. The history Klich offers up is not.

Carlson said Hitler's case was that about 15 percent of Poland had once been Germany and was given to Poland by the Allies at Versailles after World War I. This was German territory with Germans in it. Interwar Poland covered 388,634 square kilometers. The land taken from Germany and assigned to Poland was about 46,300: most of Posen, most of West Prussia, the Polish share of Upper Silesia, and the Soldau district. That is just under 12 percent. Broader counts run to 13 or 14. Fifteen is a round number. Those provinces were German state territory, and they held a large German population — hundreds of thousands in the ceded provinces.

Danzig does not rescue Klich. The Free City's 1923 census put it at about 95 percent German-speaking. At Versailles, the Allies detached it from Germany. Germany asked for a plebiscite for Danzig; the Allies refused. Poland received the conduct of its foreign relations, a customs union, control of the railways and the port, and a munitions depot on the Westerplatte. That was the functional equivalent of a transfer. In tearing Germany apart to reconstruct Poland, the Allies ignored their own principle of self-determination.

Klich then writes as if September 1939 were a war for a democratic Poland. It was not. Poland in 1939 was an authoritarian state run by a military junta. 
From that false picture he moves to a false account of Hitler's aims. He says Hitler's object was the physical extermination of the Polish population, then the conquest of the world and the destruction of every democratic state, and that Britain and France would have been attacked anyway. All false.
Hitler did not have, in September 1939, a plan or an intent to conquer the world. His program was continental: overturn Versailles, restore greater Germany, seize living space in the East, and keep Britain neutral.

He had no invasion of Britain or France prepared on Sept. 1. He wanted an accommodation with Britain and expected the Western powers to stay out of a Polish war. Britain and France turned it into a world war by declaring war on Germany on Sept. 3. On Oct. 6, with Poland defeated, Hitler offered a settlement: no further war aims against Britain or France, talks on arms and colonies, and acceptance of the new order in Poland. Chamberlain rejected it on Oct. 12. Hitler moved to knock France out only after the Western powers were in the war. After France fell, he issued the contingent order for the invasion of Britain on July 16, 1940, then made a second offer, the "appeal to reason," on July 19. Churchill, the greatest champion of the British Empire, rejected it.

London declared war because Germany invaded Poland, then did nothing to save the Polish nation-state. The British army sat in France. The air force dropped leaflets. Sixteen days later the Soviet Union invaded from the east and took more than half the country. Hitler and Stalin devoured Poland while the British stayed behind the Maginot Line. Stalin's NKVD deported hundreds of thousands of Poles and in the spring of 1940 shot about 22,000 officers and other prisoners at Katyn and at other sites.

In June 1941, after Hitler turned on Stalin, London allied with the Soviet Union, which had already conquered half of Poland. There goes the defense of the nation-state. Stalin's killing record already ran into the millions: collectivization, the famine in Ukraine, the Great Terror, the deportations, and Katyn. Hitler's did not yet. By sheer number of killings, Britain allied with the greater monster, then at Tehran and Yalta confirmed his half of Poland and a communist government for the rest. text:
India–US trade talks: Ready for an Interim Agreement—or stuck at a “plateau”?

On October 5, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said talks had reached a “plateau”, and further give-and-take was difficult for both sides.

Four days earlier, after meeting US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Milwaukee, Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said India was ready to finalise an early, balanced and mutually beneficial interim agreement under the February 6 framework.

These positions may fit together: sign a limited deal covering what is already agreed, while leaving harder issues for later. 

Whether Washington wants concessions beyond that framework remains unclear. Is that what FM was hinting? 

But the biggest unanswered question is simple: what tariff benefit would India actually receive from US?

The February 6 framework offered to lower India’s reciprocal tariff from 25% to 18% in return for major Indian concessions. On February 20, the US Supreme Court struck down that tariff regime, removing the original basis of the offer.

What replaces it? Washington’s offer remains unclear. Meanwhile, India faces a 10% forced-labour tariff despite banning forced-labour imports.

Until the tariff offer is clear, “nearly complete” tells exporters little.

No deal would not stop trade. Indian exporters could continue selling under existing rules, though uncertainty would make pricing, contracts and investment harder.

Nor would signing necessarily end that uncertainty. Fresh tariffs over Russian oil or alleged excess manufacturing capacity remain a risk. 

The US has imposed new tariffs on the EU, Japan and South Korea even after signing trade deals. Thats a risk for India. What value is a deal if it cant guarantee tariff freeze for some time.

India should sign only for lasting tariff gains and credible protection against arbitrary increases. Major concessions by India require secure benefits. There is no reason to rush.

Also, India must also stop giving away concessions while negotiations remain unfinished.

Over the past two years, India has cut duties on motorcycles, bourbon, some pharmaceuticals and Ethernet switches; allowed FDI in inventory-based e-commerce for exports; and scrapped the equalization levy on foreign platforms.

Proposed UPI fees from October 15 could further weaken India’s free payment system, benefiting Visa and Mastercard.

Every concession without a reciprocal gain weakens India’s bargaining power.

Iraqi Airways said Monday that it will resume direct flights to Iran on Oct. 8, with daily services from Najaf International Airport to Tehran, Mashhad and Isfahan.

The Iraqi national carrier said in a statement that the move was aimed at facilitating passenger travel and providing regular air transport between Iraq and the three Iranian cities.

Iraq’s Transport Ministry said on Sept. 29 that Iraqi Airways had secured a special exemption allowing it to operate flights to Iran, clearing the way for services to resume after regulatory and technical requirements were completed.

A source in the Iraqi Transport Ministry told Reuters that the exemption was granted by the US Treasury and would last for one month. Baghdad offered safeguards including passenger screening and information sharing, as well as measures aimed at preventing the flights from being used to transport weapons, sanctioned individuals or illicit funds, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter.

The exemption comes as Washington intensifies pressure on Iran’s aviation sector under Operation Economic Outcast. The US Treasury sanctioned the remaining active Iranian airlines in September, saying Iran’s aviation sector was used to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo.

On Oct. 2, the Iraqi prime minister’s office announced an agreement allowing Iranian airlines, except Mahan Air, to operate 40 flights a day to and from Najaf International Airport.

Mahan Air has been under US sanctions since 2011 over alleged financial, material and technological support for the Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force.

text:
TORM $TRMD CLOSED HIGHER WITH THE DIESEL BAN OFF. THEN A HOLDER FILED TO SELL:

TORM plc (TRMD) at $41.05, +$1.05 / +2.62% on Monday, and $40.67 after hours (as of 8:00pm ET), -$0.38 / -0.93% from Monday's close.

The verdict: Washington ruled a diesel-export ban out on Friday afternoon, and TORM still finished higher. Monday's gain is the whole move since the $40.00 close the quoted post used. After the bell, a holder of about 6% of the shares filed to sell all of them. TORM gets none of the money. The close is further ahead of the daily rates the company has already locked into contracts.

Monday was not a one-way jump.

- Range: $38.97 to $41.55. Close: $41.05.
- Volume: about 2.4 million shares, in line with Friday.

The stock traded under Friday's close and still ended at a new high close for the past year. The session high is the top of that year.

The quoted post left the Washington decision open. That decision had already closed the same afternoon.

On Friday the G7, the group of seven large economies, agreed to a release coordinated by the International Energy Agency, the body that runs emergency oil stockpiles.

- Size: 100 million barrels of oil and diesel.
- Timing: starts immediately, runs four months, with a substantial share of the diesel in the first 20 days.
- The same agreement: no energy-export restrictions among the G7 members.

President Trump told reporters Friday, as he left the White House, "And we're not going to be doing the export ban." He added that it was never really on the table. Monday was the first regular session that could trade that answer.

The diesel margin narrowed with the news. The ICE gasoil crack is the gap between the price of diesel and the price of crude.

- That gap: about $70 a barrel on Monday, from about $85 in the middle of last week.

Warren Patterson, ING's head of commodities strategy, called the release a help for now. Refined fuel moving out of the Persian Gulf again is the lasting fix, he wrote, and attacks on commercial ships there have increased. A softer gap between diesel and crude is a weaker rate story. The stock rose anyway.

Hafnia Limited (HAFN) at $10.28, +$0.03 / +0.29% on Monday.

Hafnia carries the same refined fuels. It did not match TORM's move. Hafnia is not a Len5 pick. A day this small is not the breakout the Momentum Len5 watches, and the same cargoes are not, by themselves, a discount or a payout.

TORM's own news came after the close, at 6:27pm ET. A shareholder offered shares the company is not issuing.

- Seller: OCM Njord Holdings, owned through funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management.
- Shares: 6,329,874, about 6% of the company, and the seller's whole stake.
- Proceeds to TORM: none.
- Price: not set. The company said it can still be changed.
- Timing: the company gave no date, and said the sale might not happen.

The after-hours price gave back $0.38 of Monday's gain. The announcement was already out by then. That is a piece of the day's move, not the move. Talk around the name is heavy and leans cautious. Talk is attention, not a description of the business.

TORM is not a Len5 pick on the styles that want a discount, a breakout, or a payout. Quality-Value wants a hard-to-copy business bought at a discount. Deep-Value & Special-Situations wants a strong business at a cautious price, or an event with a price and a date. This sale has no price and no date, so it is not that event yet.

- June 30 net asset value, ships at market value less debt: $36.50 a share.
- Monday's close is $4.55 above that.

That is about 12.5% higher, so neither value Len5 has a discount.

It does fit the Quality Len5, which asks only for a profitable, sound business. A low price is not required. June-quarter profit was $338.3M. Borrowings at June 30 were $1.08B. The owners' stake, what is left after the debts, was $2.55B. Debt is under that stake. What would knock it off the Quality Len5: a quarterly loss.

It is not on the Income Len5, which wants cash paid to owners that the business can keep paying. A holder selling shares is not a dividend. What would put TORM on the Income Len5: fourth-quarter bookings, ship-days already placed at a set daily rate, well above the $38,606 a day locked for the third quarter as of August 18. A later payment would then have a footing near the last dividend of $2.40 a share.

It is not on the Momentum Len5, which watches a stock breaking out on a catalyst. Monday is a new high, and a large holder is selling into it. What would put TORM on the Momentum Len5: the close still above Friday's $40 once this sale has a price.

The third quarter is already written. TORM reports on Wednesday, November 4, a date it has set. The number that decides whether Monday's close holds is the sale price, and no date is set for it. The number that decides whether the price was earned is that fourth-quarter booked rate, against $38,606.

The key risk is treating a higher close as proof the fuel shortage reached TORM's own ships. The ban came off, the diesel margin narrowed, the peer barely moved, and the shares for sale have no price yet.

One of the two open decisions closed the same afternoon the quoted post went up. The stock set another high anyway, and that holder then offered every share it owns.

Not investment advice.

text:
$CEG $GOOGL (Bloomberg) -- Google parent Alphabet Inc. is close to an agreement to buy nuclear energy from Constellation Energy Corp., as technology companies race to line up power for the data-center boom. 
The tech giant is nearing a deal to pay Constellation $1 billion or more over the course of a multi-year agreement that’s expected to be announced as soon as this week, according to people familiar with the discussions, who asked not to be named because the information is private.
Constellation, the biggest US reactor operator, and Google declined to comment on Monday. The exact scale and location of the nuclear capacity couldn’t be determined. 
The immense amount of electricity required for the artificial intelligence boom is helping to revive interest in nuclear energy, which offers around the clock power that’s also emissions-free. Recent deals have focused on existing facilities as new reactors can take a decade or more to permit and build, and the next wave of fission technology is still likely years from widespread deployment. 
Read More: Amazon Nuke Deal to Help Expand Constellation Maryland Site
https://t.co/SpqvHNUxpK Inc. struck a similar deal last week with Constellation. The cloud and e-commerce company agreed to buy 690 megawatts of power, including capacity from upgrading the Calvert Cliffs nuclear facility in Maryland.
Google already has multiple agreements with atomic power producers. It agreed last year to buy electricity from NextEra Energy Inc., a deal that will support the power company’s plans to restart its Duane Arnold reactor in Iowa that’s been shuttered since 2020. And last month the tech company lined up new capacity from Southern Co. by funding upgrades at two atomic plants.
And Microsoft Corp. agreed to buy the electricity from the shuttered Three Mile Island nuclear plant in 2024. Constellation is planning to restart its reactor at the site in Pennsylvania next year.
While safety risks and heavy cost overruns saw the world sour on atomic energy early last decade, it’s been undergoing a global revival over the last few years. As well as surging demand from the tech sector for data centers, nuclear power is being embraced by many nations as a way to cope with a jump in electricity consumption while cutting emissions.

text:
Two years of hard labor for looking at a white girl. That was the sentence a North Carolina judge handed Mack Ingram in 1951, and the girl herself testified in three separate courtrooms that he never touched her and never made a move to come closer. He was about seventy feet away, walking a neighbor's field to ask her father about borrowing a hay trailer.

There is a sentence in the North Carolina law reports about a cluster of plum bushes.

It sits in a bound volume that lawyers still pull down off the shelf. Those bushes are preserved in the permanent legal record of a state because one man stopped walking beside them on a June morning, and North Carolina then spent twenty months trying to prove that stopping there was a crime.

His name was Mack Ingram. Some records and some of the scholarship call him Matt, and the wire photograph taken during his trial ran him as Matt "Mack" Ingram, but his grave marker at Sassafras Grove reads James Mack Ingram.

He was forty-four years old, a Black tenant farmer in Caswell County, up against the Virginia line. He and his wife Linward had nine children.

By the standards of that place and that year, he was doing well. He owned his own tools, his own equipment, mules on the property, and an old automobile he drove around town.

He was better off than a good many of the white people in Yanceyville. In a segregated tobacco county in 1951 everybody could see that, and it matters later.

The white locals in that town had a phrase for him before any of this started. He was a good Negro, they said, meaning he did not cause trouble.

One morning in June 1951 he had hay to move and no trailer to move it in.

So he drove around to a few houses in the area asking to borrow one. One of the places he stopped was the Boswell farm, because he wanted to ask Willa Jean Boswell's father about using their equipment.

Nobody was home.

So he started walking the property to find Mr. Boswell. Nobody involved in this case ever said that was strange, because the Boswells knew Ingram and he had been to that house before.

He went into the woods near the property. Up ahead on the path he saw someone walking toward the family's tobacco field with a hoe in hand.

The Supreme Court would later count that walk in steps. Ninety-five.

He stopped at a cluster of plum bushes at the edge of the cultivated ground, sixty-five or seventy feet away by the state's own account.

He did not go any further. He turned around and headed back toward the road.

He never did find Mr. Boswell. So he drove to a second farm, borrowed a trailer there, drove to a third farm, and he was loading hay on that property when the police came and arrested him.

The person on the path had been Willa Jean Boswell, seventeen years old, on her way out to join her father and brothers in the tobacco field.

Her account and his do not conflict much, which is the strangest thing about this entire case.

She said she had seen Ingram driving along the dirt road earlier and that he slowed as he passed her and put his head out the window to look at her. She said that frightened her, and she kept walking, and then she saw him coming toward her in the woods.

She said he stopped about sixty-five or seventy feet away, then turned back toward the road.

She said he never touched her. She said he never made a motion to come closer, and she told three separate courts the same thing.

She reached her family and cried. Her father and brothers called the police, and Mack Ingram was arrested that afternoon and charged with assault with intent to commit rape.

There is a name for what he was accused of, and people have called it reckless eyeballing ever since. It is worth knowing that no such law ever existed.

It was never a statute in North Carolina or anywhere else. There was nothing on the books to challenge, nothing to repeal, and nothing a lawyer could hold up and call unconstitutional.

That is what made it usable. It lived inside the ordinary law of assault, where any prosecutor who wanted it could reach in and pick it up.

He was arraigned in Caswell County and waited for trial in jail.

His wife was pregnant that summer. Linward and their eleven year old son worked the fields and kept the farm alive while he sat there, because the people of Yanceyville had already turned on the family.

A local white lawyer took the case. E. Frederick Upchurch was seventy-six years old and well respected in the county, and it is believed Ingram went to him personally, knowing the man and having no money for a lawyer.

Upchurch arranged bail at fifteen hundred dollars.

Then he went to the courthouse to post it, and the prosecutor asked the judge to raise the figure. The judge raised it to eighteen hundred.

The first trial was held in Caswell County Recorder's Court. The judge, Ralph Vernon, was a local farmer with no legal training.

Willa Jean took the stand and tearfully described being afraid when she saw Ingram looking at her.

The prosecutor was W. Banks Horton, and he did not argue the facts so much as the fear underneath them. He said out loud, in that courtroom, that young womanhood had to be protected from Black men, and he used a slur to say it.

Vernon told Horton to drop the rape charge. An earlier state supreme court decision had already held that an assault with no physical contact could not be charged as rape, so the law would not carry it.

So the charge came down to assault on a female. Vernon convicted him and gave him the maximum, two years.

Ingram's lawyers appealed immediately.

The case caught national attention, and that is the only reason there is a record of him at all.

The NAACP heard about it and sent two Black attorneys with backgrounds in desegregation work. The Civil Rights Congress, a group with Communist Party ties, ran its own loud campaign in the Daily Worker and organized letter writing into North Carolina.

One of those headlines named the thing nobody in that courthouse would say out loud. Negro Was Framed For Doing Too Well On Farm.

That is the part to sit with. A Black tenant farmer in a segregated county owned his own mules and his own car and was doing better than his white neighbors, and then a look put him in a cell.

The NAACP hated the tactics, convinced that kind of noise only hardened white officials against the men they were trying to save. They may have been right, and the noise is still the reason this case survived at all.

His appeal went before a Superior Court grand jury first. Eighteen people, all white, and they returned an indictment for assault with intent to rape, putting the charge Vernon had already dropped right back on him.

The second trial came in November 1951, in front of a jury of eight white men and four Black men.

A jury with four Black men seated on it, in Caswell County, in 1951, was close to unheard of. That jury could not reach a verdict, and the judge declared a mistrial.

What happened inside that room was never written down. Twelve men went in, they could not agree, and Mack Ingram walked back out of that courthouse because of it.

The prosecutor renewed the charge and set him for trial a third time.

In November 1952, seventeen months after he went out to borrow a trailer, Mack Ingram went before an all-white jury.

His lawyers asked for a change of venue, because the local papers had already decided he was guilty in print. Judge Frank Armstrong refused.

His lawyers then put the jury itself on the record. Caswell County was forty-nine percent Black, and the pool of seventy-six people this jury had been drawn from was somehow entirely white.

Armstrong denied that motion too, along with every other motion the defense made.

At trial, Willa Jean testified that she recognized Ingram when she saw him. Her father testified that he knew Ingram as well.

Both of them acknowledged that it was normal for Ingram to be traveling that route, because he visited other homes in the community. And Willa Jean again confirmed that he never touched her and never made a motion to come closer.

That was the state's case. A man everyone knew, on a road he had every reason to be on, who did nothing.

Then Armstrong charged the jury, and what he said is worth reading slowly.

He instructed them that it is not always necessary for there to be physical contact with the person alleged to have been assaulted. He told them that if a man looks at someone in a leering manner, sly or threatening or suggestive, and watches her and then follows her, and causes her to become frightened and run or to do something other than what she would have done, then he is guilty of assault.

That instruction is the entire theory of reckless eyeballing, spoken from a bench, as law, in 1952. Ingram's lawyers objected and Armstrong overruled them.

Then Armstrong told the jury the opposite. He said they had to acquit if all Ingram did was look at her in a threatening or suggestive way.

The court solicitor got up, walked to the bench, and whispered to him.

Armstrong turned back to the jury and told them that under the last instruction, if he had said they would find him guilty, they were to disabuse their minds of that, because the court had intended to say not guilty.

So the jury had been told that a look was a crime, that a look was not a crime, and that the judge had misspoken about which. They convicted Mack Ingram anyway.

Nobody in that room was confused about the law. They were never deciding the law.

Armstrong sentenced him to six months with physical labor, then suspended it for five years. To keep it suspended, Ingram had to pay the court fees, stay on good behavior, break no laws, and appear in person at each November term of court to prove by himself and by witnesses that he had kept every one of those terms.

His lawyers appealed again, on the contradictory instructions, the refused venue change, and the all-white jury in a county that was half Black. The North Carolina Supreme Court agreed to hear it.

On February 25, 1953, Chief Justice William A. Devin took the entire thing apart.

He went back through a century of state decisions on what an assault is and laid out the requirement that had always been there, which is an overt act, an offer or an attempt to do physical injury.

Then he held the state's own witness up against that standard.

She had used the word leer. The dictionary gives that word a sly and lustful edge, and Devin noted it, and then he noted what the witness herself said when she was asked what she meant by it.

She said it meant a curious look. Nothing further, no explanation, no demonstration.

That she was frightened was not in question, the court said. But fear alone does not make an assault when there is no menace of violence behind it.

He made no sound and no gesture. He turned and walked back the way he came.

Then came the line. What may have been in his mind is not something human law reaches.

The conviction was reversed. The case should have been thrown out before it ever went to a jury.

The court did not hand him a clean acquittal, though, and this part deserves saying plainly. In that same opinion the justices remarked that his stated reason for crossing the field was rather lame, and allowed that he may well have looked at her with lustful eyes.

They cleared him without ever deciding to believe him.

There is one more passage in that opinion that people skip past. The court declined to rule on whether Caswell County had deliberately kept Black men off its juries.

But it went out of its way to note that the county commissioners had not been following the jury statute. They had been drawing names from the election registration books instead of the tax records the law specified.

In a county that was nearly half Black, in a state where Black registration was strangled at the registrar's desk, that was not a clerical preference. The court observed that careful attention to the statute would do much to improve the quality of juries in North Carolina.

That was the remedy. An observation.

Mack Ingram was cleared of everything, and it did not give him his life back.

The farmers around Yanceyville who had hired him before were now afraid to, because standing near his name would cost them their own reputations. The work went away.

So he sold off the farming equipment he owned to keep his family fed.

Go back to the beginning of this and understand what that means. The equipment was the reason he had been doing better than his white neighbors in the first place.

It was the exact thing that headline had named. He was doing too well on that farm, and by the time the state was finished with him, he was not.

While the case was in the papers, strangers sent the family money and clothes. When the papers moved on, that stopped too.

The Ingrams were still shut out of Yanceyville after the state's highest court cleared him. They took their business across the line to Danville, Virginia, instead.

Mack Ingram died in 1973. Linward outlived him by thirty years and died in 2003.

Four years after his arrest, a fourteen year old named Emmett Till was killed in Mississippi over an accusation of the same kind. Ingram had the courts and the newspapers and a chief justice on his side, and he still lost everything he owned.

The case itself was never forgotten. State versus Ingram sits in the North Carolina reports as a clean statement of what an assault requires, and lawyers cite it who have no idea whose life is underneath it.

The plum bushes are in there. The sixty-five or seventy feet are in there, and the ninety-five steps are counted and preserved, permanently, in the law of the state.

What the volume does not record is the trailer.

He borrowed one from a farmer down the road that same morning and got his hay in. That was the last thing in this entire story that went the way Mack Ingram planned it.

The law books kept the plum bushes and lost the man standing beside them. He is not hard to pick back up.

He was forty-four years old. He had nine children and a wife named Linward, he owned his own mules and his own car in a county that could not stand it, and on a June morning in 1951 he walked ninety-five steps across a field to ask a neighbor about borrowing a trailer.

Every coffee helps me keep creating.
Matt Ingram's name ended up in law books, but the real story was the farmer, husband, and father whose life changed because of a moment in a cornfield. I share stories like his because history is not only made in famous places. Sometimes it happens to ordinary people who were forced to stand their ground.

Andre Coleman’s cousin is Marvin Williams, the former NBA player from Bremerton.

Local reporting from his high-school years identifies the family link directly. Andre (the one who went missing in March 2021) grew up under his father, also named Andre Coleman, and with help from his cousin Marvin Williams, then an Atlanta Hawks forward. 

The elder Andre Coleman is the twin brother of Marvin Williams’ mother, Andrea Gittens, so the two players are first cousins. 

Marvin’s brothers also played at Bremerton High. Williams, born in Bremerton in 1986, was a McDonald’s All-American, played one season at North Carolina (2005 national champions), and was drafted second overall by the Hawks in 2005. He played 15 NBA seasons before retiring.
Coverage of the 2021 disappearance noted the connection. 

Kitsap Sun and other local outlets described Andre as a former Bremerton High basketball standout from a family that produced multiple local stars, explicitly naming cousin Marvin Williams (who had recently retired). 

The case centered on an alleged kidnapping plot involving Amber Lynn Ableman and her fiancé Steven Kerr (later killed); Coleman has been presumed dead and his remains have not been recovered. 

His mother, Leslie Taganas, has publicly sought answers and closure. National attention stayed limited compared with higher-profile cases, consistent with many unresolved local missing-person investigations that do not involve ongoing public controversy or new evidence.

The documented relative is Marvin Williams.

text:
12 AM Top-of-the-Hour News

President Trump took his midterm push to Nebraska - in hopes of helping Republicans maintain control of the Senate.  And he was quick to offer a gift to voters in the farm-friendly community in the Cornhusker state and across the country.: “President Trump tossed some red meat to voters in ruby red Nebraska by signing an executive order aimed at deferring the cost for red dye diesel to officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red dye diesel for any reason, sharing the stage with Governor Jim Piller. And Senator Pete Ricketts, Trump promised results while easing gas pains for farmers. So Pete and Jim, this should absolutely assure your election. I guarantee you that. Ricketts heads into the final month with a slim lead over independent Bob Osborne, with early voting underway. Spencer Rain, Worldwide News Network. ”

President Trump is encouraging his supporters to vote by mail. The president has for years claimed fraud is rampant in mail-in voting.
The president now says he prefers in-person voting but that his supporters could vote by mail in the upcoming midterms. He also posted a campaign video over the weekend encouraging Republicans to vote saying "Vote early, vote by mail or vote in-person on Election Day, November 3rd."
Some Republicans have expressed their concerns that discouraging mail-in voting could reduce turnout with conservative rural voters, some of whom live far from polling stations.

A bill that would make Daylight Saving Time permanent passed the House with bipartisan support earlier this year. News Nation Washington correspondent Kristen Eskow reports prospects look dim for its passage in the Senate:: “The bill's future in the Senate remains unclear, and lawmakers won't be back on Capitol Hill until after the midterm elections. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has previously expressed doubt about whether the bill can reach the 60 votes it needs to advance. ”
Republican Senator Tom Cotton is one of the biggest opponents of the bill arguing that his constituents in Arkansas, "don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark."

In baseball - the New York Yankees and Cleveland Guardians are on the brink of elimination in the American League Division Series.  The Tampa Bay Rays beat the Yankees moments ago 5-to-2 in game two of the best of five series.  The Rays could seal the deal - with a win in game three Wednesday night in New York.
Earlier, the Chicago White Sox won game two over the Cleveland Guardians 4 to 3.   Chicago now has a 2-game lead over the Guardians in the best of five series.  Game three shifts to Chicago on Wednesday.
The National League Division Series resumes tomorrow.

Starbucks is facing a lawsuit that claims protein drinks on its menu labeled as "sugar-free" may have more sugar than a Reese's peanut butter cup.
The federal lawsuit alleges the coffee giant is violating federal labeling regulations.
Starbucks says that the sugar in the drinks comes from the protein-boosted milk they use, and that they don't add sugar to the drinks, using sugar-free syrup to flavor them.

One of daytime TVs biggest heartthrobs has died...: “Hope's death is a direct result of his kidnapping her and brainwashing her to be this Princess Gina von Amberg person. I want him dead. Robert Kelker Kelly, best known for his role as Bo Brady on Days of Our Lives, has died. He played the role for three years in the early 1990s. Kelker Kelly began his career in the role of Sam Fowler on Another World. He later played the role of Stavros Cassidine on ABC's General Hospital. Kelker Kelly died on October 3. The cause of death has not been released. Bill Rakoff, Worldwide News Network. ”

Tom Cruise suffered one of the worst opening weekends of his more than 40-year film career. Warner Brothers "Digger" flopped on opening weekend. Number one in north American theaters went to Amazon MGM's "Verity." The ambitious film debuted with just $8 million, and $20million worldwide.
Reports are that it cost $160 million to make, before marketing costs. It's Tom Cruise's lowest opening in 19 years.
The movie also performed poorly at the global box office, grossing $20 million, which is surprising given how well Cruise’s films do with international audiences.

text:
🇩🇪 Germany's spy chief tells the Bundestag the country is "in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia"

The head of Germany's foreign intelligence service warned lawmakers Monday that the confrontation with Russia has "taken on a new, more dangerous dimension."

"Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia," BND President Martin Jaeger told the Bundestag's annual public hearing of Germany's intelligence chiefs, citing the attempted attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig airport in August, which Berlin blames on Moscow.

"Germany has become a major obstacle to Russia's hegemonic power projection in Europe and, as a result, a primary target of Russian actions," Jaeger said, according to POLITICO. "No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," he added.

Jaeger was careful about what that assessment does, and does not, mean. He said the BND currently sees "no evidence" that Russia intends to launch a large-scale attack on a NATO member.

"We consider it entirely possible, however, that Russia might carry out targeted, smaller-scale operations," he said, invoking the "little green men" used during Russia's seizure of Crimea in 2014.

That scenario occupies the difficult territory between covert action and conventional war: limited operations designed to exploit ambiguity, complicate attribution and test how Germany and its NATO allies respond without necessarily triggering an immediate large-scale military confrontation.

Jaeger also offered a stark assessment of the war in Ukraine. Putin, he said, "must demonstrate a success" that justifies the costs Russia has incurred and has "passed the point where he could simply call off the attack on Ukraine without jeopardizing his domestic power base."

🇺🇦 He warned that Ukraine could face Russian attacks this winter "of a severity and brutality that we have not yet seen on this scale."

Russia denies intending to attack NATO. Putin said last Thursday that if Russia were subjected to aggression, "we will have no choice but to respond."

Jaeger's testimony came amid a broader series of European warnings Monday. EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe had seen "a spike in the Russian hybrid attacks and sabotage attempts and airspace violations in recent weeks," while condemning recent Russian missile and drone violations of Moldovan airspace.

At the same Bundestag hearing, Germany's domestic intelligence chief, Sinan Selen, raised a different security concern: Chinese high-tech products, from electric vehicles to robot vacuums, and the possibility that data collected by them could ultimately become accessible to Chinese state agencies.

For Washington, Jaeger's testimony carries particular weight. Germany is Europe's largest economy and the principal hub for U.S. military forces on the continent, and the head of its foreign intelligence service is now publicly telling parliament that the risk of Germany being pulled into a violent confrontation with Russia is rising.

His warning is not that a Russian invasion of NATO is imminent. It is that Moscow may operate below that threshold, through smaller, potentially deniable actions that force Germany and its allies to decide where gray-zone confrontation ends and armed conflict begins.

text:
@marketswithmay feel free to take time out of your day to go frame by frame. I publish my work so anyone can go through it and come to their own conclusions. If you don't want to watch the video I would be happy to send you a message with the slide deck and the transcript from YouTube so you have everything at your disposal. All I ask is that you go off of what I actually argued.

I deliberately made the $HOOD comparison on purpose. I was looking at how the market prices expected earnings growth across financial services names. I know $SOFI and Robinhood get to their earnings through different business mixes. That was never the point.

When Noto came on @basispointpod he talked about valuing SOFI on earnings growth. Around the 38 minute mark he said “I actually don’t care what you call us.” What he cared about was whether investors believe SOFI has the ability to compound revenue around 30%, grow earnings around 40% and get to a 20% to 30% return on equity.

Around the 9 minute mark he walked through a PEG valuation himself. He said a comparable group of financial services companies and fintechs trades near a 1.1 PEG. He took 40% forward earnings growth times 1.1 and landed on a 44x earnings multiple.

This is why I looked at earnings growth and what the market is paying for it. I believe the bank charter is the starting point. From there you still have to work through growth, profitability, capital needs, credit exposure and the returns that SOFI can generate in the future.

That’s why I specifically included the big banks and Robinhood in my analysis. Using the FY26 to FY28 consensus from my October 2nd snapshot the expected two year EPS growth was:

$SOFI 75.1%
$HOOD 66.1%
$BAC 28.7%
$JPM 9.8%

Those are cumulative two year numbers from the end of this fiscal year through 2028. For the PEG math I used the annualized rate.

From a growth perspective, Robinhood looked a lot more like SOFI than the mature banks did. That’s why I used it as a valuation reference. You can disagree with the comp but disagreeing with the comp doesn’t mean I don’t understand the businesses.

Based on the snapshot from when I made the video SOFI traded around 19.2x FY27 consensus EPS while Robinhood sat at 38.3x. Using an annualized consensus growth the PEGs were about 0.59 for SOFI and 1.33 for Robinhood. The $31 on the slide was what Robinhood’s multiple would imply on SOFI’s FY27 estimate.

If we were to take Robinhood out of it completely SOFI still had the lowest PEG on the slide. $C was 0.67, $BAC 0.77, $WFC 0.84, $TFC 0.97 and $JPM 2.76.

Whether SOFI deserves Robinhood’s multiple, a smaller discount or the discount it has now is a fair debate. A two year PEG doesn’t settle all of it. In my opinion what can justify different multiples are earnings quality, how long growth lasts, regulatory capital and credit risk.

If you would be so kind to explain how you believe SOFI should be valued I would appreciate it as it would provide some insights as to how you are looking at SOFI.

If you think the lending book deserves a much lower multiple show me your credit assumptions. If you think growth eats too much capital walk me through the capital and dilution math. If you think consensus is too high tell me where the estimates break. I am genuinely interested to see how you are looking at this. 

I believe that this would be a real response to a valuation argument. Pointing out that Robinhood has a different business mix doesn’t tell anyone whether SOFI's current discount is the right one.

Since you want to go frame by frame the rest of the deck matters too.

Slide 12 is titled “The Bank Charter Is the Engine.” It covers deposits, funding costs and net interest margin because the bank is a core part of my thesis.

Slides 16 and 17 cover lending, credit performance, tangible book value and regulatory capital. I wouldn’t have built those slides if I thought the bank and the loan book didn’t matter.

Slide 19 is “What SoFi Still Has to Prove.” It shows Tech Platform revenue down 23% YoY with contribution profit falling from $33 million to under $12 million. It shows fee revenue at 39% of the mix against 43% for full-year 2025 and ROTCE at 7.1% against a 20% to 30% goal. It also flags the share count up about 16% and only $0.24 of EPS in the first half against a $0.60 full-year target.

I put those in there because they matter for valuation. The deck says plainly that execution still has to back up the bull case.

The thesis is also a lot bigger than SoFiUSD but I feel as if you may be singling the video out because I put SoFiUSD in the thumbnail and addressed it early. As I discussed deposit funding, member growth, cross-buy, the Loan Platform Business, fee revenue and EPS growth are very important for SOFI. SoFiUSD is one more possible growth driver that I happen to be very bullish on and it comes with its own adoption and execution hurdles.

I was specific about those hurdles as slides 8 and 9 which separate average stablecoin reserve balances from annual payment volume. A $25 billion annual payments program doesn’t automatically turn into $25 billion of reserves. The same dollar can settle a lot of transactions.

The $25 billion reserve case is labeled as my illustration and not company guidance to be clear. The income is shown before operating costs and taxes. Adoption, average balances, rates, partner incentives and execution are all listed as variables.

Those caveats are part of the work you say you want to review so I am trying to make your due diligence quicker by pointing these aspects out.

I’m comfortable defending my view that SOFI's expected earnings growth deserves a large multiple than viewing it as just a bank. I’m just as comfortable talking about what could keep that growth from showing up.

Look the reality is that I can be wrong and covering SOFI for years doesn’t make me right and neither does interviewing the CEO. The analysis has to hold up on its own and that’s why I’m asking you to engage with it since you seem to have a problem with my analysis and think that I don’t understand SOFI as a business.

Telling me I’m “still coming up to speed,” saying I don’t understand the business models and then warning me against “further escalating” when I ask for specifics doesn’t answer a single valuation question.

I offered a conversation because I think investors would get something out of hearing us work through where we differ. You passed and I respect that but don't make comments warning about "further escalating" and expect me not to respond when I already put my thesis out there for everyone to see. 

Have fun going frame by frame and feel free quoting what I said. As I send I will send you the transcript from Youtube and the slide deck. I'll be waiting for you to articulate where I went wrong, what you don't agree with and how you would approach the analysis instead. I am especially interested in what multiple you believe SOFI deserves and how far we differ on it. 

I have been publishing my work publicly for quite some time. Since you would rather engage on X rather than a live conversation I am inviting you to put your analysis  next to mine and let’s see where our views are similar and where they are different.

In 1987, West Virginia State Police serologist Fred Zain testified in a Cabell County courtroom.
The defendant was Glen Woodall.
Zain told the jury the blood evidence matched Woodall.
The jury convicted him.
The sentence was 203 to 335 years.
In 1992, DNA testing showed Woodall was innocent.

West Virginia paid Woodall $1 million.
Then the state's highest court ordered an investigation into Zain's work.
Retired Judge James O. Holliday led it.
The findings: Zain had overstated results, reported inconclusive tests as conclusive, altered lab records, and reported "scientifically impossible or improbable results."

On November 10, 1993, the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals ruled on it.
Any evidence Zain offered in any criminal case "should be deemed invalid, unreliable, and inadmissible" in later habeas challenges.
Court: "They stain our judicial system and mock the ideal of justice under law."
About 134 cases from 1979 to 1989 were in question.
If your conviction rested on his word, that ruling gave you a path back into court.

A lab report shows up in court looking official.
If you're ever the one on trial, your lawyer can challenge the analyst, the method, and the records behind it.
Zain was later charged with fraud. His trial ended in a hung jury, and he died in 2002 before a retrial.

P.S. The case is In re Investigation of the West Virginia State Police Crime Laboratory, Serology Division (W. Va. 1993).
P.P.S. This post is entertainment and educational content based on real events. It does not constitute legal advice. For legal advice, consult a licensed attorney in your jurisdiction.

text:
As a former national spelling bee participant (who, yes, studied quite a bit for spelling bees growing up), I want to offer some constructive criticism on this thread. 

First, just like competitions in any other domain, success at spelling bees requires a confluence of talent, effort, luck, and interest. The average 140 IQ kid will not know how to spell "taoiseach" unless they actually study Gaelic-origin words, the average "grinder" is at a big starting disadvantage against a kid who is just naturally well-read, and sometimes, even the kid who plays every card right can get eliminated by a word they were unlucky enough to not know. The idea that Indian-American dominance at spelling bees is solely due to one of these variables, then, strikes me as confused. 

Put another way, while it is true that Indian-Americans have set up our own Minor League Spelling Bee of sorts, and it is also (obviously) true that we do not possess any magical genes that predispose us to excel in spelling bees, it is a mistake to think that the individual Indian-American kids who do win are mindless "strivers". They have interest and talent just like high-achieving kids in other domains. 

Which brings me to my second point. A lot of the discourse around Indian-American achievement strips us of agency. When I reflect on my own experiences with spelling bees, I played a strong hand in my pursuit of them as a serious competitive endeavor. Although my parents were the ones who originally enrolled me in spelling bees, I was the one who developed an affinity for them and decided to study for them. I would set my own alarm to wake up and grind Quizlet flashcards in the early morning. 

In hindsight, is that kinda a weird thing for a kid to do? Yeah. But is it any more weird than the kid who spends his mornings at the swimming pool shaving off another second from his 100m freestyle or the kid who spends hours at the batting cage perfecting his swing? Not really, in my opinion. In all cases, you have kids pursuing something they were (presumably) introduced to by their parents/broader community which they later developed a deeper interest in. 

I want to be clear that I am not offering a defense of grind culture here - I've shared my own criticisms of the concept elsewhere (https://t.co/xddWw3ytmb). My main point is that a lot of critiques of grind culture as applied to Indian-Americans specifically are under-baked and, as a result, deny us the complexity that is routinely afforded to high-achieving individuals from other groups.

text:
The Leg-Lift Rule: Why Flat Beats Upright After a Faint
Correct answer: C. Lay him flat and raise his legs.
A sudden faint in a breathing adult with no injury is usually a brief drop in blood flow to the brain. Gravity is working against recovery if the head stays higher than the heart. Laying him flat and raising the legs about 30 cm helps blood return from the legs to the core and brain, often restoring consciousness within a minute or two.
A is risky. Sitting him upright keeps the brain above the heart and can prolong the low-flow state. Giving water before he is fully alert also raises the chance of choking.
B is worse. Holding him up and forcing him to walk can cause another collapse, a fall, or injury while he is still unstable.
D does nothing useful. Cold water may startle him but does not fix the circulation problem and can be unpleasant or unsafe if he is not fully conscious.
Once he is flat with legs raised, loosen tight clothing around the neck and waist, keep the airway clear, and stay with him. Most simple faints resolve quickly. Call emergency services if he does not wake within about a minute, has chest pain, trouble breathing, a seizure, known heart disease, or faints again. Do not offer food or drink until he is fully alert and sitting up on his own.
This is basic first-aid positioning, not a diagnosis. Recurrent or unexplained faints still need medical review to rule out cardiac or other causes.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​#MedTwitter #MedEd #MedX @IhabFathiSulima @ajaykraina @sowmiyasid @mekarora

SSH OFFICIAL

BACK HOME: 60 DAYS OF WINS

Aloha everyone, I wanted to share some good news for a change. This one is a celebration, and a little bit of a field guide.

From August 6 to October 5, 119 of the reports we shared ended with something or someone back where they belong: 51 pets home, 45 found items returned, 7 stolen vehicles recovered and 3 missing people located. 98 of those 119 were marked resolved within a day of being posted (counted from our post to the moment the win was recorded).

In this video:
A dachshund in Kapolei, still recovering from back surgery, found and cared for by a neighbor.
A pet bird in Helemano, spotted in a big tree by the property the same day.
A French bulldog in Makakilo, home by mid-morning after her owners saw the post.
A found dog in Wai'anae who went straight to someone who offered to foster her.
A pygmy goat and a tortoise in Mākaha, both home within a day.
Why a microchip helps but a post helps more: two chipped dogs went home because the post reached their families first.
How wallets and a phone came back through Liliha Bakery, Target Kapolei and the Hawaii Theatre.
How two stolen 4Runners were recovered, one through the car's own tracking.

What made the difference:
Post fast.
Show it clearly, with good photos and the marks only you would know.
Say where a found item is being kept.
Neighbors who share.

Every share, every message, every neighbor who kept an eye out. Mahalo, and stay safe out there!

Michael Kitchens
Founder & Creator
Stolen Stuff Hawaii

Because the Schumer amendment was attached to unrelated business.  A half-truth is a lie Adam.

The stand-alone measure was the Epstein Files Transparency Act (H.R. 4405, later Public Law 119-38). The House passed it 427–1 on November 18, 2025. The Senate then cleared it by unanimous consent the same day (formal passage recorded November 19, 2025), with no debate and no roll-call. Unanimous consent requires that no senator object. Marshall did not object, so the bill passed with his assent and was signed on November 19, 2025.
The only recorded Senate vote tied to releasing the files was earlier, and it was not a stand-alone bill. On September 10, 2025, Chuck Schumer offered an amendment (S.Amdt. 3849) to the defense bill S. 2296 directing the attorney general to release unclassified Epstein-related documents. Republicans moved to table that amendment. The motion passed 51–49. Marshall voted yea — to kill the amendment. Only two Republicans, Josh Hawley and Rand Paul, voted nay (against tabling).

text:
Medical records, provider depositions, expert testimony and other evidence uncovered through the malpractice litigation could potentially provide new evidence concerning Lindsay’s diagnosis, medications, symptoms and mental condition before Jan. 24, 2023 — evidence that could matter if there is a second criminal trial.

It can also work the other direction.

Statements made on Lindsay’s behalf in the civil case, and particularly statements Lindsay herself might make in a deposition, interrogatory or other discovery response, could potentially become something the Commonwealth seeks to use in a retrial. Massachusetts evidence law generally allows an opposing party’s statements to be offered against that party, and specifically recognizes deposition and interrogatory answers as potential party admissions. 

Whether any particular civil pleading or statement would actually be admissible in Lindsay’s criminal case would be a separate question for the criminal judge.

text:
So what happens next?

Lindsay’s civil team includes Rosemary Scapicchio and Lubin & Meyer attorneys Andrew Meyer Jr. and William Thompson. The malpractice litigation is already in the discovery phase, and Meyer has said testimony given by medical providers during the criminal trial will be significant in the civil case. Scapicchio has also said she intends to use deposition transcripts from the criminal proceedings once they are available.

Massachusetts medical-malpractice cases also ordinarily go through a medical-malpractice tribunal, where a judge, physician and attorney determine whether the plaintiff’s offer of proof raises a legitimate question of liability appropriate for judicial inquiry. That tribunal is not a trial and does not decide ultimate liability.

text:
Qualcomm Just Became Huawei's Net Payer. 

On October 5, Huawei and Qualcomm($QCOM ) announced a multi-year patent cross-licensing agreement covering 5G, compute, AI, and networking, with Qualcomm purchasing certain Huawei U.S. patents in compute, AI, and networking. It is the first patent licensing agreement between the two companies to cover 5G technology, and the first revenue-positive agreement Huawei has signed with Qualcomm. Qualcomm will pay Huawei, reversing a 25-year relationship in which Huawei was the payer.

The market read this as Huawei's patent strength being acknowledged. That reading is correct but incomplete. The more consequential question is why Qualcomm — a company with $1.28 billion in quarterly licensing revenue at a 69% margin — chose this moment to become a net payer.

The LogicFolding dimension is the actual story. Among the patents Qualcomm is licensing is Huawei's LogicFolding chip technology, part of the Tau Scaling Law architecture that Huawei unveiled in 2026. LogicFolding reorganizes signal transmission paths to shorten interconnect distances, improving chip performance without requiring advanced lithography. It is already deployed in Huawei's Kirin 9050 and 9050 Pro processors. Qualcomm is not buying patents for defensive cross-licensing purposes. It is buying access to a design methodology that achieves performance gains through architectural innovation rather than process node advancement.

This matters because Qualcomm's core business faces a structural ceiling. Third-quarter fiscal 2026 revenue was $9.9 billion, with QCT at $8.5 billion and licensing at $1.3 billion. Smartphone demand is softening, and the company's own guidance acknowledges near-term gross margin pressure in QCT. Qualcomm's response has been to project $40 billion in non-handset revenue by fiscal 2029, anchored by automotive ($24 billion) and data center ($15 billion) targets. The data center ambition — the $15 billion target — requires compute architectures that Qualcomm does not currently possess at scale. LogicFolding offers a proven methodology for achieving compute performance under manufacturing constraints, which is precisely the environment Qualcomm faces as it tries to compete in AI infrastructure without leading-edge foundry economics.

Huawei's patent income is becoming a second revenue curve. Huawei's IP licensing business has been revenue-positive since 2021. Cumulative R&D investment from 2007 through 2025 exceeded 1.8 trillion yuan. As of end-2025, Huawei held over 165,000 active granted patents globally, with over 270 patent license agreements signed. The Qualcomm deal pushes the total value of Huawei's patent licensing agreements above $6.9 billion.

The strategic significance is structural. Huawei's hardware supply chain has been constrained by export controls since 2019. Patents are a different class of asset: even when product and supply chains are restricted, technology that enters industry standards or is adopted by other companies' products can still generate commercial returns through licensing, cross-licensing, and patent sales. The Qualcomm deal validates that Huawei's R&D outputs in AI, compute, and networking — not just legacy communications standards — have commercial value to the world's most established licensing company.

The hidden asymmetry in the deal. Qualcomm is licensing more than 680 Huawei patents, representing just 0.23% of Huawei's 296,248 active or pending patents. But that 0.23% covers key AI and networking technologies including near-package optics interconnects and LogicFolding. Qualcomm did not disclose how many of its own patents it is licensing to Huawei or what technologies they cover. The disclosure asymmetry is instructive: Qualcomm is purchasing access to specific high-value assets while keeping its own portfolio composition opaque. The deal is not a broad mutual exchange — it is a targeted acquisition of architecture-level IP packaged as cross-licensing.

What this means for the competitive landscape. MediaTek, which has been gaining share against Qualcomm in flagship Android devices, now faces a competitor with licensed access to LogicFolding architecture. If Qualcomm integrates LogicFolding principles into future Snapdragon designs, it can offer performance improvements that MediaTek cannot match without similar licensing. This extends Qualcomm's competitive moat in mobile while building a bridge to its data center ambitions.

For Huawei, the deal signals that its patent portfolio in AI and compute is maturing to the point where global technology leaders are willing to pay for access. The next question is whether this licensing model can extend to other major chipmakers — Apple, Samsung, or Nvidia — which would validate Huawei's IP as a systemic revenue source rather than a one-off settlement.

What to watch. First, whether Qualcomm discloses any LogicFolding-derived architecture in its next-generation Snapdragon roadmap. If the licensed patents influence Snapdragon's design direction, the deal's value extends far beyond the licensing fee. Second, Huawei's next patent licensing announcements. The company said its IP business has been revenue-positive since 2021, and the Qualcomm deal raises the cumulative value above $6.9 billion. If additional agreements with other major chipmakers follow, Huawei's patent portfolio transitions from a defensive asset to a systemic revenue stream. Third, whether the regulatory review in the U.S. — which is required for the patent purchase portion — introduces conditions or delays. The deal requires review under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, and any regulatory friction would signal that the U.S. government views patent transactions in AI and compute through a national security lens.

I think France is NOW ready to [stop the immigrant-related crime and turmoil, and make it happen IMMEDIATELY]. Today, I'm going to explain how President Nayib Bukele did it in El Salvador.

At first, people were skeptical. You have to understand where El Salvador was coming from. In 2015, El Salvador was the murder capital of the world: more than 100 homicides per 100,000 inhabitants. A country of 6 million people were ruled by two gangs, MS-13 and Barrio 18, with tens of thousands of members. They controlled entire neighborhoods. Bukele’s response came the next day: a state of emergency. And he never lifted it. The army and police entered neighborhoods the state had abandoned for 20 years. Entire cities were surrounded and searched house by house. More than 80,000 arrests. A gang tattoo was enough. In a few months, he built CECOT, a mega-prison with 40,000 cells. Countries that started from much further behind than we are, did it.

The objective is simple: that every family understands that their child will no longer be able, by design, to cause trouble without the whole family paying the price. The responsibility falls on the family.

REAL CONSEQUENCES: For those who continue to offend: PRISON. For real. Heavy minimum sentences served, without an automatic parole. No more repeated suspended sentences and fifteen warnings. We must build the necessary prison spaces. Bukele built a 40,000-bed prison in a few months. France organized the Olympics in seven years and we know how to build prisons.

Thirdly, justice.

ENFORCE THE LAWS: A law is worthless if it isn't enforced. Today, a segment of the judiciary is in a state of suicidal empathy: they see the offender as a victim and the victim as collateral damage.

Activist judges, radical judges, those who judge according to their ideology rather than the law, must be investigated and removed when necessary. And there's a very simple way to align the entire system: JUDICIAL ACCOUNTABILITY.

HOLD JUDGES RESPONSIBLE: If a judge releases someone dangerous and that person commits a serious offense again, that judge will be held accountable. A surgeon is held accountable for their mistakes.

A pilot is held accountable for their mistakes.

Why not the one who decides to release a dangerous individual back onto the streets?

A judge's job is to protect victims and society, not to offer a fifth, sixth, or seventh chance at rehabilitation to people who keep reoffending.

REMOVAL OF THE DRUG TRADE: Declare a LOCAL STATE OF EMERGENCY. Looting, riots, everyday violence—all of this is fueled by drug trafficking. The drug trade finances, recruits, protects, and terrorizes. As long as we don't dismantle the networks, we're trying to bail out the ocean with a spoon. So, we're declaring a local state of emergency in each of these areas. The army is supporting the police. Neighborhood by neighborhood, we're removing the dealers and the ringleaders, one by one.

The maps already exist; the police and intelligence services know exactly where the drug dealing spots are and who controls them. [So when placed in prison] The [drug] leaders are completely isolated; no orders are coming out of their cells. What's lacking isn't information. [It is] the will [to do it].

IMMIGRATION REFORM: Fifth, a clear new set of rules for immigration. France welcomes [immigrants]. But welcoming [them] is [not] a guarantee, nor an entitlement.

ALLOW ENTRY WITH A CAVEAT of RESPECT AND ASSIMILATION: In exchange: respect for our laws, our language, our culture. A convicted foreigner [MUST BE] deported. The slightest deviation is no longer tolerated. It's not up to French victims to pay for the second chance of those who spat on the first. And finally, we measure everything.

MEASURE ALL COSTS AND SPENDING ON IMMIGRATION and the Crimes they CREATE:
Last time, I created a dashboard of public spending. We'll do exactly the same thing for Criminal Offenses. I'll call it Line Zero: a public platform that tracks in real time every offense, every crime, every assault, every demonstration that turns violent, every repeat offense, neighborhood by neighborhood, city by city.
We need to see the crime numbers go down. As long as they don't go down, as long as we're not at near-zero levels, we shall continue [with the offensive action].

We reason based on first principles: where does [public] insecurity come from?

What produces it? And, how do we cut it off at the root?

We measure, we act, we observe. Like a tech company that doesn't let go of a bug until it's fixed.

It's not a question of resources.

It's not a question of feasibility.

It's a question of willingness to ACT.

France is [FINALLY] ready to ACT.
