text:
ICYMI O/N

IRAN:

Trump said the Iran war was “essentially almost over” during his Nebraska speech, calling higher gasoline prices a “small price to pay” to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon. (Iran International)  

Saudi and Yemeni forces launched an offensive to retake Mokha and ease the threat to shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, with around 100 fighters providing air cover, the Saudi-led coalition said. A Yemeni spokesman claimed control of the strait, which WSJ couldn’t independently confirm. (WSJ)    

The Houthis said they launched missile and drone attacks against Riyadh’s airport, Aramco’s Rabigh refinery and Saudi military installations in response to the offensive. Their spokesman warned airlines that Saudi airspace had become a theatre for their operations. (WSJ)  

Fars published footage claiming a fire at an Aramco facility in Jeddah following a Yemeni attack. The facility’s identity, damage and operational impact remain unconfirmed. (Fars)  

The U.S. withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford over an IRGC-linked drone threat, U.S. and European officials told WSJ. Officials described a broader plot against aircraft and American pilots; British officials cautioned there was no evidence Tehran could execute an operation of that complexity. (WSJ)  

Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre-war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. (RTRS)

At least 50 tankers carrying Iranian oil remain backed up near Iran under the US blockade, according to United Against Nuclear Iran. Bloomberg’s preliminary tracking estimates show Iran loaded no crude onto tankers in September, the first zero-loading month since the war began. (BBG)  

Iranian Interior Minister Momeni said talks in Doha addressed Qatar and Pakistan’s mediation efforts, with proposals discussed aimed at reducing regional tensions and averting further war. (IRNA)

UN Secretary-General António Guterres arrived in Islamabad for a three-day visit, with Iran-US mediation among the subjects for talks with Pakistan’s political and military leadership. No breakthrough was announced. (IRNA)  

Recovering Hormuz crude flows aren’t resolving the diesel shortage: crude shipments reached 76% of prewar levels, but refined products accounted for just 11% of total oil flows versus over 20% before the war. Damaged refineries mean a full recovery could take well into 2027, analysts told WSJ. (WSJ)  

Trump signed an order allowing wider on-road use of tax-exempt red diesel, effectively offering a 24-cent-a-gallon federal tax saving. The IRS will waive penalties on highway sales through year-end; energy specialists warned limited distribution could constrain the benefit. (BBG)  

The World Bank warned that Asian governments’ energy subsidies may prove unsustainable, forecasting Middle East oil exports would not regain pre-war levels until mid-2027. It nevertheless raised its 2026 East Asia and Pacific growth forecast to 4.5%, citing AI investment and exports. (BBG)  

MACRO:

US borrowing costs for companies rated CCC or below reached 17%, the highest since May 2020, as the Treasury sell-off spreads into corporate credit. BofA cut its forecast for this month’s investment-grade issuance to $110bn from roughly $160bn. (FT)  

Commercial-property buyers are demanding price cuts or threatening to abandon deals as financing costs rise, WSJ reports. The share of CMBS mortgages in special servicing reached 11.42% in August, its highest since February 2013, according to Trepp. (WSJ) 

FT’s Unhedged column flags a potential dollar vulnerability: huge foreign inflows into US AI assets and falling currency hedging have left investors heavily exposed to USD. An AI reversal or renewed hedging could trigger substantial dollar selling, drawing on Nomura and BNY analysis. (FT)  

An OECD survey of 8,000 employers found just 1% of firms adopting AI were cutting headcount mainly because of the technology. FT reports economists remain sceptical of predictions of mass job losses, despite slowing entry-level tech hiring. (FT)  

HSBC maintains its call for further steepening in the U.S. 5s30s Treasury curve. Strategist Dhiraj Narula said volatility and the lack of clear technical resistance are keeping investors sidelined despite increasingly attractive long-end yields. (WSJ) 

The BoJ may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2% target, according to Reuters sources, highlighting its readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months. Many in the central bank are cautious about delivering another hike this month. (RTRS)

BoJ Governor Ueda said on Tuesday it was becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around the central bank's 2% target, signalling readiness to keep raising interest rates to blunt the risk of too-high inflation. (RTRS)

Japan’s 10-year auction was well received, where it attracted a bid-to-cover of 3.76, versus 3.29 previously and a 12-month average of 3.21; the tail narrowed to 0.02 from 0.12. JGB futures pared losses as yields above 3% brought buyers back. (BBG)  

Citi’s Tomohisa Fujiki said JGB yields are approaching their peaks, with 2.5–3% fair value for the 10-year if inflation stabilises near 2%. Citi expects curve flattening and warned crowded long-bank/short-property positioning could reverse. (BBG)  

US VP Vance told reporters that the $54bn Alaska LNG project with South Korea would proceed, despite Seoul making participation conditional on commercial viability and Trump threatening trade retaliation. South Korea said it transferred the first $2.4bn of investment funding under the US trade deal last week. (BBG)

SocGen remains neutral on Korean equities and prefers Taiwan as memory-chip earnings momentum fades and buyers disappear. Foreign investors sold $25bn of Korean stocks in August–September, while turnover has fallen around 75% from June’s peak; strategists described an “absence of marginal buyers.” (WSJ)    

South Korea’s President Lee said there were signs AI was used in attacks exposing customer data at seven financial firms. Hackers appear to have targeted third-party systems rather than core payment networks; no stolen funds have been reported. (FT)  

Australia’s Westpac consumer sentiment index fell 4.7% to 80.4 following the RBA hike and continued fuel-price pressure. Responses collected after the rate decision registered just 67.2; Westpac expects another hike in November. (BBG) 

Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers told Bloomberg TV that higher bond yields would squeeze the budget as cheap debt is refinanced. He will incorporate the impact into the year-end budget update; RBC estimates current market yields could add about A$6bn to four-year costs. (BBG)   

New Zealand’s NZIER survey showed a net 43% of firms expecting economic improvement, with seasonally adjusted confidence the strongest since 2014. Actual demand remained weak, while fewer businesses planned price rises, suggesting limited pass-through of higher costs. (BBG) 

New Zealand’s governing National Party fell to 25.9%, its weakest polling result since 2020, in an RNZ-Reid Research survey ahead of November’s election. Neither main bloc would command a majority, leaving the centrist Opportunity Party potentially holding the balance of power. (BBG)   

Germany’s coalition is struggling to agree tax measures worth more than €4bn annually, with disputes over sugar, plastics and crypto gains threatening the budget deal. One official told Bloomberg that November approval of the 2027 budget could no longer be assumed. (BBG)  

German factory orders fell 10.6% M/M in August versus -1% expected, following July’s 3.2% rise. Large orders drove the decline: excluding them, orders slipped just 0.1%, while the three-month measure remained up 1.3%. (BBG)  

Germany’s AfD is expected to secure its first regional parliament presidency in Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday with support from the hard-left BSW. The party is separately seeking enough votes to install its first state premier. (FT)  

French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen presents plans on Tuesday to cut government spending by €25 billion ($28 billion) a year, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility in the face of a growing bond market crisis. (RTRS)

France’s 10-year borrowing costs have approached 5%, with its spread over Bunds widening by almost two-thirds in a month to around 140bp. FT reports growing investor concern that political resistance to budget cuts could turn the sell-off into a broader Eurozone crisis. (FT)  

France faces more than $1tn of debt maturities by 2030 and plans roughly $380bn of issuance next year, as traditional buyers retreat and borrowing costs approach 5%. WSJ reports debt-servicing costs are projected to rise 59% by 2030, with political paralysis undermining efforts to contain spending. (WSJ)  

French teachers are joining nationwide student protests demanding more education spending, adding pressure as the government seeks budget restraint. National Rally said it wants to avoid worsening the bond crisis and acknowledged that toppling the government could contribute to an escalation. (BBG)  

Czech inflation accelerated more than expected last month after the central bank warned that tighter monetary policy may be warranted to tame price growth. (BBG)

Philippine September CPI accelerated to 7.2% Y/Y versus 6.8% expected, ending four months of slowing inflation. Food and fuel drove the upside surprise, strengthening the case for further BSP tightening at its October 22 meeting. (BBG)

Thai September CPI rose 2.82% Y/Y versus 3.1% expected and 2.53% previously. The Commerce Ministry expects further acceleration in Q4 as fuel costs feed through, with flooding estimated to add around 0.1 percentage point to inflation. (BBG)  

EQUITIES:

OpenAI is discussing a $30bn funding round with UAE investors including MGX and with BlackRock, according to Bloomberg sources. The UAE syndicate could contribute up to $10bn; OpenAI is pitching a roughly $1.4tn pre-money valuation. (BBG)  

Wall Street banks have launched a record $60bn financing tied to Broadcom chips for Anthropic, according to the FT. (FT)  

Nvidia-backed Reflection launched its first open-weight model, Beam, targeting Chinese rivals in coding and agentic tasks. Reflection says it competes with https://t.co/da7jebtExB’s GLM-5.2 and is approaching Qwen3.8-Max; the model activates 23bn of its 501bn parameters per task. (RTRS)  

SemiAnalysis estimates Claude subscriptions offer roughly five times the API-equivalent value of comparable mid-tier ChatGPT plans following OpenAI’s limit reductions. Its analysis highlights subscription subsidies as a significant drag on AI-lab inference margins. (SemiAnalysis)  

Google is nearing a multiyear nuclear-power agreement worth at least $1bn with Constellation, according to Bloomberg sources. An announcement could come this week; the capacity and location have not been established. (BBG) 

AMD’s Lisa Su said demand still exceeds supply across CPUs, GPUs and AI products, and AMD will increase its previously announced $10bn Taiwan supply-chain investment. Supply should rise substantially in 2027, but customers could absorb more; planning now extends three to five years ahead. (China Times) 

OpenAI and Anthropic told Australian parliament on Tuesday they would welcome laws requiring them to report data breaches carried out by their AI agents, acknowledging the decision to notify authorities was currently at their discretion. (RTRS)

Oracle’s 2025 healthcare breach affected nearly 20 million people, according to newly reported disclosures from the Texas attorney general. The compromised information included Social Security numbers and medical records; the scale had not previously been disclosed. (BBG)   

Banks are expanding into Asian GPU lending, broadening funding for the AI buildout despite uncertainty over chip depreciation. Citi, JPMorgan, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, Santander and SMBC are evaluating GPU-linked loans, according to Bloomberg sources. (BBG)  

KKR’s retail private-credit fund K-FITS will exceed its 5% quarterly redemption cap to meet all requests, after withdrawals reached 5.06% of shares versus 3.43% previously. The fund cited sufficient liquidity to fulfil the requests in full. (BBG)  

DayOne Data Centers publicly filed for a US IPO after previously exploring a raise of up to $5bn at around $20bn valuation. Its filing showed first-half revenue rising to $512m from $151.5m, while its net loss widened to $81.9m. (BBG)  

NextEra’s $67bn Dominion takeover faces growing political opposition in Virginia, with Governor Abigail Spanberger seeking concessions on electricity bills, jobs and investment. FT reports the backlash is raising pressure for tougher approval conditions despite improved customer credits and employment guarantees. (FT)  

Korean memory suppliers are quoting sharply higher HBM4 long-term contract prices for 2027, according to DIGITIMES supply-chain reporting: approximately $1,400–1,600 versus $500–550 in 2026. (DIGITIMES)  

Seagate and Toshiba are competing for TDK’s hard-drive magnetic-heads business in a potential multibillion-dollar deal, Bloomberg sources said. TDK is the only independent supplier of the component; its shares jumped 7.3% as the bidders seek to secure AI storage supply. (BBG)  

DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80bn yuan ($12bn), exceeding its original 50bn-yuan target, according to Bloomberg sources. Tencent and CATL are among the largest backers, with signed term sheets potentially taking the round toward 100bn yuan ahead of an early-2027 IPO. (BBG)

Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. To the community note people: Go take a very serious course on critical thinking. You truly are lost in your own lack of standards. Kabuki theater is not science, not reality, and not genuine. You are truly lost in your own head!

The flyer is the case. The note is a dictionary trick.

Health Net of California, a Centene subsidiary, published the offer itself: two thousand five hundred dollars to the pediatrician or family physician for each eligible Ambetter HMO or PPO Marketplace child when the Childhood Immunization Status Combination 10 gap is closed before the child turns two and a half. The 2026 version runs through June 30, 2027. Rotavirus is excluded because it cannot be given after eight months. The rest of the series is the bounty. Upload the record to the California Immunization Registry, or fax it to a line marked “CIS-10 Provider Incentive.”

https://t.co/8Z2Jty1ke1

https://t.co/quzIqg4h8w

That is not a rumor from a video. The payer put a price on the completed schedule and addressed it to the person holding the needle.

A kickback is a payment returned for producing the result the payer wanted. The money here moves from the insurer to the doctor when the child is brought up to date. Per child. Not a plaque for the clinic. Not a fond hope. A fee for closing the gap. Ten children behind on the series, caught up, means twenty-five thousand dollars. A hundred means a quarter of a million. The video’s arithmetic was the flyer’s arithmetic.

The community note’s theater is the swap of words. It will say this cannot be a kickback because the Anti-Kickback Statute is a federal criminal law about remuneration for referrals billed to Medicare and Medicaid, and because the check is signed by the insurer rather than by the vaccine maker. Both sentences can be true and still be a dodge. The statute is a prosecution tool. It is not the meaning of the word. A payment that arrives only when the product is delivered does not become innocent because the middleman wrote the check or because the forum picked the narrowest legal definition and answered that instead. Kabuki is performing the statute so the bounty can leave the stage.

Parents are not handed this flyer in the exam room. The doctor who urges the catch-up is the doctor who can bill for the catch-up. Consent given without that number is consent with the price hidden. The flyer even pays for a verified exclusion once Health Net accepts it, which tells you they know a gap can be closed on paper. The advertised sum is still for the shots.

Print the flyer. Print the two thousand five hundred. Print the age. The note can keep the statute. It does not get to keep the word.

Republicans have a habit of doing two things that cost them seats. They skip early voting, and they sit out midterms. This one is not optional. Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Vote early, vote RED, and Remove Every Democrat. The last two years are the case: they have not represented their constituents.
Forty-seven states and Washington, D.C., offer no-excuse early in-person voting. Alabama has none. Mississippi and New Hampshire allow it only with an excuse. Hours and sites vary by county.
Already open, or opening this week:

September 18: Minnesota and South Dakota. Idaho starts in-person absentee around this date; county early-voting sites, where offered, generally open October 19.
September 19: Vermont and Virginia. Mississippi’s excuse-only in-person absentee also began September 19.
September 24: Illinois.
October 4: Maine, Montana, and Nebraska.
October 5: California (varies by county) and Ohio.
October 6: Indiana, New Mexico, and Wyoming.
October 7: Arizona.

Still ahead:

October 13: Georgia. The statutory start is the fourth Monday, October 12, a state holiday, so it moves to the 13th.
October 14: Iowa, Kansas (counties may open later, no later than a week before Election Day), Rhode Island, and Tennessee.
October 15: North Carolina.
October 16: Washington.
October 17: Massachusetts and Nevada.
October 19: Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, North Dakota (some counties later), South Carolina, and Texas. In Texas the 17th day before the election is Saturday, October 17, so early voting starts Monday, October 19, and runs through October 30.
October 20: Louisiana (through October 27), Utah (counties may shorten this to as few as four days), and Wisconsin (no earlier than this date; towns set the start). Pennsylvania has no classic early-voting period; in-person mail-ballot voting at county offices must be available by October 20 and sometimes opens sooner.
October 21: West Virginia.
October 22: Delaware, Hawaii, Maryland, and Missouri (some listings use October 20).
October 24: Florida (counties may start as early as October 19; the required window is October 24–31), Michigan, New Jersey, and New York.
October 26: District of Columbia (some listings say October 28).
October 28: Oklahoma, through 2 p.m. Saturday, October 31.
October 29: Kentucky, through the Saturday before Election Day.

Do not wait for November 3.

“In tonight’s battle of the Chris’s only one is standing up for the education of thousands of Kiwi students. Chris Hipkins’ position to abolish charter schools shows he will trade the wellbeing and future success of thousands of students to keep his union mates happy,” says ACT Leader David Seymour.

“Christopher Luxon’s response to him was bang on. Charter schools are great, and they're getting great results for the students enrolled. In twelve months the number of schools has more than doubled and enrolments increased more than sixfold.

“Hipkins can explain to these families why their child should go back to the school they were struggling at because he wants to keep his union mates happy. Their biggest fear is that charter schools will succeed and it’s playing out in real time. They take a cut of teachers’ salaries to negotiate collective agreements, and they know charter schools sit outside those agreements.

“Families are choosing these schools because they offer something different. Some schools have had so much demand they have needed larger premises. North West College, for example, grew from 22 students in March 2025 to 150 by July this year.

“More importantly, we are starting to see the results. Five of the first seven charter schools exceeded their attendance targets in their first year, and five exceeded their achievement targets.

“At TIPENE, initial assessments in February 2025 found more than half of students were below expected levels in maths, reading and writing. By the end of the year, 81 per cent were achieving at or above the expected level in maths, 79 per cent in reading and 80 per cent in writing.

“At BUSY School, students had an average attendance rate of just 19 per cent before enrolling. Their attendance at the charter school rose to 83 per cent. These are young people for whom the existing system was not working, now attending and learning.

“There are children in classrooms today whose families have deliberately chosen these schools because they believe they better meet their needs.

“They also give taxpayers a better deal. A new primary charter school with 100 students would receive around $401,675 in establishment staff and operations funding. The same school set up as a state school would cost the taxpayer $638,249.

“ACT wants all students to have the chance to unlock their potential. For thousands of Kiwi students this will only happen with charter schools.”

text:
On a darker note, regarding the migrant crossings, if French and British authorities travel alongside the migrants to 'offer assistance if needed' for the whole journey, surely the rapes and murders that happen along the way must be witnessed by the authorities?

There is strong official evidence that French vessels sometimes remain with migrant boats for very long periods. Just last month, CROSS Jobourg coordinated continuous monitoring of one boat carrying about 60 people for more than 33 hours. 

Another French official account from April describes Cormoran and Minck monitoring a migrant boat, watching additional people board near Hardelot, and then Cormoran “securing” the boat's passage towards the British SAR region before British vessels took over. 

So the question is legitimate: if a serious assault occurs aboard a boat while a state vessel is maintaining close surveillance, what could the surveillance crew actually observe?

Suppose there were credible allegations that a rape, serious assault or deliberate killing occurred during a period of continuous French or British surveillance. Then I think the authorities' contemporaneous records become extremely important.

We would want the complete CROSS/HM Coastguard incident log, radio communications, vessel log, body-worn/video imagery where applicable, EO/IR surveillance recordings, Home Office aircraft imagery, RNLI/Border Force observations, distress calls and witness statements. The question would not merely be “Was a patrol vessel nearby?” It would be:

"At what time did the alleged offence occur, where was the migrant boat, which government assets were observing it, at what distance, what surveillance equipment was being used, what did the crews report seeing or hearing, and what happened immediately afterwards?"

There's an especially important evidential distinction. If investigators subsequently establish from passenger testimony that an assault occurred at 03:20, and AIS/operational records establish Minck was monitoring the boat at that exact time, that establishes contemporaneous state surveillance — not that Minck's crew witnessed the assault. If the vessel's optical recording then visibly captured it, or passengers were signalling for help and communications logs recorded those reports, the evidential situation would be entirely different.

The same principle applies if the authorities subsequently recover people from the boat. CPS guidance specifically recognises serious injury or a fatality aboard a small boat while the journey continues as potentially relevant to prosecution for endangering another during a sea crossing. 

If we eventually discover cases where the public narrative says something like “a woman was raped during the crossing”, while French records independently establish that the boat was under continuous state surveillance for the entire crossing, then did the French watched a rape happen?

We need to ask:
What did the monitoring authorities observe, what surveillance recordings exist, when did they first become aware of the alleged offence, and were those records secured for the criminal investigation?

That is both much harder for authorities to dismiss and much more evidentially defensible.

There is hyperbole, and then there is Donald Trump standing at a podium in Nebraska offering up Los Angeles and San Diego as sacrificial pawns in a war with Iran.

When he mused aloud that letting Iran take out those two cities was a "very small price to pay" to manage war-time economic strain, he didn't just break the presidential script. He obliterated the foundational premise of the office he holds: that the chief executive's primary, non-negotiable obligation is the defense of American lives on American soil.

We have reached a stage in our politics where partisan alienation has become so profound that an arena will cheer the hypothetical vaporization of millions of their own countrymen, simply because those countrymen live in a state that didn't vote for their candidate.

Lincoln spoke of a house divided against itself. Trump doesn't just acknowledge the division—he offers to sign off on the demolition of the Western wing if it helps the ratings.

At a certain point, we need to stop pretending this is edgy populist rhetoric. When the man holding the nuclear codes casually greenlights foreign strikes on American soil, he doesn't need another cable news panel or a fact-check. He needs a clinical evaluation. He is, quite simply, nuts.

text:
📜 THIS DAY IN DIPLOMATIC HISTORY
        October 6, 1933

On this day, the German government sent a note to the British and Italian governments. Germany, it declared, wanted either complete freedom, or to be bound by the same qualitative limits on weapons as everyone else. The note was delivered in the middle of the League of Nations Disarmament Conference at Geneva.

On its face it sounded fair. Germany had been disarmed at Versailles while the victors kept their arsenals, and for years Berlin had demanded "equality of rights." Both options meant the same thing: German rearmament. Either everyone else disarmed down to Germany's level, which France would never do for the sake of its own security, or Germany armed up to theirs. There was no answer the Western powers could give that did not hand Hitler what he wanted.

Less than a year earlier, in December 1932, the powers had formally granted Germany "equality of rights" within a system that was supposed to give security to all, and on that promise Germany had come back to the conference. Through 1933 Britain tried to turn the promise into a plan, offering Germany equality only by stages, after a trial period of several years under international supervision. Berlin wanted equality at once, with no probation and no inspectors. Hitler was not looking for a compromise. He was looking for a way out.

The Western delegates at Geneva tried to soften the German position. The German delegation, acting on strict instructions from Berlin, gave nothing. On October 14, 1933, Arthur Henderson, the president of the Disarmament Conference, received a long telegram signed by Foreign Minister von Neurath. Since the conference had failed in its "sole task" of bringing about general disarmament, it said, Germany had decided to leave both the Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations. On October 19 Berlin gave formal notice of its withdrawal from the League.

The scene at Geneva was captured by the French journalist Geneviève Tabouis. John Simon, the British foreign secretary, red with anger, called Germany a mad dog and wanted the League to stand on its dignity and give a firm answer. The American delegate Norman Davis took the opposite view. The main thing, he said, was not to make the situation worse. Sooner or later Germany would see its mistake and come back to Geneva. A little patience, gentlemen.

Germany was the second great power to abandon the League that year. In March 1933 Japan had already announced its withdrawal, after the League condemned its conquest of Manchuria. In a single year the organisation built to keep the peace lost two of the great powers it most needed to keep it.

Hitler dressed the withdrawal in the language of peace. He told the German people it was an act of "peace and honour," and even "a step toward the real abolition of war." Germany, he said, could not take part in a conference that treated it as a second-class nation without rights. He offered France a separate arms agreement, insisted that National Socialist Germany wanted only to end the old enmity between the two countries forever, and promised that if the Saar were returned, there would be no reason left to revise the border.

In Paris the advocates of a deal with Berlin grew louder. The French government agreed to "listen to the German proposals." So Hitler's ambassador received the French ambassador François-Poncet, and in meetings on November 24 and December 11, 1933, Germany laid out what its talk of peace actually meant:

the immediate return of the Saar;
an army raised to 300,000 men;
the right to the weapons such an army needed, including heavy artillery, tanks, fighters and bombers;
ten-year non-aggression pacts with its neighbours.

The "outstretched hand" was a demand to rearm.

On November 12, 1933, Hitler staged a plebiscite asking voters to approve his government's pollicy. He had called the vote the moment he quit Geneva, dissolving the Reichstag on the day of the withdrawal and presenting the plebiscite to the country as a verdict on that decision. The whole campaign was fought on it: do you back the decision to leave, to reject the humiliation of Versailles, to demand equality?

Yet the ballot itself never mentioned the League of Nations. It asked only whether the voter approved "this policy of your national government" and would profess it as his own will. The official result was 95 percent in favour, on a turnout of over 96 percent. Breaking with Geneva and preparing to rearm had been dressed up as the democratic will of the nation.

#DiplomaticHistory #LeagueOfNations #Disarmament #NaziGermany #OnThisDay

text:
NYAKASURA SCHOOL: THE INFECTIOUS ACADEMIC BEHEMOTH

Nyakasura School, one of Uganda’s illustrious educational institution has produced professionals from all walks of life. Lawyers, politicians, kings, army men, judges and doctors have all walked through “The School.” Rukirabasaija Sir George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III was educated at Nyakasura and several of his chiefs and subjects. 

Founded in 1926 by a retired British naval officer, Lieutenant-Commander Ernest Eborhard Calwell, affectionally known as “the Commander”, Nyakasura is a secondary boarding school in Fort Portal, Tooro. The Commander was posted to Kings College Budo in 1922 to teach mathematics. At that time Buddo had a sizeable number of Batooro. He met two boys from Tooro, Komwiswa and Balya who later became very close friends. When the Commander fell out with the Buddo school head, the boys urged him to start up a school in Tooro which he did.

When the Commander arrived in Tooro in December 1925, he met the reigning Omukama Daudi Kasagama Kyebambe III and his chiefs whom he requested to offer him a place with ample water, food and fertile soil to start up a school. He was offered three places, but he chose Nyakasura because of the beauty and tranquillity of the place. 

Nyakasura school was built on three foundations; God fearing, hard work and sports, which has kept it moving even in times of struggle and its students have loved to live on these foundations even after school. The old students describe it as an infectious place because whoever walks through its gates wants to always associate with it than any other places they go to. Going by their motto, ‘To Minister and not to be Ministered Unto’, Nyakasura School remains an academic behemoth in Uganda. 

The School is unique in many ways. Firstly, their uniform is a kilt, which some people think they are boys in skirts. Since Commander was a Scottish, he decided that the kilt be introduced as the school uniform. Secondly, the school has no school anthem but has a school hymn: “YEARS OF STRUGGLE LIE BEHIND US…”

Nyakasura School has been an academic and sports giant in the country over the years and is proud that the first Cricket game in Uganda was played at the school in 1929. The school dominated Uganda both academic and sports arena from 1964-1972. These were the best years of Nyakasura. In fact, for eight solid years, Nyakasura was the best school in Uganda both ‘O’ and ‘A’ level, it was second to none. The alumni and current school administration are looking forward to reviving this success. Staff quarters, the classes and all structures are undergoing rehabilitation and the school is recovering using its school hymn, “Years of struggle lie behind us…Sunshine follows after rain. Currently, Nyakasura has a secondary school boarding enrollment (S1-S6) of about 1000 students.

The notable alumni of “The School” include: 
Army officers; the late Brig Noble Mayombo, Gen David Sejusa, Major Okwiri Rabwoni;  Politicians; Adolf Mwesige Minister of defense; Margaret Mugisa Muhanga, MP Burahya county, Steven Kagwera, former MP Burahya County; Dr Chrispus Kiyonga, Ambassador and former minister; Aston Kajara, former Minister of State for privatization and MP Mwenge North , Tim Lwanga, the former minister of Ethics and Integrity.

Others are; Patrick Bitature, chairman UIA; Mugisa Micheal, former NFA boss; Richard Buteera, Director of Public Prosecutions, Beatrice Kiraso, former Secretary General of the East African Community,
Professors; Edward Rugumayo, William Banage, Kanti Eriab Kanyarusoke among others. Justices; Herbert Ntabgoba; Seth Manyindo and Patrick Tabaro
Doctors; Albert Batule, Dr Andrew Kasoro, Dr Paul Baguma, Dr Vincent Karuhanga, Dr Ategeka Gilbert among others.

東漢 「左積射五百人督印」銅印

《左積射五百人督印》銅印，出自東漢時期（公元25-220年），收藏於臺北國立故宮博物院，是一件銅製印章，高2.52公分，印面長2.44公分、寬2.43公分。該印章為鼻鈕式設計，印面以白文刻有「左積射五百人督印」八字，體現出當時軍事職階體系的特色。

此印章的文字描述涉及軍隊編制與官職等級：「積射」指的是弓箭手單位，而「督」為指揮官職稱。根據記載，掌管百人的官稱為「將」，而掌管五百人的官稱為「督」，意即「督」統領五位「將」。由此可見，「督」的權限類似於「大將軍」管理五部兵馬的架構，職權高於一般「將」。

從製作材質與尺寸分析，該銅印小巧精緻，細節刻畫工整，顯示東漢時期鑄造技術的成熟。鼻鈕設計不僅方便持握，也反映出印章在當時官署文書管理中的重要角色。印面字體為白文，輪廓清晰且布局均衡，這一點尤具觀賞與研究價值。

觀者在細看此印時，應注意銅印的氛圍與紋理變化，特別是印文的筆觸線條與輪廓，以及鼻鈕與印底面的整合度。這反映了東漢官方的行政組織和軍事編制，見證了兩漢時期刻印制度與等級劃分的體系。

此銅印同時為研究東漢軍事體系及官員層級制度提供了有力物證，也透過其實物展現了古代聲威及官方權力象徵的具體形態。在文物保存方面，國立故宮博物院依嚴格標準維護此類文物，使其得以完整面貌呈現於公眾與學術研究者眼前。

總結而言，此東漢銅印不僅是技藝的呈現，更是歷史文化與軍事制度有形的見證。研究它有助於了解兩漢官制體系和軍事單位組織，亦對古代印章工藝與行政管理制度有深入啟示。

The bronze seal inscribed with "Zuojishe wubairen du yin" — translated as "Seal of the Supervisor of Five Hundred Archers of the Left Accumulated Archery" — dates from the Eastern Han Dynasty (25-220 CE) and is housed in the National Palace Museum in Taipei. This compact seal stands 2.52 centimeters tall, with a square face measuring approximately 2.44 by 2.43 centimeters. Featuring a knop (nose button) handle, the seal's face carries an eight-character inscription carved in white script, marking it as an official military seal tied to archery troops.

The inscription provides important insight into the military hierarchy and administrative organization of the time. "Zuojishe" refers to a unit of archers (bowmen) stationed on the left flank, while the term "du" (supervisor) denotes an official rank higher than a "jiang" (general), who commands one hundred men. Here, the "du" oversees five "jiang," or five hundred soldiers, analogous to the oversight traditionally held by a "grand general" who commands five army divisions. This hierarchical nuance suggests that the rank of "du" held considerable authority, superior to standard commanders responsible for smaller detachments.

Materially, the seal is a small yet meticulously crafted bronze object, exemplifying Eastern Han metalworking skills. The knob design facilitates hold and stamping, indicating its functional role in administration and official documentation. The crisp, well-proportioned white inscriptions — where the characters are carved in relief against a recessed background — showcase the period's calligraphic and casting techniques.

Visitors examining the seal should pay close attention to the detailed contours of the inscription strokes and the seamless integration of the knop with the seal face and base. The surface texture and patina might reveal traces of age and usage, reflecting the artifact’s official function as a symbol of military command and governmental authority.

This seal not only stands as an artifact of fine craftsmanship but also as tangible evidence of Eastern Han military structuring and bureaucratic practice. Its rank designation highlights the stratified nature of military command and offers scholars material evidence for understanding Han dynasty governance and army organization.

The National Palace Museum meticulously preserves this bronze seal under professional conservation standards, enabling ongoing public display and academic research. Its significance lies equally in its physical form and the cultural-historical context it embodies — illustrating how tangible objects served as instruments and symbols of official power during ancient China.

In conclusion, the "Zuojishe wubairen du yin" bronze seal provides valuable historical testimony to the administrative hierarchy and military units of the Eastern Han era. Appreciating its craftsmanship alongside its recorded function enriches our understanding of Han dynasty political-military structures and the ceremonial use of seals in officialdom.

text:
GREATNESS, FATHERHOOD & THE MEN BESIDE MICHAEL JORDAN

The Last Dance is a rare sports documentary that works even if you don’t care about basketball.

Jason Hehir’s magnificent 10-part Netflix series follows Michael Jordan and the Chicago Bulls during their final championship season, Phil Jackson’s “last dance” in 1997–98. Around that season, it tells the story of Jordan’s rise, two three-peats, his baseball interlude, and the extraordinary personalities behind one of sport’s greatest dynasties.

Jordan is the relentless engine. Scottie Pippen is the brilliant, underpaid co-star. Dennis Rodman is controlled chaos. Phil Jackson is the Zen-like architect holding it together. Steve Kerr is the understated role player who repeatedly delivers when it matters.

But perhaps the most moving part comes about 38 minutes into Episode 9. Here, the story becomes one of fathers, older men and shared grief.

Kerr’s father, Malcolm, was assassinated in Beirut in 1984. Jordan’s father, James, was murdered in 1993. Remarkably, despite sharing this terrible experience, Kerr says they barely spoke about it.

After losing his father, Jordan increasingly found companionship among the older men in his security detail. These men provided maturity, steadiness and perspective amid the insanity of being Michael Jordan.

Especially important was former police officer Gus Lett. Gus became more than a bodyguard. He was Michael’s friend, protector and father-figure. Someone that Jordan wanted nearby, much as his own father had so often been right beside him.

And the care ran both ways. As Gus battled lung cancer during that final championship run, Jordan kept him close. After defeating Indiana in Game 7 of the Eastern Conference Finals, Michael gave Gus the game ball.

That sequence captures something profound about men. Even Michael Jordan, perhaps the most famous athlete on Earth, ferociously competitive and seemingly invincible, still needed older men.

Men who could steady him. Protect him. Make him laugh. Offer perspective. Simply stand beside him...

There’s enormous value in male friendship and intergenerational mentorship. Sometimes, when a father is gone, another good man can help carry some of the weight.

text:
The claim is a slogan, not a historical finding. Classical Islamic rule often let Jews and Christians keep their religion. It did not make Islam the most tolerant religion, and the freedom was conditional, unequal, and frequently revoked.

Under the dhimma, Jews and Christians were “People of the Book.” They could worship, keep courts for internal matters, and hold property, in exchange for the jizya and acceptance of Muslim political supremacy. That arrangement was more formal than what many medieval Christian states offered Jews, and more stable than the fate of pagans. It was still a subordinate status, not equal citizenship.

The restrictions were written into law and practice, not occasional abuses:

•  Jizya was a poll tax on non-Muslim adult males, often collected in a humiliating way. Quran 9:29 is the classical proof-text: fight those who do not believe until they pay the jizya “while they are humbled.”

•  The so-called Pact of Umar, whether or not Umar himself issued it, became the standard list: no new churches or synagogues, no repair without permission, no crosses or bells in public, no riding horses, distinctive clothing, no bearing arms, no public processions, no building higher than Muslim houses, no proselytizing.

•  A dhimmi’s testimony against a Muslim was restricted or invalid in many schools of law. Blood-money for a killed non-Muslim was often half or less. Apostasy from Islam was a capital offense in classical fiqh; conversion the other way was encouraged.

•  Polytheists, and later groups not granted dhimmi status, had a worse deal. In India, temple destruction and jizya under several sultanates and the Mughals are extensively documented. In North Africa and Spain, the Almohads (12th century) abolished the dhimma and forced conversion, exile, or death on Jews and Christians. Maimonides fled that.

There were better stretches. Early Umayyad and Abbasid cities, parts of Fatimid Egypt, and the Ottoman millet system let large Christian and Jewish communities function for centuries. Cordoba and Baghdad produced famous Jewish and Christian scholars under Muslim rulers. Those periods are real. They sit next to al-Hakim’s destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (1009), periodic forced conversions in Yemen (including the Orphans’ Decree), Timur’s massacres, and the long decline of Christian populations from majorities in the Middle East and North Africa to small minorities. Demographic collapse on that scale is not what sustained tolerance produces.

“Most tolerant” also fails the comparison. Ashokan and later Indian Buddhist policy, some Hindu kingdoms, the early Persian empires’ treatment of subject cults, Dutch and English pluralism after the 17th century, and post-Enlightenment secular states all outperform the dhimma on the measures that matter: equal legal standing, freedom to leave the ruling religion, freedom to criticize it, and freedom to build new houses of worship. Medieval Latin Christendom was often worse toward Jews than contemporary Muslim states; it was not uniformly worse, and by the 19th century the gap had reversed. Tolerance is a record of institutions and outcomes, not a property of a scripture.

So the accurate sentence is narrower. For long periods, Muslim rulers taxed and ranked Jews and Christians instead of expelling or converting them by force. That was a real, limited toleration. It was not equality, it was not consistent, and it does not make Islam the most tolerant religion in history.

Last year, a blind bet on EVERY outsider in Shanghai returned +35% ROI.

🐢 𝐂𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐞𝐝: 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟓 𝐭𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐮𝐬
CPI 2025: 32.8, down from 42.4 in 2024. Only Indian Wells (31.0) was slower among hard-court Masters.

"Compared to 2019 the courts are 25 times slower" (Medvedev, 2025). 
"The slowest conditions I have played in on the circuit" (De Minaur, 2025).

2025 stats (after 156 matches): 82% holds, 73% 1st serve pts won, 0.58 aces/game, 0.17 TB/set.

2026: too few qualifying matches so far to say whether anything changed. Update to come once the main draw gets going.

→ Night sessions play even slower ("The balls are like bowling balls, so big, especially in the evening", Griekspoor). Check the order of play before backing a big server.

🧠 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐨𝐱 𝐧𝐨𝐛𝐨𝐝𝐲 𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐤𝐬 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭
Everyone called it the slowest court on tour, yet points got SHORTER in 2025: about 5 points more rallies of 4 shots or less than in 2024, and fewer 9+ shot rallies.

Best explanation: the humidity was so brutal that players went for their shots early because they couldn't survive long rallies.

→ Milder weather this year (see below) could mean longer rallies again. Edge to grinders and elite movers, less to "survival" first-strikers.

🌤️ 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫: 𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭
2025: 30-35°C, humidity above 80%, cramps everywhere. "50% of the matches are not finishing", said Rinderknech.

2026 forecast (up to Oct 15): 24-27°C by day, 13-19°C at night, mostly dry and hazy. Showers possible around Oct 10-12 and Oct 14, then cooler, low 20s.

→ Don't copy-paste last year's chaos. The fitness and heat-tolerance edge that fueled 2025's upsets should be much smaller.

text:
W. B. Gallie
05 October 1912 – 31 August 1998
Part of a Series on the Philosophy of History
Gallie on Essentially Contested Concepts in History

Monday 05 October 2026 is the 114th anniversary of the birth of Walter Bryce Gallie (05 October 1912 – 31 August 1998), who was born a Scotsman in Lenzie, near Glasgow, on this date in 1912.

Gallie’s best known paper was “Essentially Contested Concepts” published in 1956, and his major work in the philosophy of history, Philosophy and the Historical Understanding (1964, 2nd ed. 1968), is, in part, an application of the idea of essentially contested concepts to history. Gallie also wrote a couple of book s on the philosophy of war, Philosophers of Peace and War: Kant, Clausewitz, Marx, Engels and Tolstoy (1978) and Understanding War (1991). I’d like to talk about these works, but I have other philosophical priorities for today. Hopefully I’ll eventually get back to Gallie’s writings on war since I’ve produced several episodes on the philosophical significance of war and I’d like to continue to develop that thread of inquiry.

On the first page of his Philosophy and the Historical Understanding, Gallie positions himself on the side of critical philosophy of history. In fact, the first chapter is titled “Critical Philosophy of History.” This is a tradition that understands itself as a kind of higher historiography, in which the works of historians are accepted as given, and it is the business of the philosopher of history to review and criticize the use that historians make of various concepts, and the methods by which they have arrived at their conclusions. According to critical philosophy of history, it’s not the business of the philosopher of history to understand the historical process itself, like speculative philosophers of history, but rather to reflect on the historian’s reflections on the historical process.

I just said a moment ago that, under this philosophical dispensation, part of the task of the philosopher of history is to assess how historians make use of concepts. Despite the claims by many philosophers on behalf of historians, historians use concepts with general meanings that cover many particular instances. A purely idiographic history isn’t possible because historians make use of non-idiographic concepts. Concepts are inevitable, unavoidable, and indispensible. Gallie concedes as much in his analysis of essentially contested concepts in history. But this isn’t the only thing going on in Gallie’s philosophy of history. Gallie also writes that he is interested in a narrative approach:

“What is new in my account of historical understanding is the emphasis that I have put on the idea of narrative. I have tried to analyse what it means to follow a narrative and have argued that whatever understanding and whatever explanations a work of history contains must be assessed in relation to the narrative from which they arise and whose development they subserve.”

In this connection it’s interesting to note that the first edition of Philosophy and the Historical Understanding appeared in 1964, and the second edition in 1968. Arthur Danto’s first edition of Analytical Philosophy of History appeared in 1965; the second edition, with the new title Narration and Knowledge, appeared in 1985. So here we have two philosophers of history working at the same time, both making narration central to their philosophical project. Danto has one footnote on Gallie, but no discussion of his work. Gallie makes no mention of Danto in his second edition of Philosophy and the Historical Understanding, which could have taken account of Danto’ Analytical Philosophy of History. And Gallie and Danto weren’t the only ones to focus on narrative at this time. Narration was on the agenda, but it had it critics as well. Leon J. Goldstein was highly critical of Danto’s use of narration, and went as far as to say that Danto’s discussions, “…are really no part of a critical philosophy of history.” So for Goldstein there was a relationship between critical philosophy of history and narrativism, but this was properly a negative relationship in which one excluded the other. Goldstein doesn’t mention Gallie in his book Historical Knowing, but presumably he would been critical of its narrativist strands. But I’m not going to talk about narrativism today.

I want to focus on Gallie’s essentially contested concepts of his 1956 paper. A literature has grown up around the idea of essentially contested concepts, so much so that we might say that the concept of an essentially contested concept is itself an essentially contested concept. In his 1956 paper, Gallie wrote that essentially contested concepts are, “…concepts the proper use of which inevitably involves endless disputes about their proper uses on the part of their users.” We could say that essentially contested concepts are ambiguous and cannot be made unambiguous. It’s not the case that they’re not yet precise but could be made precise with further effort. Rather, their lack of precision is traceable to a judgment involving valuation.

Many ambiguous concepts canbe made unambiguous. The concept of the color red can be considered ambiguous, since it covers a range of wavelengths in the visible spectrum of light, and there are edge cases where red transitions to orange. If human beings could see into the infrared, there would also be edge cases for red transitioning into infrared. These ambiguities, however, can be eliminated by a stipulative definition of “red” covering only certain wavelengths of light, and we can disambiguate the concept red because the concept involves no appraisive—or what I would prefer to call evaluative—elements. Similarly, many imprecise concepts can be made precise. The logical empiricists liked to focus on what they called the explication of concepts, which were intended to clarify them in just these ways of making the ambiguous unambiguous and the imprecise precise. But, if Gallie was right, there are limits to explication, and those limits are encountered with essentially contested concepts.

Gallie says we can offer legitimate philosophical arguments for or against a particular reading of a particular essentially contested concept, but because of the nature of such a concept, these arguments will never be definitive. That is to say, these arguments will never constitute a general principle for resolving what is at stake in an essentially contested concept.

It doesn’t take much philosophical acuity to see that a great many concepts we employ, and especially those concepts that attempt to capture divisive and contentious events, must fall under essentially contested concepts. This could describe not only a lot of concepts, but also a lot of kinds of concepts, so we need to significantly narrow the scope of what constitutes an essentially contested concept. Oxford Reference gives this as its entry on essentially contested concepts:

“The idea promoted by W. B. Gallie that some concepts admit of no one authoritative definition, because they are essentially the focus of different accounts, especially different moral attitudes. Concepts of which this is true might include persons, justice, equality, and others about which moral and political disagreement is apt to be endemic.”

To the moral and political disagreements mentioned here we could add metaphysical and epistemological differences. Any two philosophers with a different metaphysical understanding of the world would assign different meanings to persons, justice, and equality.  Hume, for example, said that when he looked into himself he couldn’t find anything that corresponded to a self: “I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception.” This has important consequences for the concept of a person. And Plato would have asserted that justice and equality are eternal forms that are only imperfectly mirrored in the mundane world of human activity. This, too, has important consequences for the concepts of justice and equality. Metaphysics and epistemology, then, no less than morality and political ideology, involve evaluative norms, and as such they too could be the source of essentially contested.

Gallie’s interest, however, focuses on the kind of essentially contested concepts that are likely to appear in history. He applies this framework to the concepts of religion, art, democracy, and social justice. One can easily see that many of the large concepts such as these that are employed in history would fall under the umbrella of essentially contested concepts; it might be easier to list the few uncontested concepts than to attempt to list all the contested concepts. Chapter 8 in Philosophy and the Historical Understanding focuses on essentially contested concepts, and is at pains to point out that essentially contested concepts aren’t just confused, vague, or ambiguous concepts. Between this chapter and his earlier paper, Gallie offers an exposition of essentially contested concepts that’s both comprehensive and detailed. He starts by providing five criteria for essentially contested concepts:

(I) The concept in question must be appraisive in the sense that it signifies or accredits some kind of valued achievement.
(II) This achievement must be of an internally complex character, for all that its worth is attributed to it as a whole.
(III) Any explanation of its worth must therefore include reference to the respective contributions of its various parts or features; yet prior to experimentation there is nothing absurd or contradictory in any of a number of possible rival descriptions of its total worth, one such description setting its component parts or features in one order of importance, a second setting them in a second order, and so on. In fine, the accredited achievement is initially variously describable.
(IV) The accredited achievement must be of a kind that admits of considerable modification in the light of changing circumstances; and such modification cannot be prescribed or predicted in advance. For convenience I shall call the concept of any such achievement ‘open’ in character.
(V) each party recognises the fact that its own use of it is contested by those of other parties, and that each party must have at least some appreciation of the different criteria in the light of which the other parties claim to be applying the concept in question. More simply, to use an essentially contested concept means to use it against other uses and to recognise that one’s own use of it has to be maintained against these other uses. Still more simply, to use an essentially contested concept means to use it both aggressively and defensively.

To put these in my own words, I would say that an essentially contested concept involves some evaluation, and the concept itself is internally complex so that discussion of it might involve any of its respective parts. That which falls under an essentially contested concept can be described in more than one way, and is open to revision in the light of changing circumstances. Moreover, there’s an awareness that these concepts have different interpretations, so that use of the concept is effectively made against other uses of the concept. That is to say, the use of essentially contested concepts is polemical.

These first five criteria Gallie distinguishes from a further two. Gallie says that in order to distinguish that which is merely radically confused from essentially contested concepts we need these two additional criteria:

(VI) the derivation of any such concept from an original exemplar whose authority is acknowledged by all the contestant users of the concept, and
(VII) the probability or plausibility, in appropriate senses of these terms, of the claim that the continuous competition for acknowledgment as between the contestant users of the concept enables the original exemplar’s achievement to be sustained or developed in optimum fashion.

With these two criteria we’re adding the provision that the essentially contested concept is derived from an earlier iteration of the concept that was not essentially contested, and that a given use of the concept is presented as the best use in light of further developments. Further regarding the optimum development of an essentially contested concept, in Philosophy and the Historical Understanding Gallie adds to his exposition of these concepts: “…it is quite impossible to find a general principle for deciding which of two contestant uses of an essentially contested concept really ‘uses it best’.” (p. 182) So there’s no rule we can apply to resolve the ambiguity of essentially contested concepts. At the end of his paper on essentially contested concepts Gallie makes an especially interesting observation:

“…if we want to see just what we are doing, when we apply a given appraisive concept, then one way of learning this is by asking from what vaguer or more confused or more restricted version (or ancestor) but currently accepted version of the concept in question has been derived. Commonly we come to see more precisely what a given scientific concept means by contrasting its deductive powers with those of other closely related concepts: in the case of an appraisive concept, we can best see more precisely what it means by comparing and contrasting our uses of it now with other earlier uses of it or its progenitors, i.e., by considering how it came to be.”

Gallie thus comes to a position that’s similar to what Husserl staked out in his essay “The Origin of Geometry” that was included as an appendix to The Crisis of European Sciences, and which I recently mentioned in my episode on “Peeling Away the Layers of History.” In this essay Husserl realized, as he says, that the investigation must be historical, i.e., that the investigation even of formal concepts like those of geometry must be an historical investigation. And this is what Gallie is also saying. The investigation must be historical because Gallie has built historical development into his exposition of essentially contest concepts, especially in the last two criteria. An essentially contested concept is derived from an uncontested concept, and its further development into its present form was, in part, a response to other, competing interpretations of the concept in light of changing circumstances. But, if the investigation of an essentially contested concept must be historical, and historical concepts are themselves essentially contested, this puts us in a bit of a bind.

An historical analysis of an essentially contested concept will make use of essentially contested concepts, to the extent that these concepts are part of historical thought, so this historical analysis itself will be essentially contested. This is at very least a paradox, and perhaps an outright contradiction. We could go through an inventory of historical concepts with an eye to sorting them between the essentially contested and the uncontested, which would yield us two sets of historical concepts. If we use the set of essentially contested concepts for an historical inquiry into essentially contested concepts, this lands us squarely in paradox. If, on the other hand, we use only those concepts that are uncontested for our historical analysis of essentially contested concepts, then the resulting analysis isn’t paradoxical.

Is this sorting of historical concepts into the contested and the uncontested even possible? It would require an exhaustive analysis of a comprehensive inventory of historical concepts to determine whether it is or not. But suppose it is possible. If any concepts remain belonging to history that aren’t essentially contested concepts, then our only hope for a non-paradoxical analysis of essentially contested concepts lies with these. But we would then be doing history with the smaller subset of historical concepts that constituted this remainder. We would be attempting to practise an impoverished history, probably with less powerful analytical and explanatory tools. As a result, our ability to historically investigate essentially contested concepts would be limited at best, and I can’t find that Gallie had a way out of this dilemma.

That, of course, isn’t the whole of his thought. There’s a lot more in Gallie than this exposition of essentially contested concepts. Many threads come together in his work. For example, in his Philosophy and the Historical Understanding, Gallie explicitly states that he wants to revive the philosophy of history of Windelband, Rickert and Dilthey, whom he places together in a school of thought with Croce and Collingwood. For Gallie, what unites members of this school is the idea that history has a distinctive method of its own that is not the method of the natural sciences. I’ve discussed this dichotomy between a distinctive method of historical inquiry and the method of natural science in many episodes, but Gallie’s development of this theme is quite different from what we find in the continental philosophers he cites, and he’s also quite different from Collingwood’s idealism.

And as regards Collingwood’s idealism, the final chapter of Philosophy and the Historical Understanding, “Metaphysics as History,” involves an examination of Collingwood’s metaphysics. I mentioned in my episode on Collingwood earlier this year that I’ve wanted to embark on a discussion of Collingwood’s metaphysics in relation to his philosophy of history, and here Gallie’s critique of Collingwood’s metaphysics would be particularly valuable. But I’m not there yet, and today I wanted to focus on essentially contested concepts because this has probably been where Gallie has been most influential. So I’m going to leave it at that today, and hopefully return to Gallie on another occasion.

The real power of money lies in its ability to shape economies and influence daily life. Money is not just a medium of exchange; it is a fundamental element of the economy that can create, sustain, and even destroy value. Understanding the origins and circulation of money is crucial for grasping its influence on economic prosperity and stability. Paul Sheard's book, The Power of Money, offers a comprehensive exploration of these concepts, making it a valuable resource for anyone interested in the complexities of money and its role in the modern economy.

WHO IS Warren Buffett?
Warren Buffett is an American investor, business magnate, and philanthropist, widely regarded as one of the most successful investors in history.
Warren Edward Buffett was born on August 30, 1930, in Omaha, Nebraska, the son of U.S. Congressman Howard Buffett and Leila Buffett. From a young age, he displayed entrepreneurial talent, buying his first stock at age 11 and engaging in small business ventures such as selling chewing gum and newspapers 

He graduated from the University of Nebraska with a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration and earned a Master of Science in Economics from Columbia University, where he studied under Benjamin Graham, the father of value investing 

Career and Berkshire Hathaway
Buffett began his career working at his father’s firm and later at Benjamin Graham’s partnership. In 1956, he founded Buffett Partnership Ltd., which eventually acquired the textile company Berkshire Hathaway. He transformed it into a diversified holding company, investing in insurance, railroads, utilities, manufacturing, and retail 

Buffett served as chairman and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway for six decades, stepping down as CEO at the end of 2025 while remaining chairman, with Greg Abel succeeding him 

Buffett is known for his value investing philosophy, emphasizing buying high-quality companies at fair prices and holding them long-term. His investment strategy has produced extraordinary returns, with Berkshire Hathaway shares rising over 5,500,000% since he began using it as his primary investment vehicle 

.Major holdings include Apple, American Express, Bank of America, and Coca-Cola 

Wealth and Philanthropy
As of 2026, Buffett’s net worth is estimated at around $148.9 billion, making him one of the richest people in the world 

Despite his wealth, he is known for his frugal lifestyle, living in the same Omaha home he purchased in 1958 and enjoying simple pleasures like Coca-Cola and fast food 

Buffett has pledged to give away 99% of his fortune, primarily through the Gates Foundation and family-run foundations, and co-founded The Giving Pledge in 2010 to encourage other billionaires to donate the majority of their wealth 

Legacy
Buffett’s influence extends beyond finance; he is celebrated for his clarity, ethical approach to investing, and long-term perspective. Known as the “Oracle of Omaha,” he has inspired generations of investors and philanthropists, emphasizing the moral responsibility of wealth and the power of compound interest 

His annual letters to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders are widely read for insights on investing, leadership, and risk management 
The Motley Fool
The Motley Fool
.
Warren Buffett remains active in business and philanthropy, continuing to shape the investment world and charitable initiatives even after stepping down as CEO.

text:
MARKET UPDATE — TUESDAY, 6 OCTOBER 2026

The Nasdaq just hit a record. The 10-year Treasury yield just hit its highest level since 2002.

Stocks and bonds are telling two different stories, and both can't be right forever. Today we look at who's buying the argument on each side.

🟢 STOCKS: AI KEEPS CARRYING THE WEIGHT

Monday's close:
🔸 Nasdaq 27,477.31 (+1.05%), a record, its 23rd of 2026 (Barron's). 
🔸 S&P 500 7,773.95 (+0.66%), about 0.3% shy of its 13 August record. 
🔸 Dow 51,267.90 (+0.18%), still 5.7% below its August peak.

The engine was Nvidia. It rose 2.1% to $238.90, its first record in more than four months, worth $5.76 trillion. Microsoft +1.5%, Meta and Tesla ~+2%. 10 of 11 sectors rose, led by materials (+1.2%).

Why stocks shrugged off higher yields:
🔸 Earnings season is near. Forecasts point to ~27% (Goldman Sachs) to 30%+ (LSEG) profit growth for Q3, more than half of it from AI infrastructure. Big banks report next week.
🔸 Friday's weak jobs data cut the odds of an October Fed hike. 
🔸 Oil slipped back.

"AI-linked earnings growth continues to overpower broader macro discomfort" — Patrick Munnelly, Tickmill.

But look under the bonnet:
🔸 Chip stocks fell even as tech rallied (Barron's), a rare split that has historically come before big moves, up or down.
🔸 The Nasdaq logged 57 new highs but 243 new lows. Trading volume was below average.

💡 In plain English: the index is at a record because a handful of giants are rising. Hundreds of smaller stocks are hitting new lows. That's a narrow foundation.

Deals of the day:
🔸 PTC +33%: France's Schneider Electric agreed to buy the software firm for $22.6bn in cash.

🔸 RXO +22%: C.H. Robinson is buying it for $5.8bn; C.H. Robinson fell ~11%.

🔸 Cerebras +9% after OpenAI's Sam Altman called the chip designer a "close partner".

This morning: futures are higher
. S&P 7,843.25 (+0.22%) 
· Dow 51,803 (+0.48%) 
· Nasdaq 100 31,394.25 (+0.24%)
. VIX 15.48, calm
. Euro STOXX 50 6,292.40 (+0.58%)
. Japan's Nikkei +1.1%, Hong Kong +0.7%; South Korea −~1% after a holiday. 
Brazil's stocks and currency rallied after Flávio Bolsonaro beat the polls and set up a run-off against Lula.

🟢 BONDS: A 24-YEAR HIGH, AND BUYERS ARE QUEUING

America's 10-year yield closed at ~5.31% after touching ~5.35%, the highest since April 2002. The 30-year briefly hit 5.70%. Japan's 30-year reached a record 4.24%.

This morning, slightly calmer: 10-year 5.281% (−2.6bp) · 30-year 5.638% (−2.3bp) · 2-year 4.818% · 1-year 4.483%.

💡 In plain English: a bond yield is the interest a government pays to borrow. When it rises, mortgages, car loans and company debt all get dearer. Prices of existing bonds fall as yields rise.

What pushed yields up:

🔸 Service-sector prices are hot. 
The ISM services prices index jumped to 74, from 72.6, the highest in more than four years (Reuters). 

🔸 The economy is cooling only slowly. 
ISM services 54.9 (forecast 55), still healthy. Hiring returned to growth (50.1, from 47.8). But business activity dropped sharply to 56.5, from 61.7.

🔸 Debt. 
America owes over $40 trillion, with an interest bill of ~$1 trillion a year. $1 in every $5 of tax revenue now goes on interest (Apollo's Torsten Slok).

The Fed: odds of an October hike are about 1 in 4 (23–24%), down from ~70% a week ago (CME FedWatch). The Fed's range is 3.75–4.00%; futures still price three or four more hikes by early 2028 (FT).

The twist: investors are buying.

🔸 Bond funds took in $26.4bn in the week to 1 October, 2.5x the recent average, bringing 2026's total to $520bn (EPFR/Barclays). 

🔸 Why: today's yields offer a cushion. 
"It's just math" — Joyce Huang, Vanguard. Vanguard expects stocks to return 4–7% a year long-term; bond yields "are right there".

🔸 But they're cautious: most money is going into short-term bonds, scarred by 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together.

💡 Why it matters: when safe bonds pay almost as much as risky stocks are expected to, some money leaves the stock market. That's a slow-burning headwind for shares.

What if yields keep rising? 
Reuters maps Washington's options: more short-term borrowing (already under way), then, in a crisis, an "Operation Twist" (the Fed buying long bonds) or capping yields outright, last done in 1942–51. Each step risks more inflation. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has criticised large-scale bond buying. Capital Economics thinks the risks are "tilted toward" the inflationary path, which hurts bondholders.

🟢 CREDIT: CORPORATE AMERICA FEELS THE SQUEEZE

Higher government yields are now reaching companies . 

🔸 The weakest borrowers (rated CCC or lower) now pay ~17%, the highest since May 2020. Their extra premium over Treasuries is 12 percentage points, the most since 2022. 

🔸 Bank of America cut its October forecast for top-rated company bond sales to $110bn, from $160bn.

🔸 Paramount Skydance sold $52bn of debt for its $110bn Warner Bros Discovery deal; investors wanted short bonds, not 30-year ones, and some bonds have already fallen several points.

🔸 The exception: AI. 
Data-centre builders keep borrowing because, for them, speed beats a point or two of interest.

🔸 The wall ahead: $1.45 trillion of top-rated US company debt matures in 2026–30 (Moody's), much of it borrowed near zero rates.

💡 This is where high yields bite first: indebted, weaker firms. Watch junk-bond spreads. If they keep widening, the "stocks don't care" story gets harder to sustain.

🟢 EUROPE: FRANCE'S DEBT ALARM

France now pays more to borrow than Greece or Italy (WSJ). 
🔸 Its 10-year yield hit nearly 5% on Friday, the highest since 2002, then eased to 4.86% (FT). The gap over Germany narrowed to ~137bp, from 150bp+ (Reuters). 

🔸 The numbers: debt ~120% of GDP; deficit above 5% for three years; over $1 trillion due by 2030; a record ~$380bn to sell next year. 

🔸 Missing buyers: the Banque de France has stopped buying; Japanese investors stepped back; hedge funds were burnt by the volatility, and their forced selling amplified last week's slump (WSJ). 

🔸 The politics: no majority for the €43bn budget squeeze. Spring's presidential frontrunners promise more spending: Marine Le Pen a retirement age as low as 60; Jean-Luc Mélenchon wants the ECB to cancel €488bn of French bonds.

"If we don't act, there is indeed a risk of being gradually strangled by rising interest rates... France is not Greece" — Emmanuel Moulin, Banque de France governor.

The counterpoint: Deutsche Bank's Christian Nolting says the ECB now has backstops a crisis like Greece's lacked: "I don't think we run into a real euro crisis."

Also: Spain's PM Pedro Sánchez called a snap election. And France and Germany asked the EU to get tougher on unfair trade, clearly aimed at China, ahead of EU–China talks this month.

💡 In plain English: when a country's interest costs grow faster than its economy, debt snowballs. France is near that point. That's why bond investors are demanding more to lend to it.

🟢 THE DOLLAR: WINNING BY DEFAULT

🔸 The euro hit $1.116, its weakest since May 2025, and sits ~$1.12.

🔸 The dollar index (DXY) is 102.06, up ~4% this year (The Economist), after a 0.9% weekly gain.

🔸 Gold fell 0.4% to ~$4,122 as the dollar firmed.

Why the dollar beat almost every forecast (The Economist): 
🔸 Europe's troubles push money into dollars. 

🔸 America now exports energy, so high oil helps the dollar rather than hurting it. 

🔸 The US economy keeps surprising (Q1 growth 2.5%; Q3 tracking ~2.5%, possibly 3%+). Foreigners bought a record ~$900bn of US stocks and funds in the year to July.

The catch: the old "dollar smile" (strong in booms and in crises) is becoming a "lopsided smirk". The dollar now leans on US stocks. If the AI boom pops, money could leave the dollar as fast as it came.

🟢 OIL & DIESEL: THE CRUDE IS BACK, THE FUEL ISN'T

Brent settled at $100.32 (−1.9%) on Monday, a two-week low, after being up 3.1% early. It's around $100 this morning, slipping just below. WTI ~$89.73.

Why it fell: Gulf flows (excluding Iran) recovered to 81% of pre-war levels in September, and the G7 pledged to release 100 million barrels. Saudi exports doubled to 7m barrels a day (Kpler). Iran's exports are zero under the US blockade.

But here's the real problem: diesel.
🔸 Crude through Hormuz is back to 76% of pre-war levels. Refined fuels like diesel are just 11% of cargoes, versus 20%+ before the war (WSJ/Kpler). 

🔸 Why: missile strikes knocked out refineries in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE and Iraq. China, Japan and South Korea are keeping their fuel at home.

🔸 US diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon; California $8.44.

🔸 Full recovery may take until well into 2027.

Washington's response: 
Trump let farm-use "dyed" diesel (Britain's "red diesel") onto highways, effectively suspending the 24.4-cent federal tax to year-end. With midterms on 3 November, fuel prices are political.

💡 In plain English: nobody fills a lorry with crude oil. It must be refined first. Barrels are flowing again, but refineries aren't fixed, so the fuel that moves food and goods stays scarce and pricey. That keeps inflation sticky, which is exactly what the bond market fears.

🟢 GEOPOLITICS: CALMER FLOWS, HOTTER WATERS

Hormuz:
🔸 A tanker was hit by an unknown projectile in the strait; crews fought an engine-room fire (UKMTO). Iran has launched a new wave of attacks on ships (WSJ). 

🔸 Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian called talks with Washington "meaningless" while US attacks continue. 

🔸 Dozens of loaded tankers are stuck off Iran's coast under the blockade (United Against Nuclear Iran, via Bloomberg).

Yemen and the Red Sea:
🔸 Yemen's Saudi-backed government says it recaptured the port of Mocha and launched a counter-offensive near the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

🔸 Turkey and Pakistan agreed to rapidly deploy forces to Saudi Arabia under their August defence pact, after Houthi threats to Mecca and Medina.

💡 Why it matters: Bab el-Mandeb is the Red Sea's southern gate, Saudi Arabia's route around Hormuz. Turkish and Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia mark a wider regional military commitment. That deters escalation but raises the stakes if it fails.

🗓️ CALENDAR

Today (ET):
🔸 8:15am: ADP weekly jobs (prior +20K) 

🔸 8:30am: US trade balance (forecast −$102bn, from −$88.6bn) 

🔸 9:05am: Fed's John Williams speaks 

🔸 10:45am: Fed's Michelle Bowman speaks 

🔸 1:00pm: 3-year Treasury auction (prior 4.474%), a live test of bond demand 

🔸 4:30pm: API crude inventories 

🔸 7:00pm: Fed's Lorie Logan speaks 

🔸 Also: Paramount Skydance/Warner Bros Discovery deal due to close

This week:
🔸 Wednesday: Fed September meeting minutes

🔸 Thursday: jobless claims · ECB minutes · EU–China talks in Beijing 

🔸 Friday: University of Michigan consumer sentiment 

🔸 Next week: big US banks start Q3 earnings · 14 October: US inflation (CPI)

Key dates ahead:
🔸 Late October: ECB decision · 27–28 October: Fed meeting (~1 in 4 hike chance) 
🔸 28 October: UK Budget · 3 November: US midterms

🟢 WHAT IT ALL MEANS

1️⃣ Stocks are betting on profits; bonds are betting on inflation and debt. One of them will have to give ground. Earnings season will test the stock side; CPI on 14 October will test the bond side.

2️⃣ Leadership is dangerously narrow. Nvidia at a record while chip stocks fall and 243 Nasdaq stocks hit new lows is a market leaning on a few names. Strong AI earnings are now essential, not optional.

3️⃣ High yields are finding the weak spots. France among countries, junk-rated firms among companies. Watch French spreads and CCC yields as early warnings.

4️⃣ Oil's fix is half done. Crude is flowing; refined fuel isn't. Diesel inflation won't fade until refineries recover, possibly not before 2027.

5️⃣ For savers, the bond rout is an opportunity. 5%+ on safe US government debt is the best in a generation, and record inflows show investors know it.

🔸 What would prove this reading wrong: cooler CPI on 14 October that sends yields sharply lower, broad gains beyond the AI giants, or a Hormuz deal that pulls diesel down fast.

💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"Bull markets are born on pessimism, grow on scepticism, mature on optimism, and die on euphoria."— Sir John Templeton

Bonds are in the pessimism phase today. Prices have fallen hard, headlines are grim, and that is precisely when patient buyers are quietly locking in the best yields in 24 years.

Gloom isn't the end of a story. It's often the first chapter of the next good one. Stay curious, stay calm, and have a great Tuesday.

💬 How can I make these updates better? Suggestions, corrections are always welcome.

📌 Sources: TradingView, MarketWatch (Nora Redmond, Tomi Kilgore, Joy Wiltermuth), Barron's (Naomi Buchanan), The Wall Street Journal (Collin Eaton; France debt report), Reuters (Stella Qiu, Tom Westbrook, Karen Brettell, Noel Randewich), Financial Times (Kate Duguid, Emily Herbert, Joshua Franklin, Michelle Chan, Leila Abboud, Sarah White), The Economist, Al Jazeera English, Bloomberg, CME FedWatch, ISM, S&P Global, EPFR/Barclays Research, Kpler, Moody's, LSEG, Goldman Sachs, UKMTO, United Against Nuclear Iran.
