text:
Muse is the most accessible for anyone having never done anything with the tech.

Grok Bot is a step up, offering more powerful truly agentic problem solving.

Then there is a range of products and “built in” agents with products from Anthropic, OpenAI, etc … the costs alone on using these and limitations to what you can use them for never appealed to me.

The only available true low limitation open source options are Hermes and OpenClaw.
Both too are quite different and one best has to try them both to find which one suits your working style best.

Hermes gives you more of a helping hand and is somewhat self learning.
Openclaw is strictly acting on your precise setup, particularly how you setup your agents.
Any self learning you want Openclaw to “mimic” you have to build yourself with complex memory systems and self reflection sessions (some attempts at this have been made some time ago by its introduced “Dream Sessions”).

From all offerings I have tried OpenClaw is by far the most complex and most user involved to setup and maintain.
If you are not inclined to do that or just need a product that works out of the package, don’t use OpenClaw.

For anyone interested in the tech and the time to learn, OpenClaw for that reason is one of the more interesting products as you get very deep inside the machine room.

Openclaw offers by far the most freedom how to setup your Ai compute for your very specific usecase. No other system allows for that.
For that reason it is also maintenance heavy.

Until recently every simple update of the harness (and those happened in the beginning at a pace of almost every other day) lead to a mandatory troubleshooting session.
There is a ton of learning material you can read through (and point agents to).
You will find any support you would ever need.

You are also prone to attackers, as it is as open as you allow it. You are your own security.
You can safely tinker with it in a sandbox following certain safety rules.

text:
Morning lads 👀

Tuesday’s market is telling two very different stories.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at a new all time high on Monday. $NVDA closed at a record too, and most Asian markets followed Wall Street higher overnight.

But US bonds are sending a different message.

The 10 year Treasury yield touched 5.349% on Monday. The 30 year briefly reached 5.703%. Both were levels last seen in 2002.

The dollar also hit an 18 month high.

Why are yields still pushing up while tech rallies?

Monday’s US services data offers part of the answer. Activity slowed slightly, but the prices businesses paid for inputs climbed to 74.0, the highest reading since July 2022.

So equities are looking at AI earnings and lower odds of an October Fed hike. The bond market is still looking at inflation, energy costs and debt.

Energy makes the picture even more interesting.

Brent settled at $100.32 on Monday, then slipped below $100 this morning as stronger Gulf exports and the G7’s planned release of 100 million barrels of diesel and crude eased immediate supply fears.

But the deeper export data shows the problem has shifted.

Gulf crude and condensate exports recovered to 91% of prewar levels in September. Refined fuel exports, including LPG, recovered to only 60%.

Barrels are moving again. Diesel and jet fuel remain much tighter. Tanker rates have hit records, while insurance and routing costs remain elevated.

That is why a dip below $100 Brent does not, by itself, mean the inflation pressure has disappeared. Transport, farming and manufacturing still feel the cost of fuel.

Europe is under pressure as well.

EURUSD fell to $1.1160 on Monday, its weakest level in roughly 17 months, before recovering toward $1.12. France’s fiscal worries have pushed its bond premium over Germany sharply higher, even though that spread eased on Monday. Spain’s snap election adds another uncertainty.

And on the AI side, Bloomberg reports DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80 billion yuan, roughly $12 billion, with backing from Tencent and CATL. That round has not been independently confirmed or completed, so I’m treating it as a report for now.

text:
Hard Wake-Up Call

Social media was meant to be a place where we could share ideas, challenge assumptions, learn from each other, and maybe build something better for the generations coming after us. That was the intention. That was the hope.

But that’s not what we’ve created.

Instead, we’ve built a space where oversimplified quotes and personal opinions are dressed up as #fact and #truth, ignoring real human conditions and real complexity. And the moment you offer a different perspective, not hostility, not disrespect, just a thought that doesn’t fit the script, you’re labelled critical, toxic, negative, or “not aligned.” The responses aren’t reflective; they’re demeaning.

We say we want accountability, respect, honesty.
We just don’t want them applied to ourselves.

Social media has become a mirror of the world we’re living in: adults hiding behind screens, posting moral lessons they don’t live by, ignoring the consequences of their own behaviour while preaching about everyone else’s. It’s a bubble of self importance disguised as wisdom.

And here’s the part no one wants to hear:

We are failing the next generation.

The warning signs were there years ago, but we ignored them. I wrote the quotes attached below 10 years ago, and it breaks my heart that they are far more relevant today than they were a decade ago.

We complain about governments, leaders, systems, yet refuse to take responsibility for the culture we’re creating online. We blame the world for being a mess while contributing to the mess every day through our words, our reactions, and our refusal to think beyond our own bubble.

Sometimes I tell my friends I wish I had never left the remote community where I once lived and worked. Yes, it could be hostile and violent. Some days were incredibly difficult.

But there was a difference.

Many of the people there were grateful for my experience. They wanted to learn. They wanted different perspectives. Most importantly, they wanted to make things better for the younger generations coming after them.

Think about that.

I lived in an environment where hostility and violence could be part of everyday life, yet I still witnessed people willing to listen, learn and try to do better.

And sometimes I find less willingness to do that on social media.

That tells you something.

So I’m stepping back from posting and instead focusing my efforts on writing a book. It seems Nana’s old fashioned wisdom versus social media has a market after all. 🤣

I will still occasionally share some of the graphics that will be used in the book, based on my experiences here on X.

I won’t be posting regularly, but I will still be around because I have found a wonderful group of people here who appreciate me for who I am. People who can share ideas, laugh, disagree, support each other and still treat each other with respect.

They represent what social media was meant to be.

If this feels uncomfortable, it should.
It’s meant to.

#AmandaRay #truth #HumanityFirst #SocialMedia

text:
A $500 machine just taught a $5 million tank to fear daylight.

Nobody in a defense ministry designed this. It came out of a hobby, a garage, and a war that refused to follow the script.

This is the story of how the cheapest weapon on earth broke the most expensive assumptions in modern military history.

Read to the end. The last section is the one analysts rarely say out loud.

THE SENTENCE THAT SHOULD KEEP GENERALS UP AT NIGHT

For seventy years, the rule of power was simple: whoever builds the best, rarest, most expensive machine wins.

Stealth jets. Armored brigades. Missile destroyers. Systems that took a decade to design and a country's budget to buy.

Then someone bolted a camera, four motors and a battery onto a frame that costs less than a used phone, and the rule quietly stopped working.

Not because the expensive machines got worse. Because the cheap one got good enough, in numbers large enough, at a speed no procurement office on earth can match.

That is the whole story. Everything below is detail. But the details are where it gets strange.

THE ARITHMETIC NOBODY WANTED TO DO

Start with money, because money is where wars are really decided.

A small first-person-view drone costs in the range of a few hundred dollars. A modern tank costs millions. A single air-defense interceptor can cost more than the car you drive. An armored vehicle, a radar, a howitzer, a command post: each is priced like a house, an apartment block, a small airport.

Now put them on the same field.

If the cheap thing only trades evenly with the expensive thing, the cheap thing still wins economically a hundred times over. If it trades even one time in ten, the expensive thing is a bad investment.

Military planners call this the cost-exchange ratio. Accountants call it a nightmare. And for the first time since the machine gun, the ratio is not slowly drifting. It is inverted.

The side with the million-dollar machine must now make the million-dollar machine survive. The side with the five-hundred-dollar machine only has to try again tomorrow.

THE ORIGIN STORY IS NOT WHAT YOU THINK

This did not begin in a lab. It began on weekends.

Years before any of this, a global community of hobbyists was racing small, absurdly fast quadcopters through abandoned buildings and forest courses, wearing goggles that put the pilot's eyes inside the aircraft. They traded open-source flight software on forums. They broke parts, reprinted them, tuned them, and posted the results for free.

Nobody in that community was thinking about doctrine. They were thinking about lap times.

But they were quietly building three things the defense industry had failed to build in forty years: a cheap supply chain, an enormous pool of skilled pilots, and a culture where improvement was shared instead of classified.

When a real crisis arrived, all of that was already sitting there. Components, knowledge, talent. A whole industrial ecosystem hiding inside a hobby.

The lesson is uncomfortable. The most disruptive military technology of the decade was not invented by the military. It was borrowed from people who just wanted to go fast.

THE DOCTRINE THAT DIED IN TWENTY-FOUR MONTHS

Western militaries spent decades betting on exquisite systems: few, brilliant, nearly perfect. Lose one, and you have lost a month of national industrial output.

That logic made sense against opponents who could not touch you.

It made no sense against an enemy who could produce thousands of small, replaceable, good-enough machines every week, and who treated each one as a consumable, like a bullet with a brain.

The old model asked: how do we protect this irreplaceable asset?

The new model asks: why would we ever build something we cannot afford to lose?

Military history is full of moments where quantity quietly beat quality. This is one of them, except this time quantity arrived with eyes, sensors and a pilot who can steer it at the last second.

HISTORY KEEPS RUNNING THE SAME EXPERIMENT

Every few generations, a cheap tool breaks an expensive order.

The English longbow let commoners with a few hours of training destroy armored knights who had trained since childhood. The musket made the sword a museum piece. The machine gun turned the cavalry charge into a historical embarrassment within a single war. The tank was invented to solve the trench. Then antitank weapons, cheap and portable, started solving the tank.

The pattern is always the same.

First, the incumbents laugh. The new tool looks unserious, improvised, too light to matter.

Second, a conflict forces people to use it at scale.

Third, the doctrine that took a century to build collapses in months, and those who adapted fastest rewrite the rules.

We are living inside step two and the start of step three. The only open question is who is paying attention.

THE WARNING SHOT THE WORLD MISSED

In 2020, a short, sharp war in the South Caucasus offered a preview.

Drones, along with loitering munitions that circle until they find something to hit, were used to systematically dismantle air defenses and armored columns. Footage spread online. Experts argued. A handful of defense thinkers said: this changes everything.

Most of the world nodded and moved on.

The mistake was reading it as a story about one country's good luck, one battlefield's flat terrain, one opponent's poor preparation. The real signal was structural: a cheap aircraft with a camera could now do what used to require an air force.

Some analysts say that war was the last time anyone could claim they were surprised.

THE END OF HIDING

Here is what changed on the ground, and why it matters beyond any single front.

For all of human history, armies could hide. Behind a hill. Inside a forest. Under the night. In the fog of a long supply line. Uncertainty was a defensive weapon.

Now the sky above the battlefield is saturated with eyes. Small aircraft, always there, always looking, cheap enough that you can lose a dozen a day without noticing.

The result is what analysts call a transparent battlefield.

Moving a vehicle in daylight becomes a gamble. Stockpiling fuel becomes a risk. Gathering a unit in one place becomes an invitation. Soldiers learn to move in ones and twos, to dig deeper, to stay under cover, to travel at night, to accept that anything that stands still will be seen.

The zone near the front, once a place where you could drive, rest and resupply, becomes a belt many kilometers deep where everything is dangerous.

War stops being about who can seize ground. It becomes about who can survive the ground long enough to hold it.

SOFTWARE SPEED IN A HARDWARE WAR

The strangest feature of this conflict is not the machine. It is the clock.

In a traditional arms program, a new weapon takes years to design, test, approve and field. By the time it arrives, the world has moved.

Here, improvements arrive in weeks. Sometimes days. A new technique appears in a workshop, spreads through a chat group, gets copied, gets countered, and gets replaced before a ministry could schedule the first meeting.

It looks less like a defense program and more like a software release cycle, except each patch has consequences measured in lives and territory.

Whoever learns fastest wins the current round. Whoever institutionalizes learning wins the war.

That is the quiet revolution inside the revolution: not a better weapon, but a faster loop.

THE WAR NOBODY CAN SEE

Behind every one of these machines there is a second, invisible battlefield: the radio spectrum.

Most small drones are connected to their pilots by wireless links. That link is the aircraft's lifeline, and also its weak point. So each side invests heavily in electronic warfare: systems that jam, confuse or disrupt those links, and systems that try to survive the disruption.

It is a game of move and countermove played at the speed of engineering. A defensive measure appears. An answer appears. The answer is answered.

For soldiers, it means entire areas of the front are saturated with unseen noise. For engineers, it means the competition is not really about the airframe at all. It is about who controls the invisible layer that connects the human to the machine.

The most important weapon in this fight cannot be photographed. It is a few megahertz of empty air, and everyone wants it quiet or loud depending on which side they are on.

THE LEASH THAT BEAT THE JAMMER

When radio becomes unreliable, engineers do something delightfully old-fashioned.

They stop using radio.

A new generation of drones trails a hair-thin optical fiber behind it, unspooling like a kite string over many kilometers. It cannot be jammed in the usual way, because there is no signal flying through the air to jam. The pilot's view is delivered through glass, not radio waves.

A nineteenth-century idea, communication through a physical line, defeats a twenty-first-century defensive system.

It is a perfect illustration of how this war works. The cleverest countermeasure is rarely the most advanced. It is the one the other side did not plan for.

And the fiber approach has its own costs: weight, range limits, a trail that can snag on branches, wires, and the terrain itself. Every solution creates a new constraint. That is the nature of an arms race: you never solve a problem, you only change which problem you have.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE LINK IS LOST

This is where the conversation gets serious.

For a long time, there was an obvious human limit built into the whole system: a person controls the machine. If the link breaks, the machine is blind, and the mission is over.

Engineers are now working to remove that limit. Onboard processing, computer vision, and automated terminal guidance mean that in some systems, the aircraft can continue a task without an operator's constant input.

The technical details do not matter here. The principle does.

Once a machine can make part of the decision by itself, three questions arrive at once. Who is responsible for what it does? How does it tell a legitimate target from a person who merely looks like one? And what happens when the same capability becomes cheap enough for anyone to have?

International law has been arguing about autonomous weapons for more than a decade. The technology moved faster than the argument.

Whatever your view, this is the real frontier. Not the drone you can see. The decision you cannot.

A NAVY WITHOUT SHIPS

The same story played out at sea, and it may be the most astonishing chapter.

A country with almost no conventional navy used small, uncrewed, explosive-armed surface vessels to threaten and in some cases damage a fleet of much larger warships. Ships worth hundreds of millions were forced to leave their home port and relocate far from the front.

The expensive navy did not lose a decisive battle. It lost something subtler: the ability to operate freely in its own backyard.

That is how disruptive technology works. It rarely wins by direct conquest. It wins by making the old way of fighting too expensive to attempt.

Naval planners everywhere took notice. Ports, which were once safe harbors, now look like targets with a long approach path. A fleet is no longer measured only by what it can sink, but by what it can protect against something small, cheap and patient.

THE INTERCEPTOR PROBLEM

Now flip the question. What if you are the one being attacked?

Long-range, one-way attack drones, slow and relatively simple, cost a fraction of the missiles sent to stop them. Defending a city against hundreds in a night means spending interceptors that cost many times more than what is flying overhead.

It does not take a mathematician to see the trap. Even a perfect defense, one that stops everything, is a financial defeat if it is repeated long enough.

The same logic showed up in the Red Sea, where inexpensive drones and missiles forced navies to spend enormous sums on defensive weapons to protect commercial shipping.

So defenders everywhere are looking for something that sounds almost silly: cheaper ways to stop cheap things. Guns that were once considered obsolete. Interceptor drones. Electronic defenses. Lasers, in a few cases. Anything that breaks the cost curve.

The side that solves this first does not just win a battle. It rewrites the economics of defense.

THE DAY STRATEGIC DEPTH DIED

For generations, countries felt safe because of distance. An airbase deep in your own territory was, by definition, far from the front. A bomber parked a thousand kilometers behind the lines was a bomber nobody could reach.

In mid-2025, that assumption took a hit that analysts are still unpacking.

According to multiple reports, a large number of small drones were smuggled close to several airbases and launched from concealed vehicles. They went after parked strategic aircraft, machines that cost fortunes and take years to replace.

The details are still debated, and claims on both sides should be treated carefully. But the strategic message was clear: if a small, cheap system can be moved close to a target quietly, then range stops being a shield. Geography no longer protects the things it used to protect.

Every military on earth is now looking at its own airbases, depots and ports and asking the same unsettling question: how far away is far enough?

THE KITCHEN-TABLE FACTORY

The sheer scale of production is its own story.

Official targets on the order of millions of drones per year are no longer science fiction. Workshops, small companies, volunteer groups and state-backed manufacturers now produce them in numbers that would have been unimaginable in a traditional arms industry.

It is a distributed factory: dozens of nimble teams instead of a few giant contractors. If one is hit, others continue. If one finds a better design, it spreads.

But the supply chain hides a quiet dependency. Many core components, motors, batteries, cameras, magnets, electronic parts, trace back to a small number of manufacturing hubs, most notably in Asia. Export rules, shortages and political decisions about those parts can affect the whole ecosystem overnight.

So the real contest is not only about who builds more drones. It is about who controls the boring parts: the batteries, the magnets, the tiny chips. Modern warfare turns out to be a logistics story wearing a technology costume.

THE PEOPLE BEHIND THE SCREEN

There is a human story here that rarely makes it to the viral clips.

The operator sits somewhere behind the front, sometimes in a dugout, sometimes in a basement, wearing goggles and holding a controller. Their body is relatively safe. Their mind is not.

They watch the world from a few meters above the ground, in high resolution, in real time. The distance is physical, but it is not emotional. Many describe a strange mix of focus, fatigue and moral weight that does not fade when the screen goes dark.

At the same time, the soldiers on the other end live under a different kind of stress: the constant sound of small motors overhead, the sense of being watched, the knowledge that nowhere is fully safe. People describe it as a kind of permanent background fear.

And civilians are not spared. UN-mandated investigators have documented drone attacks on people in areas close to the front, and have described some of them in the gravest legal terms.

This is the part the highlight reels leave out. Technology that reduces risk for one side increases dread for the other, and for everyone caught between.

WHAT DEFENSE LOOKS LIKE NOW

Look closely at a front-line road today and you will see a landscape that would have seemed absurd a few years ago.

Nets stretched above supply routes like tunnels. Improvised cages bolted on top of vehicles. Shotguns mounted on armored cars. Windows covered with mesh. Entire convoys that look like they were built by a very anxious craftsperson.

It looks improvised because it is. It is also deeply effective, in the way folk engineering often is.

Meanwhile, more sophisticated answers are arriving: detection systems that listen for a particular signature, drones designed to catch other drones, small radars, networks of sensors that share warnings in seconds.

The pattern is familiar. Offense invents. Defense improvises. Offense adapts. Defense adapts back.

There is no final answer. There is only the current round, and the question of who learns faster.

THE PROCUREMENT PARADOX

Back in peacetime capitals, a different crisis is quietly unfolding.

Defense bureaucracies were built for a world where weapons take ten years to field and last for forty. Their processes are careful, thorough and slow. That is a virtue when you are building a submarine. It is a fatal weakness when the thing you are buying becomes obsolete in three months.

Several large militaries have launched programs to buy thousands of low-cost autonomous systems, to bring commercial vendors into the process, and to shrink the time between idea and field test from years to weeks. Some of these efforts are promising. Some are stuck in the same old bureaucracy they were designed to escape.

The real question is not whether armies will buy drones. They already are.

The question is whether institutions designed for scarcity and perfection can learn to operate in a world of abundance and iteration. History suggests that most can't, until a crisis forces them to.

THE TECHNOLOGY IS NOT STAYING ON THE BATTLEFIELD

Here is the part that should concern everyone, including people who will never see a front line.

A technology that is cheap, commercially available and rapidly improving does not stay in the hands of states.

Drones have already disrupted major airports in Europe through sightings and closures. Criminal groups use them to carry contraband across borders and into prisons. Non-state armed groups have adopted them as an inexpensive substitute for air power.

Every conflict is a laboratory, and every lesson learned there will eventually be studied by people with very different intentions.

This is the genuine strategic shift: the democratization of aerial capability. For the first time, a tool that used to be the exclusive privilege of the most powerful states is available, in some form, to nearly anyone.

Governments will have to decide how to protect airports, stadiums, power plants and cities against something that is small, fast, cheap and hard to attribute. There is no easy answer. And the clock is already running.

There is one more effect worth naming: the psychological one. Commanders who once planned around terrain now plan around attention. Every hour of daylight becomes a question of who is watching, and every quiet stretch of road becomes a question of what is waiting. A weapon does not have to destroy everything to change behavior. It only has to make everyone assume it might. That assumption, multiplied across thousands of units and millions of decisions, is what reshapes a war.

THE COUNTERINTUITIVE TRUTH

Many people assume that drones make war easier, cleaner, more precise, more surgical.

The evidence so far points the other way.

When both sides have cheap, abundant eyes and cheap, abundant strikes, neither can advance without heavy losses. Movement becomes dangerous. Breakthroughs become rare. Fronts harden. The conflict becomes slower, more attritional, more exhausting.

Technology promised a quick, decisive war. What it delivered, at least so far, is a long, grinding one, in which the winner is the side that can produce, adapt and endure longer.

This is the oldest lesson in military history, wearing a new costume: every technology that promises to make war simple ends up making it more complicated, and often more brutal.

SEVEN LAWS OF THE NEW ERA

If you remember nothing else, remember these.

One. Mass beats elegance, as long as the mass is smart enough.

Two. Cheap things can defeat expensive things when the cost curve is on their side.

Three. The side that iterates fastest controls the tempo, not the side with the best design.

Four. Every advantage is temporary. Every countermeasure produces a counter-countermeasure.

Five. The invisible layer, radio, software, data, matters as much as the visible hardware.

Six. Supply chains are strategy. Whoever owns the boring components owns the future.

Seven. The technology will not stay where it started. Plan for it to spread.

WHAT THE NEXT TEN YEARS PROBABLY LOOK LIKE

Nobody can predict this with certainty. But the direction is clear enough to sketch.

Expect swarms: groups of small machines coordinating with each other, sharing information, dividing tasks without waiting for a human to approve every step.

Expect smarter perception: systems that can identify objects, avoid obstacles and navigate in places where signals do not reach.

Expect layered defenses: sensors, interceptors, electronic measures and physical barriers working together as a system, not as individual tools.

Expect larger and smaller versions of the same idea: bigger machines that carry more, tiny ones that fit in a pocket, and everything in between.

And expect the legal and ethical debate to remain half a step behind the engineering, which is where it has been for every major weapon in history.

THE QUESTION BEHIND THE QUESTION

Strip away the hardware, the numbers and the strategy, and one issue remains.

For most of history, using force required a person to be present, to risk something, to look at what they were doing. Distance has always eroded that. Spears, arrows, artillery, bombers, missiles: each step moved the human a little further from the consequence.

Now the human can sit in a room and see the world through a machine's eyes, and soon, perhaps, not even that.

That is not an argument for panic. It is an argument for seriousness. A technology that lowers the cost and the risk of using force will be used more often. That is not a prediction. It is a pattern.

The hardest question of the coming decade is not how to build better drones.

It is how to stay human while the machines do more of the work.

THE PART THEY RARELY SAY OUT LOUD

Here is the uncomfortable ending I promised.

The most important lesson of this entire revolution is not technical. It is institutional.

The countries that adapt fastest will not necessarily be the richest, or the most advanced, or the ones with the biggest budgets. They will be the ones willing to let go of what worked in the last war, to trust the people closest to the problem, and to build systems that learn faster than the enemy can change.

Technology is the visible part. Culture is the engine.

A small workshop with a clear problem and a short feedback loop can outpace a giant organization with every resource and no urgency. That is true in war. It is true in business. It is true in almost everything.

The drone is just the most vivid proof we have ever had.

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH THIS

You do not need to work in defense to take something from this.

Pay attention to cheap technologies that experts dismiss as toys. Pay attention to hobby communities that move faster than industries. Pay attention to any field where the cost of trying has fallen to almost nothing.

Disruption rarely announces itself. It looks small, a bit ridiculous, a little too simple. It looks like something a hobbyist built in a garage.

Then one day, it is the only thing that matters.

If this thread changed how you see the technology, repost it so more people read it. And follow along: I break down the big technology shifts while they are still easy to miss, before they become obvious.

Bookmark this post and come back in a year. Half of what sounds speculative today will read like old news, which is how every real shift begins.

One last thing.

Every revolution is celebrated by the people it helps and paid for by the people it hurts. Remember both, and the story stays honest.

The crash has thrown the military community into mourning, with Nigerians across the country joining in prayers for the fallen gallant officers.

text:
BRIEFING NOTE FOR ALL MPs — House of Commons, Ottawa  
Critical Vote on Bill C‑218 #MAID (#AMAD ) — October 7, 2026 🧵2 of 2

5. United Nations CRPD Committee Findings Relevant to Canada

The UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) has issued multiple formal observations regarding Canada’s MAID framework.

A. CRPD Position on MAID & Disability

The Committee states:  
• Disability must never be a lawful ground for assisted dying.  
• States must prohibit MAID “on the basis of disability or perceived suffering linked to disability.”  
• MAID regimes must not reinforce assumptions that life with disability is undignified.

B. CRPD Concerns Specific to Canada

The Committee expressed:  
• Grave concern that Canada’s MAID expansion risks violating Articles 10 & 14 (Right to Life; Liberty & Security).  
• Concern that MAID where natural death is not foreseeable disproportionately affects persons with disabilities.  
• Safeguards are insufficient, especially for:  
  – persons in poverty  
  – persons lacking supports  
  – persons with psychosocial disabilities  
• Disability communities were not adequately consulted.

C. CRPD Recommendations to Canada

The Committee recommended Canada:  
• Reconsider MAID provisions tied to disability.  
• Strengthen safeguards so no one seeks MAID due to lack of supports.  
• Ensure full consultation with disability organizations.  
• Collect national data on MAID involving disability

6. June 2026 Joint Committee Report to the House of Commons

The Special Joint Committee on MAID delivered a major report in June 2026.

A. System Readiness Concerns

• Canada’s health systems are not uniformly prepared.  
• Provincial readiness varies dramatically.  
• Psychiatric assessment standards remain inconsistent.

B. Lack of Consensus Among Experts

The Committee documented:  
• No psychiatric consensus on assessing irremediability.  
• Disagreement on:  
  – diagnostic reliability  
  – prognosis  
  – suicide contagion risk  
  – adequacy of safeguards

C. Safety Protocol Gaps

The report identified:  
• Incomplete national training standards  
• Insufficient oversight mechanisms  
• Lack of uniform appeal pathways  
• Gaps in data collection and reporting

D. Disability & Indigenous Testimony

• Strong opposition from disability organizations  
• Indigenous leaders raised concerns about:  
  – colonial medical structures  
  – lack of culturally safe care  
  – MAID being offered instead of services

E. Recommendation Highlight

The Committee recommended Parliament re‑evaluate whether the March 17, 2027 expansion should proceed, given unresolved safety concerns.

7. Why This Matters for the Vote on Bill C‑218 (October 7, 2026)

• MAID expansion to mental illness is not yet in force.  
• UN CRPD findings raise international human‑rights concerns.  
• Joint Committee findings raise domestic safety concerns.  
• C‑218 is a private member’s bill, meaning debate time is limited.  

MPs must decide whether Canada permanently excludes mental illness from MAID before March 17, 2027.

text:
changes circumstances; it does not rewrite revelation. A man who receives a larger house does not thereby become owner of the building code. Israel received a larger territory and remained the servant of the same LORD. Blessing should increase gratitude and responsibility, not produce the theological conclusion that God has finally moved far enough away to stop watching.

The same principle cuts directly across the assumption that liberty naturally matures into autonomy. God may genuinely loosen one restriction because circumstances change while maintaining another because the underlying truth has not changed. Immaturity asks only, “What am I allowed to do now?” Wisdom also asks, “What has God still reserved?” The flesh hears “thou mayest eat flesh” and stops listening before “thou shalt not eat the blood.” It has always been talented at selective hearing. Give it ten permissions and one prohibition, and by sundown it will be preaching a conference on why that one prohibition threatens freedom. God is not confused. Enlargement under Him is still life under Him.

2. “The Blood Is the Life”

The statement in Deuteronomy 12:23 is not ornamental: “for the blood is the life.” Moses is explaining the boundary by connecting blood with life itself. Leviticus 17:11 had already said, “For the life of the flesh is in the blood,” while Genesis 9:4 had tied blood and life together centuries before Sinai. Scripture establishes the association repeatedly so that no Israelite could honestly say the rule was arbitrary. Blood represented something the eater had no right to claim as common food. The flesh could nourish the body, but the blood carried a significance God had reserved.

That truth reaches back to the basic fact that life belongs to the Creator. Man can receive life, preserve life, reproduce life under God’s created order, and take animal life where God permits it, but he never becomes the ultimate owner of life. Genesis 2:7 says God “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” Life was not Adam’s invention. It arrived from God. Job confessed, “The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away” (Job 1:21). The blood therefore becomes a continual reminder that man lives in borrowed flesh. Every heartbeat is operating property the Creator supplied. Pride struts loudly for something that cannot guarantee its next pulse.

This makes the command far larger than a culinary oddity. Israel was being trained to distinguish eating from ownership. They could eat the flesh because God permitted it, but the blood reminded them that the life was His. Fallen man loves using a gift until he begins imagining he manufactured the gift. He eats God’s food, breathes God’s air, occupies God’s earth, borrows God’s time, and then complains that divine authority is intrusive. That is a tenant changing the locks and sending the landlord an eviction notice. Blood preached the opposite message. Life is sacred because life has an Owner.

3. The Trail of Blood Begins Long Before Sinai

Blood enters Scripture almost immediately after the fall. Genesis 4 records Abel bringing “of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof,” and the LORD having respect unto Abel and his offering (Genesis 4:4). Hebrews 11:4 later says, “By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain.” The Bible does not leave us with a religion of vegetables versus livestock as though God had developed agricultural preferences. Abel approached by faith according to revealed truth, and the sacrificial pattern involving death begins appearing very early in fallen human history.

Then Noah steps from the ark into a cleansed world, offers burnt offerings, and receives instruction concerning flesh and blood. “Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you,” God says, but immediately adds, “But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat” (Genesis 9:3–4). Key Realities of Buying Off-Grid Land in 2026
• The Federal Homestead Act Ended: The federal program ended in 1976, meaning you cannot get free public land just by living on it. However, a few local towns and counties still offer small residential land grants with strict building rules.
• Raw Off-Grid Land is Available: You can purchase private acreage that lacks connections to municipal water, sewer, or grid electricity. Buyers typically install alternative systems like solar panels, private wells or water cisterns, and septic tanks.
• Counties Matter More Than States: State-level laws set the baseline for property taxes and farming rights, but local county and township zoning laws dictate whether you can legally live off-grid, build a tiny home, or keep livestock.
• Popular States for Off-Grid Living: States frequently noted for affordable acreage and favorable regulations include Tennessee, Arkansas, Oklahoma, Missouri, New Mexico, Arizona, and Texas, depending heavily on the specific county.

text:
Indians will move 10,000 kilometres away from India and then immediately start looking for other Indians there and start living only with them.

I recently visited a friend overseas. I noticed something strange. Almost everyone around him was Indian.

It happens within India too. Someone moves from a small town to Delhi or Bangalore and immediately starts looking for people from the same place.

You have physically moved to a new place, but mentally and socially, you may have moved zero. You have only recreated the same world you left behind.

Then what exactly changed? Your address changed. Your environment didn’t.

The whole point of living in a different city or country is exposure. Meet people who grew up differently. Eat with them. Work with them. Understand how they think. Listen to opinions that would never come up in your existing circle.

Humans grow through exposure to different people, different cultures and different ways of thinking.

If the people around you never change, changing the country won’t change much.

Kathimerini: Ankara’s bid to buy an Italian-French system that Paris is blocking, and its contacts with Germany on submarines.

Ankara has launched slow but intensive bargaining with the Europeans for major weapons of European design, focused on air defense that its forces currently hold only nominally through Russian S-400s. Well-informed sources say Turkey has asked Italy to mediate past French objections to the EUROSAM SAMP/T air-defense and anti-ballistic system. Italy has in practice given the green light, and talks with Paris began last spring, but they are deadlocked. In the latest defense-ministry contacts, Italy said Paris remains opposed.

Turkey wants not only SAMP/T but the longer-range SAMP/T NG, plus industrial participation and technology transfer. The system was also offered to Greece, which chose Israel’s Achilles Shield. SAMP/T batteries cost less than Patriots. The bid fits Ankara’s wider effort to link part of its defense industry to the EU.

France is also a main obstacle on EU issues, including the SAFE regulation and customs-union modernization. Ankara fears France’s presidential election (first round 18 April 2027, runoff 2 May) could make a compromise harder.

Cooperation with Europe is not straightforward. Germany is the clearest case. Ankara has formally asked Berlin for the latest Type 212CD submarines from TKMS and proposed that part of the work be done at Gölcük. Turkey already operates six Type 214s, the same class as Greece’s Papanikolis boats. Germany is not opposed in principle, but talks will take time: Berlin wants as little industrial and technological work as possible to leave the country. Even under Chancellor Merz, who is not negative toward Turkey, those limits are clear.

Kathimerini also reports that Baykar tried to buy an important German defense-innovation firm and Berlin blocked it. What Ankara achieved in Italy about 15 months ago with Piaggio Aerospace proved impossible in Germany, which resists know-how transfers even inside the EU.

Domestic politics weigh on both Berlin and Paris. Anti-immigration, anti-Muslim parties are rising — the AfD in Germany and Le Pen and Bardella’s National Rally in France — so the talks are taking place in a tense climate.

Relations with Rome and Madrid are smoother, with defense deals moving slowly but steadily. Ankara has opened talks on Spanish Navy SM-1 missiles, likely for its eight old Oliver Hazard Perry (Gabya) frigates. The bigger Spanish program is the sale of Turkish Hürjet trainers for future Spanish pilots. With Italy, the main project is collaborative combat aircraft, or “loyal wingmen”: Turkey has developed the Kızılelma and tested it with an Italian M-346.

Revival of the Latin Mass: Appeal to Contemporary Seekers
In the dynamic spiritual environment of January 2026, the revival of the Latin Mass—formally known as the Traditional Latin Mass (TLM) or Tridentine Rite—has emerged as a compelling phenomenon, particularly resonating with contemporary seekers, including millennials and Generation Z. This resurgence embodies a profound yearning for authenticity, ritualistic depth, and transcendent experiences in an era marked by rapid technological change, cultural relativism, and existential uncertainties. For individuals investigating the revival of the Latin Mass: appeal to contemporary seekers, this ancient liturgical form provides a gateway to the rich tapestry of Catholic tradition, attracting young adults through its aesthetic splendor, doctrinal clarity, and countercultural stance. This extensive guide delves into the historical foundations, prevailing trends as of 2026, underlying motivations for its popularity, personal narratives, engagement strategies, associated challenges, frequently posed inquiries, and curated resources, all substantiated by recent ecclesiastical developments and scholarly insights.

The Historical Foundations and Evolution of the Latin Mass
The Latin Mass's origins extend to the nascent stages of Christianity, with its formalized structure emerging from the apostolic era and progressively refined through patristic and medieval influences. By the 16th century, amid the Protestant Reformation's challenges, the Council of Trent (1545–1563) codified the rite in the Roman Missal of 1570, promulgated by Pope St. Pius V, to ensure uniformity and doctrinal integrity across the Catholic world. This Tridentine Mass, celebrated exclusively in Latin with the priest oriented ad orientem (facing eastward toward the altar), emphasized the sacrificial essence of the Eucharist and fostered a contemplative mode of participation.

The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) introduced reforms via Sacrosanctum Concilium, leading to the Novus Ordo Missae in 1969 under Pope Paul VI, which incorporated vernacular languages and enhanced communal involvement to promote active participation. However, this transition sparked debates, with some perceiving a loss of sacred mystery. The revival gained traction in the late 20th century through groups advocating for the "Usus Antiquior" (ancient usage), culminating in Pope Benedict XVI's 2007 motu proprio Summorum Pontificum, which designated the TLM as the "Extraordinary Form" and facilitated its broader availability.

In subsequent years, Pope Francis's 2021 motu proprio Traditionis Custodes imposed restrictions, mandating episcopal oversight to mitigate perceived divisions and reaffirm Vatican II's liturgical reforms. By 2026, while adherence to these guidelines persists, the TLM endures in approved settings, supported by priestly societies such as the FSSP and the Institute of Christ the King Sovereign Priest (ICKSP). Initiatives like TAN Books' "Year of the Latin Mass" in 2026 further propel educational efforts, highlighting its enduring theological and aesthetic value.

Key Liturgical Elements That Define the Latin Mass
Distinct features include the exclusive use of Ecclesiastical Latin, Gregorian chant as the normative musical form, and a focus on interior prayer rather than external vocalization. The Canon's silence during the Eucharistic Prayer underscores the rite's mystical dimension, inviting participants into a profound encounter with the divine. These elements, preserved over centuries, contribute to its timeless allure.

Alito v. Scalia: Practical Considerations
Guest Post Contributed by Amy Ottaviano,
Albany Law School student and research assistant to Vin Bonventre

For the past few months, working with Professor B., I have been researching the last three terms of the United States Supreme Court. Looking at cases in which Justices Antonin Scalia and Samuel Alito had written or joined different opinions, I focused on the differences in Scalia’s and Alito’s methods of analyses. I found several.

Among the more interesting are these:
(1) The two justices treat text differently. Usually, whereas Scalia prefers to interpret statutes based on a narrow reading of plain text, Alito prefers broader readings that consider the congressional intent underlying the laws. Alito frequently looks to statutory construction, context, and the practical considerations of the law. Some examples of this difference are found in Winkelman v. Parma City School District (2007), Gomez-Perez v. Potter (2008), and CBOCS v. Humphries (2008).

(2) Related to point # 1, Justice Alito does consider practical implications, while Justice Scalia is often more tied to the plain text such that he blindly disregards them. A good example of this is in LaRue v. DeWolff (2007). There, Alito looked beyond the plain language of a statute which established regulations for federal employee retirement plans. Specifically, when the statute was enacted, federal employees were all enrolled in one kind of plan (“defined benefit”), but by the time this case arose, most were enrolled in a different kind of plan ("defined contribution”). Rather than disregard this development, Alito argued that it was more practical to give effect to the overriding congressional intent behind the law as it would apply under the changed circumstances. Scalia ultimately reached the same result in the case as Alito, but he did so in a separate opinion by drawing somewhat unpersuasive comparisons between the two types of retirement plans and insisting that his conclusion rested on the plain text.

Another noteworthy example is Indiana v. Edwards (2007). There, Scalia adamantly supported the right of a criminal defendant to refuse counsel, even where he was deemed mentally incompetent to stand trial without an attorney. Scalia ignored the practical consideration that the criminal defendant was simply incapable of mounting an effective defense without the assistance of counsel. Once again, taking practicality into consideration, Alito joined the opposing opinion that the right to self representation is meaningless if the defendant is incapable of meaningfully representing himself; that an unconditional enforcement of the pro se right does not serve the 6th Amendment’s purpose. [Other examples of the difference in the consideration of practicality may be found in United States v. Gonzalez-Lopez; Burlington v. White (2006); and Begay v. United States (2008).]

Certainly, there are more differences between these justices than the two discussed, and certainly there are many similarities. However, it seems from my research that when Scalia and Alito do disagree, it is often for the reasons discussed here.

Amy Ottaviano, Albany Law School, Class of 2010

The elite hunting group linked to Antonin Scalia is a "true knightly order in the historical tradition," according to its website
By Tierney McAfee
Published on February 25, 2016 06:05PM EST

This was no ordinary hunting trip.

When Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia was found dead at a West Texas ranch on Feb. 13, he was on a getaway with high-ranking members of an elite hunting fraternity whose origins date back to 1695.

Even after the high-profile judge’s death, the names of the 35 other guests at the remote Cibolo Creek Ranch that weekend – some of them confirmed members of a secretive Austrian society called the International Order of St. Hubertus, according to a review of public records conducted by The Washington Post – remain largely unknown.

Members of the worldwide, male-only organization had gathered at the ranch at least once before, The Post reports. The hunters, some of whom hold titles like Grand Master, Prior and Knight Grand Officer, wear dark-green robes inscribed with a large cross and the motto “Deum Diligite Animalia Diligentes,” or “Honoring God by honoring His creatures,” according to the group’s website. The Order, named after Hubert, the patron saint of hunters and fishermen, was founded in 1695 in modern-day Czech Republic. It is a “true knightly order in the historical tradition,” according to its website.

It’s unclear what Scalia’s connection was to the group, but Cibolo Creek Ranch owner John Poindexter, and C. Allen Foster, a prominent Washington lawyer who flew to the ranch with Scalia on a private plane, where both leaders in the society.

Poindexter told The Washington Post in an email that he is not aware of any association between Scalia and the group.

“There is nothing I can add to your observation that among my many guests at Cibolo Creek Ranch over the years some members of the International Order of St. Hubertus have been numbered,” he wrote.

A Scalia family attorney did not respond to The Post‘s requests for comments.

Poindexter told reporters after Scalia’s death that he met the justice at a “sports group” gathering in Washington, D.C. The U.S. branch of the Order of St. Hubertus, founded in 1966 at the Bohemian Club in San Francisco, now lists its headquarters as a suite on M Street NW in D.C. – but the address is only a mailbox in a UPS store.

The ranch owner told The Post that Scalia traveled to Houston with his friend, the lawyer Foster, and U.S. marshals. Foster and Scalia then broke off from the marshals and chartered a plane to the ranch.

According to the Presidio County Sheriff s Office incident report obtained by The Post, Poindexter told the sheriff that he and Scalia “had supper and talked for a while” on the eve of his death, before the judge “said that he was tired and was going to his room for the night.” When Scalia wasn’t at breakfast the following morning, Poindexter said he went looking for the justice and found him dead in his bed.

Law enforcement officials told The Post they didn’t know of the International Order of St. Hubertus or its connection to Poindexter or any of the guests at the ranch the weekend Scalia died.

🎬 ZODIAC (2007) 💥🍿

A mysterious killer terrorizes Northern California, taunting police with cryptic messages while an obsessive investigation turns the search for truth into a personal battle.

Robert Graysmith a quiet cartoonist at the San Francisco Chronicle who becomes fascinated by the killer's codes while his curiosity eventually draws him closer to crime reporter Paul Avery and Inspector David Toschi, who are both trying to understand a case that seems to grow more complicated with every new clue.

The investigation stretches across different police departments, witnesses, newspaper reports, handwriting analysis and possible suspects, one name begins appearing repeatedly "Arthur Leigh Allen".

The evidence surrounding him is disturbing but much of it remains circumstantial, leaving investigators unable to establish a definitive connection.

As the years pass, the case begins consuming the people chasing it. Avery's career and personal life deteriorate, Toschi's investigation eventually loses momentum and Graysmith becomes increasingly obsessed with proving his theory.

His obsession begins affecting his job, his marriage and his relationship with his children.
Graysmith refuses to let the case disappear as he continues following old clues and eventually tracks Allen down at a hardware store.

They briefly face each other but Graysmith leaves without the definitive answer he has spent years searching for.
Years later, the surviving victim Mike Mageau identifies Allen from a photograph, but even then, the mystery remains unresolved. Allen later passed on before authorities can question him further and later DNA testing from a Zodiac letter does not match him.

Insight: The story reveals how the pursuit of truth can become an obsession, especially when the mystery offers no definitive answer.

text:
DROP Program

Not every fire department in America has a DROP program. The acronym stands for deferred retirement option plan. As I understand the program, when a firefighter enters it he or she will be given the exact date of retirement. Most departments will offer a five or ten year DROP which benefits the member as well as the jurisdiction. A firefighter cannot change their mind after entering in and is bound to the date. The member benefits by receiving a check upon the date they leave the department. The jurisdiction gains because the member is in the retirement system, as far as compensation and benefits go, and the jurisdiction can better manage replacements.

“So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.”
Psalm 90:12 KJV

As Christian firefighters we do not know the exact day of our departure from this earth. But rest assured, we will all die one day—unless the Lord returns first. This should not discourage believers but rather encourage us because of the hope we have of eternal life in Christ Jesus. The Psalmist reminds us to number our days, or to live considering our soon departure so that we might apply the wisdom of God as found in His word to our hearts. Life is short. It seems like just yesterday I was graduating from the training academy in Washington, DC and now I am retired. Another blink and I will be gone. The same brevity meets us on the job: a shift can end in a routine return to quarters or in a line-of-duty death. Charles Studd wrote these stirring words of reminder in a famous poem: “Only one life, ’twill soon be past; only what’s done for Christ will last.”
Numbering our days means we do not postpone faithfulness until after DROP, retirement, or the next promotion. It means we serve the people in front of us, watch over one another, and keep our hearts anchored in Christ while we still wear the uniform.

Number your days this shift: ask the Lord to show you one concrete way to serve Him and your crew before the day ends and do it.

May our lives reflect Jesus Christ in how we choose to live and serve in the fire service.
Encouraging first responders to keep the faith!!

#fireservice #faith

text:
Hyperliquid has three fronts open in Washington, and none of them is what it looks like. How does this affect you as a HYPE holder? 

Let me explain it from the very beginning: the players, the timeline, what's actually being argued, who wants what, and what it means for you.

➡️ The players, one line each:

- @HyperliquidX (HL): the biggest on-chain perps exchange. No KYC (it doesn't ask who you are) and it blocks US users only on its website.

- A perp, or perpetual: a contract to bet on a price going up or down, with leverage and, IMPORTANT, no expiry date. As you know, it's HL's product.

- The @CFTC : the US derivatives regulator. It decides what counts as a future and who can list one. Its chairman is @ChairmanSelig .

- @CMEGroup : the biggest futures exchange in the world. The one suing the CFTC.

- @Kalshi : a CFTC-regulated exchange that listed the first legal perp in the US back in May.

- Congress: a House of Representatives committee investigating bets made with inside information.

- @HyperliquidPC , HPC: HL's lobby in Washington, funded with 1M HYPE.

- Retail: the small investor. You and me.

➡️ The real question:

Can a perpetual legally exist in the US for retail? All three fronts hinge on that. And so does whether HL can ever enter the US without ceasing to be what it is.

➡️ The timeline:

1- May 29, 2026. The CFTC approves Kalshi's BTC perp and classifies it as a future. First legal perp in the US. From that day on, any regulated exchange can list crypto perps; Coinbase and Kraken already do.

2- June 18. CME sues the CFTC, its own regulator. Its argument: a perp is not a future, it's a swap. I'll explain the difference later, because it's the key to everything.

3- August 19. Trump says the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid to the US "legally and compliantly". The White House is now calling HL by its name.

4- September 2. The CFTC asks the court to dismiss CME's lawsuit: it says CME can't sue because nobody is stopping it from listing the very same perps.

5- September 3. HL enables permissioned markets on HIP-3, the feature that lets third parties create their own markets on HL. Permissioned means only a list of wallets controlled by whoever creates the market can trade there.

In practice: whoever creates the market, Kraken for example, runs KYC on its clients, and that's how they can trade on HL through Kraken legally. It's the technical piece of onshoring, which is what making HL legal in the US is called.

6- September 9. HPC joins the lawsuit on the CFTC's side, with a brief signed by Elizabeth Prelogar, the former US Solicitor General.

7- September 16. Payward, Kraken's parent company, announces it will use those permissioned markets to offer HL perps to US clients with KYC: Bitnomial, its regulated exchange, creates the markets and handles clearing; NinjaTrader holds the accounts. Pending approval, no date.

8- September 29. Letter from the House Oversight Committee to Jeff Yan, HL's founder. It's not a lawsuit or a fine: it requests documents by October 13 on KYC, detection of suspicious trades, and contracts on Fed decisions, elections and geopolitics. 

It cites the $1.1B short on BTC and ETH opened minutes before Trump's tariff announcement on October 10, 2025, closed with more than $150M in profit. The same investigation started in May with Kalshi and Polymarket, and the same day they wrote to Crypto .com

9- October 2. CME replies to the CFTC in court. And it does so by quoting HPC: it uses a tweet from HPC's CEO ("sorry, competition is here") as proof that competition is hurting it. It describes HL as "poised to compete with CME if it enters the US". My read: CME already sees that entry as likely and is afraid of losing market share. Bullish for HL.

10- October 5. The CFTC unveils its first crypto rules, Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM. They're advance notices, not rules yet, and they draw a ladder from easiest to most demanding: spot (buying and selling directly) with no leverage, state licenses; exchanges with leverage, registration in a new category built for crypto, with proof of reserves and KYC; exchanges with perps, the full framework of the futures markets. 

And one line from Selig that sounds written for HL, even though it doesn't name it: "a person should not have to register as a broker simply because that person shipped code". The CFTC is drafting a policy so that whoever publishes software without taking orders or holding funds is not an intermediary.

➡️ Future or swap, explained with The Big Short:

Here's the concept in dispute. Is a perp a future or a swap? Let's go with an example:

- A future is a contract with an expiry date, listed on a regulated exchange. Anyone can trade it, retail included, with standard margin and a tax advantage.

- A swap, on the other hand, is an agreement between two parties to exchange payments based on the value of something. In The Big Short, Burry pays a premium every so often and the bank pays him if the mortgages collapse: that's a swap. A perp has funding, a periodic payment between longs and shorts that keeps its price pegged to the real one. CME says that payment is exactly what defines a swap. In fact, the perp was born on BitMEX in 2016 under the name "perpetual swap".

- Swaps are designed for institutions: more margin, more registration, and retail out. If CME wins, Kalshi and Coinbase have to pull or restructure their perps, and US retail loses easy access to regulated perps. Not on Kalshi, and not on a future legal HL.

➡️ What's next:

- October 13: HL's deadline to answer Congress. In my opinion it will point to the Kraken route: the protocol stays KYC-free, but whoever comes in from the US through Kraken goes through Kraken's KYC. In other words, US users could trade on HL through exchanges like Kraken, where they do pass KYC.

- October 16: the CFTC answers CME in court. After that, the judge decides whether to dismiss the case, no date.

- 60 days of public comments on the CFTC's rules.

➡️ The three scenarios:

1⃣ The court dismisses CME's lawsuit and Selig's rules go ahead. A perp is a future, the CFTC opens its on-chain path (shipping code doesn't make you a broker) and Kraken opens the door to the US. The best case.

2⃣ The court lets the lawsuit continue. Years of uncertainty, but the rules move forward on their own track and Kraken can operate in the meantime.

3⃣ CME wins: a perp is a swap. The worst case for HL, and I'll explain why below.

➡️ How it affects you today:

Not at all. HL currently blocks the US and you trade the same tomorrow. What's at stake, in my view, is what happens between now and 2027. Hyperliquid is perps. If a perp is a future in the US, there's a regulated door to walk through, Kraken is already building it, and Trump already said in August he wants it open.

If a perp is a swap, that door closes for retail: Kraken's markets on HL couldn't be futures for the small investor, onshoring would become an institutions-only product, and HL would miss out on the volume and market share of the biggest market in the world. I've held HYPE since the TGE and I'm still in, so this hits home.

Bottom line: HL's regulation has stopped being a risk nobody knew how to measure and now has a shape, dates and players, with the regulators that matter all pushing in the same direction except one: CME.

I'll keep this updated as these dates play out.

Carre.

The @CFTC just took an important step toward adopting a federal rulebook for crypto market structure: the Commission proposed rules for exchanges that let Americans trade crypto with leverage, including a new type of CFTC registration that is fit for purpose.

An exchange’s regulatory path would follow its product set: (1) state licensing for spot trading, backstopped by the CFTC's anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority; (2) CFTC registration for leverage under rules written for crypto; and (3) the existing DCM framework for perps and other derivatives. Builders shipping code onchain, and the Americans using it, would know where they stand under federal law.

Separately, the CFTC is working directly with builders to develop lawful pathways for onchain markets in the United States, and is drafting a policy so that developers who publish software but do not take orders, control execution, or hold customer assets would not have to register as brokers.

Thank you to @ChairmanSelig and the CFTC staff for the effort behind today's proposal and for putting onchain markets on the agenda.

text:
Baghdad’s Sovereignty Runs Through New York - Iraq’s principal vulnerability is the interaction between dependence on external financial infrastructure and incomplete control over domestic coercive power.

The Central Bank of Iraq’s financial statements document the establishment of an Iraq 2 account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for oil receipts and other specified funds; the arrangement establishes financial dependence without transferring Iraqi ownership to Washington. Financial Statements, 31 December 2020 — Central Bank of Iraq — 2020, Note 39. https://t.co/ezsNr7okKb

The IMF’s July 2025 assessment placed 2024 oil revenue at 36.0% of GDP, against total revenue and grants of 39.3%, illustrating the concentration of the fiscal base. IMF Executive Board Concludes 2025 Article IV Consultation with Iraq — IMF — Jul 2025. https://t.co/5BHYukjC9z

On 1 October 2026, Treasury explicitly placed Najaf pilgrimages, its pressure campaign against Iran and militia demilitarisation within the same diplomatic discussion. READOUT: Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent’s Meeting with Iraq Minister of Foreign Affairs Fuad Hussein — U.S. Department of the Treasury — Oct 2026. U.S. Department of the Treasury

The strategic implication is that Baghdad needs both dependable lawful payments and enforceable Iraqi command authority; progress in either domain remains vulnerable to failure in the other.

The decisive unresolved record is the operative Najaf aviation authorization, including its beneficiaries, duration, conditions and grounds for suspension.

Iraq’s sovereignty depends on what survives the withdrawal
The conclusion of the coalition mission in Iraq transfers responsibility to Baghdad without resolving the constraints that govern its decisions. The government must preserve financial access, administer aviation restrictions, subordinate armed organisations and sustain infrastructure whose financing creates obligations long before it delivers reliable services. The governing contradiction is that external assistance can strengthen Iraqi institutions while also increasing their exposure to creditors, licensing authorities and foreign suppliers. NATO Mission Iraq, the European Union Advisory Mission in Iraq and European investment programmes offer instruments for managing that transition, but none supplies the authority to enforce an Iraqi decision. Sovereignty will expand only when Baghdad can maintain payments, security orders and essential services through political disagreement, rather than renegotiate the conditions of their operation whenever pressure rises.

Withdrawal transfers responsibility faster than institutions acquire capacity
The UK Ministry of Defence’s announcement of 30 September 2026 confirmed the conclusion of the Global Coalition’s military mission and the departure of its forces from Iraq. Germany’s government recorded the end of its deployment after Baghdad withdrew consent. These decisions demonstrate Iraqi authority over foreign military presence, but the responsibility they transfer encompasses functions that require trained personnel, maintained equipment and dependable operational coordination. Ending a deployment establishes who may remain; it does not establish what the institutions assuming responsibility can deliver.

NATO Mission Iraq illustrates the distinction. Its advisory mission continued after personnel relocated from Baghdad to Allied Joint Force Command Naples in March 2026. Institutional assistance therefore survived a change in physical presence, while its contribution remained bounded by a non-combat mandate. Baghdad’s task is to turn advice into Iraqi procedures that persist when advisers are distant, personnel change or a regional crisis interrupts access.

The Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs made the protection problem explicit in its statement of 28 September 2026: withdrawal would occur without an alternative air-defence system, and protection of regional airspace remained a federal responsibility. The operational consequence is a requirement for warning coverage, communication and authorised response across federal and regional institutions. Sovereignty exercised through withdrawal must now be demonstrated through protection.

The investment totals conceal different kinds of obligation
The financial scale of available programmes is substantial, but their figures describe different stages of commitment. The World Bank approved US$900 million for the Iraq Transport Economic Corridors project on 4 June 2026. The UK–Iraq joint statement of January 2025 announced an export package of up to £12.3 billion. Italy’s Foreign Ministry reported in May 2025 that SACE had signed a €1 billion export-credit framework with the Trade Bank of Iraq the previous year. A financing approval, an announced package and an export-credit framework are distinct instruments; none can be counted automatically as completed investment.

TotalEnergies describes the Gas Growth Integrated Project as an investment of approximately US$10 billion, with consortium interests of 45% for TotalEnergies, 30% for Basrah Oil Company and 25% for QatarEnergy. Its announced components include a 1 GWac solar facility, first-phase seawater treatment capacity of 5 million barrels of water per day and a Ratawi production target of 210,000 barrels of oil per day from 2028. These parameters establish the project’s intended scale. Commissioning records, connected operation and sustained output determine its contribution to Iraqi resilience.

European advisory funding belongs to another category. Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/902 established a €79,078,620.21 financial reference amount for EUAM Iraq covering 1 May 2024 to 31 October 2026. Germany’s development ministry identifies a €117.7 million commitment made in July 2024. Neither amount represents an October 2026 annual expenditure figure. Baghdad’s financing decisions require these distinctions because debt service, project delivery, programme expenditure and maintenance obligations enter the public accounts through different channels.

Procurement strengthens sovereignty only when services keep operating
The Gas Growth Integrated Project connects gas recovery, electricity generation, seawater supply and oil-field development. Its value lies in those operating relationships: recovered gas must reach power plants, generated electricity must enter a functioning grid, and treated water must reach the fields it serves. An interruption at a connection point can leave completed equipment unable to deliver its intended service. The Iraqi state acquires resilience when it can operate and maintain the system, rather than simply accept its individual assets.

The same constraint applies to the Al-Qayyarah airbase rehabilitation announced in the January 2025 UK–Iraq package. Rehabilitation can support protection, but operational coverage also requires sensors, communications, authorised engagement procedures, personnel and sustainment. Financing a facility creates a procurement obligation; fielding a dependable capability requires an institutional system around it. Contracts that omit that system can leave Baghdad paying for assets whose availability remains dependent on emergency expenditure or supplier intervention.

The Iraq Transport Economic Corridors project offers a more disciplined implementation model by coupling physical investment with institutional strengthening, performance-based maintenance and evaluation of pilot results before subsequent expansion. Its significance extends beyond roads: it makes continued serviceability part of the intervention. That principle should govern Iraqi procurement more broadly, with funding released against verified delivery and credible operating arrangements rather than the political visibility of contract signatures.

Iraqi law provides authority that bargaining can still weaken
Popular Mobilisation Commission Law No. 40 of 2016 already places the organisation within the Iraqi armed forces and links it to the commander-in-chief. The Justice Ministry’s account identifies military-law obligations, hierarchy, separation from political affiliations and central authority over redeployment. The institutional problem is therefore the execution of defined obligations. A weapons transfer has limited strategic meaning if an organisation retains the command, personnel and procurement channels required to recover autonomous capability.

Articles 9 and 78 of the Iraqi Constitution establish civilian authority and the prime minister’s command responsibility. Their practical force emerges when a commander accepts replacement, a unit obeys a disputed deployment order or investigators obtain access to facilities and records. A settlement that requires a new political bargain for each such decision preserves coordination while leaving command contingent. Baghdad’s authority becomes more dependable when agreed procedures remain enforceable against an organisation that dislikes the outcome.

Aviation exposes an equivalent gap between political agreement and administrative authority. Treasury’s September 2026 action against Iranian airlines widened the sanctions problem, while its readout of the October meeting with Iraq’s foreign minister confirmed discussion of pilgrimage access to Najaf. Under OFAC’s licensing framework, the scope of an authorisation determines which transactions can proceed. Iraqi landing permission cannot by itself resolve the treatment of fuel, handling, payments or designated counterparties. The government needs a common implementation instruction that airport operators and service providers can apply without improvising foreign policy.

Financial reform carries the same requirement. The IMF’s July 2025 assessment called for restructuring state-owned banks, stronger governance and digital infrastructure, and improved anti-money-laundering controls. These measures matter because a supervised institution with reliable records can address a compliance inquiry and preserve legitimate transactions. Expanding the number of intermediaries without correcting ownership, capital and control weaknesses would reproduce the vulnerability across more channels.

European support works through mandates and contracts, not a common guarantee
Italy’s Defence Ministry statement of 29 September 2026 separated military withdrawal from continuing bilateral training and an EUAM contribution. Its commercial interests, including Eni’s Al-Zubair operations and the SACE–Trade Bank of Iraq framework, create reasons to support reliable infrastructure and contractual execution. Italy can combine technical assistance, export finance and institutional training, but each intervention needs an Iraqi owner capable of maintaining the resulting asset or procedure.

France’s exposure through the Gas Growth Integrated Project gives it a direct interest in connected energy delivery. Its February 2026 diplomatic statement also identified regional transport, water and electricity cooperation as subjects for a prospective Baghdad Conference. That channel can help clarify commitments and contain disputes; implementation still requires responsible agencies and enforceable arrangements. Germany, following the end of its deployment, retains civilian instruments addressing employment, administration, climate and energy. These can strengthen the Iraqi capacity to absorb investment without presuming a continuing military presence.

The United Kingdom’s January 2025 partnership combines export finance, infrastructure announcements and intended defence cooperation. UK statutory guidance nevertheless requires applicable licensing for military goods and technology. EUAM Iraq operates under its own Council mandate, while European transactions involving Iran also face the EU restrictions reintroduced in September 2025. Europe can help Baghdad build usable institutions, but its instruments do not supply a collective guarantee of financial access or exemption from other jurisdictions.

The EU–Iraq Partnership and Cooperation Agreement provides an established forum for coordinating that support. Baghdad should use it to require a common programme register distinguishing grants, loans, export-credit arrangements, advisory mandates and operating costs. Without such coordination, separate partners can each fulfil a contract while leaving Iraqi ministries to manage incompatible procedures and unfunded obligations.

The next two years will allocate the cost of unfinished decisions
Between October 2026 and October 2028, the decisive test will be whether Baghdad converts the coalition transition and investment programmes into operating results. The Iraq Transport Economic Corridors project needs implementation and maintenance records; the Gas Growth Integrated Project needs verified commissioning and delivery; security reform under Law No. 40 needs evidence that contested decisions are enforced. Expansion before those tests would increase obligations faster than the government’s capacity to administer them.

The IMF’s May 2025 recommendations identify the fiscal transmission of failure: weak collection, inefficient expenditure and deficient public financial management restrict the resources available for productive investment. If new facilities lack maintenance, the cost falls on the treasury through emergency spending and on households through interrupted services. If financial reform disrupts legitimate commerce without establishing usable alternatives, importers, suppliers and employers bear the immediate burden. If constitutional command remains subject to repeated accommodation, the government carries responsibility for security without dependable control over its execution.

The choice embodied in the September 2026 withdrawal is greater Iraqi responsibility. Its cost will be determined by whether that responsibility is matched by enforceable procedures, funded capability and sustained services. Baghdad can widen its freedom of action over the next two years by making those functions reliable; otherwise, Iraqi taxpayers, businesses and communities will finance a transition whose political declaration has advanced further than its institutional delivery.
