REGIONAL SPORTS ROUNDUP
October 6, 2026

COLLEGE

MSU 8TH AT MYSTIC ROCK GOLF COURSE 
Murray State men's golf shot an opening round 301 followed by a 296 in the second round and at 597, sits in 8th place out of 16 teams competing the Nemacolin Collegiate Invitational in Farmington, Pennsylvania. Lennon Albans leads the Racers with a spot in 13th place at 146 with Landon Hunt of MSU sharing a spot in 28th with a 149. 

West Virginia is the team leader after two rounds with a 582, which is a shot better than St. John's. Erik Johansson of Campbell is the medalist leader with a 139 heading into today's final round. 

COURTSIDE CLUB AT THE BANK
Murray State has introduced the CFSB Courtside Club, a new premium experience as part of the CFSB Center renovations. Located steps from the baseline, the club will offer members early entry, an all-inclusive chef’s table, drinks, a private bar, televisions and exclusive Racer apparel, along with close-up views and access to the team tunnel. Members will also have up to an hour of postgame access. The space will serve as a regional event venue outside basketball season. 

The Racer men's basketball team begins exhibition play at 6 tomorrow night at Wichita State with coverage beginning at 5:30 on Froggy 103.7 and the Varsity App. 

JACKRABBITTS HOP TO #1
South Dakota State moved into the No. 1 spot in the Stats Perform FCS Top 25 after its 31-14 victory over Illinois State. The Jackrabbits are 5-1 overall and 2-0 in the Missouri Valley Football Conference. North Dakota is ranked fourth, followed by Youngstown State at No. 8 and South Dakota at No. 10. Illinois State fell two spots to No. 12 following its loss to South Dakota State, while Southern Illinois dropped four places to No. 25. 

Northern Iowa is receiving votes but did not crack the Top 25. Other area ranked teams include Austin Peay at 9 while Tennessee Tech slipped from 9th to 15th. 

MVFC WEEKLY HONORS
North Dakota quarterback Jerry Kaminski is the Missouri Valley Football Conference Offensive Player of the Week after leading the Fighting Hawks to a 55-28 comeback victory over Murray State. Kaminski threw for 186 yards and three touchdowns while rushing for 98 yards and another score. 

North Dakota also swept the Newcomer and Offensive Lineman awards, with wide receiver Cameron Weir earning Newcomer honors after a 57-yard punt-return touchdown and 106 all-purpose yards, while guard Caleb Olson helped the Hawks rush for 303 yards. 

South Dakota State cornerback Myles Green was the Defensive Player of the Week after recording a fumble recovery and interception, including a fourth-quarter pick-six. 

South Dakota punter Brook Honore earned Special Teams honors after averaging 51.5 yards on six punts, including a 70-yarder that pinned Indiana State at its own 1-yard line.

OVC WEEKLY HONORS
Western Illinois quarterback Kennedy McGill is the Ohio Valley Conference Offensive Player of the Week after totaling 429 yards and two touchdowns in a 28-21 victory over Tennessee State.

Gardner-Webb linebacker Tre Yanez earned Defensive Player of the Week after recording 13 tackles, 2.5 tackles for loss and a sack in a 12-10 win over Charleston Southern. 

Matt Rolader of Charleston Southern and Western Illinois punter Luke Droegemueller shared Special Teams honors. Rolader remained perfect on field goals this season with a 48-yarder, while Droegemueller averaged 39.5 yards on four punts, with two inside the 20.

Gardner-Webb defensive lineman Zalen Watkins was named Rookie of the Week after recording six tackles, 3.5 tackles for loss, a sack and two quarterback hurries in the win over Charleston Southern.

text:
On January 20, 1953, Harry Truman ceased to be president of the United States.
One moment, he occupied the highest office in the nation.
Minutes later, he was simply a private citizen, carrying his own belongings toward a train.
The inauguration was over. Dwight Eisenhower had taken the oath, and Truman's time in the White House had come to an end. There was no lavish farewell, no private aircraft waiting to take him home, and no fortune waiting for him after years in Washington.
There was only a train ticket.
At Washington's Union Station, thousands of people gathered to see him off. The crowd was enormous, and police had difficulty creating a path through the station. As Truman and his wife, Bess, moved through the terminal, people applauded and cheered.
One chapter of American history was closing.
But Truman's life outside the presidency was about to look very different.
He boarded the Ferdinand Magellan, the same presidential railcar that had carried him across the country during his memorable 1948 campaign. When the train departed Washington, Truman left behind not only the White House but also the authority and influence that came with it.
There would be no presidential lifestyle waiting for him in Missouri.
There would be ordinary life.
And ordinary financial problems.
In 1953, former presidents did not receive the benefits that exist today. There were no presidential pensions, government-funded offices, staff allowances, or comparable financial support.
Truman left office without a federal retirement package.
He had no government pension specifically for former presidents.
There was no guaranteed financial cushion waiting for him.
His dependable income came primarily from a modest Army pension connected to his First World War service.
Back in Independence, Missouri, he returned to the family home.
And money became a serious issue.
People around Truman suggested that his name and reputation could make him wealthy. Corporations offered him well-paid positions. Businesses wanted him attached to advisory boards and letterheads. His former position alone could command enormous financial value.
Truman repeatedly declined.
He would not turn the presidency into a source of personal income.
Those who knew him understood why. Companies, in his view, were not really seeking Harry Truman as an ordinary private citizen. They wanted the reputation, prestige, and influence that came from having a former president associated with them.
But Truman did not believe the presidency belonged to him.
It belonged to the American people.
So he refused to sell the prestige that came with it.
There was a real financial price for that decision.
Still, he showed no sign of wishing he had chosen differently.
As Truman's circumstances became more widely known, his situation began to trouble members of Congress. It was difficult to accept that a man who had occupied the presidency during such consequential years could return home without meaningful financial security.
Truman had guided the country through the final years of the Second World War, recognized Israel, helped launch the Marshall Plan, and led the nation into the opening years of the Cold War.
Yet after leaving office, he was struggling financially.
Congress eventually responded.
In 1958, lawmakers approved legislation establishing pensions for former presidents. Truman accepted the benefit, viewing it less as a personal reward than as a sensible protection for those who would hold the presidency in the future.
When Truman's train reached Independence in January 1953, thousands of people were there to welcome him.
They saw a returning president and a national hero.
But the remarkable part of that homecoming was not the size of the crowd.
It was everything Truman had refused to take with him.
There was no accumulated fortune.
No effort to exploit his former position.
No special arrangement designed to turn presidential influence into personal wealth.
What remained was the same character he had carried into the White House.
Harry Truman had possessed extraordinary authority.
When his presidency ended, he surrendered that authority without trying to keep any part of it for himself.
Perhaps that is why his departure still resonates.
At a time when influence can easily become a commodity, Truman viewed public office as something fundamentally different.
The presidency had been placed in his hands temporarily.
When his term was finished, he gave it back.
He went home with little money, few special advantages, and the reputation of a man who had refused to profit from the office he held.
For Harry Truman, his integrity was enough.

🦠 Plague scare in Irkutsk: White House convenes meeting as Moscow stonewalls

Senior US health and national security officials met at the White House on Monday to discuss a possible plague outbreak in Russia, The Washington Post reports, citing two sources.

What we know:
▪️ The case centres on Shelekhov, Irkutsk Oblast. Daria Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the regional anti-plague institute, died in the local hospital. According to Irkutsk journalist Pavel Stepanov and Mash, she broke a test tube containing pneumonic plague on 25 September and fell ill shortly after.
▪️ Shelekhov hospital was placed under quarantine, along with at least three hospitals in Irkutsk. Local outlet "People of Baikal" reports around 200 people quarantined. The Baikalsk town administration advised residents not to travel to Shelekhov, then quietly deleted the post.

The official Russian line:
▪️ Rospotrebnadzor calls it "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and insists the sanitary situation in the region is calm. Peskov told everyone to rely on Rospotrebnadzor's statements.
▪️ A Shelekhov district deputy mayor brushed off Trump's offer of help, claiming the situation is "under full control", the dangerous diagnosis is "not confirmed", and 60% of patients have already left quarantine.

The Western reaction:
▪️ CDC, the State Department, ASPR and other agencies are trying to get details. Per WP sources, the effort is complicated by Russian officials' unwillingness to share data and by reports that Russian special services are involved.
▪️ Rubio said Moscow has shared some information on the infected lab worker and voiced concern that others may be infected, but called it no cause for alarm. Trump said the US will help Russia "as much as we can".
▪️ Biosecurity expert Dr. Ashish Jha told CNN that until more data emerges, we should assume more is happening than we can see.
▪️ Former CIA officer Dan Hoffman compared it to Chernobyl on Fox News — another systemic failure buried under information control, leaving intelligence as the only reliable window.
▪️ The European Commission says it is following the situation very closely.

Bottom line: a dead lab worker, quarantined hospitals, deleted warnings, a vague "pneumonia" diagnosis and special services in the picture. The Kremlin's playbook hasn't changed since 1986 — deny first, explain never.

text:
GAZA: HAMAS OR PALISTINE? 

**Hamas (Harakat al-Muqawama al-Islamiya, or Islamic Resistance Movement) was founded in December 1987** during the First Intifada as the Palestinian branch/political arm of the Muslim Brotherhood in Gaza. Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, a cleric who had built social and charitable networks (including al-Mujamma al-Islami from the 1970s), was the key founder. Its 1988 charter called for the destruction of Israel and establishment of an Islamic society in historic Palestine.

### Early Funding (Late 1980s–Early 2000s)
Initial support came primarily from:
- Palestinian expatriates and private donors in the Persian Gulf (especially Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states).
- Charitable networks (*dawa*), mosques, and foundations that blended social welfare with political/military activity. Western-based charities (later designated by the U.S. as Hamas fronts, such as the Holy Land Foundation in the U.S., Interpal in the UK, and others in Europe) channeled funds.

Iran emerged as a major state sponsor in the early 1990s, providing funds (initially estimated around $30 million annually, rising toward $50 million by 2000), weapons, and training for Hamas members at Revolutionary Guard facilities. Hamas opened offices in Tehran; relations deepened despite the Sunni-Shiite divide because of shared opposition to Israel. Other early or intermittent support came from Syria (hosting leadership), Sudan, and private sources.

### Path to the 2007 Takeover of Gaza
Israel unilaterally disengaged from Gaza in 2005, withdrawing settlers and military. In the January 2006 Palestinian legislative elections, Hamas won a majority, defeating the long-dominant Fatah (the main faction of the Palestine Liberation Organization/Palestinian Authority). This reflected widespread dissatisfaction with Fatah corruption and governance failures.

The international community (U.S., EU, Quartet) imposed sanctions and withheld aid because Hamas refused to recognize Israel, renounce violence, or accept prior agreements. A national unity government formed in early 2007 under Saudi mediation, but power-sharing collapsed amid mutual distrust. Fatah controlled key security forces (with some U.S./Western training and support), while Hamas built its own Executive Force.

From 10–15 June 2007, intense fighting (the Battle of Gaza) erupted. Hamas forces rapidly overran Fatah strongholds, security headquarters, and government institutions across the Gaza Strip. They executed or expelled many Fatah officials and fighters. By 14–15 June, Hamas had full control of Gaza. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas (Fatah) dissolved the unity government, declared a state of emergency, dismissed Hamas Prime Minister Ismail Haniyeh, and appointed an emergency government in the West Bank under Salam Fayyad. This created the lasting split: Hamas ruling Gaza, Fatah/PA ruling the West Bank.

Hamas framed the takeover as defensive against alleged Fatah/U.S. plans to oust it; Fatah and Western governments called it a military coup.

### Post-2007 Funding Sources
Once in control of Gaza, Hamas’s finances shifted heavily toward territorial control while retaining external patrons:

- **Taxation and local revenue** became the largest ongoing source. Hamas levied taxes/fees on imports (via Israeli crossings and Egyptian tunnels/smuggling), businesses, goods (cigarettes, fuel, etc.), vehicle registration, licenses, and more. Estimates range from roughly $300–500+ million per year in the years before October 2023. Tunnel taxes alone were significant until Egypt cracked down.

- **Iran** remained a core backer of the military wing (Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades), providing funds (commonly estimated $70–100+ million annually, with some reports of higher or fluctuating amounts), weapons technology, training, and expertise. Support dipped during the Syrian civil war (when Hamas sided against the Assad regime) but recovered. Seized documents later detailed multi-year Iranian payments totaling hundreds of millions.

- **Qatar** became a major financial and political host. It provided hundreds of millions (later structured as ~$30 million per month in cash for fuel, salaries of civil servants, and needy families) starting after the takeover and accelerating from around 2012–2014, often with Israeli and U.S. knowledge/acquiescence as a stabilization measure. Qatar hosted Hamas’s political leadership (after it left Syria). Total Qatari transfers over the decade reached into the billions; internal documents indicated some funds supported “resistance” efforts.

- **Turkey** offered political support under Erdogan, hosted investment activities, and facilitated some financial networks.

- **Investment portfolio and other**: Hamas built a network of companies (real estate, mining, farming, construction) in Turkey, Sudan, Algeria, UAE, and elsewhere, valued by U.S. Treasury estimates at around $500 million. Cryptocurrency, money changers, and smuggling supplemented this. Diversion of international humanitarian aid (including some UNRWA and other flows) and Palestinian Authority salary/service transfers into Gaza also occurred.

Overall annual budgets in the later pre-2023 period were estimated in the hundreds of millions, with territorial taxes often the single largest component, followed by state sponsors (Iran for military priorities, Qatar for governance/cash flow). Israel’s policy of allowing Qatari cash transfers was explicitly intended in part to keep Hamas focused on governing rather than escalating, while maintaining separation from the West Bank PA—though this calculation failed with the October 7, 2023 attacks.

Hamas has been designated a terrorist organization by the U.S., EU, Israel, and others, which constrains formal banking channels and drives reliance on opaque methods. Funding patterns have adapted over time to sanctions, border controls, and conflicts, but the core mix of local extraction + Iranian military support + Qatari cash has been consistent since the Gaza takeover.

text:
DID YOU KNOW??

Michael Jordan originally did not want to sign with Nike, preferred Adidas, and had a unique "Love of the Game" clause written into his NBA contract allowing him to play basketball anywhere, anytime, against anyone, regardless of injury risk or team owner approval.

When Michael Jordan entered the NBA draft in 1984, professional basketball contracts contained strict restrictions preventing players from engaging in off-season pickup games or non-sanctioned events due to the immense risk of career-threatening injuries. Jordan, driven by an unquenchable competitive spirit, refused to sign with the Chicago Bulls unless they included a custom exemption: the "Love of the Game" clause.

​This clause granted him unconditional legal authority to play recreational basketball wherever and whenever he pleased, whether in local high school gyms, pickup runs on outdoor asphalt courts, or international exhibition games. It remains one of the most famous and unique contractual provisions in professional sports history.

Furthermore, during his rookie year negotiations, Jordan was set on signing an endorsement deal with Adidas, but the German athletic brand was restructuring internally and failed to match Nike's groundbreaking offer of $500,000 per year plus his own signature sneaker line, laying the foundation for the multi-billion dollar Jordan Brand. Walk with me 👇🏾👇🏾 

The Evolution of Jordan's Historic 1984 Deals:

​The pivotal summer of 1984 set the baseline for Jordan's unprecedented career trajectory:

1. The NBA Draft & Contract Mandate
June 1984
The Chicago Bulls select Jordan 3rd overall. Jordan demands and secures the unprecedented "Love of the Game" clause before signing his rookie contract.

2. The Shoe Endorsement Pitch
Summer 1984
Jordan seeks a deal with Adidas, but the company declines to offer a signature line. Nike executive Sonny Vaccaro convinces Nike to pitch their entire basketball marketing budget on Jordan.

3. The Infamous 'Banned' Sneaker Marketing, October 1984
Jordan debuts the black-and-red Nike Air Ship (precursor to the Air Jordan 1). The NBA sends a warning letter stating the colors violate uniform rules, which Nike leverages into a legendary viral marketing campaign.

4. Global Cultural & Commercial Empire, 1985 – Present
The Air Jordan 1 releases publicly in April 1985, generating over $126 million in sales in its first year and cementing Jordan's brand as a global athletic titan.

More Surprising Facts About Michael Jordan:

A. ​The $5,000 Fines Myth: Contrary to popular belief, the NBA banned the black-and-red Nike Air Ship shoes (not the Air Jordan 1) for breaking the "51% white shoe" rule. Nike reportedly paid the $5,000 per-game fines on Jordan's behalf and capitalized on the controversy with ads claiming, "The NBA can't stop you from wearing them."

B. ​Drafted Below Two Players: Jordan was not the top pick in the 1984 NBA Draft. He was selected third overall behind Hakeem Olajuwon (Houston Rockets) and Sam Bowie (Portland Trail Blazers).

C. ​The High School "Cut" Legend: While widely reported that Jordan was "cut" from his high school varsity team as a sophomore at Emsley A. Laney High School, he was actually assigned to the junior varsity team because the varsity coaching staff needed taller post players at the time, a setback that fueled his legendary work ethic.

​SUMMARILY! 
​Michael Jordan secured a rare "Love of the Game" clause in his Bulls contract enabling him to play pickup basketball anywhere, while a missed opportunity by Adidas allowed Nike to sign him and launch the iconic Jordan Brand in 1984.

Michael Jordan once tipped a cocktail waitress a $5 chip in Las Vegas—until Wayne Gretzky stopped her, returned the chip, grabbed a $100 chip from Jordan’s stack, and placed it on her tray. Gretzky then looked at Michael and said, “That’s how we tip in Las Vegas, Michael.”

The famous tipping story comes from Rich Strafella, a former vice president of operations at the Hard Rock Hotel in Las Vegas. In a 2010 interview, Strafella claimed the exchange happened during a private, high-stakes casino game. Neither Michael Jordan nor Wayne Gretzky appears to have publicly confirmed the story.

Jordan’s interest in gambling has been widely documented. In 1993, he faced criticism after visiting an Atlantic City casino during the NBA playoffs. That same year, a golf partner claimed Jordan had lost more than $1 million to him through betting, although Jordan disputed that amount. Jordan has consistently denied having a gambling problem, instead describing himself as having a “competition problem.”

Both Jordan and Gretzky were dominant figures in their respective sports. Jordan won six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls, while Gretzky—known as “The Great One”—won four Stanley Cups with the Edmonton Oilers and retired in 1999 holding nearly every major NHL scoring record.

The banner visible behind the two reads “20th Century Sports Awards,” suggesting the photograph was taken at the Sports Illustrated ceremony held in New York in December 1999.

One of Gretzky’s most remarkable records remains his 1,963 career assists. That’s more than any other NHL player’s combined career total of goals and assists, meaning Gretzky would still rank as the league’s all-time points leader even if every one of his 894 goals were removed from his record.

THE US CASH OPEN REMAINS A LIQUIDITY TRANSITION

CURRENT REGIME

BTC defines systemic direction. ETH measures rotation. SOL measures liquid beta. HYPE and the stronger alts show where speculative demand is concentrating. The US 10Y, DXY and NQ determine whether global financial conditions support or fight the move.

text:
Every verse you just quoted was written by people who actively practiced animal sacrifice.

1. Read the end of Psalm 51: David says God desires a contrite heart, and then concludes: "Then You will delight in the sacrifices of the righteous... then bulls will be offered on Your altar" (Ps 51:19). David didn't abolish bulls; he said sacrifices must be accompanied by true repentance.

2. Look at 1 Kings 8: You quoted Solomon’s prayer about captives praying toward Jerusalem during exile. Right after that prayer, Solomon offered 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep on the altar (1 Kings 8:63). Prayer in exile was an emergency substitute, not the permanent cancellation of the sacrificial system.

3. "Preferred" doesn't mean "abolished": Proverbs 21:3 says justice is preferred to sacrifice, just like Proverbs 16:8 says a little with righteousness is better than great wealth. That doesn't abolish wealth, and it doesn't repeal the Torah's Levitical laws.

If Hosea, David, and Solomon meant that God replaced sacrifices with prayer, why did Ezra immediately rebuild the altar and slaughter bulls the moment they returned from Babylon (Ezra 3:2–3)?

text:
In Tokyo, fruit is sold inside velvet-lined wooden boxes. A single melon costs two hundred dollars and comes with a certificate of lineage.

In Kentucky, on a Saturday morning in August, fruit is sold off the tailgate of a 1994 Chevy pickup truck.

The bed of the truck was loaded with wooden bushel baskets overflowing with yellow-and-pink peaches.

Beside the scale stood an old farmer named Cletus. He was wearing a faded John Deere cap and had dirt under his fingernails from 1978.

I stopped to inspect the perimeter.

"Sir," I said, keeping my hands behind my back. "What is the certified sweetness rating of this crop?"

Cletus looked at me as though I had asked him for the algebraic square root of his dog.

"Don't know nothin' about ratings, son," he said in a slow, tobacco-stained drawl.

He pulled a curved folding knife from his pocket. The horn handle was worn white.

With one sweeping flick of his thumb, he sliced a massive crescent of peach from a fruit the size of a baseball.

He didn't offer a napkin. He didn't put it on a paper plate.

He extended the blade toward my chest, holding the dripping, glistening slice upon the steel.

"Open your mouth, buddy."

I hesitated. In my homeland, accepting fruit off a folding blade from an unwashed farmer violates every tenet of civilian hygiene.

"I have not yet transacted—"

"Eat the peach, city boy."

I leaned forward. I took the slice between my teeth.

*SQUISH.*

A warm, aromatic explosion of sugar, sun, and Kentucky rain burst across my palate.

The juice did not stay in my mouth. It ran down my chin. It ran down my wrist. It dripped off my elbow onto the dusty asphalt.

It was not sweet like candy. It was sweet like thirty days of unbroken ninety-degree sun filtered through green leaves and clay soil.

Inside my skull, forty-two years of disciplined Tokyo manners collapsed.

I wiped my chin with the sleeve of my shirt.

"This is not agriculture," I gasped. "This is concentrated solar radiation."

Cletus grinned, showing four gold teeth. He wiped his blade against his denim thigh and folded it shut with a snap.

"Trees were planted by my granddaddy in forty-six," he said softly, looking at the bushel baskets. "Watered by the creek behind the barn. Don't spray 'em. Just let the summer do the work."

I bought two entire bushels. Thirty pounds of peaches.

I lived in a one-bedroom apartment with a mini-fridge. I had no jars. I had no sugar.

I ate seven peaches standing over my kitchen sink that afternoon, juice soaking my wrists, laughing out loud at the absurdity of my wealth.

In Japan, we perfect the fruit through human restraint.

In America, an old man hands you a slice off a pocket knife, drenches your elbow in sugar, and proves that God already perfected the peach eighty years ago in the Kentucky dirt.

text:
Jean Lafitte (c. 1780 - c. 1820) was a pirate, smuggler, and one of the most notorious figures to operate around New Orleans.

Born around 1780, Lafitte and his brother Pierre established themselves in the Barataria Bay region south of New Orleans, where they built a smuggling empire. From their base at Grand Terre, Lafitte’s men captured and smuggled goods while operating outside the authority of the United States and Spain.

But when the British threatened New Orleans during the War of 1812, Lafitte found himself in an unexpected position.

In late 1814, the British approached Lafitte and offered him money, protection, and a commission if he would help them attack New Orleans. Instead, Lafitte warned the Americans of the British plans.

Andrew Jackson initially distrusted Lafitte, but the pirate eventually offered his men, weapons, ammunition, and knowledge of the local waterways to the American cause.

Lafitte’s Baratarians fought alongside Jackson’s army during the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815. His artillerymen were particularly valuable, helping man the American guns behind the earthworks.

The Americans won a resounding victory, and Lafitte’s name became forever connected with the defense of New Orleans.

Ironically, the man who had spent years evading the law became an American hero in one of the most famous battles in U.S. history.

Lafitte eventually disappeared from the Gulf Coast and the details of his later life remain uncertain. But his name never disappeared from New Orleans.

Today, Jean Lafitte is remembered throughout Louisiana—in places such as Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve, streets, and businesses. 

From pirate and smuggler to wartime ally, Jean Lafitte left  one of those most interesting legacies in New Orleans and American History.

text:
Another martyr, Jatin Das, died during a hunger strike in jail. Gandhi was in Agra at the time. When asked to offer a garland to Jatin Das’s mortal remains, Gandhi refused. Jatin Das’s supreme sacrifice stirred no sympathy in him. Yet Gandhi and the Congress supported the British in World War II — a war where soldiers did not exchange sweets out of love; it was sheer violence.
What an astonishing apostle of non-violence!

In the 1939 Congress presidential election between Subhas Bose and Gandhi’s chosen candidate Dr. Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Gandhi declared he would retire from politics if Pattabhi lost. Bose won by a landslide, though he later resigned to preserve Gandhi’s “honour.” Gandhi, however, remained in politics until death.
Similarly, Gandhi once said that Pakistan would be created only over his dead body — yet Pakistan was created with his full support.

Gandhi launched three major movements (Satyagrahas). Strikingly, he withdrew all three midway. Yet India is told that spinning a charkha gave us freedom — a laughable fiction.

Historian R. C. Majumdar wrote: “To garland Gandhi as the hero of India’s freedom is to mock the truth. To say that he won independence through satyagraha and the charkha is the height of absurdity. Calling him the hero of independence is an insult to those who bled for the nation.”

Sri Aurobindo said: “India will be free only to the extent she frees herself from Gandhism.”

Clement Attlee — the British PM who signed India’s independence document — visited Kolkata in 1956 and stayed with Governor P. B. Chakraborty. Chakraborty asked him:
“What made you leave India so quickly?”
Attlee replied: “Because Subhas Bose’s military activities had caused rebellion to grow inside the Indian Army and Navy. They were no longer loyal to the British.”

When Chakraborty asked how much Gandhi’s non-violence contributed to the British departure, Attlee smirked and said:
“Minimal.”

The very people who fled India out of fear of Netaji admitted it. Yet for 74 years, we have been banging our heads over Gandhian philosophy.

Ayan Choudhury

🇨🇳🚁⚔️🇹🇼🇺🇸 PLA Z-10 attack helicopters being prepared for amphibious operations

China is systematically adapting the Z-10 army attack helicopter for use in amphibious assault operations. Originally designed to engage armored vehicles and provide ground troop support, the aircraft is now being trained to operate from ships, strike maritime targets, and coordinate with transport aviation. The primary theater of operations is the Taiwan Strait.

This maritime adaptation has proceeded in stages. In 2014, a Z-10 landed on a Type 072A landing ship for the first time. In 2020, army aviation units practiced landing, refueling, and rearming operations on a civilian semi-submersible vessel. Later, images emerged showing eight of the aircraft on a similar platform. In 2025, Chinese state television explicitly confirmed that the Type 075 amphibious assault ship is capable of accommodating the army's Z-10s.

A Z-10 landing on the deck of a Type 075 amphibious assault ship

The significance lies beyond mere deck landings. The PLA is establishing forward maritime staging points that allow the helicopters to operate closer to Taiwan, refuel and rearm without returning to the mainland, and quickly re-enter combat. This is critical regarding operational range. The Z-10 has a combat radius of 114–294 km, depending on its configuration. The strait is at least 130 km wide; when carrying a full combat load, the aircraft might lack the range to operate over the island if launching from the Chinese coast. Ships and semi-submersible platforms eliminate this constraint, effectively moving supply points closer to the combat zone. In a major operation, semi-submersible vessels could serve not only as transport platforms for military hardware but also as temporary floating airfields. This expands the operational reach of army aviation and reduces reliance on a limited number of large amphibious assault ships.

Concurrently, China has been pre-positioning Z-10 helicopters opposite Taiwan. Satellite imagery from December 2020 recorded 12 of these aircraft at the Yuanqian heliport - then under construction - in Fujian Province (coordinates: 24.473, 117.5583). This positioning shortens the transit time to the strait and allows for the rapid reinforcement of the force grouping prior to the operation's active phase.

The Z-10’s primary mission begins once the landing force reaches the shore. During the initial hours of the landing, the helicopters can escort Z-20, Z-8, and Mi-17 transport aircraft while suppressing firing points and engaging armored vehicles, short-range air defense systems, and fortified positions. Once the landing force has secured a beachhead, the helicopters shift to providing direct fire support for ground troops. Such aviation assets are particularly valuable for units operating in confined spaces, as they respond to threats more quickly than fixed-wing aircraft and operate directly over the frontline.

The PLA is also expanding the range of targets these aircraft engage. In 2023, helicopters from an army aviation brigade of the Eastern Theater Command’s 73rd Group Army practiced missile strikes against simulated maritime targets off the coast of Fujian. The aircraft is now viewed not merely as a land-based support asset but also as a tool for engaging patrol boats, landing craft, and other targets within the littoral zone.

In February 2026, the Chinese military demonstrated joint maritime flight operations involving Z-10, Z-20, and Mi-17 helicopters. The operational concept is clear: transport aircraft deliver personnel, while attack helicopters cover the route, suppress threats, and clear landing zones.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) represent a distinct area of ​​focus. The PLA conducts exercises in which Z-10 and Z-20T attack helicopters operate alongside KVD-002 reconnaissance drones. While there is no confirmation that helicopter crews control the drones directly, the logic is evident: the drone detects a target and relays coordinates to the crew, allowing the attack helicopter to receive immediate targeting data and reduce the time between detection and engagement. This presents a major challenge for Taiwanese coastal defense units, which would have to simultaneously counter UAVs, helicopters, missile strikes, and amphibious assault forces.

The Z-10 has inherent limitations. Its maximum takeoff weight is approximately 3.4 tons lower than that of the American AH-64E Apache, resulting in reduced fuel and weapons capacity. Consequently, China is already fielding the larger Z-20T attack helicopter.

In a Taiwan scenario, the two aircraft complement each other. The Z-10 remains the primary platform for escort and close air support, while the heavier Z-20T offers greater range, advanced sensor suites, and a larger weapons payload.

According to the IISS *Military Balance 2026*, the PLA Ground Force operates 200 Z-10s, with another eight Z-10Ks assigned to the PLAAF Airborne Corps. Deploying even a portion of this fleet to the eastern theater could generate a high density of attack aircraft over the Taiwan Strait and landing zones.

text:
Jack Captein named as former New Zealand Army soldier in attempted espionage case

'A search of his address located an external hard drive containing a video of the Christchurch mosque attacks livestream and a copy of the gunman's manifesto, both being objectionable publications.' 🤔

A New Zealand soldier guilty of attempted espionage who feared retaliation if he was named has lost a bid to keep his identity secret.

Jack Alexander Captein was dismissed from service and sentenced to two years in a military detention facility in August last year, after he tried to defect and gave restricted military information to someone he thought was a foreign agent.

The Crown did not think the sentence was long enough and appealed the outcome of the first case of its kind in New Zealand history.

Captein, who has not been named until now, feared having his name published would place him and his family at risk of retaliation from the foreign power he thought he was assisting, he said in court documents.

In May this year, the Court of Appeal allowed the Crown's appeal against the sentence, but dismissed Captein's name suppression appeal.

He then sought leave to bring what Justice Christine French said would be a second appeal against the refusal to grant name suppression, which was declined in a decision released this week.

She said the Appeal Court considered it "not seriously arguable" in the circumstances that the public interest in open justice was outweighed by the interests in favour of non-publication.

Captein, who had links to two right-wing groups, admitted handing over bundles of New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) documents to an undercover officer.

The offending came to light after an undercover operation in December 2019 during which Captein met several times with an undercover officer posing as an agent of a foreign country.

He provided the officer with documentation and materials likely to prejudice New Zealand's security or defence.

Captein had also accessed a New Zealand Defence Force computer system and obtained maps, imagery and telephone directories with the intention of handing them to the undercover officer but was arrested before that happened.

A search of his address located an external hard drive containing a video of the Christchurch mosque attacks livestream and a copy of the gunman's manifesto, both being objectionable publications.

Some of the information he had found belonged to another soldier, while the bulk of it he had taken from the NZDF's internal computer system, and it included restricted information.

Captein also offered to get a covert device into New Zealand Army headquarters.

The former New Zealand Army private earlier pleaded guilty in the Court Martial of New Zealand (CMNZ) to one representative charge of attempted espionage, a charge of accessing a computer system for a dishonest purpose, and one representative charge of knowingly possessing an objectionable publication.

At sentencing, he was denied permanent name suppression.

Captein appealed the decision at the same time the Crown appealed the sentence imposed by the CMNZ.

In allowing the Crown's appeal against the sentence, the Appeal Court found that a sentence of two years' military detention did not adequately reflect the seriousness of the offending and was an insufficient deterrent, Justice French said in the Court of Appeal judgment.

"It was reinforced in that view by reference to cases from other jurisdictions which highlighted the primacy of general deterrence in sentencing for espionage and related offending," Justice French said.

The Appeal Court considered the appropriate starting point was at least four years and three months' imprisonment.

It also considered the discounts awarded by the CMNZ were "generous" but they were not reduced.

After applying these discounts to the starting point and giving Captein a further credit for the eight months already spent in military detention, the Appeal Court arrived at an end sentence of 15 months' imprisonment.

However, that was subject to a Crown recall after an error was found in the commencement date of the sentence because of a technicality in Court Martial Appeals law.

The Crown confirmed it would apply to the Appeal Court to recall and reissue its judgment to clarify the sentencing commencement date.

In dismissing his appeal for name suppression, the court held that the consequences of publication did not amount to extreme hardship and the public interest in publication outweighed the interests in non-publication.

Captein then sought leave to bring what Justice French said was a second appeal but the threshold for granting leave was high.

Captein argued he would "unjustly face public scrutiny" if named, without the ability to respond with classified details of the covert operation targeting him.

He also said he and his family would be at risk of retaliation from the foreign power he thought he was assisting and he would be at risk in a civilian prison from some prisoners, namely those who opposed his "white supremacist views" and prisoners who supported those views and may seek to radicalise him.

He was also at risk from prisoners who may try to obtain details of the offending, Captein said.

Justice French said the court was "not persuaded" that any grounds of the proposed appeal raised issues of general principle that would justify a second appeal.

"Further, we consider the merits of the proposed name suppression appeal to be weak," she said.

There appeared to be no evidence that the alleged risk to Captein or his family's safety existed, and what evidence there was pointed to the contrary, the judge said.

The court felt any risks from fellow prisoners could be adequately mitigated by the range of protective measures commonly used by the Department of Corrections.

text:
The Next Development Mandate

Why sustainable finance must become the way Sri Lanka finances development.

Sri Lanka does not lack ambition. What it lacks is room for expensive mistakes. Capital is limited. Public finances remain under pressure. Businesses are rebuilding confidence after years of disruption. At the same time, climate change is beginning to alter the economics of agriculture, fisheries, energy, tourism, infrastructure, and many of the communities that depend on them. Every rupee invested must therefore work harder.

It must generate an economic return. It must withstand new environmental and social pressures. And it must contribute to a stronger country rather than create costs that someone else will have to carry later.

This is why sustainable finance can no longer sit at the edge of the development conversation. It must become part of how Sri Lanka decides what to finance, how to finance it, and what results that capital should produce.

Development finance must move with the country

DFCC Bank was established in 1955 as Sri Lanka’s pioneering development finance institution. Its purpose was direct and practical: to provide long-term capital for the industries, businesses, and infrastructure the country needed.

That responsibility remains relevant today, although the requirements have changed.

Sri Lanka still needs investment in energy, enterprise, infrastructure, and productive capacity. But those investments must now respond to climate risk, pressure on natural resources, changing international standards, and the need to extend opportunity more widely.

A project cannot be judged only by whether it is financially viable when a loan is approved. The more difficult question is whether its economics will continue to hold as environmental and social conditions change.

For DFCC Bank, this has meant carrying its original development mandate into a different era. The task is no longer simply to finance development. It is to finance development that works over time.

Sustainability belongs inside the decision

Sustainable banking is often discussed in terms of targets, disclosures, and specialized financial products. These are important, but they are not the whole answer.

The real test comes earlier, inside the decision. Which sectors receive capital? How are environmental and social risks assessed? What conditions should accompany financing? How will impact be measured? And what happens when a project that appears financially sound carries risks that may emerge only several years later?

DFCC Bank has applied environmental and social assessment to lending through its Environmental and Social Management System for more than two decades. This incorporates applicable IFC Performance Standards and provides a structured basis for identifying and managing risks associated with financed projects. That foundation has since expanded into a broader approach to sustainability-related risks and opportunities across the Bank. Board oversight, management responsibility, ESG policy, risk processes, disclosure, and external assurance connect sustainability to how decisions are made and reviewed.

This work attracts less attention than a new green or blue financial instrument. Yet its importance should not be underestimated. Sustainable finance is only as credible as the definitions, governance, data, and monitoring behind it. Without that discipline, capital may acquire a new label without producing a different result.

Finance must make a new investment possible

The value of sustainable finance is not limited to supporting projects that would have found funding anyway. Its greater contribution lies in helping important but underserved areas become investable.

Sri Lanka’s renewable energy sector offers a useful example. DFCC Bank supported the development of the country’s private-sector renewable energy industry, including financing
Sri Lanka’s first grid-connected mini-hydropower project. Working with international development partners, the Bank helped direct private capital into a sector that was still establishing its commercial foundations.
What began with mini-hydropower later expanded to include wind, solar, and waste-to-energy projects. The lesson was straightforward: finance can do more than fund an established market. It can help create one.

That principle continues to apply to newer financial instruments. In 2024, DFCC Bank introduced Sri Lanka’s first listed Green Bond, providing a route for domestic capital to support renewable energy. Sri Lanka’s first Blue Bond, listed in 2025, extended the use of sustainable finance to water security, wastewater management, sustainable fisheries, marine ecosystems, and climate-resilient coastal infrastructure.

In 2026, a Basel III-compliant GSS+ Bond brought sustainable use-of-proceeds principles more deeply into the Bank’s capital management.

The significance of these instruments is not found in their colors. It lies in the discipline they require: defined uses of funds, clear eligibility criteria, governance, reporting, and evidence of impact.

When done properly, they give investors greater confidence in where their money is going and provide important projects with access to capital that may not otherwise reach them.

Global climate capital needs a local route

Sri Lanka’s climate financing requirement is greater than conventional bank balance sheets or public finances can meet alone. International climate finance must therefore become part of the solution. Access, however, is only the beginning.

Global funding must translate into viable local programs, credible project pipelines, and results that reach the sectors and communities most exposed. That requires institutions capable of connecting international funding requirements with local knowledge, implementation capacity, and financial discipline.

DFCC Bank became the first Sri Lankan entity accredited by the Green Climate Fund in 2023 and remains the country’s only accredited entity. That accreditation provides Sri Lanka with a direct institutional route to the world’s largest dedicated climate fund.

A climate-resilient fisheries initiative now being developed with the Food and Agriculture Organization illustrates the work needed to convert that access into practical action.

Fisheries sit at the intersection of several national priorities: food security, employment, exports, coastal livelihoods, and climate vulnerability. Financing resilience in this sector, therefore, serves both environmental and economic purposes.

This is where a bank can contribute something distinctive. It can help turn a development need into a credible financial structure, bring together different sources of capital, manage risk, and track results after funds have been deployed.

The objective is not merely to bring climate finance into Sri Lanka. It is to ensure that the finance works when it arrives.

The transition must reach beyond large institutions

A sustainability transition confined to governments, banks, and large companies will not be enough.

Small businesses, farmers, fishing communities, women-led enterprises, and households must be able to participate. Many are already among those most exposed to changes in weather, resource availability, energy costs, and economic conditions. Yet they often have the least access to capital, technical knowledge, and protection against disruption. This is both a social and an economic issue.

If smaller businesses cannot adapt, supply chains weaken. If farming and fishing communities cannot respond to climate pressure, food security and rural incomes suffer. If households cannot access affordable solutions, the cost of transition becomes another source of exclusion.

Finance must therefore be accompanied by knowledge, capacity, and products suited to the realities of the people expected to use them. The environmental and social dimensions of sustainable finance are inseparable. Progress in one will eventually be limited by neglect of the other.

A mandate for the decade ahead

The coming decade will determine whether sustainable finance becomes part of the ordinary machinery of Sri Lanka’s economy or remains a specialist category discussed largely through reports and conferences.

The outcome will not be measured by the number of commitments made. It will be visible in the quality of investment that follows: more reliable energy, stronger businesses, better-prepared communities, healthier ecosystems, and projects whose economics remain sound as conditions change.

DFCC Bank has a clear role in that work. Our history in development finance gives us experience, but it does not give us permission to rely on the past.

We must continue improving our risk practices, data, disclosures, and financial instruments.

We must build partnerships capable of channeling capital into sectors where the need is clear, but the path to investment remains difficult.

We must also be candid about the obstacles. Sri Lanka needs stronger project preparation, better data, deeper technical expertise, and financing structures that recognize both urgency and affordability.

Sustainable finance will not remove every trade-off. Nor will it replace the need for sound commercial judgment. It demands better judgment.

Profit remains essential. But the quality of that profit increasingly depends on what stands behind it: resilient businesses, secure communities, functioning ecosystems, and investment decisions that continue to make economic sense. That is the next development mandate.

“According to preliminary reports confirmed by the Nigerian Air Force Director of Public Relations and Information, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, the aircraft, an ATR-42 with tail number NGR 931, was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when it crashed in a swampy area opposite the Naval Base in Igbokoda.

“The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr. Festus Keyamo, has confirmed that 25 passengers and seven crew members were on board.

“On behalf of the government and good people of Ondo State, Governor Aiyedatiwa expresses his heartfelt sympathy to the Chief of Air Staff, the entire Nigerian Air Force family, and the families of all personnel and passengers on board the ill-fated aircraft.

“The governor has been in contact with the leadership of the Nigerian Air Force, the Ilaje Local Government Chairman, Maurice Oripelaye, and security agencies on ground.

“To aid ongoing efforts, Governor Aiyedatiwa has directed the State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA, the Ministry of Health, and relevant security agencies to immediately mobilise and offer full logistical and human support to the Nigerian Air Force and other emergency response agencies in the search and rescue operations currently ongoing at the crash site.

“The governor has also directed that the area be cordoned off and secured to allow for smooth and unhindered rescue operations, while urging residents of Igbokoda and adjoining communities to remain calm, cooperate with emergency responders, and refrain from spreading unverified information.”

Panic in coastal community as residents recount loud sound

Meanwhile, a resident, who said many occupants of the aircraft might have died, said: “It happened this morning (yesterday). We heard a very loud sound from the area where the incident occurred, but we couldn’t get there because the place is a swampy area inside the creek. We were just looking at it from afar.

“The accident caused panic as both the young and old people in the community fled in different directions.

“But the police and the military later came around for rescue, but the occupants may have died there,” he said.

Another resident, Oluboyo Olusola, said “after the accident, I was here personally. I saw many things. I saw parts of the aircraft, I saw body parts that were scattered and clothes. That means everybody inside that aircraft are dead.”

Monarch fears no survivor, says aircraft submerged in swamps

Also speaking, the traditional ruler of the community, the Olu of Igbokoda, Oba Afolabi Odidiomo, said he initially feared it was a commercial aircraft because of the potential number of casualties.

Oba Odidiomo said: “I was in court when the incident happened, and I directed some of my palace officials to visit the site. 

“At that time, nobody could determine whether it was an airplane or a helicopter. I was worried because it must not be a plane, because the number of casualties would be just too high. Our first thanks to Almighty God is that it did not happen inside the town; otherwise, the casualties would have been too many.

“The aircraft crashed into the river and a swampy area. It was raining when the accident happened and the place was waterlogged.

“The aircraft did not catch fire, but a substantial part of it has gone into the water. We cannot describe the exact situation for now, but from my investigation and what we have gathered so far, there was no survivor.”

Tinubu mourns NAF personnel in Ondo jet crash, orders thorough investigation

In his immediate reaction to the crash, President Bola Tinubu expressed profound sadness over the accident

A statement by the presidential spokesman, Bayo Onanuga, said the aircraft was on a routine mission from Benin to Lagos when the accident occurred.

text:
Nick Saban’s departure left college football with a void, and the ripple effects were felt quickly at Alabama. The current head coach, Kalen DeBoer, has faced immediate pressure from a restless donor base, despite matching Saban’s early 25-8 start. The contrast in how the two coaches handle administrative power offers a clear lesson for DeBoer: establish and enforce a firm boundary between football operations and outside financial influence.

Saban's approach became famous for drawing a hard line between the athletic program and the university’s most powerful boosters. He prioritized on-field needs—recruiting, player development, and program culture—while limiting distraction from exclusive fundraising circles. He even scaled back or eliminated traditional booster activities that could intrude on football decisions. By keeping the focus squarely on football performance, he avoided letting external money dictate internal priorities.

When DeBoer arrived, reports indicated that wealthy boosters were already scrutinizing the program’s direction after a rough start, signaling that the old dynamic can re-emerge if not checked. DeBoer’s calm and amiable style, while appealing, risks being interpreted as openness to outside influence. The key is to balance respect for donors with a clear stance that football decisions remain rooted in competition, development, and program integrity rather than financial leverage.

As financial realities evolve, with private equity and corporate funding increasingly involved in roster payrolls, coaches may face diminished autonomy. The warning is clear: without a decisive, Saban-like boundary between football operations and booster influence, a program can drift from its competitive core. The path to lasting success in Tuscaloosa appears to favor a strong, unwavering leadership style that keeps external interests from shaping football strategy.

For DeBoer to secure a durable legacy at Alabama, the best move is to assert boundaries and focus relentlessly on recruiting and player development, rather than courting every donor or trying to appease the boardroom. The coach who can effectively tell the fat-cat financiers where to place their influence—and keep the program’s priorities laser-focused on the field—will be better positioned to weather the modern funding landscape and build sustained success.

text:
AI is making diversification harder than it looks.

The technology isn’t just driving a handful of US megacap stocks anymore: its influence is spreading across equities, bonds, commodities, venture capital, private markets, and infrastructure.

That means investors who think they’re spreading their bets may still be loading up on the same underlying theme.

Take stocks. Developed-market indexes are heavily weighted toward tech, while emerging-market benchmarks have their own AI concentration through South Korean chipmakers and Taiwan’s TSMC.

The same dynamic is showing up in credit markets, where hyperscalers are issuing more corporate debt to fund their buildout.

That supply is even spilling into government bonds by competing for investor demand and nudging yields higher.

Then there’s energy. Data centers need enormous amounts of electricity, and the AI buildout is adding to power demand at the same time as energy supply remains constrained.

Copper is part of the story too. After all, data centers, power grids, and the infrastructure connecting them all require plenty of the metal.

And the effects stretch into private markets. Data centers and their supporting infrastructure are becoming an increasingly important theme across private equity and private credit, while venture capital has become heavily concentrated in AI startups.

So the diversification problem isn’t just that AI is everywhere. It’s that seemingly different assets can react to the same shock.

That raises an obvious question: where can investors hide if the AI boom turns into an AI bust? Government bonds may be one answer.

A sharp pullback in AI investment could weaken growth, cool inflation, reduce energy demand, and prompt central banks to cut interest rates.

Hyperscaler bond issuance could also fall, easing competition for capital, while a risk-off move could send investors toward traditional safe havens.

Those forces would all tend to support government bonds. And unlike much of the past two decades, bonds now offer investors a meaningful yield while they wait.

In other words, government bonds could provide both income today and a potential hedge against the very theme that is making diversification harder in the first place.

text:
A 16-year-old high school student  
YouTube channel from 0 to monthly earnings of $5000+  

Opens a group chat every day after school  
Assigns tasks to 5 AI employees  
Half an hour later, a complete YouTube video is ready  

Never shown his face, never edited a single frame of video  
Topic selection → Script writing → Voiceover → Thumbnail → Publishing  
Fully automated  

I've broken down the entire process 👇

> Pick the right niche. This is 90% of the game. Most people pick a niche they like instead of a niche that pays and has room to grow. Get this wrong and nothing else matters.

> Find who's already winning. Use Manus to pull 10 channels in your niche under 100K subs that are still doing 1M+ views a month. Small channels beating the algorithm = a niche that's wide open right now.

> Steal the pattern (legally). Use Claude's extension to rip the top 40 videos from each of those channels over the last 6 months. Titles, view counts, upload dates. This is your blueprint of what's already proven to work.

> Train your own title machine. Feed that list into Claude and tell it to study the topics and titling like a channel manager. Now it writes titles in the exact language your niche already rewards.

> Go deeper than the surface. Run deep research on the niche to find what people actually want to watch then narrow to your top 3 content pillars. Direction beats guessing every single time.

> Generate trending titles on command. Off those 3 pillars, pull 5 high-CTR titles each. That's 15 videos ready to hand off before you've filmed a thing.

> Hire your team. UpWork. Fiverr. A scriptwriter, an editor, a thumbnail designer. You're the operator now, not the labor.

> Nail your SEO. Google Trends for timing, ChatGPT for optimization, TubeBuddy to VidlQ for the tags and search data that get you found.

People aren't on camera. People are not "influencers." They built systems.

What the system actually looks like:

1. Choose a high-CPM niche (finance, health, travel, tech = $8-40 RPM)
2. Hire a 4-person team on Upwork for $600-1,300/month
3. Produce 2-4 videos/week using the outlier method
4. Direct all traffic to one ultra-long Money Video (45-90 min)
5. Money Video sells a digital product or affiliate offer
6. Email list captures viewers for $1/subscriber/month recurring

That's the whole system.

The 6 highest-potential niches right now:

→ Finance & Investing ($12-35 RPM)
→ Business & Entrepreneurship ($10-25 RPM)
→ Real Estate ($15-30 RPM)
→ Health & Wellness ($8-20 RPM)
→ Travel — especially cruise content ($5-15 RPM)
→ Technology & AI ($8-18 RPM)

That's the whole loop. Niche + proof + titles + research + team + upload. Run it for 60 days and you'll be shocked how fast it moves.

The time to build is now.

text:
#Amagimedialabs

Is a 50x 1 year Forward P/E worth the Consumer Behavior Bet?

What Amagi Actually Does: The Dual SaaS + Ad Monetization Logic

Amagi is not a streaming application; it is the invisible, cloud-native logistics network supplying them. Today, legacy media giants and premium news networks are facing a dual challenge: they must maintain traditional satellite broadcasts while aggressively expanding to IP-based (internet) broadcasting, smart TVs, and direct-to-consumer digital endpoints.

Amagi captures value across this transition using two completely distinct, yet complementary, revenue pillars:

The Predictable Foundation (B2B SaaS Model): Amagi's software takes a network’s massive archive of video files, schedules them, overlays graphics, and broadcasts them as continuous 24/7 linear channels over the internet. For this infrastructure playout (Amagi CLOUDPORT), they charge flat, recurring monthly enterprise software fees.

The High-Leverage Supercharger (Programmatic Ad-Revenue Share): Apart from fixed SaaS subscriptions, Amagi operates a highly lucrative Monetization & Marketplace engine (Amagi THUNDERSTORM). Every time a commercial break occurs on a streaming screen, Amagi's ad-insertion tech dynamically swaps the ad file on the server side in real time. For mid-sized content brands, Amagi sells these ad spaces directly to global brands and takes a direct commission cut (revenue share). For massive networks with their own ad-sales teams, Amagi takes an "inventory split," keeping a percentage of the total ad slots to monetize for themselves.

The Operational Balance Sheet: Amagi serves 45% of the world’s top 50 media companies, including global titans like NBCUniversal, Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount, and Samsung TV Plus. In FY26, it generated ₹1,506 crore in total revenue (combining SaaS licenses and ad-revenue shares) with an EBITDA margin of ~10.36%, finally crossing into PAT profitability (₹72 crore). However, because it handles massive video payloads, Amagi spends roughly 27% to 29% of its revenue renting cloud infrastructure from AWS and Google Cloud, creating a structural variable cost floor.

The Economic Moat: Can It Be Defended?

Amagi's current premium rests on the strength of its competitive advantages, which face distinct long-term threats:

Current Moat (High Switching Costs & Friction): Once a network like NBCUniversal plugs Amagi into its master control rooms, digital ad insertion pipelines, and scheduling logic, removing it creates massive operational risk and downtime. This stickiness shows up in Amagi's phenomenal Net Revenue Retention (NRR) of 126%. Furthermore, Amagi acts as a unified hub pre-integrated into over 300 global smart TV platforms—a massive logistical moat that would take competitors years to replicate.

The Ad-Network Effect: Through its marketplace, the more streaming channels Amagi aggregates, the more programmatic advertisers it attracts, optimizing fill rates and ad targeting data.

Future Threats: The moat is heavily exposed to coopetition risk. Tech giants like AWS offer foundational media services (AWS Elemental) and could theoretically build out competing application layers. Additionally, legacy hardware giants (Harmonic, MediaKind) are aggressively moving their systems into hybrid cloud code, crowding the enterprise space.

The Big Bet: Global Consumer Behavior & The Streaming Paradox

Evaluating Amagi requires analyzing global viewing shifts. The tech is device-agnostic—whether pixels load on a Connected TV (CTV), laptop, or phone, Amagi's cloud engine still processes the stream and dynamically injects the ad. The true vulnerability lies in the format of consumption and the unpredictability of user habits:

• The Macro Trend (Subscription Fatigue): Globally, consumers are hitting a spending wall with premium, ad-free services (Netflix, Disney+, Max). This subscription fatigue has triggered an explosion in FAST (Free Ad-supported Streaming TV) networks. Aggregated FAST viewing hours recently grew by a massive 55% year-on-year.

• The Dynamic Ad Upside: As viewers migrate to free tiers, Amagi's ad-monetization engine thrives. The firm processed a massive 13.6 billion ad impressions in a single quarter (Q1 FY27), taking a lucrative commission slice of programmatic video ad revenues.

The Uncharted Risks: We cannot be entirely certain how sustainable this viewing pattern is. Consumer choices are highly cyclical. If premium ad-free tiers drop their prices, or if macroeconomic factors pressure consumer wallets differently, viewing preferences could easily pivot again. More critically, Gen Z is actively moving away from traditional horizontal, 24/7 linear feeds toward short-form vertical algorithmic content (TikTok, YouTube Shorts). If long-form viewing hours drop globally, Amagi's addressable format pool will shrink, directly hitting both its SaaS processing volumes and its ad-revenue splits.

Conclusion: The Premium Verdict

A 50x 1-year forward P/E is a statement of extreme confidence by the public markets. It assumes that the current consumer shift toward FAST networks is an irreversible, multi-decade structural trend rather than a passing economic phase. To justify this price tag, global corporate video ad budgets must continue expanding rapidly into internet TV channels, and Amagi must seamlessly capture that traffic.

Today investors are not buying a stable enterprise software utility; they are making a highly concentrated macroeconomic bet that the world will keep leaning back to watch television with commercial breaks.

[Not a buy/sell recommendation, DYOR]

The historical symmetry between the destruction of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline and the destruction of the Herodian Temple in Jerusalem offers a compelling framework for analyzing the transition from the Old Covenant age to the New. From a covenantal fulfillment perspective, this timeline highlights the radical shift in the locus of God’s presence—from a localized, temple-centric system in Jerusalem to the universal reality of the New Creation inaugurated by Christ.

The Chronology of Covenantal Shift
The rapid succession of these events creates a powerful "bookend" effect to the close of the Old Covenant age:
 *December 69 AD: The destruction of the Temple of Jupiter symbolizes the instability and collapse of the pagan Roman order amidst the Year of the Four Emperors.
 August 70 AD: The destruction of the Second Temple by the Roman legions, led by Titus, marks the terminal point of the Old Covenant. As the Jerusalem temple was the geographical anchor of the Mosaic system, its annihilation finalized the transition that had been in progress since the death and resurrection of Christ.

Theological Implications: The "Fiscus Judaicus" and the New Creation
The use of the *fiscus Judaicus* (the "Jewish Tax") to rebuild the Roman temple is a poignant illustration of the "transfer of symbols." The wealth and tribute previously dedicated to the maintenance of the Jerusalem cult were literally diverted to bolster the religious authority of Rome.
From a fulfilled eschatology perspective, this irony underscores several key points:
 1. The End of the Ritual System:  The destruction of the Jerusalem Temple effectively ended the Aaronic priesthood and the sacrificial system, fulfilling the prophecy of Hebrews 8:13 regarding the "obsolescence" of the Old Covenant.
 2. The Shift in Authority: The transfer of temple funding signifies the total collapse of the political-religious hegemony that had historically stood in opposition to the early Church.
 3. The Manifested Kingdom: With the physical barriers and the symbolic center of the Old Covenant removed, the Church was definitively freed from its Jewish ethnic/geographical constraints, fully entering into the "New Creation" reality where God’s presence is no longer localized in stone or mortar, but in His people.

The transition from the earthly, localized temple to the cosmic reality of the New Jerusalem serves as the backdrop for the final "passing away" of the heaven and earth of the Old Covenant order.

text:
KALIBRATE: THE REAL REASON FUEL PRICES ARE SO HIGH

The company you are referring to is Kalibrate (officially registered as Knowledge Support Systems Inc.). While the company is globally headquartered in Manchester, United Kingdom (with US corporate offices in Michigan and New Jersey), it became a household name across California due to a massive federal antitrust lawsuit filed in the state.

Kalibrate provides AI-powered fuel pricing and location analytics software, including a widely used mobile app that allows fuel retailers and dealers to manage and deploy gas prices directly from their phones.

Key Overview of Kalibrate:

The Software & Mobile App: Kalibrate acts as an AI-driven pricing ecosystem. Fuel dealers input their private store data, volumes, and local competitor metrics. The AI then analyzes historical patterns, traffic volume, and market demand to recommend optimal, profit-maximizing fuel prices.

Widespread Adoption: The platform is utilized by nearly all major US fuel brands and big-box retailers. Its clients and defendants in recent litigation include 7-Eleven, Circle K, BP, Marathon Petroleum, Speedway, Walmart, Albertsons, and TravelCenters.

The California Antitrust Controversy:

Kalibrate dominated national headlines due to class-action litigation filed in the Eastern District of California.

The Accusation: The lawsuit alleges that Kalibrate operates as the "central nervous system" for an illegal, algorithmic price-fixing scheme. Instead of stations competing naturally to offer lower prices, the AI allegedly coordinates high pump prices across competing brands simultaneously.

The Impact: According to the legal complaints, in areas where US fuel dealers heavily adopted the Kalibrate app, gas prices artificially increased by up to 30 cents per gallon compared to what normal market competition would dictate.

Legal Precedent: This case serves as a critical test for California's updated antitrust laws, which explicitly restrict competitors from using shared algorithms to artificially drive up the cost of living.

Mace wrote on X on Friday, August 7, 2026, “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic.
