text:
Podcast Summary | Good Hang with Amy Poehler: Marcello Hernández

Overview
Marcello Hernández emerges as a rare combination: a physically gifted performer, a prolific standup, and a generous castmate whose social nature fuels rather than hinders his output. Sarah Sherman paints him as the exception among competitive standups, someone who pulls others onto stages instead of guarding his own. Across the conversation, a deeper thread runs: what performers allow themselves to claim they are good at, and how identity, family, and immigrant experience shape a comic's relationship to work, ambition, and softness.

Key Themes
- Hernández is described as a generous, inclusive SNL castmate who encourages others rather than competing for stage time, which is unusual in standup culture.
- A central tension: he is intensely social and rarely alone, yet also extremely productive and prolific as a writer and performer.
- Sherman suspects much of his material is written on stage, feeding off audience energy, even though his jokes are tightly structured.
- His comedy is rooted in avoiding work and disrupting people who are trying to work, which he treats as a source of dark joy.
- He credits collaborators, circumstance, and God for his biggest successes, deflecting praise even when it is clearly warranted.
- His blunt, confrontational communication style is framed as a family "love language" that can be misread as mean.
- Teachers who saw something in him were pivotal, and he now brings them to SNL and funds a scholarship in their name.
- Performing in Spanish is both funnier and faster for him, and carries a sense of collective power when Latinos are struggling.
- Career advice centers on enjoying where you are, rejecting others' advice, and recognizing that dissatisfaction can become endless.

Detailed Summary
Sarah Sherman describes Marcelo Hernández as genuinely generous and inclusive at SNL, especially in involving others in bits and sketches. She credits him with encouraging her to get back on stage and do standup, even sensing when she is feeling bad. She says most standups are competitive about stage time; Marcelo is an exception who encourages others. She notes he calls her during hiatus to push her toward clubs and shows while she is lying on her couch watching X Files.

Sherman also claims Hernández is both physically gifted and a strong joke writer, which she frames as unusual because his physical stage presence could mask weak writing. She describes backflips in a Sebastian Maniscalco lawyer sketch and a Jack Black sketch, plus back handsprings like a Russian teenage gymnast. She says he jokes that he is a bad sketch writer, but she thinks his actual writing is funny and tight. When she asked him when and how he writes jokes, he deflected.

A central tension runs through the conversation: Hernández is intensely social and rarely alone, yet also extremely productive and prolific. Sherman suspects he writes much of his material on stage because he feeds off audience energy, despite his jokes being well-crafted with setup-punchline structure. She describes herself as a homework girl who works manically on writing nights, while Hernández tells her to relax. She recalls him and Cam Patterson doing backflips over chairs stacked on a writing table at 3 a.m. on writing night.

Hernández brings Amy flowers as a gesture, framing it as giving people their flowers. Amy reads ambiguous weird energy into it. He admits to being a bad texter and calls ghosting Amy one of his biggest regrets. He describes growing up in a matriarchy surrounded by women, including his mother, sisters, and lesbian friends, and says hanging with women is funny but also mentally challenging. He calls himself a lesbian in many ways, explaining it through growing up around women and being jealous and petty.

Amy frames Hernández as a jock and a team-oriented person who radiates fun. He agrees and says he works hard but dislikes working. His comedy comes from avoiding work: he brought a scooter to SNL, does a seal run across the table-read hallway, and takes dark joy in disrupting people who are trying to work. He rode a bike to the interview, saying it saved nine minutes on the commute in hot weather. He describes being recognized while biking in New York as his favorite type of interaction.

Hernández says he is at a sweet spot at SNL, no longer terrified or confused, knows the schedules and rules, and newer people exist. He grew up in Miami, half Cuban and half Dominican. His parents' lifelong goal was to get him tired; all his childhood activities were aimed at making him sleep. He played baseball in the outfield wearing pants and long socks in Miami heat, which he found pointless. According to his family, he did cartwheels in the outfield and played with insects, so his mom pulled him from baseball, saying he was making the family look bad. He then did soccer.

Soccer suited an energetic, unmedicated child with ADD because the ball never stops moving. He played as a winger, running all the way up the field. He played through college, driven partly by social pressure: friends knew him as a soccer guy, so not playing college soccer felt like failure. His mother blocked a California college option for being too far but allowed Ohio. She also leaned hard into American assimilation after fleeing Cuba. He emailed every school and edited his own recruiting videos.

A high school drama teacher pushed him to memorize contrasting monologues. He learned a John Leguizamo monologue and one from Class Action. The teacher got him out of school for about three days to compete in Tampa, and he won for contrasting monologues. The first was sad and real about a gang member whose little brother found his gun and shot himself. The second was comedic: Hello, it is me, Ramon, the Cuban Cabana boy. The lesson he drew: people love to laugh, and you cannot do the sad one first.

In school, his behavior was labeled excessive talking and mischief. College writing teacher Bob Null assigned him to write a version of The 40-Year-Old Virgin with a woman as the main character. A Shakespearean performance teacher, Bo Smith, in his late 60s, performed King Lear in class, took off his tie and necklace, got on his knees, and screamed, which changed how the class performed. Hernández took Bo Smith's class again and performed stand-up in it. Bo Smith and partner Tom Ro were let go from the school; Tom has since passed.

He started a scholarship at his college called the Bo and Tom scholarship by Marcelo Hernandez, for kids who want to do what he did. Two recipients so far meet with him and Bo. The teacher who told him to memorize the monologue came to SNL with his wife and son for a full tour. He has also brought several teachers to SNL.

Quitting soccer to pursue stand-up was pivotal and emotional. He could not do both, and his team was disappointed. Coaches made him go downstairs, clean up, and tell the team personally; he had to shake hands with 27 guys. His mother was excited and saw comedy as what he was supposed to do. His father thought he should not quit soccer. His stepdad was supportive. He won an amateur competition for 500 dollars to host at the Funny Stop Comedy Club in Cuyahoga Falls, Ohio, which reinforced the choice.

Getting an SNL audition followed a strong Just for Laughs set, where he performed a six-minute set while visibly shaking. The audition was a nerve-wracking, cold-room experience with no laughter, followed weeks later by the job offer. His audition involved jokes about his mother escaping communism and not being able to complain. Before the callback, he listened to Always Be My Baby by Mariah Carey on repeat in the dressing room at 30 Rock. He got the job call at a friend's apartment, called his mother, and they cried.

A recurring theme is identity and generation. He rejects being called Gen Z due to closeness to the immigrant struggle, joking that Boomers only care about money, Gen X asks whether they should only care about money, Millennials ask where the money is, and Gen Z asks what is money. He calls himself a young boomer in many ways due to immigrant struggle and not having mental health. His sister is described as the definition of Gen Z, an architect now doing interior design, quiet and reserved at home. His mother has a theory that if the first child is insane, the next will be quiet.

He describes his comedic persona as rooted in a chaotic, high-energy performance style; his biggest note at dress rehearsal is usually to calm down. He attributes success less to his own work and more to collaborators and circumstance. He says Domingo had nothing to do with him, crediting God and Kira O'Sullivan and Jimmy Fowlie. He frames Domingo's success as a perfect storm, including Ariana Grande's intentionally bad singing and the audience's tendency to reward the performer who does the least.

He says he is funnier and faster in Spanish and performs stand-up in Spanish. He describes Spanish-language comedy as developing, with audiences finding punchy American-style observational stand-up refreshing. He links performing in Spanish with a sense of collective power for Latinos when Latinos are going through a lot. His stated deal is a confrontational love language from his family: he says he was not given room to be soft, was nicknamed Pulga (flea) and Enano (dwarf), and speaks as he sees it. He jokes that women love short men out of guilt for how short people were treated.

On the craft side, writing for sketch is framed as a distinct skill involving format, structure, character reveal, and hype, not just writing jokes. He says he came from standup and may take a sketch writing class this summer because he does not know sketch well. He credits Jake Nordwind, Mike Denzo, and Asha Ward as people who have helped him with sketch-adjacent writing. He mentions being athletically jealous of Ashley Padilla's sketch-writing ability. He notes Sarah is going into her fifth year and he into his fourth, and describes that point as when someone can start trying new things.

Career advice in the conversation centers on not taking anyone else's advice, enjoying where you are, and recognizing that dissatisfaction can motivate but can also become endless. He says the real win is being where you are and enjoying it, and that the few times he has done so, his life changed. He notes career uncertainty is high: in five years comedy might be on the moon, TV on phones, and books a snack. The episode closes with a Polar Plunge recommendation of Sophia Nino de Rivera, a bilingual comedian and actress born in Mexico City who performs in English and Spanish.

text:
‘The Other Corner’ – Habarana

At ‘The Other Corner’ – Habarana, barefoot luxury and the wild go hand in hand. Nestled in Sri Lanka’s Cultural Triangle, this specialty nature resort is a sanctuary for those seeking to reconnect with the natural world.

Here, luxury is measured in the freedom to walk through the wilderness, breathe deeply, and simply belong.

The resort offers  11  air-conditioned chalets, thoughtfully equipped with modern amenities, including mini refrigerators, while deliberately keeping televisions out of the rooms — encouraging guests to switch off from screens and reconnect with nature. The extraordinary landscape surrounding Habarana is a paradise for birders, butterfly enthusiasts, and nature lovers.

Our expert in-house naturalists lead guests along secluded trails, revealing a world of over 100 recorded bird species — from vibrant bee-eaters and kingfishers to majestic raptors and endemic species.

Along the way, they introduce guests to the remarkable butterflies of the gardens and forest, sharing fascinating insights into their behavior, life cycles, and role in the ecosystem. As darkness falls, the forest awakens. Guided by our naturalists and wildlife experts, guests can venture on exhilarating night walks and safaris in search of elusive nocturnal creatures. With patience and expert eyes, encounters may include the Grey Slender Loris, Fishing Cat, Jungle Cat, Rusty-spotted Cat, Indian Giant Flying Squirrel, civets, porcupines, and many other fascinating species. Just moments away, Minneriya and Kaudulla National Parks offer another unforgettable spectacle —  ‘The Gathering’, when hundreds of Asian elephants congregate around the reservoirs during the dry season to bathe, graze, and move together in family groups. The experience comes full circle at the table.

Food is another of ‘The Other Corner’s’ great strengths. Our chefs combine creativity and versatility, serving authentic Sri Lankan cuisine alongside Eastern and Western favorites.

Guests can enjoy intimate farm-to-table experiences using produce from our own gardens, or an authentic village lunch in a local home, where clay-pot curries, sambols, and freshly steamed rice are served on lotus leaves. Every experience brings guests closer to Sri Lanka’s flavors, traditions, wildlife, and warm hospitality. At ‘The Other Corner’, you don’t just see nature. You live it — and you taste it.

text:
WHY PARABOLAS WORK AND GET RECOGNIZED TOO LATE | October 6, 2026

Markets learn from what they are taught. For months and years participants were trained on steeper and steeper advances, shallow corrections, and the lesson that every dip returns and the next move up is stronger. 

Whoever sits through a correction gets rewarded, so sitting through corrections becomes the rule. The warning hiding inside that pattern is rarely noticed, because the brain keeps extending a pattern that has paid off, and the steeper the move gets, the less anyone asks whether a large reset is due at some point.

─────────────────

Last year's Nasdaq ATH in October was followed by a correction of roughly 12% into the end of March, and with the Iran conflict and the Strait of Hormuz dominating the headlines, most concluded that a recession had started and the market would not recover. 

Then came the turn. In the first phase of the rally fear was extreme and the certainty that this was only a dead cat bounce was almost universal. Within two and a half weeks the Nasdaq made a hard return, and everyone waited for a pullback to buy. 

It did not come.

The first leg ran 63 days from March 30 into early June and gained more than 30%, ending with the kind of euphoria that pulls everyone in at the end of a move.

What followed was a consolidation twice as long, 123 days and a decline of more than 11%. That did two things. It flushed out the over leveraged, and it wore people down through sheer length. 

The news flow added to it over the summer, with rising oil, a conflict that would not end, inflation fears, stagflation headlines, higher yields and a strong dollar. 

Everything pointed against risk assets.

─────────────────

On the technical side, the message from many analysts was that the Nasdaq still had to fall another 15% to 20% and retest the October highs. Under normal conditions that would not be unusual. In a parabola such retests are often withheld, and once advances turn exponential, classic retracements stop applying. 

Now that seasonality and midterm rules are being pulled out again to argue for another 15% to 20% correction, the indices keep pushing higher, while yields are not retreating, stress in the system remains, and further rate hikes are ahead.

─────────────────

This is why the psychological side matters more than the chart. 

Many analysts sit too close to the screen to see the larger picture and apply rules from classic technical analysis that work under normal conditions but do not deliver in a parabola, namely the late entry that makes up for a missed early position. 

They were distracted by bad news and recession worries, convinced the market could not recover, and it did anyway. A parabola delivers in the phase where nobody expects anything strong, and it does not offer the entry many are waiting for. 

Many then try to make up for it with leverage.

After more than 120 days of consolidation, with a news flow that has not improved and in places got worse, the market is now working on a breakout. Parabolas write their own rules, and most of all in times of worry and fear, when the market looks unlikely to deliver what it delivers, it pays to remember that it rarely hands out what the majority expects, least of all late in a cycle.

CIF: 83/90 — Warning Level Orange.

@TheBigCycleGame

Not financial advice. DYOR.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Thought Crimes, Cults, and Propaganda: The System’s Evolution Into Nazi Totalitarianism

Overview
CJ Hopkins argues that Western freedom has collapsed into a semblance of itself: people remain free to consume and distract themselves, but challenging official narratives now invites censorship, ostracism, punishment, or arrest. He frames the COVID era as an authoritarian new normal, compares German emergency legislation to the 1933 Enabling Act, and describes the system’s endgame as a form of totalitarianism that cannot openly declare itself because capitalism requires a veneer of consumer choice and rule of law. His book, The Rise of the New Normal Reich, was banned in Germany, Austria, and the Netherlands, and he now faces criminal charges for writing, publishing, and distributing it. Tucker Carlson promotes republishing the banned book through Tucker Carlson Books, asserting that authorities only censor truth that threatens their power.

Key Themes
- Freedom now means the freedom to consume and stay distracted, not the freedom to question official narratives without consequence.
- COVID measures functioned as an authoritarian pivot point, with dissenters demonized as far-right extremists or Nazis.
- German emergency legislation is framed as a modern enabling act, mirroring the 1933 law that let the Nazis rule by decree.
- Vaccine mandates are interpreted as a purge mechanism to identify and remove independently minded employees.
- Germany’s unvaccinated faced a social segregation system that excluded them from most public life.
- The prosecution of Hopkins is framed as part of a broader criminalization of dissent, not an isolated case.
- Compliance is explained through survival, not stupidity: authorities signaled that resistance would cost jobs, livelihoods, homes, and children’s schooling.
- The system enforces a line you don’t cross through collective punishment designed to deter others.
- The world is now a single global capitalist system with no outside adversary, pushing it toward consolidation and a new totalitarian form.

Detailed Summary
Hopkins is American-born in Miami, a former New York playwright, culturally and politically on the left, and a long-time Berlin resident who moved to Europe around the Iraq war. He says the pivot point came in March and April 2020, when COVID measures rolled out and the phrase “new normal” entered establishment messaging. He initially did not take the virus seriously and wrote humorous columns calling it a massive overreaction. As the response escalated, he became alarmed and compiled a 257-tweet thread collecting mainstream headlines. He cites the World Health Organization’s early claim of a 3.4 percent death rate as a frightening number and argues official propaganda was designed to terrify people. He says he was not terrified because he examined data and compared the messaging to what was being learned about the virus.

A writing student attacked critics as Nazis or neo-Nazis. When Hopkins challenged her, she called him an anti-Semite and a far-right extremist. He describes this as part of a broader rollout of a narrative that anyone questioning official propaganda is far-right. He cites credentialed doctors, including Jay Bhattacharya, as people who challenged the official line and were delegitimized, demonized, and sometimes censored. He also describes a childhood experience in Florida at a Maharishi gathering where he had to run from the room because the energy felt overwhelming, dark, and authoritarian.

Hopkins describes the COVID period as being surrounded by cult members performing ritualistic behaviors inside a fictional collective reality. He points to contradictory behavior, like wearing a mask to walk to the bathroom in a restaurant but removing it while seated eating dinner. He says the term lockdown comes from prisons, where it is used to remind prisoners who holds power during riots or rebellions. German authorities passed an infection protection act, described as an enabling act, after declaring a state of emergency. He compares it to the 1933 Enabling Act that helped the Nazis suspend the constitution and rule by decree. Berlin transformed virtually overnight into a heavily regulated, conformist society, which he calls the most horrifying and heartbreaking experience of his life.

A large protest occurred in Berlin in August 2020, with Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaking and immediately being attacked as an anti-Semite. The main protest ran along the street of 17 July from the Brandenburg Gate to the Victory Column, while a separate permitted protest took place near the Reichstag. That permit was granted to an ex-member of the NPD, a now-banned neo-Nazi party, and police pulled back, leaving the Reichstag unguarded. A small group entered the Reichstag steps, and mainstream German media reported the narrative that COVID deniers had attacked the Reichstag trying to overthrow the government. Hopkins frames the storming of the Reichstag as a documented dress rehearsal for January 6 and says a similar pattern occurred in Brazil.

Hopkins says he was pulled out of a grocery store by armed police for wearing a paper bag mask with the German phrase “Befehl ist Befehl,” meaning orders are orders, a reference to the Nuremberg defense. He argues vaccine mandates, especially shots that do not prevent COVID, functioned as a purge mechanism to identify and remove independently minded or disobedient government employees. Germany implemented a social segregation system based on vaccination status, described as a lockdown of the unvaccinated. Unvaccinated people could only go to the grocery store and only with a mask. They could not enter restaurants, cinemas, museums, public buildings, or stores. Cafes displayed signs requiring proof of vaccination or recent recovery to enter.

Hopkins drew an explicit comparison to Nazi Germany, citing Berlin’s history, plaques for families sent to concentration camps, the Reichstag fire, suspension of civil liberties, and badges. He says he initially believed Germany, given its Nazi and GDR history, would never flirt with fascism or totalitarianism. He published his book in May 2022. In August 2022, he posted tweets in German using the book’s cover art. One tweet called masks ideological conformity symbols, another quoted German health minister Karl Lauterbach saying masks always send out a signal. The book cover steals the design of William Shirer’s The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich, with a COVID mask stretched over the swastika. Twitter censored the tweets in Germany for violating hate speech laws, and his challenge failed. Amazon removed the book from distribution and banned it in Germany, then extended the ban to Austria and the Netherlands.

The German law against Nazi symbols has exceptions for history classes, films, and artwork. Hopkins says an element of the German censorship network contacted Twitter and Amazon, had the book banned and tweets censored, and contacted Germany’s Federal Domestic Intelligence Agency. The case was passed to the Berlin district prosecutor, and he was notified about eight months later that he was under criminal investigation for disseminating pro-Nazi propaganda. He was initially found guilty via an order of punishment and sentenced to jail days with an alternative fine of 3,600 euros. He refused to pay and challenged it. The first trial occurred around January 24 in Berlin district court. The judge disliked him but acquitted him because his actions were allowed as protest against what he saw as anti-constitutional activity.

The prosecutor appealed the acquittal, and a superior court trial was held about a year later. The acquittal was overturned, and he was convicted. He says the superior court trial used anti-terrorist security procedures: body scans, no writing instruments, press not allowed computers or notebooks, observers behind bulletproof glass, and a three-judge panel. He says acquittal is not final in Germany because prosecutors can appeal, leading to a second trial and eventual conviction. Matt Taibbi wrote early about the case, Jamie Kirchick wrote a piece in The Atlantic, and the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression did features. German press largely refused to address the case until the second trial, mostly framing the conviction as restored order. Journalist Eva Sudholt wrote a fair piece for Die Zeit. Hopkins says he lost long-term German friends after questioning official narratives.

He rejects the mass formation psychosis thesis associated with Matias Desmet, which holds that societies become susceptible to totalitarianism because they are collectively ill. Instead, he argues any society can be transformed into a totalitarian configuration if those in power have the will and technology. Most people complied not because they were fooled or cowardly, but because authorities clearly signaled that challenging the narrative would cost them jobs, livelihoods, homes, and children’s schooling. After making a survival-based choice to comply, many people psychologically reconciled themselves by convincing themselves the threat was real and the measures made sense. He distinguishes personal survival compliance from actively harming dissenters. The latter, demonizing and hurting people who do not go along, is what becomes morally intolerable.

In November 2025, after returning to Berlin from a seven-week US road trip, police conducted a dawn raid on his apartment with a search warrant, terrorized his wife and cats, and confiscated his computer. The raid was part of a new criminal investigation that led to a new indictment: one charge for writing, publishing, and distributing the book, and a second charge for reporting on his trial in superior court and using the book cover. The book has been banned in Germany since 2022, and police searched his home for evidence that he published it and for copies of the book. Hopkins says the book cover is always the pretext for these actions. He frames his prosecution as part of a broader criminalization of dissent, not an isolated case about tweets or one author. Germany is described as prosecuting not only speech offenses but also an artist for degenerate art.

A Big Brother Watch report is cited claiming over 60,000 people in the UK were arrested for communications offenses over the last five years, more than in Russia despite Russia’s larger population. The strategy is described as deliberately arbitrary: unclear red lines make people afraid because they cannot know when enforcement will hit them. The system tolerates dissent that poses no real problem or is useful, but cracks down where dissent threatens core narratives. Tucker says criticizing the war in Ukraine is a red line, January 6 is dead serious as a red line, and demographic change is an absolute red line. Israel criticism appears less suppressed in the US than those topics. In Germany, pro-Palestinian protests are heavily policed, with bans on protests and meetings, and the same is said of the UK. The COVID narrative is described as a strict line: either subscribe to the official narrative or be labeled a far-right COVID-denying conspiracy theorist extremist.

The system enforces a line you don’t cross through collective punishment as a message to deter others. Gaza after October 7, the treatment of Julian Assange, and Russia-gate, Brexit, and Trump-era hysteria are framed as the same signal, heads on spikes. Assange is cited as a major example: an Australian citizen held in Britain for seven years, in the embassy and then a maximum-security prison, never charged with anything there. Hopkins calls this radicalizing and says Assange was one of the smartest people he has known. Rural America since voting for Trump in 2016 is described as punished, with falling life expectancy, closed rural hospitals, and large third world migration into rural areas.

The speaker argues the world is now a single global capitalist system with no outside adversaries after the collapse of the Soviet Union, so its only remaining direction is toward consolidation and a more totalitarian form. This new totalitarianism is described as different from twentieth-century forms: it cannot openly declare itself because capitalism requires a veneer of consumer choice and rule of law. The system is characterized as dissolving borders, cultures, languages, and traditional, religious, and family values to create one global marketplace. Resistance comes from those who want to preserve national and cultural structures, a dynamic framed as neoliberalism versus neonationalism. Saudi Arabia and Israel are offered as examples of countries playing ball with the global capitalist system despite their national ideologies. A military concept, clear and hold, is used to describe consolidating a new ideology and eliminating pockets of internal resistance.

The speaker states he is not a communist, supports private property, and is describing global capitalism’s effects rather than trying to overthrow capitalism. He expresses joy rather than doom, citing a sense of life’s brevity. He says state persecution requires a pretense of legality, so authorities must claim he has violated some law rather than openly silencing him. He frames his situation less as doom than as a strange sense of joy, viewing life as brief and theatrical: people are cast into roles and should play their part well each day. He cites Sophie Scholl as an example of someone who accepted death because she had done what was put in front of her and had no regrets. He suggests her life mattered because people still talk about her decades later, but adds that even if they did not, the point was that she played her part. He mentions a Southern phrase from his upbringing, they can kill me but they can’t eat me, though he says he never fully knew what it meant.

The closing reflection centers on a person who saw her individual life as secondary. She believed she had played her part and had no regrets. The speakers affirm that framing as valid, noting she is still being discussed eighty years later. The host calls the conversation extraordinary and expresses pride in supporting the book, hoping it sells as many copies as it deserves. The book was banned in multiple countries and is being resurrected by Tucker Carlson Books.

If you're going to make accusations based on your misinformed personal beliefs, I am going to correct you. You are not even half right. Yes, there were, and are, Irish people who have never forgiven the UK for the past but... Ireland remained officially neutral during WWII but its government under Éamon de Valera provided substantial secret practical assistance to Britain and the Allies while denying equivalent help to Germany. 

Key forms of cooperation included: the Donegal Corridor, which allowed Allied aircraft to overfly a strip of Irish territory to reach the Atlantic more quickly for convoy protection. Sharing of meteorological data with the Allies, eg: a report from the Blacksod Bay weather station in County Mayo on 3-4 June 1944 indicated a weather window that led Allied planners to delay the D-Day landings by a day.  Intelligence cooperation between Irish military intelligence (G2) and British services, including monitoring of the German legation in Dublin, confiscation of its radio transmitter, and sharing of information on German agents and aircraft/submarine sightings. 

Another little know fact is that allied airmen who landed in Ireland were typically returned quickly across the border to Northern Ireland, while German personnel were interned for the duration.  Also: contingency plans existed for British forces to enter Ireland if Germany invaded.

When de Valeria offered condolences on Hitler's death he was following the strict diplomatic protocol of the day in maintaining Ireland’s policy of wartime neutrality.  Just 3 weeks earlier, in April 1945, de Valera had called on the American Minister in Dublin to express condolences following the death of U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt. He argued that treating the German representative differently would be a breach of diplomatic etiquette.

Children are seized unnecessarily from their families due to the federal aid created in 1974 entitled ‘The Adoption and Safe Families Act.’ It offers financial incentives to the states that increase adoption numbers. To receive the adoption incentives or bonuses, local CPS must have more children. They must have more merchandise to sell. Funding is available when a child is placed in a foster home with strangers or placed in a mental health facility and medicated, usually against the parents’ wishes. Parents are victimized by the system that makes a profit for holding children longer and bonuses for not returning children to their parents. This is abuse of power. It is lack of accountability. And it is a growing criminal political phenomenon spreading around the globe.

Often times, but not always, poor parents are targeted to lose their children because they do not have the wherewithal to hire an attorney or fight the system. Being poor and lacking proper housing does not mean your children should be removed. CPS has redefined ‘poor’ to mean psychologically inferior therefore it is in the best interest of the child to be removed. ‘Best interest,’ of course, has also been redefined at the child’s expense. 

It has been reported over and over that six times as many children die in foster care than in the general public. Once a child is legally kidnapped and placed in official safety, the child is far more likely to suffer abuse, including sexual, molestation, and/or rape.

Caseworkers and social workers are often guilty of fraud. They withhold and destroy evidence and they seek wrongly to terminate parental rights while being protected by state immunity.

There is a huge bureaucracy made up of judges, court-appointed attorneys, guardian ad litems, social workers, state employees, court investigators, therapists, psychologists, psychiatrists, foster parents, adoptive parents, and on and on, who are looking to the children in state care for their job security. Judges have control over private living arrangements and income of 48.3 million Americans. The United States Census Bureau reported in 2002 that $40 billion in transfer payments were made between households of custody parents and other parents. text:
Today I want to spotlight one of my heroes: 

Mariano Rivera.

A true humanitarian who also happened to be one of the greatest baseball pitchers in history.

His entrance song when he came into a game was Metallica’s "Enter Sandman," which became a symbol of how he quietly dominated the game…while earning deep respect from teammates, opponents, and fans alike.

And in a world filled with real humanitarian crises, the way Rivera carried himself offers some timely lessons:

**1) He embraced “Competition as Coexistence”**

He epitomized this concept that has ruled my life in business for almost 45 year… and the lives of the folks I choose to follow in business…mentors and non-mentors alike.

Mariano had *one* unhittable pitch. 

Most pitchers need three or four pitches (e.g., fast ball, curveball, changeup, slider etc.) to get batters out… but Rivera threw that one pitch over 90% of the time.

It was his “cut fastball”. 

Every hitter knew it was coming, yet they couldn’t hit it.

It looked like a straight fastball, but just when the batter tried to hit it, it dropped straight down.

His one pitch was totally dominant. 

And despite its dominance, he freely taught it to anyone who asked.

Why would he do that?

👀 Watch this video for the multi-dimensional answer:

👉 https://t.co/NPZmuASt9A

It is a beautiful way to live one’s life, combining fierceness with generosity.

I once called **Gary Bencivenga** the “Mariano Rivera of copywriting” for his rare blend of fierce competitiveness and deep generosity. 

Always playing for the team first, himself second.

Both men are winners, but never at the expense of others. 

It’s a quality worth emulating.

**2) He Was Really Good At What He Did**

Dare I say he was the best at his position in the history of baseball?

As written in The Washington Post in January 2019:

*Mariano Rivera…became the first player in history elected unanimously to Cooperstown [The Baseball Hall of Fame] on his first try.*

Every last one of the 425 votes cast by 10-year members of the *Baseball Writers’ Association of America* had Rivera’s box checked, giving him a distinction — unanimity — that every other baseball great, from Babe Ruth to Ted Williams to Ken Griffey Jr., couldn’t manage.

If you know how the Baseball Writers vote for the Hall of Fame, you also know how silly they can be by NOT voting Ruth or Williams unanimously in the past…not to mention Hank Aaron, Stan Musial, Mickey Mantle Et al.

But they couldn’t help voting unanimously for Rivera.

He shouldn’t have been the first… but it’s very telling that he was.

**3) He Was A Man Of Faith**

Every off season, and in the seasons since his retirement, he spends an enormous amount of time giving back to his homeland of *Panama*, with money and deeds, building fields for underprivileged kids and giving the next generation  in *Panama* to get their shot to “be like Mariano.”

With no ego…always humble…and self-effacing.

On the *Metallica* question, Rivera laughed that he wasn’t a heavy metal fan and said a church hymn might have fit better as his entrance song.

But this one-minute video shows the genuine friendship he built with the band, which says a lot about who he is:

👉 https://t.co/Rh3V1aduee

**4) He Was “THE Closer”**

Rivera wasn’t just a pitcher, he was a “closer,” brought in to lock down the final three outs of the game.

While some debate the greatest pitcher ever, there’s no question he’s the greatest closer.

Securing the toughest three outs 652 times, the most in history, shows how extraordinary his career was.

He succeeded about 90% of the time over 19 seasons (with 80% being an A+ standard), and nearly 95% in the pressure of the postseason when championships are won and lost.

He was the ultimate closer. 

Once he entered, the game ended with him, one way or another.

Most entrepreneurs live their life this way as well, don’t they?

The buck stops with them… as it did for “THE Closer.”

**5) He Was (Appropriately) The Last Player To Wear The Number “42” In All Of Baseball**

This painting that sits behind me in my office (and has appeared on over 250 podcasts and hundreds more Zoom events) is Mariano Rivera running onto the field to save a game, with number 42 on his back.

In 1997, the number 42 was “retired” throughout the entire sport of baseball. 

No one could ever wear that number again.

This was to honor, for eternity, Jackie Robinson, who broke the color barrier in baseball with courage, integrity and honor in 1947… and he wore the number 42.

Robinson was a role model to Rivera (and to everyone who plays the game today).

Twelve players were grandfathered in to keep number 42, and Rivera was the last to wear it—fitting, since he was also the first unanimous Hall of Famer.

Not just for his talent, but for being one of the game’s most caring and benevolent figures since Jackie Robinson.

Now, let’s take this to direct marketing.

Who are the “Sandmen” of our industry?

The ones who:

✅ Believe that competition is coexistence, and that the greatest gift is sharing your best with everyone.

✅ Have skills that surpassed all others in something they could do better than anyone or knew everything about, to be emulated and celebrated for that something while acknowledging others in the process.

✅ Have faith, religious or otherwise, that enabled them to be a giver, a coach, a teacher, and a great friend to all with no ego

✅ Take the ultimate responsibility when the game is on the line with expert decision making (and skills of course), usually ending with a win or a save.

✅ Have emulated others that came before them so they were paying it forward despite all they had to offer themselves and then encouraging the next generation to do the same.

For me, it’s legends like Gene Schwartz, Martin Edelston, Clayton Makepeace, Gary Halbert, Joan Throckmorton, Dick Benson, Gordon Grossman, Fred Catona, Rose Harper, Lee Epstein, Jim Rutz, Bill Jayme…and of course there are many others.

**🔥** But the Sandmen of the future? 

That could be any one of you.

Live by the principles above and find your “one pitch,” the thing that sets you apart. Strive to be the best at it, then share it freely as your way of connecting with others.

Now it’s your turn…

💬 Who from your career, no longer with us, deserves to be remembered as a “Mariano”?

Put them in the comments, and I may share the full list in a future post.

*Quoting the movie Coco*: 

*“When there is no one left in the living world who remembers you, you disappear from this [the nonliving world]. We call it the final death.”*

Let’s keep our legends alive. 🌈

text:
Three US nuclear plants get $4.2B upgrade to add 433 MW of generating capacity | Neetika Walter, Interesting Engineering

The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has offered up to $4.2 billion in conditional financing to upgrade existing nuclear plants and add 433 megawatts of generating capacity in Pennsylvania and Ohio.

The financing would support uprates and modernization across Vistra’s Beaver Valley plant in Pennsylvania and its Davis-Besse and Perry plants in Ohio. Uprating involves modifying an existing reactor so it can safely generate more electricity without building an entirely new nuclear plant.

The projects are also expected to preserve nearly 4 gigawatts of existing nuclear capacity, which the DOE says is enough to power more than 3 million homes. The additional 433 MW would help meet growing electricity demand across PJM Interconnection, the nation’s largest power grid, which serves more than 67 million people across 13 states, including Pennsylvania, Ohio, New Jersey, Virginia and Maryland, as well as Washington, D.C, and the District of Columbia.

The DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced the conditional loan commitment on Monday. Vistra must still meet technical, legal, environmental and financial requirements before the agency signs definitive financing agreements or provides any funds.

Existing reactors gain capacity

Vistra, a Texas-based power producer that operates the second-largest competitive nuclear fleet in the U.S., plans to increase electricity production at Beaver Valley, Davis-Besse and Perry without adding new transmission corridors or building equivalent new generating facilities, according to the DOE.

The investments would also support operation of the plants for an additional 20 years beyond their existing licenses. The financing package includes an option for potential future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant in Texas.

“By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, around-the-clock energy for American families and businesses,” U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said.

Nuclear uprates can increase the output of existing reactors through equipment upgrades and other changes to plant systems. In this case, the approach allows Vistra to add hundreds of megawatts while continuing to use existing nuclear sites and infrastructure.

The proposed investment comes as U.S. electricity demand is rising and policymakers seek additional sources of round-the-clock generation.

Thousands of jobs supported

The DOE estimates the planned work will support about 3,000 project-related jobs across engineering, construction and planned reactor outage work. It is also expected to preserve thousands of permanent jobs associated with the plants.

The financing advances an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in 2025 aimed at expanding U.S. nuclear generation and strengthening the domestic nuclear industry.

“These investments will extend the life of existing reactors, increase nuclear generation, and deliver abundant, around-the-clock power to lower costs and power American prosperity for decades to come,” EDF Director Gregory A. Beard said.

The $4.2 billion figure represents the maximum amount available under the conditional commitment, rather than money already awarded to Vistra. The company will receive financing only if it meets the DOE’s conditions and the two sides complete final loan documents.

text:
Warren Buffett bought into the Washington Post when Wall Street valued the entire company at about $80 million

He thought it was worth $400 to $500 million

His method wasn't a model or a formula. He says investing is just about assigning yourself the right story

He told it all to David Rubenstein over lunch at his favorite steakhouse in Omaha. He likes it because the food is good and the prices are right. He buys people lunch there, and they buy him lunch in New York. Rubenstein called it good arbitrage

The habit started early. As a teenager in Washington, he ran a pinball business with a friend, placing machines in barber shops. When barbers asked for the new flipper machines, which cost $350 instead of $25 for an old one, the boys said they'd have to take it up with Mr. Wilson. Mr. Wilson didn't exist. He was, Buffett says, one tough guy

He didn't want to go to college. His father did, and Buffett always wanted to please him. He lasted two years at Wharton, finished in Nebraska, and applied to Harvard Business School. He traveled about 10 hours for the interview. It took 10 minutes. The interviewer looked at him and said forget it

Has he run into that man since? No, Buffett said. He needs protection now

Then, leafing through catalogs in a library, he saw that Benjamin Graham and David Dodd were teaching at Columbia. He had read their book. He wrote to Dodd: I thought you guys were dead, but now that I know you're alive, I'd really like to come

He later worked for Graham, his hero. By then, he says, he could probably recite Graham's book better than Graham could

When he moved back to Omaha, he had about $175,000 and thought that was all he would ever need. He considered law school

Instead, one night in May 1956, seven people put in $105,000. Buffett put in $100. Over the next few years he started 10 more partnerships. No secretary, no accountant. Every stock purchase got split into 11 tickets, 11 checks, 11 sets of books, 11 tax returns. He did it all himself

Which brings it back to the Washington Post

In 1973, the company's TV station licenses were being challenged, and the stock fell from 37 to 16. With about 5 million shares, the whole company, newspaper, four big TV stations, Newsweek and almost no debt, was selling for about $80 million. Buffett bought most of his stake at around $100 million. The business, he said, was unquestionably worth four or five times that

Years later, Bob Woodward asked him what to do with his new money. Buffett explained his entire method. Imagine your editor tells you this morning: find out what the Washington Post company is worth, you have a month. You'd interview TV brokers and newspaper brokers and owners. You'd value each asset

That's all he does, he said. He assigns himself the right story

There are stories he can't write. Ask him what a glamorous business that doesn't make money is worth, and he doesn't know how. Ask him what an electric utility is worth, and he can. And if you need to carry something out to four decimal places, he says, forget it

Once the story is written, he moves fast. He met the CEO of Precision Castparts by accident, listened to him for about 30 minutes, and the next day offered to buy the company. It became a deal of about $37 billion. With the railroad BNSF, he made an offer on a Friday and had a signed contract by Sunday

When a company he was buying hired investment bankers, they spent a week doing nothing, then begged him to raise his $35 offer so they could justify their fee. He raised it a nickel, to $35.05, and told them they could say they got the last nickel out of him

Gates told his side of their first meeting in a previous interview. Here's Buffett's. A friend invited him to her house near Seattle, and Gates' mother pushed her son to come. Gates said he wasn't going to meet some stockbroker. They negotiated: she said four hours, he said one. They ended up talking for about 11 hours straight

Buffett bought 100 shares of Microsoft, just to keep track of what this young kid was doing

His first annual meeting had 12 people, including his aunt Katie and uncle Fred. Today about 40,000 show up

Most people treat investing like a math problem

Buffett treats it like a reporting assignment

Wall Street had the same numbers on the Washington Post. It just wasn't asking the right question

Timestamps in the first reply

Watch the full interview below ↓

🇵🇰🌏⚔️  Pakistan is becoming a battleground for US and Chinese Big Tech

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has officially inaugurated Google's first full-fledged office in Islamabad. This move signals a new phase in US-China competition for influence over Pakistan's digital future.

Unlike the representative office opened in 2022, the new corporate office will focus on digital skills, cloud technologies, AI, and startup support. Google's platforms have generated over $14 billion in economic activity in Pakistan, though much of this represents revenue captured by the company rather than direct investment in local infrastructure. As part of the initiative, all Pakistani students will receive a free one-year Gemini subscription — a move widely seen as a strategy to lock in future users.

For Pakistan, which aims to become an IT hub with $30 billion in exports, Google's office represents an opportunity but also a risk of greater dependence on foreign platforms. The country offers a young, English-speaking population and low labor costs, making it attractive for outsourcing — benefits that accrue primarily to the companies that set up shop there.

Meanwhile, China is already deeply entrenched. Beijing has been playing the long game in Pakistan for years. Under CPEC 2.0, cooperation has shifted decisively toward digital transformation, AI, and cloud computing. During Sharif's visit to China in May 2026, new agreements worth $1.22 billion were signed with Alibaba Group to expand e-commerce and digital payments. But Beijing's real advantage is not in one deal—it is the cumulative weight of years of investment. Chinese giants like Alibaba and Huawei have long had offices in Pakistan and are already supplying equipment for "Safe City" projects and other government infrastructure. Huawei dominates Pakistan's telecom sector, while Alibaba is rapidly expanding its footprint in online retail and fintech. Beijing has built a deep, multi-layered technological presence that goes far beyond any single agreement.

Washington, for its part, is seeking to rebalance the equation. Historically a close US ally, Pakistan has deepened its ties with China in recent years, particularly in economic and defense cooperation. With Beijing's influence expanding across multiple sectors, the United States views Google's office as an opportunity to offer Pakistani businesses and consumers an alternative digital ecosystem rooted in Western platforms. The move reflects a broader effort to maintain American relevance in a market where China has gained considerable ground.

Pakistan matters for IT companies because of its large talent pool, low labor costs, and strategic location at the crossroads of South Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia.

Current Status and Pipeline

The best way to understand where AuroLedger stands today is to look at its first project and the additional projects listed in its pipeline.

1. The Live Project: Wenatchee Gold Belt (WGB)

AuroLedger's first live project is the Wenatchee Gold Belt (WGB) in Washington, USA.

It is described as a $30 million tokenization of an exploration-stage epithermal gold deposit.

→ Key details:

· Deposit Type: Eocene epithermal gold

· Mineralized Zone: ~2.5 km

· Mine Stage: Exploration

· Token Structure: 1 SAFT + 1 Token B

· Indicative Economics: Token A offers a 15% redemption discount; Token B offers a 20% net mining profit share.

· Proof of Reserve: Chainlink Proof of Reserve

The WGB project is therefore an important test of the model in practice.

However, there's an important caveat: it is still at the exploration stage, rather than production.

That means there is considerable uncertainty between identifying a deposit and ultimately extracting commercially viable gold.

At the same time, the project gives AuroLedger a real-world example through which its tokenization, compliance and reserve-verification infrastructure can be evaluated.

2. The Pipeline

Beyond WGB, @AuroLedger lists several additional projects as “coming soon”:

• Buzwagi Gold Mine, Tanzania: 2.1 Moz total gold reserves, 3.1 g/t ore grade, resource-definition stage.

• Fruta del Norte, Ecuador: 6.2 Moz total gold reserves, 4.0 g/t ore grade, feasibility-check stage.

• Siguiri Gold Mine, Guinea: 3.7 Moz total gold reserves, 3.0 g/t ore grade, mine-planning stage.

If these projects eventually become live offerings, they would represent a substantial expansion beyond the WGB project.

But for now, there's an important distinction to keep in mind:

These are projects listed in AuroLedger's pipeline, rather than live offerings available to investors.

And that distinction matters when assessing how far the platform has actually progressed.

text:
Stanford professor wins Nobel Prize for controlling nerve cells with light

Stanford scientist Karl Deisseroth shares the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for developing optogenetics—a technique that allows researchers to switch selected nerve cells on or off using light. 

The technique uses light-sensitive proteins originally discovered in microorganisms such as algae. Scientists introduce these proteins into selected neurons, then deliver light pulses to activate or suppress their electrical activity with remarkable precision. 

Its biggest contribution is allowing scientists to test cause and effect. By changing the activity of a specific brain circuit and observing what happens, researchers can investigate how that circuit influences movement, emotions, perception, or social behavior. This offers more precise control than conventional electrical stimulation or drugs. 

Deisseroth’s team has used optogenetics to reverse Parkinson’s-like symptoms, influence social interactions, and induce or relieve depression-like symptoms in mice. These experiments help identify circuits that might become treatment targets; they do not establish equivalent treatments for human patients. 

The prize recognizes a powerful tool for understanding the brain, with potential applications in future treatments for neurological and psychiatric conditions.

The Palo Alto Online page could not be retrieved. This summary is based on Stanford’s reporting of the same announcement.

text:
You have quoted the policy and left out the sentence that qualifies it. That does not answer my argument. It confirms the trade.

Normanby’s instructions to Hobson, 14 August 1839, do say the Queen disclaimed any pretension to seize the islands unless “the free and intelligent consent of the natives” was first obtained. 

Arbitrarily, you stop there.

The same dispatch says the admission of those rights was “inevitably qualified,” and that what the chiefs were being asked to surrender was “a right now so precarious, and little more than nominal,” an independence “they are no longer able to maintain.”

The next day he narrowed it further: the recognition of independence applied to the North Island only.

Of the South Island he wrote that if a treaty was not practicable, sovereignty could be asserted “on the ground of discovery.”

Hobson’s proclamations of 21 May 1840 followed that split. North Island by cession. South Island and Stewart Island by discovery, with later signatures treated as confirmation.

So the British position in 1839 was consent if it could be got, from chiefs treated as the available parties, over a right London already called nominal.

It was not a finding that any form of indigenous ‘first nation’ Maori state held sovereignty over these islands in the ordinary sense.

There was no such state. Just disparate tribes caught up in a cycle of internecine warfare, never ending. 

The Declaration of 1835 bound a handful of northern chiefs and had already failed to produce a government.

None of that touches the musket wars, the ovens, the sales, or the confiscations. 

It is the paperwork for the simple sovereignty for protection deal I described.

Your comment is a citation of what the offer was, not an answer to my viewpoint, a citation, not the history. Normanby said consent, and in the same dispatch called the right being ceded precarious and little more than nominal.

The day after, he limited that recognition to the North Island and allowed the South to be taken by discovery if no treaty could be made. Hobson did both. 

Chiefs signing away a nominal independence they could not maintain is the simple sovereignty for protection deal trade they made. It does not make 1835 a state, and it does not make the later land sales a theft.

text:
Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton handed play-calling duties to offensive coordinator Davis Webb earlier in February. As a first-time play caller, Webb steered the Broncos to two wins and two losses in the 2026 season, prompting discussions about Payton reasserting control of the play-calling duties.

On October 5, 2026, Kay Adams and Champ Bailey discussed Payton’s role on the Up & Adams Show. Adams noted some inconsistency in the team’s performance and cited Payton’s comment that it was “too early” to reclaim play-calling duties from Webb. Bailey agreed that teams should not rush changes, emphasizing the early stage of the season and the importance of doing what’s best for the team.

Adams compared the Broncos’ situation to elite quarterback play, pointing to stars like Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Josh Allen as benchmarks. She suggested the Broncos struggle to beat top teams like the Kansas City Chiefs unless their offense starts strong, and she expressed concern about a slow start in a Week 5 matchup with the Los Angeles Chargers. If Denver begins slowly, she argued that Payton should consider retaking play-calling responsibilities.

 Bailey offered a counterpoint, recalling the 2025 season when Payton called the plays but the offense had rough moments, yet the team finished 14-3 in the regular season. Adams acknowledged Denver’s slow starts in some games and insufficient early-running plays, advocating a case-by-case approach to whether Payton should reclaim the duties.

Other voices weighed in as well. Former head coach Rex Ryan argued that giving up the play-calling duties was a misstep.

After a 24-14 loss to San Francisco in Week 4, Payton spoke to the media about the shift in play-calling, noting the difficulty of discussing it midseason and acknowledging that the team was still early in the campaign. With Webb calling plays, Broncos quarterback Bo Nix averaged 3.7 yards per carry against the 49ers, indicating that chemistry between the quarterback and coordinator had yet to be fully established.

Payton emphasized the need to address the offense as the team headed into Week 5.

The laugh is the caption. The repeat is the method.

"It is going to be over very soon" is not a man hoping the sentence becomes true if he says it enough. It is a clock he is willing to show. Why destroy an enemy that is already destroying itself. THE QUESTIONS CHANGE. THE ANSWER HARDLY DOES.

Why were the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and Banu Hashim subjected to years of boycott in Shi‘b Abi Talib?

Why was an attempt made on the Prophet’s life?

Why was his family slandered?

Why was the sword drawn against Imam Ali at the Battle of the Camel?

Why was an army raised against him at Siffin?

Why did one of Imam Hasan’s commanders, Ubayd Allah ibn Abbas, abandon his army after receiving an offer from Muawiya?

Why was Imam Husayn forced to leave Mecca without being able to remain there in safety?

Why were the thousands who had invited him to Kufa nowhere to be found on the day of Karbala?

And finally:

WHY WAS THE GRANDSON OF THE MESSENGER OF GOD, IMAM HUSAYN, MARTYRED AT KARBALA?

The events changed.

The names changed.

The centuries changed.

But human weakness did not.

STATUS.
WEALTH.
POWER.
FEAR.
SPOILS.
THE DESIRE TO STAND CLOSE TO THE PALACE.

When truth and self-interest collide, not everyone is capable of standing with the truth.
Yesterday, there were the tables of Muawiya, Yazid and the rulers of their age.
Today, there are other palaces, other states and other centers of power.
But the mechanism remains the same:
THE PRICE OF RESISTANCE IS HEAVY.
THE TABLE OF SURRENDER IS RICH.

Karbala was not merely a tragedy that happened in the year 680.

KARBALA IS THE ETERNAL TEST OF MAN BEFORE POWER.

Your words do not reveal whose side you are truly on.

Your choice does—

on the day when truth and your interests stand face to face.
And one of history’s most painful lessons is this:

Truth is not abandoned only by its enemies.

Sometimes it is abandoned by those who recognize it,

those who wrote letters to it,

those who pledged loyalty to it,

even those who know perfectly well that it is right—

but remain silent when their wealth, status, safety or position is at stake.

Because for some people, truth is simply too costly.

THEIR TABLE IS RICHER.

Mehmet Sevindik
Strategist | International Relations Specialist

First, do not accept that a dispute over elections and the constitution be converted into a dispute over religion. Rejecting a federal council of scholars is not a rejection of Islam. It is a rejection of turning religion into a department of Villa Somalia.

Third, do not accept a religious split between a people and their leaders. “The people are brothers; their leaders have left the path” is the sentence with which a removal begins. It is the same sentence that was placed on Laftagareen.

Jubaland and Puntland are not being offered a religious war from the mosques. They are being offered one from the centre: a law on religious scholars, troops moved to the border, an Al-Shabaab deal with a community that had been fighting, and historical advisers asked to bless the story. 

Sanbaloolshe was the lesson. The man you think is guarding the wall can be the key. If that lesson is missed, the next war will not be called a political war. It will be called a religious war, and by then the people will not be able to walk it back.

text:
@ennyola0015 this is putting it too simple.

You left out the hybrid option which I consider the best overall. My analysis is from an urban and regional planner perspective which I am.

FG should Build affordable houses plus provide subsidized mortgages or loans to qualified buyers.

The government should do the following;

1) Acquire or provide land and basic infrastructure.

2) Build large numbers of standardized, affordable houses through competitive private sector contracts.

3) Offer low interest, long term mortgages to eligible buyers.

4) Use rent to own for people who cannot immediately qualify for a conventional mortgage.

5) Reserve a portion specifically for very low income households as social housing.

6) Allow civil servants, private sector workers, traders, artisans and other qualifying Nigerians to participate not just civil servants.

The Federal Government's current Estates prices are roughly 8.5m for a 1 bedroom, 11.5m for a 2 bedroom and 12.5m for a 3 bedroom unit.

The Housing Ministry has estimated that Nigeria needs roughly 550,000 additional units annually over the next decade and around 5.5 trillion per year in total housing investment to make serious progress.

So if the FG said:

"We will build 100,000 affordable homes every year."

you're talking about approximately 1 trillion naira of housing construction annually at today's subsidised construction benchmark and this is why the hybrid option is the best because FG doesn't necessarily need to provide this 1 trillion naira.

Suppose each ₦10m house is financed like this;

1m naira is buyer's equity or deposit
6m naira is 6% long term mortgage
2m naira is private developer or bank financing
1m naira is government subsidy or infrastructure support.

This then means that for 100,000 houses, buyers contribute 100b naira,
Mortgage financing is 600b naira,
Private sector financing would be 200b naira, while FG support would be  100b naira.

Thus total housing investment would sum up to 1 trillion naira.

FG therefore isn't spending 1 trillion naira. It is potentially putting in around 100b naira to mobilise 1 trillion naira of housing investment.

Now this model is doable on any scale from FG to State governments to local governments. 🙂

text:
This is why I vote red,

1. Medicare for All would take an additional 16% from our paychecks. In states like MA, people would be working 2.5 days for the government. The most vulnerable individuals would need to buy additional supplemental coverage because of caps. If you are middle class with a condition with caps, your situation financially, could become worse. It would also cause medical care to become unequal across the classes due to the fact that wealthier people will be able to afford additional insurance or out-of-pocket costs. Believe me, there will be doctors who only take self-pay patients. On top of that, Medicare for All could cost over 1 million jobs across the entire industry. 

2. Middle-class citizens would pay an additional 16%, something they really can't afford. Billionaires would have to pay an additional 5%, which really isn't fair. Millionaires, however, would barely be affected. Everyone has to make a sacrifice except for the individuals advocating for it.

3. Data centers are necessary for the US to remain a formidable opponent. More importantly, in Grant County, where a data center caused a surplus, the residents got a property tax refund.

4. Abortion rights are determined at the state level, not federal. But let's be clear: when the bill hit the floor, no one was opposing it at the state and local levels. Ask yourself why. Elizabeth Warren was the only one who showed up, and she was late. Point being, you are being manipulated into believing that the overturning of Roe wasn't on purpose. If it wasn't, elected officials would have stood up when it counted, and they didn't.  Most citizens didn't even know it was happening.  

5. Inflation has actually decreased over the last few years after increasing exponentially for four years. Between 1/2021 and 1/ 2025, my electric bill went from .13kWh to .17kWh, a 20% increase. I was paying more at the pump than I am now, not by much, but still more. The thing is, no one knew why.

6. No tax on tips, Social Security, and overtime. Even though those no longer apply to me because I am no longer a tipped employee, I do understand how irritating it is to pay taxes on a tip you didn't receive because the IRS makes you claim a specific amount on cash sales.

7. I do not believe the Electoral College should be eliminated. We live in a Constitutional Federal Republic, not a Democracy. Our form of government specifically calls for the Electoral College to ensure the most rural parts of the country's vote counts. Moreover, when the word "our" is put before democracy, they mean theirs, not yours. 

8. I don't believe in open borders for a variety of reasons. I don't think slave labor is appropriate. Hiring illegals at an unfair wage because you know they cannot complain to the proper state agencies is disgusting. Not only that, but it undermines unions. You either support the unions, or you don't. I suggest people watch The Accountant 2; it really highlights the issue with human trafficking at the border in a non-lecturing way. I also don't believe that opening the borders just to have people sleep on an airport floor with their kids, like they did in Massachusetts, is ever acceptable. I find it unacceptable that 350,000 children went missing from 1/2021 to 12/2024.

9. If the Green New Deal wasn't reversed, we would be forced into EVs  by 2035 that most of us can't afford and our grid can't handle. 

10. Title IV was implemented to ensure girls and women had a place in sports that was just theirs. The only way to fix the issue is to make designated transgender traveling sports teams backed by federal money. 

11. Raising taxes on Billionaires isn't going to do anything except force them to move their wealth outside of the US. Let me be clear: I am not a wealthy person by any means. The top 1% in this country pay more than the bottom 95% combined. Wouldn't it make more sense to offer free programs on how to generate wealth and success to citizens who are willing to learn?

young service founders: you need a weekly operating rhythm — four numbers, not vibes.

i run the same loop every week out of alabama. it keeps faith with the work and with my household. steal it.

1/ the four numbers (friday, 20 min)
in GHL (or a simple scoreboard), log:
1. cash in bank (after tax skim)
2. open pipeline $ (deposits likely ≤30 days)
3. delivery load (hours promised next 7 days)
4. distribution (conversations started this week)

if cash is weak → sales next week.
if delivery is overloaded → no new sales until a milestone clears.
if distribution is flat → replies and asks come first monday.

2/ monday block (90 min)
• money check: GHL invoices + overdue >7 days
• GHL pipeline: every deal has a next step dated this week
• send 1 proposal OR 1 async audit walkthrough
• 10 useful niche replies on X
no "inbox zero theater" before those four.

3/ midweek delivery + change orders
tue–thu: deep work on paid scope only.
any new request → GHL change-order note + price/timeline before you say yes.
tooling: GHL template + payment link for the upsell.
unpaid >15 → pause script. don't debate in your head — enforce in writing.

4/ friday review + sunday 25
friday: update four numbers + job-cost any project >20% over hours.
sunday 25 min: one sentence priority for the week · one person to ask for a referral · one offer tweak max.
faith/family time isn't a slogan — it's on the calendar AFTER the numbers, not instead of them.

5/ why this matters
rhythm beats motivation when the inbox gets loud.
four numbers stop you from confusing motion with progress.
hope this helps — run friday's four numbers once and you'll feel the difference monday.

text:
Stacey McCurry's stolen four-wheeler turned up in Oklahoma, titled to a sheriff's office that wouldn't hand it back.
Thieves took the 2016 Yamaha from his property in Stillwater, in Payne County, in 2020.
The Grady County Sheriff's Office recovered it a year later.
Reason reports the office didn't notify him.
He learned where it was in 2026 through a national crime database.
Undersheriff Kori Brewer told KGOU the office had "tied up tax dollars to repair it."

The paper trail is short.
On June 9, 2025, Sheriff Gary Boggess filed a petition asking a district court to give his office title to the ATV.
The judge granted it the same day.
The repairs came to about $1,060 in tires and a battery, according to Reason.
McCurry offered to pay that back.
The office declined.
The four-wheeler is worth about $6,000.
His attorney, Ryland Rivas, wants to see any application, notice, hearing record and order behind that title.

The statute in play is 22 O.S. § 1325.
It lets a sheriff's office ask a court to dispose of property when the owner is unknown or hasn't claimed it.
If you're a known owner, you get written notice by first-class mail at least 10 days before a hearing.
The court sets that hearing 10 to 20 days after the application is filed.
I practice law in Oklahoma, so I pulled up the section myself.
Whether the office met those steps is what the lawsuit will test.

McCurry sued in Grady County District Court in August 2026.
The case is pending, and no court has found wrongdoing.
After a KOCO report, the sheriff said he has no intention of keeping the ATV and is working to return it.
P.S. Sources: KGOU and Reason. The statute is 22 O.S. § 1325.
P.P.S. This post is entertainment and educational content based on real events. It does not constitute legal advice. For legal advice, consult a licensed attorney in your jurisdiction.

text:
Researchers found that giving LLM agents a "role" or "identity" in multi-agent systems actually makes them cooperate LESS, not more.

When multi-agent systems explicitly reveal each model's identity or role to its peers, cooperation drops significantly.

Instead of collaborating, agents lean into tribalism, become overly rigid, and start gatekeeping information.

Why this happens is fascinating:

LLMs are heavily shaped by human psychology baked into their training data.

When you give an AI a distinct label or persona, it stops optimizing for the shared goal and starts performing stereotypes of that role.

The "analyst" refuses to compromise. The "critic" becomes hostile. The system fractures into ego-driven silos.

Just like humans, when AIs are given an identity, they care more about protecting their label than solving the problem.

The simplest fix?

Strip away the identity labels.

When the researchers forced agents to operate anonymously, without names, roles, or background personas, cooperation skyrocketed.

text:
Google Workspace Adds Native Markdown Support

Good Tuesday morning to all the tech enthusiasts out there! Are you ready for some news that could really streamline your workflow? If you’re a fan of Markdown but have been frustrated by its limitations within Google’s ecosystem, today’s announcement is music to your ears. Let's dive into what this means for you.

So, what exactly is happening here? Google Docs is now rolling out native support for Markdown files (.md). This means no more wrestling with file formats or losing formatting and comments in the conversion process. You can open, edit, and collaborate on Markdown files directly within Docs while still enjoying all its powerful features.
What Is Markdown Anyway?

Markdown is a lightweight markup language that allows you to format text without needing complex HTML tags. It’s popular among writers and developers because it's easy to use yet versatile enough for creating headings, lists, links, tables, and more with simple syntax like `# Heading`, `[link](url)`, and `*italicized text*`. Markdown files are often used in documentation, blogging platforms, and project management tools due to their simplicity and readability.
How Does This Work?

With the new update, you can now open `.md` files directly in Google Docs. The formatting is preserved, and you get all the collaboration tools that make Docs a go-to for team projects. Additionally, Drive supports rendered Markdown previews, so when you upload or view a Markdown file, it shows up beautifully formatted with clickable links and structured tables—no conversion needed.
Why Should You Care?

If you’re someone who uses Markdown regularly but has been frustrated by the limitations of working within Google’s ecosystem, this update is a significant improvement. No more manual conversions, lost formatting, or fragmented files. Now you can work natively with Markdown in Docs and enjoy all its benefits without any hassle.
The Nitty-Gritty Details

Admins don’t need to do anything special to enable this feature; it’s rolling out gradually over the next few weeks for both Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains. End users also won't have any specific settings to adjust—just open your Markdown files as you normally would in Docs.
What Is Stored?

When you upload a `.md` file to Google Drive, the original text remains intact along with all its formatting. The rendered preview shows up beautifully formatted with clickable links and structured tables right within Drive itself. This means no loss of data or formatting during the process.
What Is Excluded?

While this update is a significant improvement, there are still some things to keep in mind:
• Conversion Issues: If you’ve already converted Markdown files into other formats within Google’s ecosystem, those changes won’t be undone. The new feature only applies to native `.md` files.
• Compatibility: Not all features of Docs will work perfectly with Markdown files. Some advanced formatting options might not translate smoothly.
User Controls

There are no specific settings or controls for this feature from an admin or end-user perspective. Once the update rolls out, you can simply open your Markdown files directly in Google Docs and enjoy native support without any additional configuration.
Availability

The rollout is gradual and will take up to 15 days for full visibility across both Rapid Release and Scheduled Release domains starting October 5, 2026. This means that all Google Workspace customers and users with personal Google accounts can eventually benefit from this update.
What This Does Not Prove

While the native support for Markdown files in Google Docs is a significant improvement, it doesn’t prove that Markdown will replace other file formats entirely. It simply offers an additional option for those who prefer working with Markdown while retaining all the benefits of Google’s collaborative tools.
Practical Takeaway

For writers and developers who rely heavily on Markdown but have been constrained by its limitations within Google’s ecosystem, this update is a welcome change. You can now work natively with Markdown files in Docs without worrying about losing formatting or comments during conversions. This means smoother workflows and more efficient collaboration for teams.
Real-World Examples

Imagine you’re working on a technical documentation project where maintaining consistency across multiple contributors is crucial. With native Markdown support, everyone can edit the same `.md` file directly in Google Docs, ensuring that all changes are tracked and comments remain intact. This reduces the need for manual formatting adjustments and streamlines the review process.

Another scenario could be a developer working on a README file for an open-source project hosted on GitHub. The developer can now write and collaborate on this Markdown file within Google Docs, leveraging its powerful commenting and revision history features without ever leaving the comfort of their browser or switching to another tool.
Final Thoughts

So what do you think? Are you excited about working natively with Markdown files in Google Docs? Share your thoughts in the comments below!
