text:
Sumatra is the Indonesia most people never quite reach — and that’s exactly why it still feels wild. Venture into the lush rainforests of Sumatra, where the critically endangered Sumatran tiger still roams.  Wake up to orangutans swinging through the canopy in Gunung Leuser. Drift across Lake Toba, the world’s largest volcanic lake, ringed by the Batak highlands. Hike toward the crater of Mount Sibayak or watch the sunrise over Mentawai waves that surfers still call their secret. Rice terraces, jungle rivers, and coastal villages that haven’t been polished for mass tourism sit just a flight from Medan or Padang.  From incredible wildlife encounters to vibrant local culture, Indonesia offers adventures like no other and @Capricorn_Vacay  will help planning your dream journey!

text:
Democratic socialism’s $50 trillion price tag
A hole big enough to bury the American economy

This is the dystopian, dangerous reality of the DSA’s utopian vision. Every “free” promise comes back as a higher mortgage rate, a bigger tax bill, a smaller paycheck and a deadlier street.

The White House Council of Economic Advisers has weighed and measured the Democratic Socialists of America’s agenda and found it wanting, to the tune of a $52.8 trillion federal fiscal burden over 10 years, or about $49 trillion after crediting a billionaire wealth tax.

Just how big is a $49 trillion DSA budget hole? Deep enough to bury the American economy.

Under the Congressional Budget Office’s baseline, debt held by the public is already on track to reach 120% of gross domestic product by 2036. Borrow that $49 trillion to cover the DSA deficit, and that ratio more than doubles, to 254%. Interest payments alone could exceed projected federal revenue.

That is the macro picture. Now for the micro.
The Council of Economic Advisers modeled all eight pillars of DSA’s 2026 program. Seven carry direct fiscal and budget consequences, totaling a crushing $52.8 trillion in potential federal costs and lost revenue before factoring in a billionaire wealth tax that comes nowhere close to covering the deficit. The eighth pillar carries a human cost.

“Medicare for All” is the Big Kahuna. It adds $47.4 trillion to federal deficits. Canceling all student debt and making tuition free at every college would cost $3.6 trillion.

Add roughly $530 billion more for open borders and mass amnesty.

How about a 32-hour workweek with no cut in pay? That costs $918 billion in lost federal revenue, cuts 4.2 million to 6.9 million jobs, concentrated among workers earning $14 to $24 an hour, and pushes unemployment from 4.1% to between 6.6% and 8.2%.
Advertisement

Then there is the Green New Deal. It costs the Treasury $370 billion in lost tax revenue. The far larger hit, more than $12 trillion over 25 years, lands on families and businesses through higher electricity, heating and car costs. Add rent control, and the gross DSA policy total is $52.8 trillion.

To fill that DSA fiscal hole, Washington must either borrow the money or take it from you in higher taxes.
Borrow it, and America’s deficit rises from 5.8% of GDP to more than 21%. The 10-year Treasury yield rises by nearly 6 percentage points, and 30-year mortgage rates could top 12%.

Meanwhile, the Council of Economic Advisers estimates that inflation would climb into double digits — and could rise as high as 160% over the next 10 years. The reason is simple: When Washington spends trillions of dollars that it has no plan to repay, that money chases the same goods, and investors expect the debt to be inflated away. Either way, prices rise.

Tax Americans to plug the DSA fiscal gap, and the math is no kinder. Income tax collections would have to rise to about 2.6 times current levels, and the average effective individual tax rate would jump from 14% of adjusted gross income to nearly 40%.

Meanwhile, the effective corporate rate jumps from 11% to 30%.

The Council of Economic Advisers’ model shows the capital stock shrinking by 11.5%, labor hours falling by 16.2%, and real GDP permanently 14.6% smaller. After-tax hourly wages drop 28.4%, about $22,000 a year for the average household.

That is an American economy on life support. Now here is the human body count.

DSA calls for steps toward “fully abolishing the police and prison system.” The research the Council of Economic Advisers cites is blunt. Every 1% cut in police presence raises homicides by about two-thirds of a percent, and the dead are disproportionately Black. Per capita, the homicide effect of police staffing is twice as large for Black victims as for White ones.

This is the dystopian, dangerous reality of the DSA’s utopian vision. Every “free” promise comes back as a higher mortgage rate, a bigger tax bill, a smaller paycheck and a deadlier street.

Gallup found in August that 57% of Americans ages 18 to 34 now view socialism favorably. These are exactly the Americans that the DSA agenda would hit hardest. It is their generation that would inherit a debt more than twice the size of the economy.

The Trump agenda offers the alternative: Build, produce and reward work. A manufacturing economy defended by tariffs that offers rising real wages and job security while bolstering our national security. Safe cities. A border closed to human traffickers, drug traffickers, terrorists and interlopers driving down wages and stealing American jobs.

This November’s midterm elections are very much a referendum on the Trump agenda versus the DSA agenda. Put the Senate and House in the hands of the Democrats, and the DSA agenda moves from the fringe to the floor.

In today’s Democratic Party, DSA members and their allies win primaries: Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee in Florida; Darializa Avila Chevalier, Brad Lander and Claire Valdez in New York; Melat Kiros in Colorado; Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania. text:
Detroit has a second road network about 1,200 feet below the first one.

Not sewers.

Roads.

More than 100 miles of them run through the Detroit Salt Mine, which spreads beneath more than 1,500 acres of the city.

Getting down there was a nightmare before anyone could enjoy the privilege of mining salt beneath Michigan.

Salt was discovered in the area in the late nineteenth century. A company began sinking a shaft through glacial deposits and rock, ran into serious engineering trouble and spent enough money to go bankrupt before reaching the deposit.

That is a painful way to confirm that the salt really is down there.

The operation that followed eventually reached it, and mining developed into the underground world that exists today. Huge rooms are cut through the salt while large pillars are left behind to hold up the roof.

Then there is the machinery.

Anything too large for the shaft has to be taken apart above ground, lowered piece by piece and rebuilt underground.

Detroit somehow managed to turn salt mining into an assembly job.

Loaders and trucks then travel through a road network beneath a city famous for building vehicles above it. The rock salt they remove is used for things such as keeping icy roads passable in winter.

The mine is still active, but public tours are not offered.

The shaft entrance is on Sanders Street.

Drive past it and there is very little to suggest that another Detroit begins 1,200 feet below you.

text:
Stuff like this really makes you hate politics, because the attitude is basically: let them take out Los Angeles or San Diego, right? Never mind the fact that there are probably people who support him living there too; simply because they reside in the wrong locality, they are treated as expendable. Yet, we cannot talk about anyone taking out Israel, no matter the shaky footing we've been on for ages regarding geopolitical relations and resource management. This is coming from a sitting U.S. president. Unfortunately, plenty of people will eagerly cheer and swallow this whole because they are completely bought into the red-versus-blue continuum.

At this point, if you aren't entirely black-pilled on the political system as it stands, I don't know what it will take to wake you up. There is virtually nothing that makes this situation reconcilable through ordinary political means. I'm not saying conflict or total collapse is something I'm rooting for, it truly isn't; and I believe maintaining the status quo for the sake of stability is far preferable to watching the entire structure crumble. At the same time, you have to look at reality: even the safe play of maintaining the two-party theater isn't functioning anymore. The extremes are stretching further apart, and the political center now thoroughly dominated by discourse demanding unconditional support for Israel at the expense of our own domestic stability, has completely displaced what used to be a pragmatic, moderate middle ground.

It raises the fundamental question: where do we go from here? Most people lack the political nuance required to synthesize a coherent worldview across both left and right without treating the entire ordeal like a tribal football match. It is an exhausting and depressing place to be, because all roads appear to point toward systemic breakdown. In that kind of fallout, you don't get a sudden restoration of sanity; you just get a resumption of the same destructive dynamics. You are effectively forced to participate in the charade regardless of which side you lean toward, unless you choose to disengage completely. But opting out simply allows the existing machinery to grind forward unimpeded.

The entire apparatus is untenable. The cost of living is suffocating, mass surveillance continues to expand, and Silicon Valley power brokers have successfully courted both political factions, playing them against each other like a synthetic skin they can shed whenever convenient. Now, the broader economy is propped up by their prized speculative asset, generative AI, which artificially inflates valuations and underpins systemic stability. If that bubble bursts, the fallout will cascade across every sector due to how hyper-concentrated institutional investment has become; all while baseline costs for healthcare and housing remain out of reach.

This is why systemic breakdown feels inevitable. If you weren't preparing yesterday, you are already behind. Yet even if you have prepared, the crisis moves at a paradoxical pace: fast enough to demand urgent mobilization, but slow enough to gradually bleed your resources dry before the climax arrives. 

Ultimately, clear solutions are hard to find. Many have bowed out because the polarization completely drowns out rational voices. Platforms like twitter, which once offered a viable digital town square, have been distorted by ideological vanity. While the previous administration operated with a similar disregard, the current trajectory feels more reckless because the execution is so overtly ham-fisted. The only silver lining is that this lack of subtlety makes the institutional machinery painfully obvious, machinery that used to operate discreetly under far more polished, deceptive management.

text:
Gulliver accounts tower on Instagram and TikTok

Did you wake up to a flurry of notifications about something called "Gullivers"? If not, you might be missing out on the latest social media craze sweeping through Instagram and TikTok. So, what exactly are these towering figures that everyone's talking about?
The Rise of the Giants

The term “Gulliver” comes from Jonathan Swift’s classic novel *Gulliver's Travels*, where the protagonist encounters various miniature and giant societies. In today’s social media parlance, Gullivers are users who present themselves as towering figures compared to regular-sized humans. These accounts have been popping up all over Instagram and TikTok, drawing in curious followers like moths to a flame.

Two notable examples include Emma Tallgirl on Instagram and VeryTallGinna on TikTok. Their accounts are flooded with images and videos showcasing these towering figures, often in everyday situations that highlight just how large they appear compared to normal-sized humans. For instance, one video shows a Gulliver dwarfing cars or walking through city streets where buildings look like tiny dollhouses.
Why Are People Obsessed?

So what’s the appeal? First off, it's a clever way to play with perspective and scale. Gullivers offer a fresh take on familiar scenes by exaggerating size and proportion. It's like seeing your mundane life through a funhouse mirror. Plus, there’s an element of novelty and surprise—seeing someone towering over buildings or dwarfing cars is just plain entertaining.

But it’s also about community and shared experience. Followers connect over the absurdity and creativity of these posts, forming a kind of digital tribe united by their fascination with giants. It's like being part of a secret club where everyone gets to marvel at something extraordinary together.
The Technical Side

Creating Gulliver content isn’t just about imagination; it requires some technical know-how too. Many creators use augmented reality (AR) tools or post-production software to make these illusions possible. Apps like Snapchat and TikTok offer AR filters that can stretch a person’s image, making them appear much larger than life. It’s all about blending the real with the surreal.

For instance, Emma Tallgirl might use an app that stretches her body vertically while keeping her head in proportion. This creates the illusion of towering over everything around her. Similarly, VeryTallGinna uses TikTok's AR filters to make herself appear gigantic in everyday settings like parks or city streets.
What Is Stored and Excluded

When you dive into Gulliver content, what exactly are you looking at? The accounts typically store a mix of edited images and videos that showcase the creators as towering figures. These posts often include everyday scenes where the creator appears to dwarf cars, buildings, and other objects. However, they exclude any raw or unedited footage showing the actual size of the person.
User Controls

If you’re intrigued but want to keep things in perspective, there are ways to manage your exposure to Gulliver content. You can follow specific accounts that interest you without getting overwhelmed by a constant stream of exaggerated proportions. Additionally, most social media platforms allow you to customize your feed and mute or hide posts from certain users if they become repetitive.
Availability

Gulliver content is widely available on Instagram and TikTok. Simply search for popular Gulliver creators like Emma Tallgirl (@emmatallgirl) and VeryTallGinna (@verytallginna), and you’ll find a plethora of entertaining posts to explore. However, it’s worth noting that the trend might not be as prevalent on other social media platforms.
What This Does Not Prove

While Gulliver content is visually impressive, it doesn’t prove anything about real-world proportions or physical capabilities. The illusions are heavily edited and rely on AR filters, so what you see isn’t always a true representation of reality. It’s important to remember that the appeal lies in the illusion rather than actual size.
Practical Takeaway

So what changes for you? If you’re into social media trends and enjoy a good laugh at exaggerated proportions, Gullivers are definitely worth checking out. But if you prefer your content grounded in reality, this might just be another fleeting fad that passes by without much impact on your daily feed.
Privacy and Data Considerations

While the trend is fun to watch, it’s important to consider privacy rules and data handling practices. Social media platforms have strict guidelines about sharing personal information and ensuring user safety. Gulliver creators must adhere to these regulations when posting content that might attract a wide audience. Users should also be cautious about oversharing their own information while engaging with such trends.
Final Thoughts

The digital world is always evolving, and the latest trend of Gulliver accounts shows no signs of slowing down anytime soon. Whether it’s a long-term phenomenon or a brief blip, one thing is clear: these giants are here to stay for now. So go ahead, take a peek at some of those towering figures, and see if they capture your imagination.

What do you think? Are Gullivers the next big thing in social media, or just another passing trend? Share your thoughts in the comments below!

text:
Rupert Lowe is simply disgusting.

In yet another of his divisive, inflammatory, misleading tweets he accuses the police of going to “astonishing” lengths “to import these men”, calls 149 people brought in from the Channel “third world invaders”, declares their housing “treason”, and promises prison for any official who “knowingly placed unvetted dangerous criminals in our communities”.

Precisely none of it survives contact with the record, and some of it is contradicted outright.

On Sunday a small boat that had set out from Normandy reached the Hampshire coast. @RNLI lifeboats brought 149 people ashore at Gosport that evening. The government said the migrants would be transported to “short term holding facilities in Kent where they will be processed as normal and undergo stringent health, security and biometric checks.” This was the second attempt: on 22 September, a planned landing in Gosport was called off and that boat’s occupants were taken to Dover by sea.

Hampshire police used two powers. A Section 14 Public Order Act condition directed protesters to Walpole car park until 4pm on Monday. A Section 34 dispersal order covering the whole town runs until 7am on Tuesday. Police said officers were there to support the emergency response at sea and to facilitate peaceful protest.

Lowe called Sunday “a humiliation for the British people”, but he says nothing about what happened on Gosport’s own streets.

Police put the crowd at around 350 over the evening; a BBC report the next morning said about 150 had tried to get into the former naval base where the boats were due. Police officers were treated for injuries. Twelve people were arrested on suspicion of offences including assaulting a police officer, affray, criminal damage and racially aggravated public order. One man was arrested on suspicion of obstructing a highway after ambulances were prevented from travelling along Clayhall Road.

An MP who campaigns on law and order found no words for injured officers or obstructed ambulances. Just think about that. Decent British people who risk their wellbeing on the frontline, upholding our laws and helping the sick and injured, are not even deemed worthy of a mention.

His contempt was not for whoever injured officers that night, but for two groups: the police who held the line, and the people brought in from the sea.

The only mention of officers in his post is the claim that they went to astonishing lengths “to import these men”. Police who stood on a cordon on a Sunday night, some of whom were injured doing it, got an accusation from him instead of thanks.

Whether a dispersal order covering an entire town was proportionate is a fair question. But Lowe never asks that. He presents the policing as proof that the establishment arranged the landing. But the boat was already in the Channel when the order was made.

Policing a crowd around a landing tells you how that crowd was managed. It tells you nothing about why the boat came, and Lowe offers no other evidence.

I could find no published breakdown of the nationalities of the 149, so “third world” is Lowe’s own assumption. “Invaders” conjures armed conquest. These people were taken off a dinghy by volunteer lifeboat crews and put on coaches.

“Treason”, under the Treason Act 1351, includes levying war against the Crown and helping its enemies. The Treason Felony Act 1848 covers plotting to depose the monarch, to levy war in order to force a change of policy, or to stir a foreigner to invade by force. A critic might say that receiving small boats is the last of these: that processing and housing the arrivals is what brings the next boat. The Act does not say that. It was written for encouraging a hostile armed entry, and it requires an intention to bring one about. A civil servant applying an asylum law passed by Parliament has neither the force nor the intention.

These are category errors, and they work together. A moral panic needs folk devils, and it needs someone to blame for letting them in. “Invaders” supplies the first and “treason” the second, recasting officials who follow the law as enemies of the nation. Words like that, aimed at public servants on the night police officers were injured in the street, should be judged by what they do to an angry audience.

Small-boat arrivals are not screened before they reach shore, and some past arrivals have turned out to have serious criminal records. That is a real weakness in the system. But the government’s stated process for these 149 was transfer to Kent for health, security and biometric checks.

Lowe produces zero evidence that any of them has been identified as dangerous, and none that any official knowingly placed a dangerous person anywhere.

If Lowe means officials who wilfully abuse their position, the law already covers misconduct in public office, and he would need evidence he has not offered. If he means officials who applied the asylum law as it stood, he needs something much darker.

Restore Britain’s policy paper, Mass Deportations: Legitimacy, Legality, and Logistics, which Lowe presents and endorses, proposes leaving the European Convention on Human Rights, repealing the Human Rights Act, and passing a “Great Clarification Act” so the Commons can overturn court rulings by simple majority. Leaving the Convention would remove Article 7’s international ban on retrospective punishment. As far as I can find, the paper does not set out a prosecution of officials. That pledge is his.

What would remain is the common law presumption, affirmed by the House of Lords in Waddington v Miah (1974), that criminal statutes do not reach back to punish conduct that was lawful when it happened. It is a presumption only, and Parliament can override it with express words.

Taken at its word, Lowe’s pledge would need a Parliament willing to make past lawful work into a present crime, and then to jail the civil servants who did it: retrospective punishment of the state’s own employees for obeying the state.

The principle that pledge would breach has a history worth knowing. In July 1934, after the Night of the Long Knives, the Nazi regime passed a law declaring the killings retrospectively lawful. In June 1935 it amended the criminal code so that an act could be punished by “analogy” if it offended “the fundamental idea of a penal law and healthy popular sentiment”, even where no statute covered it.

In Stalin’s Soviet Union, officials who had loyally carried out one party line were recast as wreckers and enemies of the people when the line changed. Formally they were charged with sabotage or treason; in substance, their offence was obedience to the state as it had been, judged by the state as it had become.

Lowe is proposing neither purges nor show trials, and the comparison has limits. His paper still assumes a Parliament, a majority and express words. But a Parliament that expressly overrode the common law presumption to jail civil servants for processing asylum claims under the law then in force would be making the move those regimes made: legality made to depend on who later holds power. The danger lies in what those words would be asked to do.

Lowe ends his post by insisting that “We need to deport millions, and send those responsible to prison. It’s that simple.”

Really?

He said something very different when launching Restore Britain as a party in February. He told supporters that it was “not offering you a miracle cure”, that its programme would require discipline, courage and patience, that “it will be painful”, and that he would “always be honest with you about the extent of the task ahead.”

On 16 March he wrote of his party’s 113-page mass deportation policy: “It is complicated - it requires a lot of thought and planning.” In the same post he said “we should be honest with the British people”, and called removing the illegal migrant population “an incredibly challenging task - more than anybody realises.”

So which is it? “Simple”? Or “painful”, “complicated” and “incredibly challenging”?

On 28 September, when another @ user complained that he never defined what he meant by a “hostile environment”, Lowe replied: “We’ve published a 113 page policy paper outlining exactly what we mean.”

The Restore paper plans for roughly 1.8 to 2 MILLION people, with 150,000 to 200,000 forced removals a year, an expanded Immigration Enforcement, charter and military flights, withdrawal from the Convention, new legislation and a carve-out for Northern Ireland.

One returns route is already gone. Dublin III, which let the UK ask another EU state to take back an asylum seeker already registered there, stopped applying when the Brexit transition period ended on 31 December 2020, and no EU-wide equivalent replaced it. Lowe, then a Brexit Party MEP, campaigned for the Brexit that ended it.

In February and March, honesty with the British people meant admitting that this was hard. In October, after a boat landed in Gosport, it was “that simple”.

Lowe has been specific about the culture he says he is defending. In July 2025 he listed what built Britain: “Duty, decency, self-reliance, fair play, humour, freedom, personal responsibility.” The same month he demanded “One law for all - no parallel systems.”

In December 2025 he described British culture as one that “respects women, rewards hard work, values discipline”, that is “polite, fair, good-humoured”, and “where personal responsibility matters”.

Launching his party in February, he named the Christian heritage behind the country’s moral and civic foundations as “responsibility, duty, restraint, forgiveness and fairness”, and pledged to “uphold one legal system. One rule of law. One standard. No parallel justice.”

On Saturday, the day before the boat landed, he restated the principle at his party conference: “One law, one standard. Again, that principle is simple. The state should be frightening to criminals and reassuring to decent Brits.” He then described a father of two jailed, in his account, for throwing a plastic bottle at police and swearing at officers during an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth. He said violence against the police was unacceptable, but objected to the state making “a cruel example of those with rightful anger”, and promised: “We will not have law-abiding peaceful protesters crushed under the state’s boot while invading scumbags from the third world are fed into our harbours.”

The very next evening, a boat came into a harbour.

Police officers in Gosport were treated for injuries. Twelve people were arrested on suspicion of offences including assaulting a police officer, affray, criminal damage and racially aggravated public order, and one on suspicion of obstructing a highway after ambulances were prevented from travelling along Clayhall Road.

On Saturday, Lowe called violence against the police unacceptable. On Monday, with officers injured, he said nothing about it. “One law, one standard” would reach the people arrested in Gosport that night. In Lowe’s post, the only people facing the law are the civil servants.

The rest of his list fares no better. A culture that is “polite, fair, good-humoured” does not describe people taken off a dinghy by volunteer lifeboat crews as “third world invaders”, a phrase close to one he had used at his conference the day before. Restraint and forgiveness do not end in “treason” and prison for civil servants who applied an Act of Parliament.

Let’s turn his own test on his own party.

Jared Taylor, the American white supremacist banned from entering Britain, announced in February that he had joined Restore Britain, as Lowe was celebrating passing 90,000 members. The Southern Poverty Law Center describes his organisation, American Renaissance, as a white-nationalist hub. Searchlight says it has for decades hosted conferences attended by neo-Nazis, Ku Klux Klan figures and European identitarian activists.

Steve Laws, who calls for the expulsion of ethnic minorities including British-born citizens, joined the same month and, according to The Times, urged his supporters in April to become Restore candidates and organisers to “create a stronghold in that party”. He resigned at the end of August.

HOPE not hate has reported members of Patriotic Alternative, which it describes as Britain’s largest neo-Nazi group, campaigning for Restore at the Makerfield by-election in May.

In August, Allister Heath, editor of the Sunday Telegraph and certainly no friend of the Left, wrote that “Rupert Lowe’s racist cheerleaders can no longer hide their despicable extremism”. Lowe dismissed it as the “12th Restore Britain hit piece this week”.

Lowe wants migrants deported for putting their “clan” above “our British rule of law”. On these reports, his own party has room for a “clan” of its own: people who would put ethnicity above British citizenship.

Unlike Lowe, Gosport’s own representatives have been precise. Council leader Zoe Huggins says the town is not the right location for small boat arrivals, that the Home Office keeps ignoring the council’s concerns, and that the government should urgently find a suitable alternative site for disembarkation and processing. Constituency MP Caroline Dinenage and Hampshire’s police and crime commissioner Donna Jones want all boats taken by sea to Dover, wherever on the south coast they arrive. All three are Conservatives.

Those demands are specific, achievable, and made by people answerable to Gosport. Lowe, the MP for Great Yarmouth, more than 200 miles away by road, offers the town nothing it can use. He takes its complaint, strips out every workable detail, and hands it back.

Gosport asked for a safer landing site. Lowe gave it a slogan of invasion, treason and prison sentences for civil servants, and broke his own list doing it.

He says the young men on the boats come from “alien cultures that share none of our values”. He claims that he fears a future in which “our own culture and laws are gradually eroded”, and wants Britain to stop appeasing “cultural practices that clash with British law and values”.

Apply that test to his own post.

His one law for all had nothing to say about the people arrested in Gosport.

His restraint and forgiveness ended in “treason”.

And the presumption against punishing past lawful work is exactly the British legal value his pledge would have to override.

If anything in this sorry episode is a “humiliation for the British people”, it is a British MP writing the post below. Nazi Germany declared its own killings lawful after the fact. Stalin’s Soviet Union turned officials’ obedience into treason when the line changed. Both remade the meaning of past acts to suit whoever held power. Neither has any place in twenty-first-century Britain.

I am sick of him. The British people are sick of him.

It’s that simple. 🧐

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
The Law of First Mention is a well-established principle in biblical hermeneutics. It asserts that the first occurrence of a concept, word, or practice in Scripture sets its fundamental character and establishes a guiding pattern for its interpretation throughout the rest of the text.

When applied to the doctrine of tithing, this principle reveals a striking theological disconnect in modern pulpit teaching.

A strictly scriptural examination of tithing across biblical dispensations shows a consistent definition of what the tithe actually was, and, crucially, what it was not.

1. The Patriarchy (Genesis 14): When Abram tithed to Melchizedek, he did not give from his personal wealth, silver, or gold. Scripture explicitly specifies that he gave a tenth of the spoils of war (Hebrews 7:4). Furthermore, this was a voluntary, single recorded event, not a recurring obligation or an ongoing financial command.

2. The Mosaic Law (Leviticus 27, Deuteronomy 14): Under the Covenant of the Law, the tithe was strictly defined as agricultural produce, crops, and livestock from the Holy Land. Money and precious metals existed and were widely used for commerce, temple ransoms, and taxes, yet God never permitted silver or gold to serve as the required tithe.

This exposes the core issue: There is no verse in the New Testament that commands believers under Grace to tithe, nor is there any passage that defines “God’s tithe” as a percentage of income, silver, or gold.

If the Law of First Mention defines the tithe by its origin, and the Mosaic Law formalizes its precise elements as agricultural yield, altering the definition to mean “10% of monetary income” under the New Covenant requires scriptural authorization that simply does not exist in the text.

To preach monetary tithing as a mandatory New Covenant obligation presents three serious theological hurdles:

Silence of the Text: The Epistles, written specifically to instruct the Church in the Dispensation of Grace, contain zero instructions regarding a mandatory tenth, zero directives establishing money as the element of a tithe, and zero warnings of a curse (Malachi 3) applied to New Covenant believers.

Hermeneutical Inconsistency: Taking Abram’s single act of tithing spoils to establish a perpetual obligation, while simultaneously discarding the actual substance of what he offered (spoils) and the frequency of his act (once), cherry-picks the principle to enforce a modern financial model.

Redefining the Covenant Basis: The New Covenant explicitly shifts the paradigm of Christian giving from a legal requirement to a heart condition. As Paul writes:

2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV) Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, [so let him give]; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

How, then, can a compulsory monetary tithe be preached as a required doctrine under Grace?

It cannot, at least not through a consistent, literal reading of Scripture. To teach that God demands a mandatory ten percent of monetary income today requires binding New Covenant believers to a modified element (money) under a legal framework, while claiming freedom from the Mosaic Law itself.

Under the Dispensation of Grace, the required “tithe” does not exist in the text. In its place, the New Testament establishes a higher, non-percentage-based standard: voluntary, sacrificial, proportional, and joyful stewardship driven by love rather than legal mandate.

text:
Greetings, brother, and thank you. It is good to hear from you again. God bless you too.

I am not a dispensationalist. I hold that God has one people and one plan, and that His promises to Israel find their fulfilment in Christ and in all who belong to Him. "If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham's descendants, heirs according to promise" (Galatians 3:29). Christ has made Jew and Gentile "into one new man" (Ephesians 2:15), and there is one olive tree and not two (Romans 11:17-24).

On a rebuilt temple, I find nothing in Scripture that requires it before the Lord returns. Jesus said the temple was His own body (John 2:19-21). Now His people are the temple. "Do you not know that you are a temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16). And the sacrifices cannot return with God's approval, because Christ "offered one sacrifice for sins for all time," and "there is no longer any offering for sin" (Hebrews 10:12, 18).

What must happen before the end is this. "This gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all the nations, and then the end will come" (Matthew 24:14).

I do believe God still has mercy in store for the Jewish people, and it will come the same way it comes to anyone, through faith in Christ (Romans 11:23).

One word about your pastor. Godly men have differed on these things, and some who taught me much hold his view. So I would not call him a false teacher over this. Sit with him and an open Bible, and be patient. "Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls" (Hebrews 13:17).

Full disclosure on how this page actually runs. This is the only time I’m addressing it seriously, then it's back to funny business as usual. 😤

To the people obsessing over every post in the replies: I run this account to write jokes, have fun, and make some extra cash. I aim for three to seven posts a day, which comes out to roughly twenty to fifty a week. Anyone who writes comedy knows not every post is going to be gold...

When a post hits hard and goes viral, the algorithm routinely throttles the account right after. I’m not going to burn my best original material during algorithmic dead zones, so on those days, I use writing tools, basic observations, AI images, or filler to keep the account fed. If a mediocre post sends you into a rage, hit unfollow. 👍🏻

If you harass me or my friends in the replies, you get blocked immediately...

There is also a reason this account stays anonymous. My family and personal life stay completely separate from this platform. You won’t see my face, my home, or my family. The internet is full of unhinged people, and I don't need a joke about Michelle Obama's testicular cancer to get my house burned down by some radical 50-year-old man in a dress and a diaper. I have zero interest in trading my family's safety or privacy for internet clout.

For some context without giving away my life: I was born in Tampa and went to college in Southwest Florida to get a writing degree that turned out to be a total waste of time and energy. “Ken Michaels Creative”(c)1988,2026 - "The Music Makers..." was my "community radio station" company’s name as a kid.

Hey there, it’s Ken Michaels, I was an 11 year old that wanted to be a "DeeJay"-AND- "weatherman." I ran into a few problems... I didn't have a drivers license and, well, I sounded like "a little girl!" (Haha!)

NOBODY WOULD HIRE ME!

With my Dad’s help, we found out that you could have a "Community Radio Station..." There was no age limit, you could play what you wanted to, and no "Federal License" was required if you only covered a small area. 

It's still referred to today, as a "PART 15 RADIO STATION" in the "rules and regulations" of The Federal Communication Commission, Washington, D.C.

We ordered a small FM Transmitter Kit, that you had to build yourself, "the kit" was made for this exact type of station.

He helped me turn an old storage shed into a small radio station building. I was able to buy old used studio equipment from a friend who did actually work at one of Meridian, Mississippi's biggest station as the engineer. First thing I needed was a mixer. Then, a mic 🎤 and two record players and a cassette tape player.

My engineer friend said that I needed to come up with a name for the station, decide on what type of music we'd play, and go from there! I named it, "POWER 88 Gospel!" ...and I wanted to put together the absolute best music collection. So... every weekend we went in search of records at yard sales. It worked out perfectly!

My engineer friend said that my music collection was "kind of, officially" known as the stations, "music format." -and since I was "the formats creator" and wanted to pick every song played, the format needed a name. I decided to name it, "Home Grown Gospel." ...And (haha) I was very picky about what songs played. I wanted to play the best, "Southern and Country style Gospel & Church Hymns!

I grew up, s l o w l y... but eventually was hired by one of the "BIG STATIONS" in Meridian, and decided to close my little community station. -But, I heald onto the company name: "Ken Michaels Creative"( and all of my records and tapes) -AND- kept my "music format name" with all of my notes as to what songs should play. I had future plans for my "Home Grown Gospel" format!

Since then, my "Home Grown Gospel" format became the musical format for a 50,000 watt FM station, and was heard all across two states... Later down the road, a guy called me and said, I own an AM and FM station in Meridian. 

I would love for you to bring your music collection and have "Home Grown Gospel" air on both the AM and FM station. I accepted the offer and became those stations, "Operations, Program and Music Director." 

My "Home Grown Gospel" format went on both the AM and FM...How long did they stay with me? 14 years...

As of a few weeks back (September 6th), it marked my 35th year in radio and weather. 

Today, my company "Digitally Kennected, LLC" has a "music format division" and not only is that division known as, "Ken Michaels Creative" but I not only still have "Home Grown Gospel" available, but I own almost 20 others that I have created. What about the weather? I'm a "Severe Storms Specialist" and have covered numerous stations across the South with my "LIVE" (non-stop) coverage.

And, without question... "Digitally Kennected, LLC's" 3rd division is, "Ken Michaels Weather." My (multi-year) weather partner is "Forbes Magazine ranked #1!" - "WeatherTAP" of Crossville, Tennessee.

I also have "Ken Michaels Channel" on Spotify. One of my most popular music shows is known as, "Home Grown Gospel!" Below you'll see my "listener link" to hear this weekends, "Ken Michaels Channel" (K M C) -Special 3 hour presentation, it's music and name are now heard around the globe 🌎 on Spotify!

https://t.co/Euns3LHLiI

text:
🇿🇦 Sjoe! South Africa’s State Capture Story Isn’t Over — It Just Changed Chapters 📖🔄 ~ 🚰🇿🇦 Dry Taps. Thin Newsrooms. Delayed Consequences. The Pattern Is the Story ~ 🇿🇦 The Capture Circuit: Loyalty In, Accountability Out, Bill Sent to Everyone 💸🔄
The nozzle clicks. Another litre of imported petrol slides into the tank. The price edges toward R30. In the same crowded week a former chief justice reminds the country that investigations must produce consequences, and a foreign government attaches personal travel restrictions to selected South African nationals.

The question that matters is not which event arrived first. The question is which unfinished business sits underneath all three.

South Africa’s democratic-era state capture is not a closed historical episode ended by formal inquiry. It is a continuous multi-chapter operating system whose past diagnosis, present mutation and future trajectory must be read as one unfinished circuit. 

The Zondo Commission did not write the final page. It wrote the opening sentence of a longer story that is still being lived at the pump, the tap, the child-protection desk and the thinning newsroom.

That is the claim. The converging evidence that follows is independent, reinforcing and testable.

1. The Diagnostic Opening That Never Closed

Between 2018 and 2022 the Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture catalogued loyalty networks, institutional hollowing and the systemic diversion of public resources across state-owned enterprises, revenue collection and procurement. 

Its reports were treated by many as the final chapter. They were not.

In October 2026 former Chief Justice Raymond Zondo publicly expressed disappointment that the preventive institutions and mechanisms he identified as essential remain substantially incomplete more than four years after the inquiry concluded. 

Asset recoveries have risen toward R11 billion and some legislation has been enacted, yet soft consequences persist. Individuals against whom findings were made have continued in senior positions because disciplinary processes were deferred pending criminal charges—a stance Zondo himself has described as nonsensical (Zondo, 2026; Presidency progress reports, 2025).

Continuity is measured not by the absence of discrete scandals but by the persistence of missing ceilings, loyalty over competence, and an enabling circuit that simply adapts. 

Formal inquiry without structural interruption leaves the system free to reconstitute itself under new stationery. 

Constitutional design after 1994 deliberately created independent institutions and investigative commissions precisely to constrain the concentration of power. When those mechanisms produce formal findings that are then buffered by the same political networks they were meant to check, the original design intention is partially inverted.

Sjoe!
A recommendation that can be survived for years without career-ending cost is not quite the same instrument as one that cannot. The difference is the buffer—and buffers have a way of looking thinner once the price of staying inside them rises.

Stirring Questions:
What independent metric would show that the consequence gap identified by Zondo has actually closed?
If formal findings can coexist for years with continued high office, what remains of their deterrent value inside the networks that matter?

Why these questions together matter:
They convert abstract accountability language into a concrete cost-benefit calculation that networks must now perform. They test whether the prior fact is still treated as optional or has become the necessary starting point for any evaluation of later chapters.

2. The Loyalty Filter That Learned New Languages

Cadre deployment was found unconstitutional and facilitative of capture. The practice itself was retained. Preferential procurement and BEE instruments that had already become extraction channels for connected networks were then intensified through harder ownership and eligibility gates. 

Draft regulations contemplated 100 percent designated-group ownership requirements for significant contract bands, excluding even highly compliant mixed-ownership or listed firms (Judicial Commission, 2022; draft General Public Procurement Regulations, 2026).

Subsequent legislation has sought to reduce political interference in appointments, yet the dual movement—retention of the filter plus radicalisation of the racial cover—remains the structural feature. 

Under-delivery is met with stricter thresholds rather than competence reform, locking the system into winners’ bias: the networks that benefited keep control of both the problem statement and the design of the solution. 

The original enabling practice outlived the commission that named it unlawful by converting failure into justification for a more elaborate protective casing.

Political scientists have long observed that systems prioritising upward loyalty over outward accountability generate distinctive incentive structures. 

Survival and advancement depend more reliably on network protection than on the avoidance of formal findings. When those findings arrive and produce years of uninterrupted high office rather than rapid equivalent consequence, the protected individual receives repeated confirmation that the ordinary rules of cost still bend.

Sjoe!
A system that answers its own under-performance by raising the racial threshold for entry has a peculiar genius: it can fail at its stated purpose indefinitely and still succeed at its operational one.

Stirring Questions:
Why was the loyalty filter treated as non-negotiable while the intensity of racial eligibility was treated as indefinitely expandable?
If under-delivery is met with more of the same racial instruments rather than reform of the appointment practice, what mechanism remains for course correction?

Why these questions together matter:
They force a choice between two incompatible accounts: one in which radicalisation is the cure, and one in which radicalisation is the method by which the original capture protects itself. They determine whether future policy can escape the closed loop or must continue to travel inside it.

3. The Coalition Multiplier

Post-2021 hung councils and multi-party arrangements did not dilute the operating system; they multiplied its opportunities. Frequent mayoral and administrative churn, prolonged acting appointments, delayed budgets and weakened oversight became normal in major metros.

Political energy is consumed by holding the chamber and distributing portfolios. No single actor owns the multi-year outcome, so emergency contracting becomes the reliable default.

Service failures are then attributed to coalition complexity rather than the underlying loyalty logic that adapts to every configuration of power. The same soft-consequence buffer identified after Zondo reappears in fragmented local government, proving the system is configuration-agnostic. 

Crisis becomes the generator of bypass contracts. 

Comparative governance research shows that technical networks—water, electricity, rail—punish deferred maintenance more relentlessly than most other public services. 

Pipes and pumps do not respond to press statements. They respond to spare parts, skilled operators, and budgets that actually reach the asset.

Sjoe!
Loyalty is an excellent quality in a friend. It is a less reliable quality in a pump station.

Stirring Questions:
When political energy is spent holding the chamber rather than fixing the pipes, what measurable recovery in non-revenue water or treatment compliance has been achieved?
Does the addition of more parties reduce the visibility of differential outcomes or merely shift their expression into quieter channels?

Why these questions together matter:
They convert household cost into a demand for design change rather than further temporary relief. They test whether the soft buffer can survive once continuity itself is priced by the daily experience of dry taps and dark classrooms.

4. The Measurable Signatures

National non-revenue water stands near 47 percent; Gauteng metros frequently record 40–50 percent. Johannesburg Water alone lost approximately R2.8 billion in one recent year. Wastewater works collapse. Sewage reaches the Cradle of Humankind. Free State municipalities endure decade-scale dry taps and empty coffers. 

Specialised child-protection organisations face chronic under-funding while unspent allocations return to Treasury (Auditor-General, 2025; SAHRC, 2026).

Past under-maintenance and loyalty-based capacity gaps created the fragility. The present converts every outage into emergency tanker or repair spend that absorbs the budget which could have reduced the losses. 

Future pressure under a strong-to-very-strong El Niño for 2026/27 and fiscal constraint converts chronic shortage into prolonged humanitarian risk for the same communities (South African Weather Service, 2026). 

Grants and bulk supply may still exist on paper. Reliable delivery and the professional layer that turns cash grants into actual safety for the highest-risk children do not. 

The institutional signature is consistent across water, electricity and specialised welfare: missing ceilings, deferred consequence management, and crisis-as-opportunity logic.

Sjoe!
The weather has the manners to send advance notice. The infrastructure appears not to have RSVP’d.

Stirring Questions:
What single measurable control point—verification before payment, capacity before premium—has been permanently closed since the first residual claims were recorded?
If reform announcements themselves have become a recurring stage, what would interrupt the circuit rather than decorate it?

Why these questions together matter:
They move the discussion from individual cases to the operating system that repeatedly generates them. Without changes to that system, each new crisis simply reproduces the previous one at larger scale.

5. The Informational Closure

The independent press is already under severe commercial duress from platform dominance, circulation collapse of 70–85 percent in major categories, and staff cuts. Into that shortage the National Department of Health spent R181.9 million between September 2024 and September 2026 on uncapped communications contracts with two private agencies, portions drawn from NHI implementation, HIV, tuberculosis and child-nutrition lines. One major recipient is directed by a former City Press editor. Neither agency employs investigative reporters (Karrim, 2026; Competition Commission, 2025).

The press receives none of the residual public narrative oxygen and is left reading the receipt of money spent next door. 

This closes the informational feedback loop: extraction continues while the institution whose constitutional function is scrutiny is itself thinned by the same missing-ceiling logic visible in service delivery. 

Section 16 protects publication. It does not replace a lost advertiser, a cut post, or a programme budget turned into a billboard.

Sjoe!
You cannot capture a newspaper with an advert you never offered. You can only spend the last air next door, then ask why the paper is wheezing.

Stirring Questions:
Did any of the R181.9 million buy newsroom space, or only production around it?
When the residual state advertising tank is spent where the newspaper is not in the room, what remains of the local capacity to read the next set of receipts?

Why these questions together matter:
They reveal the self-protecting character of the circuit: the system that requires scrutiny systematically reduces the oxygen available for that scrutiny. They hold the opportunity-cost claim without requiring a theft verdict.

Synthesis

The converging evidence forms a single, testable sequence. The consequence gap identified by Zondo is the prior fact. The loyalty filter was retained and protected. Coalition instability multiplied opportunities rather than diluted them. Service collapse and welfare erosion are institutional signatures, not external shocks. 

The residual media oxygen is being spent next door to the newsrooms that should be reading the receipts.

Independent lines of evidence—from commission statements, capacity data, audit outcomes, climate forecasts, funding records and advertising contracts—reinforce one another like overlapping fingerprints at the same scene. 

The argument is falsifiable. If future data show restored processing capacity that eliminates structural premiums, contemporaneous physical verification before major payments, rapid and equivalent personal consequence for senior figures under formal findings, the establishment of the preventive institutions Zondo recommended, and reliable funding of both specialised protection and independent reporting capacity, the description of an open circuit will have to be revised.

Until such data appear, the pattern stands.

The stakes are measured in the price paid at every pump, the residual claims that accumulate on public balance sheets, the developmental years of children growing up with intermittent water and thinned protection, and the quiet erosion of the only institution left to make the other failures visible and costly.

Sjoe!
Five independent witnesses, one shortage. They did not have to meet. The newsroom, the tap and the clinic felt all five.

Objections

Some will argue that external pressures invent problems that are purely domestic. The capacity collapse, verification lag, consequence gap and funding patterns predate the external measures. External cost merely prices patterns already documented.

Others will note that formal recommendations are not convictions and that process must be allowed to run. Process that repeatedly produces soft personal cost for those inside the core network while generating harder outcomes for comparable figures outside it is itself data. The differential is the observation.

A third view holds that temporary task teams, bulk increases and grant expansions demonstrate ongoing commitment. Announcements are not outcomes; the losses, pollution metrics and funding gaps remain.

Conclusion

Zondo First is both diagnostic and prescription. Look inward at the unfinished business before evaluating the legitimacy or utility of any outward pressure or temporary relief. The coherent response is not prolonged finger-pointing but the harder work of interrupting the circuit—verification before payment, consequence after finding, capacity restored under glass walls, and oxygen returned to the desks that read the receipts.

The pipes do not negotiate. The climate does not attend press conferences. The residual oxygen of the fourth estate does not replenish itself. 

Until ceilings are fixed, consequences are equivalent, and competence is elevated above loyalty across appointments, procurement, service delivery and public narrative funding, the chapters will keep accumulating.

The ballot and the institutional redesign remain the only remaining levers that still belong to the people who live with the consequences.

Sjoe.
The beloved country has faced tougher tests. Clear-eyed action on the prior fact remains available. The receipt at the pump, the differential outcomes, the dry taps, the waiting clinics and the wheezing newsrooms are all still waiting for the circuit to be closed.

Individuals who associate themselves with that, or other racist groups, have committed acts of violence. They should be prosecuted, and have been.

Unless you can show he was directly involved with the planning or execution of any illegal acts, he can't be prosecuted.

Holding an animus towards a racial/ethnic group is not a crime. Making abhorrent statements about a group or individual based on their racial/ethnic background is not a crime.

Allow me to offer examples.

Let's say that the leader of the Black Hebrew Israelites was to make the following statement:  'I hate white people. I think they are trash, and the world would be a better place if there were no white people'.

That is an abhorrent statement. It's also within that person's rights to hold those beliefs, and to make that statement.

Now, let's say he made the following statement: 'I hate white people. I think they are trash, and the world would be a better place if there were no white people. So, I'm calling on everyone to eliminate every white person you see. When you leave here today, don't wait, don't hesitate. Just kill whites.'

That would be a crime. 

Why?

It's a call to imminent illegal acts, and under the Supreme Court ruling in Brandenburg v Ohio, that's not protected speech.

Like I said, I find the individual's racist views to be abhorrent. But if you're going to support the Constitution, you have to support ALL of it, or none of it. 

If you want your freedom of speech and association to be protected, you need to want his freedom of speech and association protected.

High-Fiber Nigerian Foods
• Beans and Legumes: Black-eyed peas, brown beans, and dishes like moi moi and bean porridge provide heavy amounts of soluble and insoluble fiber.
• Leafy Greens and Vegetables: Local vegetables like ugu (fluted pumpkin leaves), bitter leaf (onugbu), waterleaf, and ewedu (jute leaves) add great bulk and nutrients to meals.
• Okra: Okra soup contains natural mucilage (a gel-like substance) packed with soluble fiber that aids comfortable digestion.
• Whole Grains: Unpolished local rice (Ofada rice), sorghum (guinea corn), millet (oka baba), and acha (fonio) contain high amounts of fiber compared to polished white rice.
• Tubers and Plantains: Unripe plantain, sweet potatoes, and cocoyam offer healthy complex carbohydrates and good dietary fiber.
• Snacks and Seeds: Tiger nuts (kunnu aya), groundnuts, and local corn are budget-friendly and natural sources of roughage.

Wiley: A Fresh Voice for Colorado’s Elections

Colorado voters have a clear choice in the 2026 Secretary of State race—and it goes far beyond party labels.

James Wiley is not business as usual. His background in business, management and election-integrity activism has given him a different perspective on how Colorado runs its elections. He is proposing major changes, including removing non-citizen voters, securing the vote, requiring citizenship checks at registration, and using blockchain technology to improve public records.

If we have to show an ID to buy a beer or a firearm, it's reasonable to show an ID when registering to vote.

Amanda Gonzalez represents the corruption that has saturated our state. As a longtime Democratic official and Jefferson County Clerk and Recorder, her priorities largely focus on maintaining secrecy and business as usual. That means mailing out invitations for non-citizens to vote, releasing passwords, and creating a toxic environment in the SoS office with high turnover.

For voters who believe Colorado needs new ideas, greater transparency and fundamental accountability, Wiley offers a fresh perspective rather than more of the same.

The choice is simple: business as usual—or a new direction for Colorado.

James Wiley brings a fresh perspective. Colorado deserves nothing less.

text:
Farley says Ford’s Fathom launch will be ‘a heck of an effort’

Ford CEO Jim Farley says launching the upcoming Fathom electric pickup at scale, while hitting its aggressive price and production targets, will require a major effort as the automaker retools its Louisville plant.

– Farley said launching the Fathom “at this scale, at cost, on time” will be a major challenge.

– The Fathom is priced from $28,350, or $29,945 including destination, positioning it among the most affordable new EVs on the market.

– Ford plans to begin building the five-seat electric pickup in 2027 at its Louisville, Kentucky, plant, which is undergoing a multibillion-dollar retooling.

– Order books are expected to open in early 2027, with customer deliveries planned for later that year. Farley has not confirmed a delay.

– The Fathom will offer more passenger volume than a Toyota RAV4, along with a pickup bed and front trunk.

– Standard technology includes BlueCruise capability, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, digital key and bidirectional charging.

– Ford’s Universal EV Platform uses fewer parts and welds and replaces the traditional moving assembly line with an assembly-tree process designed to improve manufacturing efficiency.

– Ford began producing LFP battery cells in Michigan in June, with launch-ready cells expected before the end of 2026.

Ford has yet to reveal the Fathom’s official range or full specifications, leaving the automaker’s ability to hit its sub-$30,000 price, production timeline and cost targets as key milestones ahead of its 2027 launch.

text:
Former Dallas Cowboys quarterbacks Troy Aikman and Tony Romo have long since retired from playing and pursued broadcasting careers. As their on-air paths have evolved, Dez Bryant, a three-time Cowboys Pro Bowler and former wide receiver, offered a candid piece of advice to the organization.

“Troy Aikman and Tony Romo need to be part of the Cowboys organization,” Bryant posted on social media.

Aikman brought three Super Bowls to Dallas, and his rise began with a strong supporting cast, including Emmitt Smith, Michael Irvin, Jay Novacek, and a formidable offensive line. His 11th season featured one of the sport’s memorable comebacks: on Sept. 12, 1999, he sparked a rally from a 21-point fourth-quarter deficit against the Washington Redskins, sending the game to overtime and delivering a 76-yard touchdown pass to Rakim Ismail for a 41-35 win. He retired in April 2001 and quickly transitioned to broadcasting, joining Fox Sports as a game analyst in 2001 and remaining a familiar face in the booth.

Romo’s Dallas tenure spanned 14 seasons, ending without a Super Bowl victory but highlighted by his loyalty to the franchise. He retired in 2017 and signed a three-year, $9 million contract with CBS, making him one of the higher-paid NFL color commentators at the time.

Recent seasons have brought scrutiny. Aikman faced criticism for on-air mistakes, including a Week 2 misidentification during a Rams-Giants broadcast. Romo has also drawn attention for not always anticipating plays, with some viewers noting a perceived preference for certain quarterbacks. Off the field, Romo faced legal issues earlier, leading CBS to place him on leave and ultimately part ways with the network.

Meanwhile, Aikman’s broadcasting contract with ESPN, set to expire after Super Bowl LXI in February 2027, could influence his future options. As for Romo, his career in the booth has concluded, prompting discussion about potential roles within the Cowboys organization, whether in coaching or front office capacities.

With Dallas currently led by a steady quarterback in Dak Prescott, many believe the franchise could benefit from the guidance and experience of former legends in advisory or leadership positions. The idea of bringing Aikman and Romo back into the Cowboys fold—whether in coaching, front office, or anotherStrategic capacity—continues to be a point of conversation for some fans and analysts.

text:
Pathogen diplomacy and the propaganda theatre of the absurd. Faced with mounting concern over a possible leak of a dangerous pathogen — amid reports of suspected Yersinia pestis infection and pneumonic plague linked to a Russian laboratory — Moscow is resorting to a tried-and-tested tactic: reversing roles.

Rospotrebnadzor has, in all seriousness, announced its readiness to provide assistance to the United States, offering to send Russian specialists and laboratory equipment to America in the name of ‘resuming joint work on biological threats’.

Meanwhile, in Washington, the atmosphere surrounding the Russian outbreak is growing increasingly tense:

▪️ Rubio demands transparency: At a press conference in Reykjavík, Secretary of State Marco Rubio adopted a markedly tougher tone. While he had sought to calm concerns barely 24 hours earlier, he now stressed that the US was monitoring the situation in Russia ‘hour by hour’. Rubio demanded full transparency from Moscow and urged it to share data with the international community, invoking the lessons of the COVID-19 pandemic and the risks associated with laboratory incidents. He also said that Washington had the capacity to assist Russia should the situation spiral out of control — provided that reliable information on the scale of the threat was available.

▪️ Trump on the ‘army of microbes’: President Donald Trump also declared his readiness to provide assistance, stressing that the US was prepared to help Russia ‘as much as it possibly can’, because the situation represented a ‘huge problem’ for Moscow. In his characteristic style, however, he added a remark about the nature of modern pathogens: ‘These microbes have become stronger and smarter; they’re like an army.’

Rospotrebnadzor’s statements amount to a classic smokescreen. Rather than allowing independent international scrutiny and clarifying the circumstances surrounding the death of the laboratory worker, the Kremlin prefers to cast itself as a global benefactor — while evading questions about its own biosafety procedures.

Bacteria do not respect national borders, and any attempt to turn a potential laboratory incident into a bargaining chip in relations with the West is playing with fire.

The world does not need offers of support from the Kremlin.
It needs hard facts before the ‘army of microbes’ escapes Russian test tubes.
