Pezeshkian claims Europe’s view of Iran is "inaccurate." Yet the truth is that Europe’s "view" is accurate, it precisely reflects Europe’s hostile stance toward Iran.

Europe does not misunderstand Iran; Europe opposes Iran. It opposes Iran because the country refuses to submit to the U.S.-Israeli regional order; because it supports the resistance in Palestine and Lebanon; because it challenges U.S. military hegemony in the Strait of Hormuz; and because it refuses to capitulate in nuclear negotiations.

Denmark does not misunderstand Iran. Denmark is a NATO member part of the alliance that is militarily encircling and economically strangling Iran.

Iran can continue its dialogue with Denmark and the rest of Europe. It can continue to demonstrate its desire for peace on the international stage.

But Iran must harbor no illusions. Dialogue does not equate to friendship; the presentation of credentials does not equate to support. The very same hands that present credentials to Iran also deliver bombs to Israel.

Pezeshkian is right: Europe’s view "does not reflect reality." But the reality is that Europe’s view is not a "misunderstanding," it is "hostility." And Iran must survive amidst this hostility through resistance, not through illusions.

No… I am simply pointing out that Trump has potentially roped the US into a military defence deal with Greenland (and any other nato / Eu forces based on Greenland (subject to the agreement of Denmark and Greenland that the US can never veto) and its environs that deals with some big problems for nato and Europe and Canada.

For north Western Europe a more robust US presence on Greenland deals with the threat of Russia coming to our north and west via the Greenland / Iceland Gap given that Sweden, Denmark, Poland, Germany, Norway, and the Baltic states would prevent the Russian navy finding its way to the north sea via the Denmark Strait.

The Uk’s nuclear submarines access the Atlantic and high north from 3 bases on the Uk’s west coast to now protect many states in Europe via the Greenland / Iceland gap also to get north of Russia for faster launch to strike times.

We really need to be right on Russia’s door step under the ice ready and a strong US presence on Greenland is an enabler for that.

Trump though and many in his party… don’t want to do Europe any favours… and won’t realise how this helps us… and hopefully the remaining right minded people in the pentagon who Trump never listens to anyway will not spell it out for him.

Trumps motivation regarding Greenland is purely commercial dressed up as defence.

For so many reasons any plan to make a viable commercial business mining minerals on Greenland is doomed to failure for the US.

This is due to the fact that energy on Greenland is limited to poorly connected hydro and does not have the capacity to much improve due to limited resources. 

Greenland does not have the geothermal power potential that Iceland has which sits directly over the mid Atlantic ridge where the earths crust is separating making it one of the best places for very cheap geothermal power on earth.

In fact Greenland is pretty cold for geothermal.

Greenland’s mineral wealth therefore should not be confused with easily exploitable mineral wealth. 

The deposits are usually remote many miles from the ports, the climate is extremely hostile, infrastructure is minimal, industrial power is limited and many locations face difficult or seasonal access. 

The US would have to invest heavily in mines, roads, ports, power generation, processing and Arctic shipping before it could extract anything at scale. 

High-value mineral concentrates can make the long sea journey to America viable; bulk, lower-value ores generally cannot. 

Greenland therefore offers the US potentially valuable strategic resources, but it is hardly a ready-made mineral warehouse waiting to be exploited now.

There is another major vulnerability to the Trump plan: the economics depend on high-value minerals remaining sufficiently valuable to justify the enormous cost of developing mines and infrastructure in Greenland. 

If rare-earth or other critical-mineral prices fall substantially, the business case could deteriorate very quickly while the roads, ports, power systems and processing facilities remain expensive to operate and difficult to repurpose. 

Governments could subsidise strategically important production, but that would effectively transfer some of the commercial risk to taxpayers. 

Greenland therefore offers potentially valuable resources, but exploiting them at scale carries a considerable long-term commodity-price risk on top of the already formidable logistical and infrastructure costs.

As the climate changes it may become more viable many decades from now.

Trumps whole Greenland scheme is built on very tenuous assumptions based on little more than hope.

text:
🇮🇷🇦🇫|The Iran-Afghanistan Railway: A Strategic Breakout Amidst Imperial Encirclement, or a Neocolonial Conduit for Resource Plunder?

On October 6, 2026, Hamid Ghanbari, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Economic Diplomacy, met in Tehran with Mohammad Naeem, the Deputy Foreign Minister for Finance and Administrative Affairs of the Afghan Taliban government. The talks centered on a single, critical issue: the Herat-Mazar-i-Sharif railway project.

This was no ordinary consultation on infrastructure cooperation. It took place against a backdrop where the Strait of Hormuz was blockaded by a US military standoff, Iranian oil exports were stifled by sanctions, and Afghanistan remained locked out of the international financial system. Two nations, simultaneously encircled by the imperial order, were attempting to carve out an overland lifeline bypassing the US dollar and Western control using railway tracks and mineral resources.

Yet, the reality is far more complex than the simple label of "economic cooperation" suggests. Behind this railway lie Iran’s strategic breakout, Afghanistan’s resource-for-infrastructure swaps, Turkey’s involvement, the shadow of China, and a power struggle between factions within the Taliban.

Part I: The Dual Dilemma of Imperial Encirclement

Iran: Blockaded at Hormuz, Seeking an Alternative Path

By 2026, the war between the US-Israel alliance and Iran had been raging for six months. The US Navy had imposed a maritime blockade on Iran in the Strait of Hormuz, placing unprecedented pressure on Iranian oil exports. Although Iran responded by enforcing regulations through its "Persian Gulf Waterway Authority" and launching anti-ship missiles, Tehran was acutely aware that it could not afford to put all its eggs in the Hormuz basket.  Jabbar-Ali Zakeri, CEO of the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways, stated clearly in an interview with ILNA: "Completing this railway will not only boost trade between Iran and Afghanistan but also connect the regional rail network to China and strengthen Iran's position within international transport and cargo transit corridors."

Iran needs not only to bypass the Strait of Hormuz for oil exports but also to secure a land-based trade artery to China. Regarding China-Iran trade, a Xi'an-Aprin freight train service was launched, reaching Iran via Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan; however, this route traverses multiple countries, introducing uncertainties. The Herat-Mazar-e-Sharif railway represents a crucial link in Iran's strategy to build an "East-West railway corridor."

Afghanistan: A Trade Lifeline Choked by Sanctions

Since coming to power in 2021, the Taliban government has faced economic sanctions and financial blockades imposed by the international community. Afghanistan's traditional trade routes rely on Pakistan's ports of Karachi and Gwadar. However, relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan deteriorated sharply in 2025; Islamabad accused the Taliban of supporting the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) in launching attacks within Pakistan and closed the border for nearly a month in October 2025, causing losses of approximately $200 million for Afghan merchants.

Afghanistan urgently needs an outlet to the sea and a trade route that does not rely on Pakistan.

Iran's Chabahar Port offers a potential solution. However, U.S. sanctions have severely restricted the port's operations. Although the U.S. granted a limited sanctions waiver for Chabahar Port in 2018, this waiver was revoked in 2025, and subsequent temporary waivers expired in April 2026. Acting Afghan Foreign Minister Muttaqi has even publicly called on India to negotiate with the U.S. to secure the lifting of sanctions on Chabahar Port.  The Herat–Mazar-i-Sharif railway represents the only viable strategic alternative for Afghanistan, given the dual predicament of an unreliable route through Pakistan and sanctions restricting the use of Chabahar Port.

Part II: "Railways for Minerals"—A Raw Resource Swap

Who is footing the $780 million bill?

According to reports from Iranian and various regional media outlets, the Herat–Mazar-i-Sharif railway spans approximately 657 to 800 kilometers (figures vary by source), with an estimated project cost of $780 million.

Iranian companies will undertake the construction, yet "financing is the responsibility of the Afghan government."

This statement sounds plausible on the surface, but the actual deal structure is far more complex. Zakari, the Managing Director of the Railways of the Islamic Republic of Iran, explicitly stated that the project would be executed under a "railways-for-minerals" model whereby Iran secures the right to build the railway infrastructure in exchange for participating in the development of and investment in Afghanistan's mineral resources.

The CEO of the Iran Railway Development Alliance further confirmed on August 2, 2026: "The project will be directly awarded to the applicant Iranian party, and its financing is expected to rely on the government's share of proceeds from mineral extraction."

In plain terms: Afghanistan lacks the cash to pay for the railway's construction. Instead, it is using its underground mineral wealth to settle the bill.

What minerals does Afghanistan possess?

Afghanistan boasts abundant mineral resources, including lithium, copper, iron, rare earth elements, gold, marble, and coal. Its untapped mineral wealth is estimated to exceed $1 trillion. Among these, lithium stands out as one of the country's most strategically valuable assets; against the backdrop of the global shift toward electric vehicles and energy storage, lithium is often dubbed "white oil."

What are the implications of Iran securing the rights to develop Afghanistan's mineral resources?

It means Iran gains not only a land route that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz but also access to strategic resources that are critical to the global energy transition.  Yet Afghanistan, a nation besieged by sanctions, isolation, and crushing poverty is trading its last remaining underground wealth for a railway line on the surface.

This is not "economic cooperation." It is a forced exchange driven by the pressure to survive. Afghanistan has no choice. It lacks cash, credit, and access to international financial channels. It possesses only mineral resources, which serve as its sole bargaining chip.

Part III: The Five Nations Corridor and Regional Rivalry Winners and Losers

The Five Nations Railway Corridor (FNRC): A Land Bridge from Iran to China

The Herat–Mazar-i-Sharif railway is a crucial component of the Five Nations Railway Corridor (FNRC). Spanning approximately 2,100 kilometers, this corridor connects Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan to China, ultimately terminating in Kashgar, Xinjiang.

The corridor utilizes the 1,435mm standard gauge the international standard enabling direct integration with railway networks in both China and Europe. Upon completion, it will establish an East-West Eurasian corridor more competitive than maritime shipping, with Afghanistan and its northern neighbors playing pivotal roles as connectors.

Turkiye’s Involvement

Notably, Türkiye is a third party in the construction of this railway. In October 2025, during the 36th Regional Conference of the International Union of Railways, Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkey signed an agreement in Istanbul to jointly construct the Mazar-i-Sharif railway.

Turkiye’s involvement is no coincidence. Ankara has long sought to expand its influence across the Caucasus and Central Asia. By participating in this railway project, Türkiye can embed itself into the overland trade route stretching from Europe to China.

India: The Marginalized Loser

India is losing ground in this geopolitical game.

For a long time, India has sought to establish connections with Afghanistan and Central Asia via the Chabahar Port, aiming to bypass its arch-rival, Pakistan.  In 2016, India, Iran, and Afghanistan signed a trilateral agreement regarding Chabahar Port, with India pledging to invest in a railway line connecting the port to the Afghan border.

However, U.S. sanctions derailed this plan. With the 2018 sanctions waiver revoked in 2025, India was forced to scale back its investment in Chabahar Port. While India hesitated and awaited permission from Washington, Iran and Afghanistan opted for direct cooperation bypassing India through a "railways-for-minerals" arrangement.

India’s influence in Afghanistan is being supplanted by that of Iran and China. Furthermore, the diplomatic cover and arms supplies India provided to Israel during the genocide in Gaza have further eroded its moral standing in this Muslim-majority region.

Part IV: Power Struggles Within the Taliban. Backstabbing Beneath the Negotiating Table

The Meeting Between Naeem and Gambari: Superficial Cooperation

The talks held on October 6, 2026, appeared on the surface to be a consultation on economic cooperation. However, the official statement released by the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan in addition to discussions on railways, minerals, and power cooperation also addressed issues regarding migration and visas.

This was no coincidence. The plight of Afghan refugees in Iran is a long-neglected yet highly sensitive issue in bilateral relations. With millions of Afghan refugees living and working in Iran, their visa status, employment rights, and social treatment represent practical challenges that the Taliban government must confront.

Internal Divisions Within the Taliban

Yet, even more perilous than the refugee issue is the power struggle within the Taliban itself.

The Taliban has never been a monolithic organization; it is divided into at least three major factions:

1. The Kandahar Faction: Centered around Supreme Leader Hibatullah Akhundzada, this faction represents the Taliban's religious conservatives and its fundamentalist core.  2. The Haqqani Network: Centered around Sirajuddin Haqqani, this faction controls the Ministry of Interior and security agencies; it is known for its hardline stance and extensive combat experience.
3. The Doha Faction: Centered around the group's negotiators, this faction signed the Doha Agreement with the U.S. in 2020 and advocates for engagement with the international community.

To which faction does Mohammad Naeem, the Afghan representative at this meeting, belong?

Naeem serves as the Taliban government's Deputy Foreign Minister for Finance and Administration. While his specific factional affiliation has not been explicitly disclosed, his presence at the negotiating table for economic talks with Iran underscores the internal power struggle within the Taliban over control of economic resources.

What lies at the heart of the railway project? Mineral resources. Control over these minerals is a focal point of contention among the Taliban's various factions. The Kandahar faction holds ultimate decision-making power, yet the Haqqani Network controls the security apparatus, and the Doha faction manages diplomatic channels. Whoever controls the mineral development contracts effectively controls Afghanistan's largest stream of cash revenue.

As Naeem shook hands with Ghanbari in Tehran, other factions within the Taliban were likely plotting in Kabul or Kandahar either to undermine his authority or to secure a share of the profits from the mineral contracts.

Part V: Who Pays for the Railway?

Local Communities: Displacements Ignored

The Herat–Mazar-e-Sharif railway is slated to traverse vast swathes of northern Afghanistan, cutting through provinces such as Herat, Badghis, Faryab, Sar-e Pol, and Balkh. These areas are far from uninhabited; they are home to diverse ethnic groups, including Pashtuns, Tajiks, Uzbeks, Hazaras, and Turkmens.

The construction of the railway will inevitably necessitate land requisition and the relocation of local residents.  Records from the Asian Development Bank regarding the Hairatan–Mazar-e-Sharif railway project in Afghanistan indicate that the project required "minimal land acquisition and resettlement" and was classified under the category of "involuntary resettlement." Although the project was small in scale, it highlighted a fundamental reality: building railways in Afghanistan inevitably means people must leave their land.

The Herat–Mazar-e-Sharif railway is far larger in scale than the Hairatan–Mazar-e-Sharif line. It will traverse more densely populated areas and affect a greater number of communities. Yet, there are currently no publicly available environmental impact assessments, social impact assessments, or resettlement plans.

Seismic Risk: An Overlooked Engineering Hazard

The Herat–Mazar-e-Sharif railway route passes through a seismically active zone in northern Afghanistan. A study published in the journal *Seismology* established a specific seismic catalog for this railway to facilitate seismic hazard assessment.

Northern Afghanistan is a region prone to frequent earthquakes. In October 2023, a series of powerful earthquakes struck Herat Province, killing over 2,000 people and destroying thousands of homes. Constructing a railway spanning 657 to 800 kilometers through a seismically active zone demands exceptionally high engineering standards and entails massive additional costs. However, current public information contains no details regarding seismic-resistant design.

Environmental Cost: Railways Are Not Inherently "Green"

Railways are often viewed as more environmentally friendly than roads because they reduce carbon emissions associated with trucking. However, the construction process itself exacts a heavy environmental toll; activities such as roadbed excavation, bridge construction, and tunneling cause irreversible impacts on landscapes and hydrological systems. Afghanistan’s fragile northern ecosystem is ill-equipped to withstand the environmental shocks of large-scale infrastructure development.

In the absence of any environmental assessment, the construction of this railway could inflict permanent damage on the water resources, soil, and biodiversity of northern Afghanistan.  Part VI: The Truth—Not "Economic Cooperation," but a Struggle for Survival

Iran’s Calculus

◾Strategic Breakout: Bypassing the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz by establishing an overland route to China.
◾Resource Acquisition: Trading railway construction for rights to develop Afghanistan’s mineral deposits specifically strategic resources like lithium and copper.
◾Regional Influence: Using the railway network to draw Afghanistan and Central Asian nations into Iran’s economic orbit, thereby countering US and Saudi influence.

Afghanistan’s Calculus

◾ Breaking the Blockade: Reducing reliance on trade routes through Pakistan and opening new paths to Iranian ports and Central Asian markets.
◾ Generating Revenue: Securing much-needed cash flow through mineral exports to alleviate the economic crisis.
◾ Gaining Leverage: Exchanging mineral rights for railway infrastructure represents the best available option given the lack of alternatives.

Who Loses?

◾ Pakistan: Loses its monopoly over trade routes to Afghanistan, weakening its political influence over Kabul.
◾India: Sees the Chabahar Port project crippled by sanctions and its influence in Afghanistan supplanted by Iran and China.
◾The Afghan People: Their mineral resources are used to pay for railway construction; their land is requisitioned; their communities are neglected. Once the railway is built, profits will flow to Iranian enterprises and the Taliban elite, not to ordinary Afghans.

Conclusion: Empire and Resistance on the Rails

The Herat–Mazar-i-Sharif railway is no mere infrastructure project. It represents a strategic breakout against imperial containment, an unequal exchange of resources for infrastructure, a new battlefield for regional geopolitics, and an extension of internal power struggles within the Taliban.

Iran needs this railway to circumvent US sanctions. Afghanistan needs it to break Pakistan’s trade monopoly. China needs it to complete the overland network of the Belt and Road Initiative. Turkey needs it to expand its influence in Central Asia.

But what do the people of Afghanistan need?  What they need is peace, security, food, and dignity. They do not need a railway designed to transport their underground resources to foreign nations or to hand over their land to foreign corporations. What they need is a railway that belongs to the Afghan people, serves the Afghan people, and is controlled by the Afghan people.

Yet, this railway does not belong to them. It belongs to Iran’s strategic interests, the Taliban’s power games, and China’s geopolitical designs. As for the Afghan people, they are merely the compacted earth beneath the tracks.

While Gambari and Naeem shook hands in Tehran, Afghanistan’s mineral resources were being priced and its lands surveyed; meanwhile, the future of the Afghan people was being laid inch by inch along a track beyond their control, heading toward an unknown terminus.

This railway bears the name "Cooperation." Yet, in essence, it is a forced exchange born of the desperate struggle for survival. And in this exchange, the only ones whose voices go unheard are the people who must live beside the tracks or those forced to leave them behind.

text:
Fair point that there's an asymmetry, and some of the WWII questions that get shouted down are legit. Area bombing, Dresden, unconditional surrender, Yalta handing half of Europe to Stalin. Those should be debated.
I'll go further on WWI, that one is genuinely debatable and there's merit on both sides. Niall Ferguson argued we should have stayed out, a German-led Europe might have been something like an early EU, we'd have kept the empire, and maybe no Lenin, no Hitler. Max Hastings argued the other way, and he's got the documents. Germany's September Programme in 1914 set out what they wanted, chunks of France, Belgium as a vassal state, the Channel coast, the rest of Europe in a German-run economic bloc. And when they did win in the east they forced Brest-Litovsk on Russia and took a third of its population. Tucker was right about the cost too, the Eton chapel names, a generation gone. I can see both sides of that one.
WWII I can't. The difference isn't a taboo, it's that we know what the other side intended because they wrote it down and started doing it. The camps, the plans to clear Eastern Europe, a navy built to fight ours, invasion plans for Britain. The other wars look like disasters because the threat was overstated or the war failed. This one the threat was real and the war did what it set out to.
From where we sit it's not close. Hitler signed Munich and broke it six months later by taking Prague. Every British government for 300 years fought to stop one power owning the continent, Napoleon, the Kaiser, then him, and the Kaiser was nasty but he wasn't running death camps. Hitler's peace offer in 1940 meant accepting a Nazi Europe with a fleet being built to take on ours. And if you want to know what German rule over British soil looked like, look at the Channel Islands, forced labour and Jews shipped off to the camps.
Question how it was fought all you like, I'll happily have that argument. Whether it had to be fought, I don't think there's an argument.

Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., sparked bipartisan backlash after posting on X that every Muslim elected official in the United States is a security threat, a claim she made in the wake of Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s Democratic primary win.
Mace wrote on X on Friday, August 7, 2026, “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic. We refuse to be silent.” She posted the message roughly two months after she finished fifth in South Carolina’s Republican gubernatorial primary. She went on to name New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and El-Sayed specifically, telling followers Americans should be “very concerned” about the two progressive Muslim politicians.
When a British commentator criticized the post, Mace doubled down, writing, “If not wanting to be blown up, st*bbed, or rammed by a car by a radical Islamist in the United States of America makes us Islamophobes, then so be it.”
Two days later, CNN anchor Omar Jimenez pressed her on the remarks during an appearance on “CNN Newsroom,” asking whether she meant every Muslim elected official. Mace replied, “Uhh, that’s not what I said, that’s not what I said. I do think we have a real issue with radical Islamic—” Jimenez interjected, “I mean, it sounds like that’s what you’re saying,” to which Mace responded, “No, I was talking about elected officials.”
Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington condemned the post, writing on X, “This is absolutely disgusting and dangerous. Republicans must denounce this blatant Islamophobia. To Muslim communities across America: I will always stand with you.” Mace answered Jayapal directly, writing in part, “Islam must be confronted and Islam must be removed from civil society in the US.” California state Sen. Scott Wiener also criticized Mace, accusing her of demonizing Muslims. Neither Mace’s campaign nor her congressional office has offered further clarification on the original post. See less

There has never been a bigger gap between what is technologically possible and what the world understands to be possible.

For AI-native builders, the world has fundamentally changed. Things that once required months of effort and millions of dollars can now be built by one or two talented people in hours or days.

Business leaders outside the AI bubble know that AI can radically change their business, from how they run it to what they offer their customers, but they have no idea where to begin, or even who to trust to help them find out.

I don’t blame them. AI is accelerating so fast right now that if you aren’t actively building and learning at the frontier, your entire strategy is almost certainly built on wrong assumptions.

To use an analogy from history, right now some people are flying jets across the country while others are still dying of dysentery on the Oregon Trail.

It doesn’t have to be that way.

Today we’re launching Foundations Design & Engineering (FDE) to bridge that gap.

Over the past two years, Foundations has grown into a community of 300+ committed AI builders across Seattle and SF. Increasingly, the scarce resource for many of them isn’t the ability to build.

It’s finding great problems worth solving.

FDE is our attempt to connect these two worlds.

For existing companies eager to embrace AI, FDE should feel like magic. You express a business problem in plain English. We analyze your problem through an AI-native lens, assign the right team in our community to solve it, and help you get to the best outcome for your business as quickly and cheaply as possible.

No armies of junior consultants. No incentive to maximize billable hours. Just founder-grade technologists applying hard-fought lessons from the edge of what’s possible today.

Sometimes the answer is a few hours of expert help or a product that already exists. Sometimes it’s a full build. Sometimes it’s “the tech isn’t there yet, let’s find another way”.

You have problems. We have builders looking for them.
Let’s make the connection.

text:
BREAKING NEWS: Ross Hotel Partners Buys The Doyle Hotel For $22 Million

CHARLOTTESVILLE, VA — Ross Hotel Partners and its investment team have purchased The Doyle Hotel in Charlottesville for $22 million, Butch Ross, principal of Ross Hotel Partners, confirmed exclusively Tuesday morning with Jerry Miller of The @iLoveCVilleVA Network.

The sale of the prominent hotel at 499 W. Main Street closed Friday, October 2, 2026, Ross said. 

Ross partnered with Dipan Patel, CEO of Buckhead America Hospitality, on the acquisition. The partners used a "friends and family raise to capitalize our project," Ross told The I Love CVille Network.

THE DOYLE NAME WILL CHANGE AGAIN

The property will continue operating as The Doyle Hotel for approximately four to six months. Ross and his partners then plan to rebrand the hotel under a new name while transitioning the property into Hilton's Tapestry Collection, a move expected between the first and second quarters of 2027.

"It's not wise to have another name change in such a short time," Ross explained to The I Love CVille Network. "We will announce a new name for the hotel next year."

The Hilton affiliation will become a significant component of the new ownership group's strategy.

"Joining The Hilton Tapestry Collection is necessary because the consumer is hunting for that Hilton brand," Ross said. "They want their rewards points. That's where we saw an opportunity [with this deal]."

PINK GROUSE TO BECOME ELEVATED SUSHI CONCEPT

One of the first major changes Charlottesville residents will see won't require waiting until 2027.

Ross confirmed that ownership plans to reimagine The Pink Grouse, the farm-to-table restaurant and lobby bar inside The Doyle. Before the end of 2026, management intends to pivot and rebrand the restaurant into an elevated, first-class sushi concept.

The Indigo Road Hospitality Group of Charleston, South Carolina, will manage The Doyle's food-and-beverage operations.

Dreamscape Hospitality, a Dallas-based third-party hotel and hospitality management company, has been contracted to manage the hotel itself.

"We are like kids in a candy store right now," Ross told The I Love CVille Network. "We are going to breathe life into The Doyle."

ROSS WANTS THE DOYLE TO CLIMB CVILLE'S HOTEL MARKET

Ross was candid about where he believes The Doyle currently sits within Charlottesville's competitive hotel landscape — and where the new ownership group intends to take it.

"Right now, we are competing at the bottom of our competitive set, and that is going to change quickly," Ross said. "It's all about getting heads on beds right now."

Ross expects The Doyle to compete directly with some of Charlottesville's most recognizable upscale hotels, including The Draftsman, The Graduate, Kimpton The Forum Hotel and the Omni Charlottesville Hotel.

The strategy suggests Ross Hotel Partners isn't simply acquiring The Doyle and maintaining the status quo. The new ownership group plans to reposition the property, strengthen its food-and-beverage offerings, tap into Hilton's massive loyalty ecosystem and compete more aggressively for Charlottesville's leisure, business, university and event-driven hotel demand.

ROSS TO DISCUSS $22 MILLION DEAL LIVE ON THE I LOVE CVILLE SHOW

Ross will join Jerry Miller, CEO of @TheMillerOrg and host of The I Love CVille Show, live at 12:30 p.m. Tuesday, October 6, to discuss the $22 million acquisition, the future of The Doyle Hotel and his group's plans for the property.

The interview will offer Charlottesville an opportunity to hear directly from the new ownership about one of the city's most significant hospitality transactions of 2026.

The I Love CVille Show With Jerry Miller, 12:30 pm, Monday - Friday.

text:
First of all, this response was originally much shorter, but I thought some points warranted more development and explanation (and citations), thus it became a bit long. Apologies in advance for that.

I think this way of framing the new covenant risks doing a disservice to God’s prior dealings with Israel, and with man as a whole—even with Adam. Was Yahweh the God of only some Israelites, or of Israel as a whole? Were only some members of the covenant? I would argue that the whole people were in covenant with God (Exod. 24:7–8; Deut. 29:10–15), even though many proved faithless. I think Paul makes this distinction clear in 1 Corinthians 10:1–5: all Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,” all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank from the same spiritual Rock, which “was Christ,” yet “with most of them God was not pleased.” Such typology runs throughout the OT and into the NT. Israel could bear the Name of Yahweh and yet bear that Name in vain; likewise, we should not assume that being baptized into that same Name makes covenantal unfaithfulness impossible (Matt. 28:19; 1 Cor. 10:1–12; Heb. 3:7–19; 6:4–6; 10:26–31). This is why the prophets repeatedly insist that outward signs were never sufficient in themselves: circumcision of the flesh always pointed to circumcision of the heart (Deut. 10:16; 30:6; Jer. 4:4; Rom. 2:28–29), and God rejected ritual observance divorced from faith (Isa. 1:11–17; Hos. 6:6; Heb. 10:1–10). Indeed, “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Heb. 10:4). God has always called his people to faith—he does not and never has wanted faithless ritual. The rites themselves were never the point; they all pointed beyond themselves to Christ (Col. 2:16–17; Heb. 8:5; 10:1; cf. Rom. 10:4). It has all been Christ in all of God’s dealings with man (John 1:1–3; 1 Cor. 10:4; Heb. 11:26; 1 Pet. 1:10–11; Col. 1:16–17).

For that reason, much of Jeremiah’s new-covenant promise is not really all that novel in substance. God had already commanded Israel to place his words upon their hearts (Deut. 6:6; 11:18). God had already promised to be their God and make them his people (Exod. 6:7; Lev. 26:12; cf. 2 Cor. 6:16). God had already revealed himself as the God who forgives sin (Exod. 34:6–7; Ps. 103:8–12; cf. Rom. 4:6–8). The most novel characteristic of Jeremiah 31 is the promise that “they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jer. 31:34; Heb. 8:11). But I would argue that this points to a transformation of the old priestly order: under the Mosaic administration, access to God—his presence and instruction—was mediated through a tiered priesthood, while the new covenant expands that priestly vocation to the entire people as a whole (1 Pet. 2:5, 9; Rev. 1:6). Yet even this is not new! Israel was already called “a kingdom of priests” (Exod. 19:6), and Adam himself was placed in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Gen. 2:15), language associated with priestly service and guardianship (cf. Num. 3:7–8; 8:26). Therefore, Jeremiah is not speaking of something wholly new—he is speaking of a restored created order, with sin removed and humanity directed back to Yahweh; restored to the state which God called “very good” (Gen. 1:31; cf. Rom. 8:19–23).

Furthermore, if we read ahead to Jeremiah 33, it cannot be said that the new covenant simply replaces the Abrahamic covenant, for that promise is still being fulfilled in Christ (Gal. 3:16, 29; Phil. 2:9–11; Rev. 11:15; 15:4; 21:24–26); nor can it be said to replace the Davidic covenant, for that is fulfilled in Christ as our King (Jer. 33:17; Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:29–36); nor can it be said simply to abolish the priestly promises, for those too reach their fulfillment in Christ as our High Priest and in the expanded priesthood of the kingdom of Christ (Jer. 33:18, 21–22; Heb. 4:14; 7:11–28). Rather, the new covenant can only be said to supersede the Mosaic covenant, whose shadows and sacrificial order find their intended end in Christ (2 Cor. 3:7–14; Gal. 3:23–25; Heb. 8:6–13; 10:1–14). That old order was then brought to its visible and historical end in A.D. 70 with the destruction of the temple, after Christ had already offered himself as the definitive Sacrifice once for all.

This is why I do not think Jeremiah 31 requires us to conclude that the new covenant consists only of the elect. Jeremiah is not announcing that God has abandoned his former covenantal purposes, but that those purposes are being brought to their climactic fulfillment in Christ. Humanity’s original vocation was to image God, dwell in his presence, and serve him faithfully; sin corrupted that vocation, and Christ restores it and bestows it back upon us. Not only that, Christ, the Last Adam (1 Cor. 15:45), restores creation as creation and humanity as humanity—he does not abolish what God called “good.” He is the true image of God (Col. 1:15; 2 Cor. 4:4), and in union with him we are conformed to that image by his Spirit (Rom. 8:29; 2 Cor. 3:18).

The new covenant is therefore “new,” not because God has changed his purpose or dealings, but because what was promised and typified throughout all of salvation-history is brought to its intended end in Christ (Rom. 10:4; Gal. 3:23–25; Col. 2:16–17; Heb. 10:1). Therefore, I cannot see how one can argue that the new covenant is so vastly different than the old, for they had the same substance and goal. The newness is that the shadows are gone—Christ is unveiled. Christ has come. He has definitively re-created humanity through his own work and bestowed that renewed humanity back upon us.

text:
Ethiopia rejects pressure over Nile and Red Sea access
Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia have declared that Nile decisions require consultation and consensus amid a longstanding dispute with Ethiopia over its dam
Published 5 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/14C5G09rfG
Ethiopia has warned that coercion and aggression will not undermine its interests in the Red Sea and Nile, a day after Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia declared maritime governance the exclusive responsibility of coastal states and rejected unilateral measures harming downstream water supplies.
In a statement on Monday, Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry cited the East African country’s historical and geographical connections to the Red Sea and its position as the source of the Blue Nile, saying these realities cannot be altered by coercion or destabilization measures.
“Actions taken through proxies or acts of aggression will not change the facts on the ground,” the ministry said, declaring Ethiopia ready to defend its sovereignty and “core national interests.”
The statement did not name the four countries, whose leaders met in New Alamein, Egypt on Sunday for talks on regional security and cooperation. In a joint declaration following the summit, Egypt, Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia reaffirmed “the principle of freedom of navigation” and called for cooperation on transboundary rivers, including the Nile, through “prior notification, consultation and consensus.”
Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan have long clashed over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Africa’s largest hydroelectric dam with a generating capacity of 5,150 megawatts, which Ethiopia built on the Blue Nile and inaugurated in September 2025. Egypt and Sudan fear its operation could threaten their water supplies and demand a binding agreement on filling and operation. Ethiopia considers the dam essential for electricity generation and development and maintains that it will not harm its downstream neighbors.
According to the Foreign Ministry’s statement, the Blue Nile originates almost entirely in the Ethiopian highlands and supplies around 85% of the Nile’s total flow.
Ethiopia became landlocked when its former province, Eritrea, gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long liberation war. Its pursuit of sea access, which Ethiopia considers vital to its economy and security, has fueled tensions with neighboring countries. In January 2024, it signed a deal with Somaliland to obtain coastline access for a naval base in exchange for recognition. Somalia condemned the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty.
A Turkish-mediated agreement in December 2024 eased tensions and provided for negotiations on commercial sea access under Somali sovereignty. Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud told Al Jazeera over the weekend that his government has “no objection to Ethiopia gaining access to the sea through Somalia.” He said the country could offer Ethiopia access to up to three ports for trade.
Ethiopia’s push for sovereign access to Eritrea’s Assab Port has also strained relations with Eritrea, which accuses the country of plotting to take its ports by force. The two countries broke diplomatic ties last week after Ethiopia accused the Eritrean authorities of financing armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed

text:
The ad is a campaign commercial, and the government paid for it. Everything else is detail.
It's a near-copy of Trump's 2024 campaign spot with one change: the disclaimer now reads "Paid for by the U.S. Government." House Democrats say the White House budget office moved $20 million in Customs and Border Protection money on Sept. 19 into an account for border-security commemorative events that had held $500,000. The next day, DHS awarded a $20 million national media contract. The White House calls the ads public service announcements. They name enemies, they echo a campaign, and they air weeks before the midterms. That isn't public service. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican, says taxpayers shouldn't foot the bill. Whether a court calls it illegal is still open. Either way, money Congress gave to secure the border is promoting the president.
Now look at what the ad promises.
"Demolish the deep state." That means the career civil service, people bound to carry out the law no matter who wins. Their offense is refusing to treat the president's preferences as statute.
"Expel the warmongers." This comes from a president who struck Iran's nuclear sites and has ordered lethal strikes on boats in the Caribbean. The phrase is an insult, not an account of anyone's record.

"Throw off the sick political class that hates our country." Most of his critics don't hate the country. They oppose his policies, including immigration enforcement that has killed American citizens. Federal agents in Minneapolis killed Renee Good in January and Alex Pretti 17 days later. Both times the administration claimed a deadly threat, and both times bystander video contradicted it. An agent in Texas killed Ruben Ray Martinez in March 2025, and DHS didn't acknowledge it publicly until records surfaced nearly a year later. Challenging an official story is not disloyalty. A free country requires it.

"Drive out the globalists." Oil trades on a world market, and disease crosses oceans. Trade, finance, and migration ignore slogans. Isolation is not a policy.
"Rout the fake news media." In September, Trump revoked the White House passes of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, calling their work fake news. A federal judge, a Trump appointee, ordered the passes restored. He found the outlets were likely denied due process and that nothing in the record supported the national-security rationale. The White House may manage access to its grounds. It may not use access to punish coverage.

On Monday, Trump reversed course. He said MAGA Inc. would pay for the ads going forward, while calling the use of taxpayer money "a rather standard thing to do." The second claim undercuts the first. If the spending had been proper, there would be nothing to fix. Moving the bill to a super PAC concedes what the White House still won't say out loud: these are political ads, and political ads are not the public's expense. The concession only looks forward, though. Taxpayers have already covered an estimated $10 million or more, and neither the White House nor MAGA Inc. would say whether that money will be repaid. Trump himself said earlier that he would "gladly pay the money" if anyone thought the ads were wrong. Plenty of people have said so, his own party's Senate leader among them, and MAGA Inc. reported roughly $416 million in cash in August. Repayment is the honest remedy, and so far nobody has offered it.

The ad targets the civil service, the press, and anyone who disagrees. It's a campaign ad, recycled and charged to the public, and now that he has been caught, it's being moved to a different account. Calling it a public service never changed what it was. Changing who pays from here on doesn't change what was already taken.  Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in part, lost her job for promoting herself using Homeland Security funds to make films, but the only people who can hold Trump accountable are the voters and he should hear from them loud and clear during the midterm elections.

text:
OIL IS BACK AT $100 BY LUNCH. STOCKS ARE STILL CELEBRATING THE DROP:

The big indexes kept their morning gains into lunch, and the S&P 500 is still above its record close. One of the two reasons they rose is gone. Brent crude, the global oil price, has climbed back to about $100 a barrel and erased nearly all of its early slide. The other reason, slightly cheaper borrowing, is still standing. The midday answer: the mood held, the support under it got thinner, and smaller companies have already turned red.

Where the indexes sit at 12:46pm ET:

- S&P 500: 7,832.78, +58.83 points / +0.76% today.
- Nasdaq composite: 27,664.19, +186.88 points / +0.68% today.
- Dow Jones Industrial Average: 51,577.05, +309.15 points / +0.60% today.

iShares Russell 2000 ETF (IWM) at $282.18, -$1.20 / -0.43% today.

That fund holds about 2,000 smaller US companies.

The S&P 500's day so far:

- Open: 7,805.96.
- High: 7,844.52, at about 11:25am ET.
- Record close to beat, from August 13: 7,798.99.

It has slipped about 12 points from that high. It still sits about 34 points above the record. The small-company fund went the other way. It opened at $284.40 and has spent most of the morning under Monday's close.

The turn is in oil.

- Brent crude futures, December: $100.11 a barrel, -$0.21 / -0.21% since Monday's close.
- West Texas Intermediate futures, November, the US benchmark: $89.67, +$0.24 / +0.27% since Monday's close.

Brent bottomed at $97.06 around 8:50am ET. The US price is now above Monday's close. About half of the climb back came in a single hour. At 11:15am Brent was near $98.50. By 12:15pm it was over $100. The S&P 500 set its high for the day inside that same hour.

Cheaper oil was half of this morning's case for stocks. It eases the fear that fuel costs keep inflation, and interest rates, climbing. That half has expired, and energy stocks show the switch.

Energy Select Sector SPDR (XLE) at $63.89, +$0.44 / +0.69% today.

It opened below Monday's close and has climbed with crude since. Shortly after 10am it was the weakest of the 11 sector funds.

The other half is still standing. The 10-year Treasury yield is what Washington pays to borrow for a decade, and it feeds mortgage rates and company loans.

- 10-year Treasury yield: 5.273%, down 0.038 percentage point from Monday's 5.311% close.

Its low for the day, about 5.25%, came around 11:20am. It has edged up since.

The weak spot is narrow. The typical large company is keeping pace with the giants.

- Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) at $212.53, +$1.41 / +0.67% today.
- SPDR S&P MidCap 400 ETF Trust (MDY) at $676.70, +$4.43 / +0.66% today.

The equal-weight fund holds the same amount of every S&P 500 company, so a handful of giants cannot carry it. It is up almost as much as the regular index, and mid-size companies are keeping up too. The selling is concentrated in small companies, and much of it in one corner.

SPDR S&P Biotech ETF (XBI) at $151.25, -$4.94 / -3.16% today.

Its low came at about 10:45am, the same time as the small-company fund's. Biotech is a bigger slice of the small-company fund than of the S&P 500, which helps explain why small companies are red while mid-size ones are not.

The sharpest selling is in vaccine makers that jumped Monday on a plague scare. A 28-year-old worker at a plague research institute in Irkutsk, Siberia, died last week of pneumonia of undetermined origin. On Tuesday, World Health Organization spokesperson Christian Lindmeier said the WHO sees "a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole."

- Moderna (MRNA) at $190.91, -$12.31 / -6.06% today.
- Novavax (NVAX) at $11.20, -$1.37 / -10.87% today.

Novavax rose about 20% on Monday. Moderna rose about 7%. This morning Moderna touched $212.19, its high of the past year, before the selling hit. Moderna is on none of the six Len5 watchlists, because it still loses money. Novavax is on none either: it loses money and owes more than it owns.

The leader sits at the other end of the sector list.

Utilities Select Sector SPDR (XLU) at $40.98, +$1.01 / +2.53% today.

Constellation Energy (CEG) at $306.62, +$39.00 / +14.57% today.

Constellation, which runs the largest fleet of US nuclear plants, jumped after announcing two long-term power supply deals before the open. It is on none of the six Len5 watchlists: at about 30 times its past year of profit at today's price, the value styles have no discount to weigh. Its jump has nothing to do with oil, so the day's leading sector does not need cheap crude.

Into the close, Eastern time:

- 1:00pm: the Treasury sells $58B of new 3-year notes. The 3-year yield goes in at 4.921%, down 0.04 percentage point from Monday.
- 4:00pm: the close. A finish above 7,798.99 would give the S&P 500 its first record close since August 13.
- Wednesday: $39B of 10-year notes at 1:00pm, then minutes of the Fed's September 15-16 meeting at 2:00pm.

With oil back where it started, cheaper borrowing is the only one of this morning's reasons left. That makes the 3-year sale matter more now than it did at the open. If buyers demand a higher yield than the market offered minutes before, borrowing costs rise again.

The morning has truly turned if the 10-year climbs back above Monday's 5.311% close. It has also turned if the S&P 500 finishes under its 7,798.99 record. The rally is widening instead if the small-company fund gets back above Monday's $283.38 close.

Stocks are still trading as if oil got cheaper this morning. It did, for a few hours. The afternoon rests on what money costs, and nothing else from 9:30 is left to lean on.

text:
Another FF/FG Budget. Another failure to make Ireland affordable.

This could have been a Budget to make life more affordable for workers and families. Instead, for the second year running, over 1.5 million workers are being left worse off.

After years of record tax receipts, people are entitled to ask: why is it still so expensive to live in Ireland.

Renters get just €150, while big developers once again benefit from hundreds of millions in tax breaks.

Home heating oil has risen by around €700 a fill this year, yet the Government offers a reduction of less than €43.

Fuel Allowance is being increased by €5 a week but cut by four weeks, meaning people will actually be €12 worse off over the winter while energy prices continue to rise.

Students are still paying €350 more in fees than when the promise to abolish fees was first made. At this rate, free fees are nearly 16 years away.

And people with disabilities who were left €1,400 worse off last year are still waiting for meaningful support. A €10 increase next January is nowhere near enough.

FF and Fine Gael have spent billions, but they haven’t tackled the costs that are putting families under pressure every single day.

Sinn Féin proposed practical measures to put money back into people’s pockets: cutting USC for every worker on the first €40,000 they earn, removing carbon tax from home heating oil, restoring €400 energy credits, cutting fuel costs, reducing student fees, doubling the renters’ tax credit, investing in affordable housing and delivering €10-a-day childcare.

This Government had the money and the opportunity to make a real difference.

Instead, workers, renters, students and people with disabilities are being told to wait while developers continue to benefit.

Ireland doesn’t have a money problem.

It has a priorities problem.

And once again, FF/FG have shown exactly whose side they are on.

text:
The 'Cornell 7' haven't been charged. The mob doesn't care | Opinion
What's most troubling in the Cornell University rape allegations is that onlookers have already made up their minds about who is to blame.
Ingrid Jacques
USA TODAY
Oct. 2, 2026, 4:02 a.m. ET

The allegations of a gang rape at a Cornell University frat house in 2024 that are dominating headlines have transported me right back to the preceding decade, where cases of regret too often turned into accusations of rape.

These were the years of the Obama administration, during which colleges and universities were pushed to investigate allegations of sexual misconduct in ways that favored the accusers. The accused – almost always young men – were essentially stripped of their constitutional due process rights, and the accuser’s word was all that mattered. Many male students were kicked off campus, with their reputations in ruins while they often lost judicial protections.

This problematic and unfair framework was fixed during President Donald Trump’s first term, and as of Sept. 28, those guidelines have been officially reinstated.

There is a rush to judgment in the Cornell rape allegations

The heated reaction to the Cornell allegations and the rush to judge the young men involved before they’ve had their day in court makes me fear the country has learned nothing about the dangers of simply “believing women.”

The woman at the center of this latest case, who conveniently gets to be “Jane Doe” while her alleged rapists are all named, caused an uproar when she filed a civil suit on Sept. 16 – nearly two years after the initial incident occurred. Her story has changed “dramatically” since she first told it in October 2024, according to Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who is reopening the case in light of the “new” information.

Biden's Title IX rules bring back 'kangaroo courts.' They will hurt, not help, women | Opinion
At the time, Van Houten reviewed the statement Jane Doe made to campus police and decided that what had happened during that alcohol-and-drug-fueled night was voluntary and consensual and did not run afoul of New York law.

Fast-forward two years, and Jane Doe has remembered things very differently. In her civil complaint, she alleges she was “sexually assaulted and raped” by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity. Also named in the lawsuit are the university, the fraternity, her sorority and even a local bar for all neglecting to protect her from the assault that allegedly followed.

Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time, apparently takes zero responsibility for her actions. The lawsuit lays out that – on her own accord – she consumed “10 standard drinks” within three hours before she “stumbled” to the frat house – also her own decision.

In the public's eye, the accused men are already guilty

What’s most troubling in the Cornell allegations is that onlookers have already made up their minds about who is to blame.
From politicians to celebrities to TV and social media personalities, the accused (who’ve never been charged with a crime) may as well have been convicted.

In a statement, and in an interview with NPR, U.S. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat, called the allegations in the rape case “serious and horrific.”

“I am glad the district attorney is reopening this case,” Gillibrand said. “Regardless of what this grand jury concludes, the larger truth is clear: a system that forces survivors to these lengths is a system that is fundamentally broken.”

New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, also a Democrat, referred to a “culture of rape” on elite campuses like Cornell.

Actress Florence Pugh posted on Instagram that she felt “uneasy and sick and anxious” about the allegations.

“I know this has happened before, and I hate the idea of it happening again,” Pugh wrote.

Actor Josh Gad also took to Instagram, saying he thought the “Cornell boys lost the right to a future when they stole a future from a helpless young woman,” calling the allegations a “violent and sick criminal act.”

I was pleasantly surprised to hear Sunny Hostin, a host of “The View” and a former federal prosecutor, offer a fair take on air, calling out the contrasting accounts by the alleged victim and how this is affecting the accused men:

“The pictures of these young men who have not been charged, not been adjudicated, are being plastered all over the internet. I think people are reporting this story inaccurately. I think they are reporting it unfairly. And while this is something that we have to take very seriously, there is no way, according to her statement in 2024, that any prosecutor would have brought this court case.”

For this, Hostin has been derided for her “disgusting” comments and not showing enough “empathy” for Jane Doe.

I remember instances in the not-so-distant past when other accusations of gang rape turned out to be made up and false.

This happened in 2006 in the infamous Duke lacrosse team rape allegations and in 2014 when a salacious account in Rolling Stone (later retracted) detailed reports of a gang rape at a University of Virginia fraternity house. Both stories garnered reactions similar to the Cornell case, with knee-jerk support of the alleged victims.
Not all women tell the truth, and not all men are rapists.

The DSA agenda may cost $200 trillion. Guess who pays for it? | OpinionTrump's public charge rule puts taxpayers first on immigration | OpinionHigh prices are killing date night – and GOP's midterm hopes | Opinion

At Cornell, however, a shocking 1 in 3 undergraduate women reported in 2025 that they experienced unwanted sexual contact or penetration since enrolling.

It defies belief that there are so many sexual predators who attend the Ivy League school. But it does point to underlying issues between the sexes.

A new report from the American Enterprise Institute’s Survey Center on American Life showed a startling 66% of young Democratic women blame men for the challenges facing women in American society. A majority of young women identify as Democrats.

Regardless of the outcome in the Cornell civil lawsuit and the reopened criminal investigation, young women must take responsibility for their actions. Everyone at that Cornell party – including the alleged victim – made mistakes, from drinking too much to taking drugs to partaking in unwise sex. Why should the men involved be held to a higher standard?

Women shouldn’t expect coddling. And regretting one’s bad decisions is a far cry from rape.

text:
If you haven't listened to the 37-minute JxW “THIS MAN” audiobook, let me actually explain the entire story from beginning to end, because there is so much more happening here than “Wonwoo is a mysterious man who appears in people's dreams.” The story is built around two completely different figures: Wonwoo, the Protector who enters people's dreams to bring them back to reality, and Jeonghan, who creates an entire dream world because he cannot accept the reality of losing someone. And the tragedy is that, from the outside, you don't immediately understand which one is saving people and which one is trapping them.

Wonwoo is the Protector. He moves through the space between dreams and waking life, entering the dreams of sleeping people and seeing the things they carry with them when they fall asleep: their regrets, failed exams, unanswered messages, lost relationships, people they never got to say goodbye to, and all the things that continue hurting even when nobody else can see them. When he finds someone suffering inside their dream, he doesn't erase what happened to them. He simply approaches them, leans down, whispers into their ear, and gives them a peaceful, dreamless sleep.

 When they wake up, they can't properly remember him. All that remains is a vague image of a tall man in a dark coat, a presence they can't quite place. Those fragments slowly turn into a rumor, the rumor becomes an urban legend, and the figure comes to be known as “THIS MAN.”

Then there is Jeonghan, whose story exists somewhere completely outside the normal flow of reality. His world is permanently stuck at 8:47 AM. The same morning keeps repeating because Jeonghan created this world for one reason: someone called “A” has disappeared from his life, and he cannot accept that A is gone.

So instead of returning to reality and grieving, Jeonghan builds a place where A can still exist. Breakfast is always prepared. The surroundings remain familiar. Everything stays exactly as he wants it to be. But there is a problem with the world he created: a dream can recreate the appearance of something you remember, but it cannot truly bring back someone who is gone. And Jeonghan's memories are beginning to disappear.

At first, it's small details. Then A's voice becomes harder to remember. Eventually, Jeonghan can no longer remember A's face. That is what frightens him most, because as long as he can remember A, he can continue pretending that A is still there. So he covers A's head with a white cloth and cuts two holes for the eyes. He no longer has to look at a face he can't remember. The figure underneath the cloth can remain A simply because Jeonghan chooses to believe it is A.

But eventually, A runs away.

And once A disappears, Jeonghan's dream world begins to deteriorate. The sanctuary he created needs something to keep it going, so Jeonghan starts entering other people's dreams. He approaches sleeping people and offers them the same escape he created for himself: “Come with me to a place where wishes come true.”

People follow him because the offer is almost impossible to refuse. In their dreams, they can have the things they don't have in reality. They don't have to deal with regret, loneliness, failure, or loss. They can simply stay somewhere beautiful. But the more people Jeonghan brings into his world, the more their dreams become part of the world he has created.

And while all of this is happening inside the dream, something terrifying is happening outside.

People across the city begin falling asleep. They collapse on buses, in offices, on the streets, and in other public places, but they aren't screaming or fighting it. They are sleeping peacefully, often with happy expressions on their faces. Even television broadcasts begin to disappear because the people working there have fallen asleep. Little by little, the waking city becomes empty because people are choosing the dream over reality.

text:
Three deals hit this morning. One is signed, one is signed with cash, & one is still just a bid.

Energy Transfer($ET) agreed to buy Vaquero Midstream for about $2.625Billion. The mix is $1.95Billion in cash and about 33.3 million new Energy Transfer common units. Close is aimed at the fourth quarter, still subject to regulatory approval. Vaquero runs about 300 miles of pipe in the southern Delaware Basin, Loving, Reeves, Ward, and Winkler counties. The Caymus Processing Complex has three trains at about 675 million cubic feet a day, with land for two more trains that could take the site toward 1.2 billion cubic feet a day. Contracts are fee based, about 100,000 dedicated acres, average life about 10 years. Energy Transfer says the buy is immediately accretive to distributable cash flow per common unit, and that the gas ties into pipes, fractionation, terminals, and export it already runs. Kelcy Warren’s partnership has been guiding $5Billion to $5.5Billion of 2026 capital, mostly on the gas network.

Uber($UBER) said it will buy ezCater for $2.3Billion in cash. Boston company, founded in 2007, is the site offices use when a meeting needs trays instead of a single lunch. More than $2.5Billion in gross bookings over the last 12 months. Average order above $400. Uber wants those orders on Uber Eats, next to the Uber for Business accounts it already has. Dara Khosrowshahi said catering is a large line for restaurants. Close is aimed at the coming months, and is still in need of approval. In July Uber agreed to buy Delivery Hero for $14.8Billion. ezCater is the smaller of the two, and the one with a $400 ticket already on the books.

Seagate($STX) is the one that is not done. Bloomberg reported today that Seagate and Toshiba are both after TDK’s magnetic heads unit, the read and write heads inside a hard drive. Toshiba opened talks in the spring. Seagate came over the summer with a higher offer. The figure being discussed is as much as several billion dollars. TDK is the only independent maker of those heads and sells them to Seagate, Toshiba, and Western Digital($WDC). TrendForce puts 2026 drive share near 48% Western Digital, 42% Seagate, 10% Toshiba. A buyer would own a part the other two still purchase. Antitrust is the obvious review, because data center storage is being treated as strategic. TDK has been moving spend toward batteries, passives, and sensors. Seagate and TDK have not commented. Toshiba has said the report does not match its understanding.

Vaquero’s customers will get paid first if the fourth quarter close holds and the two extra trains get built. Uber Eats restaurants are next if a $400 catering order actually lands in the app. Seagate only if a bid becomes a contract and a regulator lets one drive maker own the independent head line. Western Digital has a reason to read that filing carefully.

Watch the Energy Transfer close, the ezCater approval clock, & whether TDK names a buyer.

A person perceiving audio that is not being delivered through ordinary external speakers.

The patent specifically discusses modulating speech onto an RF carrier so that intelligible subjective sound can be produced through the RF hearing effect.

https://t.co/0VrzWtpcsC

“Apparatus for audibly communicating speech using the radio frequency hearing effect.”

text:
🚨 Arsenal are preparing a double bid worth a reported £119m in the January window for two left-wing targets: RB Leipzig’s Antonio Nusa and Juventus’s Kenan Yildiz.

The club sold Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli for a combined £77m over the summer and missed out on Morgan Rogers and Vinícius Júnior before signing Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for around £34m. 

Tzolis has started well under Mikel Arteta but is expected to miss two to three weeks with a hamstring injury picked up on international duty, prompting Arsenal to look for a higher-impact option.

On Nusa, #Arsenal are working on a formal offer of about €40m (£34m), while Leipzig are said to want €60–65m (£51–55m). 

Arsenal and Tottenham had already shown interest in the 21-year-old Norwegian in July.

On Yildiz,  Arsenal sporting director Andrea Berta is ready to table a €100m (£85m) bid to beat Real Madrid to the 21-year-old Turkish forward, who extended his Juventus contract to 2030. 

Juventus will not sell him in January under any circumstances, though a summer exit could become possible if they miss Champions League qualification and the player pushes for a move. 

Arsenal are prepared to “go crazy” for him.

Nusa is the more realistic January option, while Yildiz would represent the bigger long-term upgrade.

ii. However, many other commentators believe it is unlikely that Paul wrote this book. Dods quotes Farrar: “The writer cites differently from St. Paul; he writes differently; he argues differently; he declaims differently; he constructs and connects his sentences differently; he builds up his paragraphs on a wholly different model… His style is the style of a man who thinks as well as writes in Greek; whereas St. Paul wrote in Greek but thought in Syriac.”

iii. F.F. Bruce quoted Calvin on this point: “The manner of teaching and the style sufficiently show that Paul was not the author, and the writer himself confesses in the second chapter (Hebrews 2:3) that he was one of the disciples of the apostles, which is wholly different from the way in which Paul spoke of himself.”

iv. The early commentator Tertullian (who wrote in the early 200s) said Barnabas wrote Hebrews, but he offered no support for this statement other than that Barnabas was a Levite (Acts 4:36) and a man of encouragement (Acts 4:36).

v. Martin Luther believed that Apollos wrote the book of Hebrews, because Acts tells us Apollos was eloquent and had a strong command of the Old Testament (Acts 18:24).

vii. No matter who the human author of Hebrews was, there are indications that it was written fairly early in the New Testament period, probably somewhere around AD 67 to 69. The reference to Timothy (Hebrews 13:23) places it fairly early. The present lack of physical persecution (Hebrews 12:4) puts it fairly early. Finally, the lack of any reference to the destruction of the temple probably puts it before AD 70, when Jerusalem and the second temple were destroyed. Since the writer to the Hebrews was so concerned with the passing of the Old Covenant, it seems unlikely that he would ignore the destruction of the temple if it had already happened before he wrote.

text:
The Night of the Paris Riots

It was neither a battle nor a siege, nor even quite a revolt, but rather a series of riots pitting the populace against the garrison. While the nobility busied themselves with the business of war, the common people took to the streets in a fury. The French Civil War between the Armagnacs and the Burgundians offers a prime example of this facet of medieval society; for the first time since the Jacquerie, and perhaps even before, the common people, regardless of status, played a significant role in the unfolding of the civil war, particularly in Paris.

The violence reached its peak, transcending mere factional conflict, on the night of June 12, 1418. Parisians had already endured nearly a decade of street violence when a sudden rumor threw everything into chaos. Although the Armagnacs had been driven out of Paris on May 29 and the Burgundians held the capital, a rumor began to spread that the Armagnacs were returning to slaughter the entire population and dump their bodies into the Seine in sacks.

The situation spiraled out of control. Upon hearing the cries of "Alarm!" and "To arms! We’ve been betrayed!" at 11:00 PM, tens of thousands of Parisians, 60,000 of any "society level" according to Monstrelet, poured into the streets, fueled by a rage unlike anything the city had ever known. Everyone took up arms, wielding old mallets, axes, hatchets, and clubs. Believing the Armagnacs were on the verge of entering the city, they decided to kill all the prisoners: "Kill! Kill! Kill every last one of those Armagnac traitors! I renounce God if even one of them escapes!" or even "Kill all these foreigners!", referring to the Armagnac troops from Brittany and Gascony regions, at a time when the concept of a nation was merely geographical and local. The Burgundians were overwhelmed; even the mightiest knights in full armor were forced to retreat, so uncontrollable had the crowds become. The Provost of Paris, Jean de Villiers de L'Isle-Adam, stepped before the mob, pleading for calm, mercy, and justice. But the people shouted back: "To hell with your reason, mercy, and justice!"

More than five prisons across the capital were targeted; that night, Armagnacs, civilians, and Burgundians alike were slaughtered by the hundreds amidst total chaos:

At the Palace, gates and bars were smashed in. The Constable and faction leader Bernard VII d'Armagnac, the Chancellor, and a squire had their throats slit despite their pleas, and the courtyard filled with corpses. Victims were stripped of their clothes, even their breeches, before they had even breathed their last. They were beaten about the face until unrecognizable; only the Constable and the Chancellor could be identified, having been killed in their beds. The Constable suffered a broken leg, and a strip of skin was carved from his torso in the shape of his emblem, the Armagnac band. 
At Saint-Éloi, everyone was hacked to death with axes. At the Petit Châtelet, a Burgundian accomplice inside called out the prisoners' names; each man was struck down as he lowered his head to pass through the wicket gate. The bodies were dragged to a cesspool. Some prisoners fought back, shouting "Long live the Dauphin!" and wounding many attackers, only to be thrown from the windows onto waiting pikes. 
At the Grand Châtelet, according to the chronicler Pintoin, armed royal officials held out for nearly two hours before the massacre ensued: prisoners were hurled from the windows, even those imprisoned merely for debt. According to Monstrelet, the prisoners, armed with armor and projectiles, killed several attackers and were only captured the following day, driven out by fire and smoke.
Other prisons included Saint-Martin-des-Champs, Saint-Magloire, the Temple, and Four-l'Évêque. Those that could not be forced open were set ablaze, leaving the prisoners to burn or suffocate.

Ultimately, the night's toll stood at between 2,500 and 5,000 dead, victims of indiscriminate slaughter, with most bodies left uncollected for two or three days.

And the irony? The rumor that had spread was false. No Armagnacs were planning to enter Paris this night; following their defeat at the Battle of the Bastille in early June, their troops had all retreated to the south.
