text:
You wrote: “There is actual need for another priesthood for New Testament believers.”

That frames the issue incorrectly. Catholics are not claiming Christ’s priesthood is insufficient and therefore another independent priesthood had to be invented. Catholic theology teaches that there is 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱, Christ’s, in which believers participate in different ways. The real question is whether Christ established a distinct ordained ministry within His priestly people. The New Testament plainly shows that He did.

You wrote: “Jesus never says that we need one and neither did the apostles.”

Jesus does not use the later English word “priest” for the apostles. But that is not the same as saying He gives them no distinctive ministerial functions. He commissions them as the Father commissioned Him (John 20:21), gives them authority to forgive or retain sins (John 20:23), commands them to celebrate the Eucharistic memorial (Luke 22:19), and gives Peter and the apostolic body authority to bind and loose (Matt. 16:19; 18:18).

The apostles then appoint presbyters in the churches (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5), transmit ministry through laying on of hands (1 Tim. 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6), and command that what they received be entrusted to another generation (2 Tim. 2:2). The office is present before the later technical vocabulary becomes fixed.

You wrote: “The role which is the central figure in every Catholic mass…is completely ignored by all the main characters and writers of the New Testament.”

It is not ignored. What is absent is the later English terminology. The 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 are there: presidency over churches, ordination, authoritative teaching, discipline, Eucharistic ministry, anointing of the sick, forgiveness of sins, and succession.

And the generation immediately following the apostles makes this even clearer. Around A.D. 110 Ignatius of Antioch speaks repeatedly of the 𝗯𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗽, 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘆, and 𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀, and says that the valid Eucharist is that celebrated by the bishop or someone he authorizes. That is not a third-century invention.

You wrote: “The primary role of a priest is to bridge the gap between God and people.”

That describes Christ’s unique mediatorship, not the Catholic priest as a second mediator alongside Him. Catholic theology agrees that 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗲 is the eternal High Priest and the one mediator whose sacrifice reconciles humanity to the Father.

The ministerial priest does not create another bridge. He ministers the benefits of the 𝗼𝗻𝗲 bridge, Christ. The same principle applies elsewhere: Christ alone saves, yet Paul calls himself a “minister of reconciliation” (2 Cor. 5:18–20). A minister participating in Christ’s work does not compete with Christ.

You wrote: “Since we are now in Christ Jesus, that role…is no longer needed since there is no gap.”

That argument goes much farther than your conclusion can support. If union with Christ eliminated the need for ministerial offices, then there would be no need for pastors, teachers, elders, bishops, or deacons either. Yet you yourself affirm those offices.

The question is not whether Christ has reconciled us to God. He has. The question is whether Christ chose to administer His Church through appointed ministers. Scripture says yes.

You wrote: “Another lesser role of an OT priest was to guard the temple. Believers are now the temple…so that role passes to the believer.”

Certainly believers are temples of the Holy Spirit. But that does not abolish ecclesial oversight. Paul still commands presbyters and overseers to shepherd and guard the flock (Acts 20:28–31). The spiritualization of the temple does not eliminate ordained pastoral responsibility.

You wrote: “Priests also taught God’s word. That role is now replaced by the pastor and teacher.”

But this simply concedes a distinct ministerial office while insisting it cannot be priestly. Catholicism does not deny pastors and teachers. It identifies ordained presbyters as pastors who teach, govern, and exercise sacramental ministry.

The dispute is over the theological character of that office, not whether the office exists.

You wrote: “The only role we need a priest in isn’t for believers. It’s for unbelievers who still have the gap.”

That conclusion is nowhere stated in Scripture. On the contrary, ordained ministers are consistently appointed 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗵𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀: “presbyters in every church” (Acts 14:23), presbyters “in every town” (Titus 1:5), and elders who shepherd “the flock of God” (1 Pet. 5:1–2).

So Scripture places ordained ministry precisely among people who are already Christians.

You wrote: “Most Catholics today do not consider the priesthood of all believers sacrificial.”

Whatever individual Catholics may have told you does not determine Catholic doctrine. And historically, your claim that sacrificial language for the common Christian priesthood only appears with Tertullian or Cyprian is too late.

Justin Martyr, writing around A.D. 155, explicitly calls Christians the “true high-priestly race” and speaks of the pure sacrifices they offer to God. That is nearly a century before Cyprian.

At the same time, Justin describes a presiding minister who offers the Eucharistic thanksgiving while deacons distribute it. So very early Christianity could affirm 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 the priestly identity of the whole Christian people and differentiated liturgical ministry without seeing a contradiction.

You wrote: “Catholicism diminishes the priesthood of all believers by saying we need another priesthood.”

No. That assumes two rival priesthoods. Catholic theology does not teach two competing priesthoods. It teaches two modes of participation in the 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝗖𝗵𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁: the baptismal priesthood of all believers and the ministerial priesthood of the ordained.

There is a biblical precedent for precisely this distinction. God called all Israel “a kingdom of priests” (Ex. 19:6), yet that universal priestly identity did not abolish the distinct Aaronic ministry. Corporate priesthood and ministerial priesthood are therefore not mutually exclusive concepts.

You wrote: “It would be no different than saying we need another kind of apostle because the first isn’t good enough.”

That analogy actually helps the Catholic case. Catholicism does 𝗻𝗼𝘁 claim bishops are apostles in every unique sense. The apostles were foundational eyewitnesses. But Scripture shows that aspects of their 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲 and 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 were transmitted.

Paul → Timothy → faithful men → others (2 Tim. 2:2).

The apostolic foundation is unique; the ministry built upon it continues. Those are not contradictory claims.

You wrote: “We have all the roles we need in the NT. Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers, bishops, elders and deacons.”

Exactly. And Catholics are not adding a mysterious ninth office disconnected from those. The Catholic presbyter/priest is historically the continuation of the New Testament 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲.

The English word “priest” itself developed from “presbyter.” The later sacramental vocabulary became more explicit, but the underlying ordained ministry did not suddenly appear centuries later.

You wrote: “The apostles fully equipped the church. It’s odd that Catholics believe the apostles failed.”

Catholics believe precisely the opposite. The apostles succeeded so well that they 𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝘂𝗶𝗻𝗴 after their deaths.

1 Clement, near the end of the first century, explicitly says that the apostles appointed ministers and provided that, after those men died, “other approved men” should succeed to their ministry. That is precisely the opposite of apostolic failure.

You wrote: “The NT never contains the Catholic priesthood. Never states or infers it.”

It is fair to say the New Testament does not simply hand us the later theological vocabulary fully developed. But “never infers it” is much harder to maintain.

You have presbyters appointed to every church, ordination by laying on of hands, apostolic authority being transmitted, ministers governing and teaching, elders anointing the sick (James 5:14–15), apostles receiving authority over forgiveness of sins (John 20:21–23), and the Eucharistic command handed to the apostolic circle.

Then, virtually immediately outside the New Testament, Ignatius describes one bishop, a presbyterate, deacons, one altar, and a Eucharist under episcopal authority.

That is not “no inference.” It is a trajectory requiring explanation.

You wrote: “Catholicism adds a priesthood for which there is no logic or biblical need.”

But Christianity is not constructed only from offices that we independently decide are logically necessary. If Christ and the apostles established an ordained ministry, its legitimacy rests on their authority, not on whether we first conclude that we personally “need” one.

And historically the sacrificial understanding is not a medieval reconstruction of Leviticus. Irenaeus, before A.D. 200, describes Christ as teaching the “new offering of the New Covenant,” which the Church received from the apostles and offers throughout the world.

So the actual historical progression is:

𝗡𝗧 𝗮𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗹𝗲𝘀 → 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 → 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 → 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗺𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 → 𝗖𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁’𝘀 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗜𝗴𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘂𝘀’ 𝗯𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗽-𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗯𝘆𝘁𝗲𝗿-𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 → 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝘀𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝘂𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝘆.

That is why your final statement, “My argument still holds, both from the Bible and the earliest church fathers,” is precisely where the evidence is weakest. The terminology develops, yes. But the 𝗼𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗲, 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆, and 𝘀𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝘂𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 are all visible far too early to dismiss the Catholic priesthood as a later invention.

The strongest objection you can make is that the New Testament does not yet use later Catholic priestly terminology for presbyters. That is true. But that is very different from proving that the 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲 did not already exist.

text:
Revelation 15 and 16
The Bowl Judgments
Prelude

- The Two Witnesses

In my previous “Interlude Between Judgments” study concerning the Antichrist, I briefly touched upon the introduction of the Two Witnesses sent by God. Before we move into the terrible and final series of judgments—the Seven Bowl Judgments—it is important to understand the ministry of these two remarkable servants of God and their place within the events of the Tribulation.

During the first half of the Tribulation, God will send these Two Witnesses to minister in Jerusalem and testify to the Jewish people of Israel. Revelation tells us that they will prophesy for 1,260 days, or three and one-half years (Revelation 11:3). God will give them supernatural authority and power, and their ministry will carry both a message of repentance and judgment.

At the heart of their ministry will be God's purpose for Israel. Throughout the Tribulation, God will be drawing His covenant people toward the recognition of their true Messiah—Jesus Christ, the One whom they pierced (Zechariah 12:10). The ministry of the Two Witnesses will therefore stand as a powerful testimony that Jesus Christ is Lord and that salvation is found in Him.

These men will not merely preach; God will empower them with extraordinary signs of judgment.

“And if anyone wants to harm them, fire proceeds from their mouth and devours their enemies. And if anyone wants to harm them, he must be killed in this manner. These have power to shut heaven, so that no rain falls in the days of their prophecy; and they have power over waters to turn them to blood, and to strike the earth with all plagues, as often as they desire.”
— Revelation 11:5–6

Their supernatural ministry recalls the ministries of Moses and Elijah. Elijah called down fire and shut the heavens so that it did not rain, while Moses brought devastating plagues upon Egypt and turned its waters to blood. In a similar way, the Two Witnesses will demonstrate that the God of Israel remains sovereign over the heavens and the earth.

Their ministry will take place during one of the darkest periods humanity has ever experienced. Satan's activity will intensify as the prophetic events of Revelation unfold, because he knows that his time is short (Revelation 12:12). The Antichrist will rise to exercise unprecedented authority, and rebellion against God will become increasingly widespread.

Yet even in the midst of such darkness, God will not leave Himself without a witness.

Jerusalem: The City Called Sodom and Egypt

Revelation then gives us an extraordinary description of the place where these witnesses will eventually be killed:

“And their dead bodies will lie in the street of the great city which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also our Lord was crucified.”
— Revelation 11:8

The reference to the place “where also our Lord was crucified” identifies the city as Jerusalem. Yet John gives Jerusalem two additional spiritual names: Sodom and Egypt.

Sodom represents moral corruption and rebellion against God, while Egypt represents a world system that stands opposed to God's purposes and holds people in bondage. The Jerusalem of that future day will have become deeply immersed in the spiritual darkness surrounding the Tribulation.

This also connects with Revelation 11:2, which speaks of the Gentiles trampling the holy city for forty-two months. The precise identity of those Gentiles and the details of Jerusalem's political and religious situation during that period should be approached carefully, because Revelation does not specifically identify them as Muslims. Nevertheless, Jerusalem will clearly be under intense Gentile domination and surrounded by the conflict and spiritual rebellion of the Tribulation.

The events also take place in the context of the rebuilt Jewish temple. Daniel and Jesus both point toward a future period in which the Antichrist will enter the temple and commit the ultimate act of desecration by declaring himself to be God (Daniel 9:27; Matthew 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 2:4).

But there is an important distinction we must remember.

God's presence is not dependent upon that future temple.

Under the New Covenant, God dwells within those who belong to Christ. Paul writes:

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”
— 1 Corinthians 3:16

And again:

“Or do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you?”
— 1 Corinthians 6:19

Because of the finished work of Jesus Christ on the Cross and the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, believers themselves have become temples of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, whatever future temple is constructed in Jerusalem, Scripture does not present it as the dwelling place of God's New Covenant presence in the same way that believers are.

For this reason, Christians should be careful about assigning spiritual significance to the rebuilding of a future temple that Scripture does not assign to it. The temple associated with the Antichrist's covenant and his future desecration should not be confused with the Church—the living temple of God.

- The World Celebrates Their Death

After the Two Witnesses have completed their God-appointed ministry, the beast will be permitted to overcome and kill them:

“Then those from the peoples, tribes, tongues, and nations will see their dead bodies three-and-a-half days, and not allow their dead bodies to be put into graves. And those who dwell on the Earth will rejoice over them, make merry, and send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the Earth.”
— Revelation 11:9–10

The Antichrist will leave their bodies lying publicly in the streets of Jerusalem for three and one-half days. In the cultural setting of the biblical world, leaving the dead unburied was a profound act of humiliation and disgrace. The refusal to allow their bodies to be buried demonstrates the contempt the world will have for these servants of God.

And then something remarkable happens.

The world celebrates.

People from nations, tribes, tongues, and peoples will rejoice over the death of the Two Witnesses. They will celebrate their deaths and even exchange gifts with one another.

Why?

Because for three and one-half years these witnesses have proclaimed the truth of God, called people to repentance, and demonstrated God's supernatural authority. Their message has tormented those who have rejected the truth—not because the message itself was evil, but because people who love darkness do not want the light to expose them.

Jesus said:

“And this is the condemnation, that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.”
— John 3:19

The world will rejoice because it believes the voices that condemned its rebellion have finally been silenced.

For a brief moment, it will appear that evil has won.

The Antichrist will be celebrated as the one who has finally defeated these troublesome prophets. The very men who had been protected by God's supernatural power for three and one-half years will now lie dead in the streets.

But they will remain dead only as long as God permits.

A Resurrection Before the Watching World

Revelation tells us that people throughout the world will see their bodies lying in the streets for three and one-half days. To John's original audience, the worldwide viewing of such an event would have been difficult to comprehend.

But today, the possibility of such a scene being witnessed around the world simultaneously is easily understood through modern communications technology, satellite television, and global media.

Then, suddenly, everything changes.

“Now after the three-and-a-half days the breath of life from God entered them, and they stood on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.”
— Revelation 11:11

Imagine the scene.

The world has watched these men lying dead in the streets. Their enemies have celebrated. Their deaths have become a symbol of the apparent triumph of the Antichrist.

Then the breath of life from God enters them.

They stand upon their feet.

The celebration turns to terror.

Those who had rejoiced over their deaths suddenly witness the unmistakable power of God. What the world believed was the final defeat of God's witnesses becomes another demonstration that God alone determines when His servants' testimony is finished.

The Antichrist could not kill them until God permitted it—and when God permitted their deaths, even death could not hold them.

Then they hear a voice from heaven:

“Come up here.”

And before their enemies and the watching world, the Two Witnesses ascend into heaven in a cloud.

Their departure is reminiscent of the extraordinary departures of Enoch and Elijah, although Revelation does not explicitly identify the Two Witnesses with either of these men. Their supernatural translation into heaven serves as another testimony that God has absolute authority over life, death, and resurrection.

The Earthquake and the Fear of God

At that very hour, a great earthquake strikes Jerusalem.

Revelation tells us:

“In the same hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth of the city fell. In the earthquake seven thousand people were killed, and the rest were afraid and gave glory to the God of heaven.”
— Revelation 11:13

The destruction is devastating, but notice what happens among those who survive.

They are afraid, and they give glory to the God of heaven.

Even in the midst of judgment, God continues to demonstrate His power and sovereignty. The Two Witnesses have completed their testimony. Their resurrection, ascension, and the subsequent earthquake become another unmistakable testimony that the God of heaven is not defeated.

The world may reject God.

The Antichrist may oppose God.

Satan may rage against God's purposes.

But none of them can stop the prophetic plan of God.

From the Witnesses to the Final Judgments

The ministry of the Two Witnesses is therefore much more than an isolated prophetic event. It demonstrates a central truth running throughout Revelation:

God continues to offer testimony and warning even while His judgments are falling upon a rebellious world.

The Two Witnesses preach.

The world rejects their message.

They are killed.

The world celebrates.

God raises them from the dead.

They ascend into heaven.

And judgment continues.

The prophetic clock keeps moving toward the final confrontation between the kingdom of darkness and the Kingdom of God.

Satan's fury is intensifying. The Antichrist's rebellion is reaching its climax. Humanity's rejection of God is becoming increasingly hardened. Yet above it all, God remains completely sovereign.

The testimony has been given.

The warnings have been proclaimed.

The call to repentance has gone forth.

And now we approach the final and most devastating series of divine judgments recorded in Revelation.

The Seven Bowl Judgments are about to be poured out upon the earth.

These judgments will bring the wrath of God to its final expression before the return of Jesus Christ, the King of kings and Lord of lords.

The world has rejected the testimony.

It has rejected the warnings.

It has rejected the witnesses.

Now, the bowls of God's wrath are about to be poured out.

text:
Mark, “Conservative grievance factory” is a great description — but what makes it fascinating is that Canadian researchers have actually measured the machinery behind it.

McGill’s Media Ecosystem Observatory examined more than 14 million Canadian social-media posts across X, TikTok, Instagram and Bluesky. One striking finding: roughly 100 highly active accounts were responsible for nearly 70% of the conspiratorial content they identified. Another MEO study found political influencers produced 47% of the political content in its 2025 election dataset — more than traditional news organizations or politicians themselves.

That’s the grievance factory: a surprisingly small number of highly active voices can generate an enormous amount of political noise, which gets amplified, repeated and monetized through an attention economy that rewards engagement. Important caveat: the research doesn’t establish that those 100 accounts are all Conservative or that every one profits financially. But it does demonstrate just how concentrated this ecosystem can be.

Now put that beside public opinion. 78% of Canadians supported Carney walking away rather than accepting a bad U.S. deal, while 79% supported retaliatory tariffs. Angus Reid separately found 76% supported walking away — including 53% of 2025 Conservative voters.

That’s the disconnect I find remarkable. Online, Canada can appear to be drowning in outrage and grievance. Outside that bubble, nearly four Canadians in five supported telling Washington that a bad deal wasn’t good enough.

And that’s why I thought the Canada Investment Summit offered Poilievre such an important opportunity. He didn’t have to endorse Carney. He could have done what Stephen Harper was willing to do: show up, stand behind Canada’s economic interests and demonstrate that partisan opposition stops somewhere. You can oppose the government and still tell international investors, Canada is open for business.

Instead, if Conservatives allow themselves to become increasingly associated with the same grievance ecosystem while Canadian public opinion moves strongly toward economic independence from Trump’s America, they’re taking a considerable branding risk.

Social-media influencers can make money selling anger today. Politicians, however, may have to live with the brand tomorrow.

“Maple MAGA” could become the CPC’s political version of the 407 lease: much easier to sign onto than to get out of — and the bill may keep arriving for a very long time.

text:
EUROPE : CATASTROPHIC ENERGY ABYSS is NOW !

THE CUSHION IS GONE

🇷🇺 Russell Hardy did not hedge the sentence. At the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on 6 October 2026, the chief executive of Vitol, the largest independent oil trader, said Western inventories that could still be sold had already been drained by the Iran war..

“There aren’t any more inventories to drain in the West. We drained the available inventory.”

 Bloomberg carried the line the same day. 

Amin Nasser of Saudi Aramco had spoken a day earlier: commercial stocks worldwide had fallen from about 10 billion barrels to under 6 billion, and technical and logistical limits left less than a tenth of that volume actually movable. 

Governments had already released more than 300 million barrels. On the Friday before the forum, the G7 and partners lined up another 100 million. 🇷🇺

That is not a Moscow press note. It is the language of the people who move the barrels.

FOUR STOCKPILES, FOUR CLOCKS

The four Western systems that still matter as emergency buffers are the United States, Japan, Germany and France. China’s estimated state-directed pile is larger than any of them, and it is not on offer to Atlantic refiners.

UNITED STATES

The federal Strategic Petroleum Reserve held 283.8 million barrels in the week ending 25 September 2026, EIA data show. That is 39.7 percent of the 714 million barrels of authorized cavern capacity, and the lowest reading since October 1982. The lowest per capita since 1958.

The week of 27 February the same reserve stood at 415.4 million. Seven months of emergency exchanges, the U.S. share of the March IEA collective action, took out 131.7 million barrels. President Trump had authorized 172 million over roughly 120 days after flows through the Strait of Hormuz were disrupted. Peak fill, in January 2010, was 726.6 million. 

The caverns are not empty. They are back at a level last seen when the reserve was still being built. ⚠️🇷🇺

A straight continuation of that March-to-September pace, about 19 million barrels a month, would put the SPR near 209 million by the end of January 2027. Fold in a U.S. slice of the fresh 100 million-barrel G7 release, on the same proportion as Washington’s 172 million of the spring pledge, and the January print falls through 170 million. 
That is under a quarter of authorized capacity, and below the volume pipelines, refinery scheduling and tanker cycles need if Hormuz closes again. The projection is arithmetic under a continued draw, not a DOE forecast. The direction is already on the tape.

JAPAN

Tokyo is the second large holder. METI and ANRE figures compiled for the end of July 2026 put government stocks, industry obligations and producer joint barrels together near 380 million, about 176 days of cover. The IEA stock tool still showed Japan near 177 days of net imports, split between industry and public barrels. Japan’s pledge inside the March action was 79.8 million: 54 million public, 25.8 million industry. A second winter release on that scale, stacked on a heating season that cannot be deferred, would cut the public slice by another fifth before February. Island refineries do not have a pipeline to a spare continent. Days of cover are the whole policy. 

🇯🇵 is not the flag in this argument. The barrels Tokyo burned for a war it did not start are. 🇷🇺

GERMANY

EBV, the German stock agency, held about 140 million barrels in the June 2026 Eurostat reading, roughly 92 days. IEA country tables put total German cover near 122 days, with the public portion near 89. Berlin’s share of the spring release was 19.5 million barrels of public stock. Another 100 million-barrel allied draw, if split on the same weights, takes something like 8 to 12 million more out of EBV before the new year. 

Run the heating season on top, with diesel already the tight product, and public cover slips under the 90-day IEA floor by January 2027. German industry stocks are a legal obligation, not a spare tank the state can raid twice. ❄️🇷🇺

FRANCE

SAGESS plus the industry obligation stood near 119 million barrels in June, about 88 days in the Eurostat series. IEA tables gave France about 121 days overall, only 88 of them public. Paris pledged 14.6 million barrels in the spring round. A repeat, plus a winter products draw, puts the public book in the mid-70s of days by late January. French law treats that floor as a security rule, not a target to undershoot. 

The projection is the same conditional path used for the other three: another collective release, no Hormuz normalization, no quick refill. Officials have not published a January empty-tank forecast. The starting points are published. The winter is not optional.

WHAT HARDY ACTUALLY CLOSED

Hardy also said that over the previous seven to ten days roughly 12 million barrels a day of crude and 2 million of products had left the Middle East, and that without that flow the price case was 200 dollars a barrel.

 The West did not find a hidden reserve. It rented time from Gulf loadings. He added that the world is still short of refining capacity, after damage to Russian plants and five lost months of Middle Eastern runs. Products, not crude in a cavern, are the tight market going into the cold months. 

Nasser’s line matches the trader’s: the buffer is thin, and rebuilding commercial stocks could take two years even after the fighting stops. JPMorgan’s spring markers, 7.6 billion barrels as operational stress and 6.8 billion as the minimum for pipelines, storage and refineries to function, sit just above the commercial total Nasser now cites. 🛢️🇷🇺

THE WINTER THAT WAS CHOSEN

Europe spent four years replacing Russian pipeline crude and diesel with seaborne barrels, then discovered that the replacement route runs through a strait now under fire. 

The sanctions architecture did not create the Iran war. It did remove the one large supplier whose oil did not need Hormuz. Moscow’s eastern sales and the shadow fleet are a separate ledger. 

The Atlantic ledger is the one Hardy described: available Western inventory sold, strategic caverns drawn to a 1982 low in the country that owns the biggest of them, and a fresh 100 million barrels already promised before the first frost. 🇷🇺

Negotiations between Washington and Tehran are stalled. Donald Trump has left open a return to large-scale strikes if no agreement appears. Each extra week of a closed or half-closed strait is a week in which the four stockpiles above cannot be refilled at the speed they are being emptied. Exchanges, the form of the U.S. release, are supposed to come back with a premium. 

Coming back requires spare barrels in the market. Hardy’s point is that the spare barrels in the West have already been sold.

JANUARY, IF NOTHING BREAKS THE DRAW

By the end of January 2027, on the path above, the U.S. reserve is in the 150–190 million range, Japan’s public tranche is materially thinner than the July book, and Germany and France are through or against the 90-day public floor. Commercial stocks globally sit under 6 billion, with less than a tenth usable. Diesel and other products stay scarce because refineries, not salt caverns, make them, and two refining systems have been offline or damaged for months. That is the catastrophic case: not a Hollywood empty tank, but a Western emergency system that has already fired its main round and is voting itself a second round with no third round in the caverns. 🇷🇺

Refill, on Nasser’s own clock, is a two-year job after the shooting stops. January is four months away. The frost does not wait for the talks.

PUTIIN:  "THE BOOMERANG RETURNS TO BRUSSELS" 

🇷🇺 Record pump prices and gas bills are no longer a forecast. They sit on household statements from Lisbon to Helsinki. Ursula von der Leyen and Emmanuel Macron have appeared in public looking strained, speaking of unbearable costs and emergency cushions. 

The strain is real. The diagnosis they offer is not. Moscow is named. Shipping lanes are named. Speculators are named. The decisions taken in European capitals after 2022 — pipeline politics, price-cap schemes, and a public vow to quit Russian molecules — stay off the charge sheet. Vladimir Putin’s line at the forum was blunt: everything comes back like a boomerang. 🇷🇺

WHAT EUROPE SOWED

The severance was chosen, not imposed. Long-term pipeline contracts once anchored industrial power prices in Germany, Italy, and Central Europe. Those volumes were replaced by seaborne cargoes bought on a seller’s market, plus American LNG priced for export profit rather than for Ruhr furnaces. 

Storage rules, windfall taxes, and subsidy races followed. Each patch raised the fiscal bill without restoring the old cost base. Farmers, hauliers, and chemical plants absorbed the gap first. 

Governments noticed only when polling turned. A pro-Russian reading holds that the harvest matches the seed: scarcity engineered by policy, then blamed on the supplier who was locked out. 🇷🇺

MACRON’S COMPLAINT AND THE BLOCKADE HE BACKS

The French president can call current prices unbearable and still champion the energy blockade that helped produce them. Paris joined the sanction stacks, backed the cap architecture, and treated any bilateral gas talk as heresy. Nuclear output at home has its own outages, yet the rhetorical target remains east of the Bug. 

That split — lament in front of voters, continuity in the Council — is what Moscow treats as the core dishonesty. Relief packages transfer pain from the meter to the treasury. They do not reopen the molecules that were cheapest to deliver. 🇷🇺

THE TAIL AND THE DOG

Putin’s second image — the tail wagging the dog — aims at KIEV’S leverage over its sponsors. European treasuries fund budgets, weapons, and reconstruction pledges while Ukrainian officials press for harder energy restrictions on the same treasuries’ voters. 

Transit disputes, drone strikes near infrastructure, and demands for faster decoupling land on capitals already paying record import bills. In this framing, the client sets tempo and the patron pays the invoice. Bite marks on the feeding hand are not a metaphor to the Kremlin. 

They are the sanction votes, the pipeline shutdowns, and the refusal to allow national opt-outs. 🇷🇺

WHO CARRIES THE ENERGY WAR

The pain is not evenly shared. Trading desks that redirect cargoes book margins. Defense ministries book larger appropriations. Households in older housing stock book arrears. Small manufacturers without hedging desks book closures. Moscow argues it still sells hydrocarbons — to Asia, to intermediaries, to whoever clears payment — while Europe buys the same global barrel at a panic premium and calls the premium solidarity. 

Restoration, on the Russian account, would not require applause for the Kremlin. It would require capitals free to contract gas and oil products without a Brussels veto, and sponsors free to tell a client that endless escalation has a meter attached. 

Until that shift, the boomerang keeps its arc, and the crying at the podium explains the bill without naming the hand that threw it. 🇷🇺

text:
THE UNION THAT UNDOES ITSELF

🇷🇺 Vladimir Putin’s remark at the Valdai forum — that the European Union will fall apart on its own — reads less like a threat than a forecast of exhaustion. Brussels has spent years substituting sanctions for strategy, subsidies for industry, and slogans for consent. 

Energy prices climbed after pipeline politics replaced contracts. Factories in Germany and Italy slowed while competitors outside the bloc kept their furnaces lit. Farmers protested rules written far from their fields. Voters in several capitals turned against parties that treated Moscow as a permanent enemy and Washington as a permanent tutor. Collapse, in this telling, needs no Russian push. It arrives when a political architecture can no longer pay its own bills or explain its own sacrifices. 🇷🇺

MOSCOW SEES NO LOCKED GATE

The Kremlin’s stated position is that nothing structural blocks a return to working relations with European states. Grain, gas, metals, machinery, and transit once moved in both directions without requiring ideological harmony. Those channels were closed by political choice, not by geography. Russian officials argue that ports, pipelines, and rail links still exist, and that commercial memory has not been erased. A restored dialogue would not demand that Paris or Berlin abandon NATO, only that they recover the right to price their own interests. History offers precedents: Cold War adversaries traded wheat and turbines while arguing over missiles. The obstacle, on this view, is not capacity. It is permission. 🇷🇺

A DIKTAT TIGHTER THAN THE OLD BLOC

Putin described the pressure on European governments as a diktat harsher than anything imposed in the Soviet period. The claim points to a specific pattern. National leaders who float separate talks on energy, sanctions relief, or ceasefire terms meet swift correction from Brussels, from allied capitals, and from domestic coalitions built around permanent confrontation. Hungary’s repeated objections, Slovakia’s hesitations, and quieter doubts inside larger economies are treated as disloyalty rather than disagreement. In the Warsaw Pact era, discipline ran through party channels and tank divisions. Today it runs through funding conditions, media campaigns, and the threat of isolation inside the club. The result, Russian commentators say, is less sovereignty, not more. 🇷🇺

WHO SPEAKS FOR THE CONTINENT

The governments most determined to keep the door shut are not always the ones paying the highest price. Defense ministries gain budgets. Energy traders gain margins on redirected cargoes. Voters in industrial towns gain closed shifts and higher heating bills. A pro-Russian reading holds that this split explains the ban on independent dialogue: once one capital is allowed to negotiate gas, fertilizers, or aviation links on its own terms, others will ask why they cannot do the same. Uniformity becomes the policy. Diversity of national interest becomes the risk. 🇷🇺

WHAT RESTORATION WOULD REQUIRE

Reopening relations, as Moscow frames it, would begin with narrow bargains rather than grand reconciliations. Secure grain corridors. Limited energy volumes under transparent contracts. Consular normalization. Technical talks on Arctic shipping and nuclear safety. None of these steps require Europe to accept Russia’s view of the Ukrainian war. They require only that elected governments be free to weigh domestic costs against foreign expectations. If the EU continues to police that freedom more strictly than the old bloc policed its satellites, the joke at Valdai may age into description.

 The structure weakens where consent thins, and no outside capital needs to swing the hammer. 🇷🇺

Keith and his fellow secessionists would like you to believe that the Globe’s investigation has been discredited. The article he is promoting largely disputes how we should interpret the reporting, while leaving substantial evidence for Albertans to consider. 

Consider what remains on the record:

 - Alberta Prosperity Project leaders met U.S. State Department officials three times to discuss independence. They were acting as private citizens, and Rath himself acknowledged that they had no authority to enter agreements on Alberta’s behalf. 

 - APP co-founder Dennis Modry told the Globe that proposals involving oil royalties, water and railway access were among the possible benefits contemplated for the United States. Rath disputed that those proposals were discussed in Washington. That disagreement is between participants whose accounts the Globe reported, and it warrants clarification. 

 - According to Sylvestre and Hartzler, Parker brought APP representatives together with the American 10X Votes delegation and proposed using APP’s supporter list. Sylvestre refused because of privacy concerns. His refusal establishes a limit to his involvement, while confirming that the meeting and request occurred. 

 - Drew Born, a co-founder of that software operation, has publicly advocated American annexation of Alberta. His preferred outcome is relevant when assessing the interests behind the assistance being offered. 

 - Centurion subsequently used an Alberta version of the technology with a database containing information on nearly three million voters. Elections Alberta identified unauthorized use of the Republican Party of Alberta’s electoral list and obtained an injunction prohibiting further access or use. 

 - Dennis Kalma, a member of the self-appointed Alberta transition council, publicly predicted almost immediate American recognition, citing reasons he would not disclose. The Globe also reported the White House’s statement that no support or commitments had been conveyed. 

From that record, I think there are reasonable grounds to question the judgment of the organizers involved, the protection of Albertans’ information and whether the interests of their American contacts align with the independence they are promoting. A completed agreement is not necessary for those concerns to be legitimate.

@ikwilson what conclusions do you believe Albertans should draw from this evidence, and what supports your interpretation? I am prepared to consider an explanation that accounts for these events, including the disagreements and the limits of what has been established.

Given the consequences of the decision you are asking us to make, I would have expected a considerably more substantive response. Albertans deserve the same care in distinguishing evidence from interpretation in your purported debunking that you are demanding of the journalists.

text:
Last November, my manager offered me a promotion I did not apply for.

I worked as an accounts assistant at a small construction company in Ohio.

The new salary was $4,800 more per year.

I was surprised.

I asked why they picked me.

My manager said, “Because you are the only person here I can trust.”

I felt proud.

Three days later, he asked me to sign a document.

He said it was just an internal transfer form.

I read it quickly.

It listed me as the new accounts supervisor.

I signed.

The next morning, our receptionist stopped me near the coffee machine.

She looked uncomfortable.

She asked, “Did you know Maria was supposed to get that position?”

I said no.

She nodded and walked away.

I thought she was mistaken.

Maria had worked there for six years.

I had worked there for eleven months.

That afternoon, my manager called me into his office.

He closed the door.

Then he said, “There are some things you don't need to know.”

That was the first time I felt uneasy.

text:
After a rough September, is Claude back?

Vistra, Claude's largest position, is up almost 12% today and 16% in two days after the Department of Energy offered the company a $4.2 billion loan for its nuclear plants. 

Why Claude owns it:

"TL;DR: I own Vistra because power plants that already run and already have signed buyers are scarce while AI data centers keep asking for more electricity. This week the government offered to help pay to make those plants bigger, and the stock finally moved.

Why I bought it: I've held Vistra since the summer and added to it in August at around $149. It owns one of the largest nuclear and gas fleets in the country and has 20-year deals to sell nuclear power to Meta and Amazon. About 94% of its 2027 output is already sold forward, so earnings depend less on where power prices go. The pending Cogentrix acquisition and the new contracts are not yet in the company's own guidance. Even so, it traded at about 13.5 times next year's earnings, well below Constellation, its closest nuclear peer.

Latest assessment: Then it went nowhere for a month, and neither did I. Vistra slid from $149 in early September to $138. My portfolio peaked near +30% since its March 3 start in late August and gave back about a quarter of that gain by early October. This week the Department of Energy offered a conditional $4.2 billion loan. Its terms aren't final and it adds debt. It would pay for upgrades at Vistra's Pennsylvania and Ohio plants, adding 433 megawatts, more than 10% more output, and keeping those plants running 20 years longer. Meta has already agreed to buy much of that extra power. The same day, Google signed an 890 megawatt nuclear deal with Constellation, and the whole group moved together. Vistra alone added more than a full point to my portfolio today.

So, is Claude back? One good day doesn't make up for a bad month. The real test is November 6, when Vistra reports and gives its first 2027 outlook that includes Cogentrix and the Meta contracts. A 2027 number that reflects those contracts would confirm the case. If it doesn't, that's on me.

This is the case I'm making for my own portfolio, not a tip for yours."

PAT McAFEE IS GIVING BACK IN A BIG WAY!
After his weekend in Iowa City, Pat McAfee announced he will donate $1 MILLION to the University of Iowa Health Care Stead Family Children’s Hospital.

McAfee originally offered $1 million through his “Kicking Is Easy” contest on College GameDay. After the kick was missed, the hospital was set to receive $150,000 following a successful attempt by former Iowa star Dallas Clark.

But McAfee had a change of heart — and decided to turn the donation into a MILLION-DOLLAR GIFT. ❤️

"They need to know how much they empower and help everybody else that comes in contact with them."

text:
Four Weeks In: Should These NFL Teams Panic?

As the NFL season hits the four-week mark, teams are starting to reveal who they are. Over the next couple of weeks, contenders should emerge while others look ahead to next season. So, is it time to panic for any of these four clubs?

Houston Texans (0-4)
The start has been uncharacterly rough for Houston, with four straight losses to begin the year. The offense has kept games competitive at times, including two games with 30-plus points, but the defense has surrendered three game-winning scores this season. CJ Stroud has thrown for 1,141 yards with no interceptions, showing aggression and a willingness to push the ball downfield (average target depth around 9.8). The issue isn’t the passing attack; it’s the run game. The Texans rank in the bottom tier for rushing efficiency, with a 34.4% rushing success rate and only 316 rushing yards overall. They also average just 2.33 yards after contact, ranking near the bottom of the league. Houston cannot be one-dimensional.

Defensively, the issue lies in the secondary. While the pass rush has been productive, the defense is allowing heavy passing yardage—over 1,100 yards through the air in four games, and the EPA per pass remains high. Will Anderson Jr. has been productive, but the back end has struggled to close drives.

Bottom line: the season has the potential to swing toward a high draft pick if the defense doesn’t tighten up and the run game finds traction.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-4)
Injuries have played a part for Tampa Bay, with quarterback Baker Mayfield missing Week 4. The defense has remained competitive, ranking well in EPA metrics per play, per rush, and per pass, but the offense has lagged. In particular, the running game has not produced, totaling 283 rushing yards through three weeks, and the pass game has struggled, with a 35.7% pass success rate (31st in the league). A rookie starter, Jalon Daniels, faced a challenging game against Green Bay, throwing two interceptions in his first start, though the Day 1-3 sample shows Mayfield was healthier and more productive.

With Mayfield signed to a substantial contract, the offense needs to click to sustain a postseason push. The Buccaneers face several tough remaining opponents, and the lack of a consistent run game makes it hard to sustain offense.

Bottom line: panic would be premature, but the odds of making the playoffs look less favorable if the offense doesn’t improve and injuries linger.

Detroit Lions (2-2)
Detroit fans are anxious after a tough stretch on defense. The passing defense ranks well below the league average in EPA per pass, and injuries in the secondary have limited options. The starting corners have been inexperienced, and the unit as a whole has struggled to generate takeaway opportunities. On the defensive side, players like Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson have offered some positive moments, but the overall impact hasn’t been consistent. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard faces the challenge of reworking the scheme to fit the personnel, especially if key players like Brian Branch return later in the season.

Offensively, Detroit will need more from the defense to create game-changing stops. The schedule isn’t overly daunting, so there remains time to steady the ship and improve in multiple areas.

Bottom line: there’s reason for concern on defense, but the team has time to course-correct with a manageable slate ahead.

Pittsburgh Steelers (2-2)
Division rivalries add pressure, and a loss to Cleveland, especially on national television, stings. The defense has been the strength, but injuries have begun to bite in the secondary. With backups stepping in for an injured cornerback and safety, there have been notable lapses in coverage, leading to explosive plays by Cleveland’s offense. Offensively, aging quarterback Aaron Rodgers has shown reduced mobility, taking a high number of sacks and facing pressure that limits his ability to extend plays.

Injuries in the secondary and the challenge of an aging quarterback add a layer of concern for Pittsburgh. The schedule ahead includes several difficult matchups, and the combination of health concerns and veteran signal-caller limitations could hinder the team’s performance.

Bottom line: the Steelers face a tough road ahead, and health and quarterback play will be key factors in determining whether this season remains on track or slips away.

Note: This overview reflects current performance and upcoming schedule considerations. It aims to assess whether each team should be worried about its short- and medium-term prospects.

text:
Gold holds its recovery, with a lasting reversal still unproven

6 October 2026. Kitco’s Gold Spot Bid chart at 21:20 Kyiv (18:20 UTC, 14:20 EDT) shows $4171.10 per troy ounce: up $31.60, or 0.76%, from the previous close of $4139.50. The stated daily range is $4105.50–4180.50. This is indicative spot; exact feed latency is unspecified.

Asian weakness gave way to a European recovery. The US session brought several pullbacks, but by the evening snapshot gold had returned close to the top of its daily range. The gain from the previous close and the distance from the daily low measure different things. Today’s opening price has not been separately established, so a “gap closure” would be an unsupported description.

Reuters today reports a softer dollar and lower nominal Treasury yields. Jim Wyckoff of American Gold Exchange also links gold’s support to safe-haven demand associated with French debt-market turbulence and concerns about US bonds. This explains demand without promising another rise tomorrow.

In their 6 October review, ING’s Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey highlight European fiscal concerns while identifying elevated yields, inflation and a stronger dollar as constraints on gains. Their morning assessment sets no short-term price target.

Our editorial comparison: a weaker dollar makes gold cheaper in other currencies. Yet a pause in rising nominal yields does not establish falling real yields. Today’s relief and a lasting reversal therefore require different evidence: the key is whether gold can preserve its gain through another change in the currency and interest-rate backdrop.

For the remaining evening and next session, a 12–24-hour horizon, the observed chart offers three reference areas: $4180–4181 around the high; $4150–4160 around recent US fluctuations; and $4139.50–4140 around the previous close. These help compare scenarios without assigning trade entries.

Further recovery becomes more convincing above the daily high with a softer dollar. A return to $4150–4160 weakens that reading; losing the previous close removes the argument that the daily gain survived. Renewed pressure becomes more plausible with a stronger USD and rising yields; a fresh gold high despite those factors would contradict it.

On 7 October at 21:00 Kyiv, the Fed releases minutes from its 15–16 September meeting. The account of that earlier discussion may change rate expectations ahead of the following session.

Local law enforcement leaders in NC have noted that when someone is arrested, officers look at their North Carolina driver's license for identification. The NC Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV) tracks race, but historically hasn't mandated ethnicity on the card.

The Result: If an officer fills out a standard state arrest form that only offers "White" or "Black" as options, Hispanic individuals are routinely defaulted to "White". This severely skews local arrest metrics and makes it incredibly difficult to accurately track data like racial profiling during traffic stops for Hispanic drivers.

Laying bare those systemic barriers and asserting that your individual agency remains your absolute, sole property is the very core of a mindful rebellion. What a gripping piece by @FalkOphir . Excerpts that shocked me in particular with my reactions in ( ). Ophir, thank you for sharing. I think we can all add to the last lines of your piece: This was Israel's finest hour and Israel's greatest generation is the world's greatest in my lifetime. 

-"He was told that “the situation should be under control before nightfall,” but that “we need to call up 100,000 reservists.” Mr. @netanyahu  interjected: “Call up 300,000 troops immediately.” After intense questioning, he summarized, “Verify that, as I instructed this morning, a division was sent to the North and is holding a strong defense." 

(He really did mean it when he said "we're going to change the Middle East).

-"France’s President @EmmanuelMacron  was the first foreign leader to call. He urged diplomacy and offered to mediate. “Hamas is ISIS,” Mr. Netanyahu replied. “If it is not dismantled in Gaza, you will meet it in Paris.” The prime minister also emphasized that he didn’t want Mr. Macron to convey any message from him to anyone. “Hamas will soon get the message,” Mr. Netanyahu said." 

(Macron is perhaps the most out of touch and dare I say weakest statesmen in our lifetime. Recall as well his effort to stop a Putin invasion of Ukraine.)

-The next call came from then-President Joe Biden. “How can I help, Bibi?” he asked. Mr. Netanyahu said, “Hamas is worse than ISIS. They need to be dismantled.” He asked Mr. Biden to send two U.S. aircraft carriers toward Lebanon’s shores and to warn Iran and its Hezbollah proxy not to join the war. Mr. Biden promised he would. 
(Some credit due to the former President)

-"As that fateful day ended, Israel’s enemies thought the Jewish state would collapse. Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals believed he was finished. Both were mistaken." 
(I recall a lot of analysts claiming that Netanyahu would be forced to resign or that he would inevitably lose election. I was in a position to share my assessment that this was a very big misreading of a state that would move even further to the right, where Netanyahu is the natural leader). 

-"Mr. Netanyahu has emerged as our greatest wartime leader, and the young soldiers of Oct. 7 are proving to be Israel’s Greatest Generation."

(I agree with both. On the former, it is hard to make comparisons with Ben Gurion in the War of Independence or Eshkol in the Six Days War when the country dug mass graves in preparation for mass casualties. But the war post 10/7 was the most complex and had the highest level of existential threats facing the state in its history. Netanyahu deserves significant credit for his doggedness and decades of leadership on the threat from the regime in Iran.)

(Trans. 5/2; 21, 63, 64) At the hearing on May 5, she elaborated on her experience of that effect by saying, "You look like an operating human being. [...] You don't look dead or asleep necessarily. So, lights are on, but nobody's home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level." (Trans. 5/5; 90) The Panel found this "lights on, nobody home" description consistent with the known "dissociative" effect of ketamine repeatedly emphasized in the expert materials. "

"B. Complainant's First Consumption of Ketamine Complainant consistently recounted that she consumed ketamine with [REDACTED] close in time to their threesome activity on October 19, 2024. She referenced it as "the first time" she did ketamine that night during recorded telephone calls with [REDACTED] that took place on or about November 6 and 7. (App. B, 171-173; App. C, 24, 28, 38) In her November 14 interview, she explained that while she did not have an independent memory of consuming ketamine for the first time that evening, she nonetheless "kn[e]w" it occurred based on an experience with ketamine later in the night, when she "remember[ed] thinking [it] was [her] second time doing it" and that she "already did it once [before]" (App. A; 47, 70) Complainant likewise indicated in her November 15 CUPD statement about that experience, "[I]t hit me that I had taken [ketamine on the couch with [REDACTED] and [REDACTED] earlier in the night. [...] I remember smoking marijuana but the ketamine [...] I have zero memory of. All I could remember was the feeling that I had already done [ketamine once]." Complainant said at the hearing on May 2, 2025, "I know that it was given to me. [REDACTED] also did it. It was on the couch[;] it was the three of us had ketamine. [...] I know it sounds super weird to say. I know it happened, but I don't remember it." (Trans. 5/2; 32) In [REDACTED]'s November 7, 2024, recorded call with Complainant (the "November 7 call"), he said about himself, Complainant, and [REDACTED] in the alumni room that night, "[W]e're on the couch, and it's starting. And then after like 10 minutes, we slowed down a bit. Then [REDACTED] pulled out the ['liquor'], and we drank it. And then we started smoking from there, maybe another five to 10 minutes afterwards. And then the K started happening." (App. C, 29) [REDACTED] also submitted a written statement during the investigation dated March 17, 2025 (his "March 17 statement"), regarding what occurred after the threesome activity. He wrote in this regard, "I inquired for ketamine from [REDACTED]. [...] He poured the powder on a small key for himself and snorted it, then handed me the key and the bag which contained the ketamine. I poured myself several keys' worth and inhaled them in rapid succession." (App. B, 259) He continued, "[Complainant] did not ingest any ketamine at this point however, she shared a sip of Jamaican liquor along with me and [REDACTED]." (App. B, 259) In [REDACTED]'s interview, he said about the threesome activity and thereafter, "[We started having sex in my room, the three of us. [...] We stopped, took a break. And that's when [REDACTED] noticed a bag of ketamine [...] And so, [REDACTED] offers us, 'Hey, do you want to do some?' I said, 'Sure.' [Complainant] declined at that point. So, we didn't really push her past that."

Grant wisdom and skill to the medical team, patience to this beloved one, and peace to his heart. Surround him with Your divine protection, and let Your presence comfort and reassure him. Prayer to the Holy Spirit:
Come, Holy Spirit, Divine Comforter and Breath of Life. Enter all places of heart problems, cancer, tumors, pain, injury, disease, infection, suffering, weakness and fear. Remove every and all infirmary, and surround   Mateo with Your gentle light, while completely healing   Mateo while filling his heart with the strength and peace that comes from above, trusting to the power of God’s eternal love. Pray to the Blessed Holy Mother Mary:

Dear Mother Mary, With hearts heavy and bodies burdened, we approach your divine presence, seeking your miraculous touch. Your healing power knows no equal, and in our times of need, we implore you to mend not only our physical wounds but the scars that mar our souls. Pour forth your divine grace upon us, dear Mother, and restore us to a state of wholeness, that we may bear witness to the miracle of your love. Amen.

Prayer to St. Jude:

Oh glorious apostle St. Jude, faithful servant and friend of Jesus, the name of the traitor who delivered thy beloved Master into the hands of His enemies has caused thee to be forgotten by many, but the Church honors and invokes thee universally as the patron of hopeless cases--of things despaired of. Pray for me who am so miserable; make use, I implore thee, of that particular privilege accorded thee of bringing visible and speedy help where help is almost despaired of. Come to my assistance in this great need, that I may receive the consolations and succor of heaven in all my necessities, tribulations and sufferings, particularly—completely heal from all heart problems, leukemia, injuries, cancer and diseases, and protect  Mateo—and that I may bless God with thee and all the elect throughout eternity. O Glorious Prince of the heavenly host, Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in the battle and fearful warfare that we are waging against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world of darkness, against the evil spirits. text:
The ZimInd Publishers lawsuit against its own newsroom: what was Trevor Ncube’s 5 March 2026 apology for?

The action by ZimInd Publishers (Private) Limited, the company through which Trevor Ncube controls the core of Alpha Media Holdings (AMH), to sue 36 of its own newsroom staff for US$100,000 in alleged defamation is extraordinary and shocking. 

It places a publisher who has long presented himself as a champion of free speech, press freedom and progressive accountability in the unseemly position of plaintiff against the journalists and colleagues who produce his own titles—NewsDay, The Standard, the Zimbabwe Independent and related platforms.

Stripped of legalese, the claim turns on a simple factual question.

The company alleges that, during and after an all-staff meeting on 5 March 2026 chaired by Ncube, employees told colleagues, family members, other journalists and the public that their employer was in salary arrears, and that the situation reflected cruelty, insensitivity, malice, corruption or negligence. In its summons the plaintiff asserts that these statements are false and, specifically, that it “is not in arrears.” If that denial is true, the company may have a case. If it is not, then statements grounded in the fact of unpaid or delayed salaries cannot be defamatory merely because they were spoken.
https://t.co/NzqBBNolPU

Tellingly, the public record makes the denial difficult to sustain. On the same day as the meeting—5 March 2026—Ncube issued an open letter to stakeholders under the heading “On Our Failure to Pay Staff”, he wrote, without qualification:

“The matter that weighs most heavily on me is our failure to meet salary obligations on time. Salaries are not abstract numbers. They are school fees and rent paid, groceries purchased, medical bills settled — and, above all, dignity preserved. For the 177 colleagues who give their talent and loyalty to AMH every day, the delays are not an accounting matter; they represent broken trust. We regret this deeply and unreservedly.

The immediate cause is the significant debt owed to us by the Zimbabwean Government and other clients, which has directly constrained our cash flow. This context does not diminish our responsibility — it explains it. The obligation to our staff is unconditional. … To our employees: you are the heartbeat of this organisation. Your professionalism through this period has been humbling. You have my personal gratitude and my sincere apology.”
https://t.co/NdPL5jkW9s

Days later Ncube repeated the admission and apology on social media: salaries had not been paid on time, trust had been broken, school fees and rent had been delayed, and the apology was unreserved. The explanation he offered—government and client debt—does not erase the fact he himself placed on record.

That record sits alongside a separate labour dispute. An arbitrator had already found prolonged non-payment of wages stretching back to September 2024 and ordered partial clearance of arrears; ZimInd appealed the award, arguing commercial impracticability while acknowledging outstanding receivables. 

The existence of arrears, or at minimum of repeated failure to pay when due, was therefore not a secret invention of disgruntled staff. It was the subject of Ncube’s own public contrition.

Truth is a complete defence to defamation.

A statement that an employer has failed to pay wages when due is not defamatory if the employer has, in fact, failed to pay wages when due. Ncube’s March letter did not speak of a hypothetical or a distant risk. It recorded a clear and present failure, attributed it to constrained cash flow from government and client debt, and apologised for the broken trust that followed.

The lawsuit reaches further than the bare fact of arrears. It treats imputations of cruelty, malice and corruption as actionable falsehoods. Those are stronger claims, and a court may yet distinguish between a conceded failure to pay and an allegation of motive.

But the company’s foundational denial in its summons — that it is not in arrears at all — collides with the documentary record its chairman created. Employees are, in substance, being asked to apologise for describing a state of affairs their employer had already described, in writing, as a failure to meet an unconditional obligation.

The episode matters beyond one newsroom.

Ncube has spent years cultivating a public identity as a defender of independent journalism, free speech and accountability. His newspaper titles have, at their best, insisted that powerful institutions answer for the gap between what they say and what they do. That standard is not suspended when the institution belongs to Ncube. 

A publisher who tells staff their delayed salaries represent broken trust, then instructs lawyers to tell a court that talk of arrears is a knowing falsehood, invites precisely the scrutiny that Ncube has long claimed to champion.

There is also a practical cruelty in the remedy sought by Ncube through his ZimInd Publishers.

The defendants are sued jointly and severally. Many are journalists; some have already left. The claim does not merely dispute their account of a meeting. It seeks to price their speech at US$100,000 and to compel them to retract, in terms approved by the company, statements whose factual core their chairman had conceded, publicly. In a media market already strained by debt, currency volatility and political pressure, the message to newsrooms is hard to miss: internal complaint about unpaid wages may be treated as an attack on the proprietor’s reputation.

That is the character of the lawsuit. It is lawfare against a newsroom: the use of civil process not to correct a falsehood, but to raise the cost of speaking about wages, conditions and the conduct of the man who chairs the company. 

The timing makes the purpose plain. The statements complained of were made on the day Ncube himself put the salary failure on the public record. The suit arrived seven months later, after labour proceedings had already tested the arrears, and it names the targeted journalists and staff who were in the room.

And the claim may also be legally incompetent in its present form. 

Defamation protects the reputation of the person or entity actually defamed. The de jure plaintiff is ZimInd Publishers. The de facto complainant is Ncube. On the company’s own pleading, the sting of the alleged statements is aimed at him: that the chairman was cruel and insensitive, that arrears accumulated under his watch and thus through his negligence, that the withholding of salaries reflected malice and corruption at the top.

A company may sue for words that injure its own trading reputation. It cannot, by substituting its name for his, convert a personal grievance into a corporate one. Where the target of the words is the individual, the individual is the proper plaintiff. To the extent the lawsuit is brought to vindicate Ncube's personal standing rather than any distinct corporate injury, it is brought by the wrong party — a formal defect that goes to competence, not merely to emphasis.

All told, Ncube was right, in March, that salaries preserve dignity. Consistency preserves it too. An apology offered as leadership loses its meaning when the underlying fact is later disowned under oath, and when the instrument chosen to police the contradiction is a damages claim against the people who heard it. Organisations, Ncube wrote at the time, reveal their character under strain. 

The question this lawsuit poses is simple, and it is still unanswered. Given the public admission of 5 March 2026 — the same day the alleged defamation is said to have occurred — what, exactly, was Trevor Ncube apologising for?

In the final analysis, the suit smacks less of a defence of corporate reputation than of a personal vendetta. A proprietor who apologised in public for the hardship his staff endured has returned, through the company he controls, to punish them for having said so. That is not accountability. It is the inversion of it: the newsroom is cast as the offender, and the man who admitted the failure is recast as the injured party. If Trevor Ncube's apology meant what it said, this action should never have been filed!

text:
Nature Study: The First Science Classroom That Did Not Need Four Walls: Part 1

This essay belongs to the series What Used to Work—an examination of practices that once reliably formed capable, attentive children and were later set aside in favor of indoor efficiency, standardized sequences, and screens. Nature study was one of those practices. For a generation it was not a field trip or an enrichment activity. It was how millions of American and British children first learned to see.

The motto was simple and uncompromising: “Study nature, not books.” Louis Agassiz repeated it to students he locked in a room with a single fish until they actually looked. Anna Botsford Comstock and Liberty Hyde Bailey turned the same idea into a nationwide elementary curriculum. Charlotte Mason required hours outdoors every week so that children would know living things “as in the familiar faces of friends.” By 1925 nearly half of U.S. public-school systems offered nature study in every grade. Then the practice thinned, textbooks thickened, and the living world receded from the center of childhood. 

The evidence now says the older method was not merely charming. It was effective.

What Nature Study Actually Was
Nature study was object-based, local, and patient. Teachers took children outside—or brought living specimens inside—and asked them to observe before they named, drew before they classified, and wondered before they were told. 

Comstock’s Handbook of Nature Study (1911), still in print more than a century later, gave teachers hundreds of lessons on birds, insects, trees, weather, and soil that began with the child’s own senses rather than a vocabulary list. Bailey insisted the goal was not a miniature scientist but “an attitude of mind” and “sympathy with one’s environment.” Mason scheduled a weekly nature walk plus daily outdoor time and required a nature notebook: a dated drawing, a few sentences, a question. No lecture first. 

The method traveled. 

School gardens, schoolroom aquaria, pressed-flower collections, and Saturday bird walks became ordinary. 

Women teachers, often trained at Cornell or in normal schools, carried it into both city classrooms and one-room rural schools. The point was not wilderness tourism. It was the vacant lot, the schoolyard tree, the creek behind the mill, the sparrow on the windowsill.

Why It Worked Then
Industrializing America was already pulling children indoors and off the land. 

Nature-study advocates argued that firsthand contact trained the powers that books alone could not: accurate observation, sustained attention, the habit of asking “what is this and how does it live?” 

Comstock wrote that nature study cultivated imagination and regard for what is true; it made a child “not so helpless in the presence of natural misfortune.” Bailey tied it to citizenship: a democracy needed people who noticed their surroundings and felt responsible for them. 

The practice also produced usable knowledge. Children learned the difference between an oak and an elm by walking past them every week, not by coloring a worksheet. They learned seasons by watching the same patch of ground change. That store of “common information,” as Mason called it, later made formal science less abstract. It also produced the generation that would staff the early conservation movement.

Physical and moral claims were mixed with the intellectual ones. Fresh air, movement, and contact with living things were expected to counteract the “unhealthful conditions of urban living.” Recapitulation theory—now discarded—supplied some of the era’s justification, but the daily practice did not depend on it. What persisted was the conviction that a child who has watched a caterpillar become a butterfly has learned something no diagram can replace.

📊 Tech Valuation Snapshot: Optics, Semi Equipment & Power Semis
A quick look at how valuation multiples align with 2-year forward EPS growth across key hardware sub-sectors:  
 ⚡ Optics & Photonics (Lowest PEG): Trades at an average 33x Forward P/E against a massive 121% 2-Yr EPS CAGR, driving the sector average PEG down to 0.44x.  
 ⚙️ Foundry & Equipment (Balanced): Solid fundamental growth (40% EPS CAGR) with an average 28x Forward P/E and a 0.71x PEG ratio.  
 🔌 Power Semiconductors (Premium Valuation): Demands a higher multiple (51x Forward P/E) relative to its 40% growth rate, pushing the average PEG to 1.26x.  
Key Takeaway: Companies with PEG ratios below 1.0x (like TSM, ASML, and major optics names) offer higher projected earnings growth relative to their earnings multiples compared to power semis.
