text:
እሾክን በሾክ: The Counterinsurgency Triangle
Tigray Peace Force, Gadaa Commando and Amhara Peace Force

I have been watching an interesting pattern take shape across Tigray, Oromia and Amhara. Former rebel commanders and fighters who switched sides are not simply being disarmed and sent home. They are being reorganized, armed and deployed against the movements they once belonged to.

At first, these may look like three separate regional developments, but I do not think they are. The Tigray Peace Force, Gadaa Commando and Amhara Peace Force increasingly point to a common counterinsurgency logic in which former rebels are used to penetrate, weaken and fight the insurgencies from which they emerged. The calculation has obvious advantages, as these fighters know the people they are fighting, the terrain they operate in, the networks that sustain them and the internal weaknesses outsiders may struggle to understand. What concerns me is what this strategy could produce once the immediate wars are over.

All three are state-backed armed formations built largely around former rebels who switched sides and joined the government.

The Tigray Peace Force was formed from commanders and combatants who broke away from the TPLF and turned against it after aligning themselves with the federal government. Its main objective is to confront the TPLF inside Tigray in cooperation with federal forces.

Gadaa Commando follows a similar logic. It was built largely from former OLA commanders and combatants who surrendered or defected to the government. Rather than simply disarming and demobilizing them, the government reorganized and deployed them within the counterinsurgency effort. Their primary target has been the OLA, although they have also been deployed against Fano forces in parts of Wollega.

More recently, the Amhara region announced the formation of the Amhara Peace Force, bringing together former Fano combatants who joined the government side at different times. It is reportedly commanded by Captain Masresha Sete, one of the founders and important commanders of the Amhara Fano insurgency. Other regional armed formations, including the Tekeze Guard and Raya Guard, are also reportedly expected to come under its command structure.

Former rebels offer the state advantages that conventional security forces cannot easily reproduce. They know insurgent commanders, supply routes, hiding places, recruitment patterns, support networks, communication channels and battlefield tactics from firsthand experience. Some also defected after serious disagreements with their former comrades, adding personal rivalries and unresolved grievances to their willingness to fight them.

The experience in Oromia already shows both the value and the limits of this approach. Former OLA commanders who switched sides have reportedly worked with military intelligence, national intelligence and Oromia security institutions. Their insider knowledge can help expose supply and support networks, penetrate insurgent structures and persuade fighters still in the bush to surrender or defect. Their performance as frontline combat units, however, appears less decisive than their usefulness in intelligence, infiltration and political persuasion.

In Tigray, the advantages appear more pronounced, with former TPLF fighters operating under the Tigray flag giving federal forces a locally rooted partner and helping soften the perception that the campaign is being conducted entirely by an outside army. TPF commanders also appear capable of reaching former comrades in ways federal forces cannot. Some fighters can be persuaded to defect, others to cooperate, and still others may provide information while remaining inside TPLF structures. During the latest fighting, that combination of local knowledge, political symbolism and access to former networks appears to have given federal forces an important advantage.

It is still too early to judge the Amhara Peace Force in the same way. Former Fano commanders and fighters aligned with the government have nevertheless already reportedly provided information about Fano commanders, operational methods and support networks. They have also been used in information operations intended to deepen existing divisions and exploit rivalries within the insurgency. Their formal organization now raises the possibility that former Fano fighters will increasingly confront their former comrades directly on the battlefield.

For the government, the short-term appeal is obvious, as the model can weaken insurgencies from within while giving security institutions something conventional forces often struggle to acquire quickly, trusted local access and insider knowledge. Yet the same qualities that make these formations useful today could make them difficult to manage later, particularly if they retain their weapons, commanders and separate identities after the immediate counterinsurgency mission has passed.

These are former ethno-nationalist rebels who are once again being organized into armed formations with strong regional and ethnic identities. Today their mission is to fight their former comrades. Yet the same forces are operating in a country where territorial disputes, communal tensions and competing regional claims remain unresolved.

Complaints have already emerged against Gadaa Commando over alleged attacks involving Amhara civilians. There are also reports of tensions and clashes involving the Tigray Peace Force and Raya Guard around Alamata. If the Tekeze Guard is eventually incorporated into the Amhara Peace Force, the implications could become even more sensitive along the contested western border areas.

Those immediate tensions are only part of the risk, as former rebel formations that are armed, organized, given commanders and allowed to operate as identifiable forces can begin developing interests of their own. Commanders accumulate loyal followers, fighters develop institutional identities, weapons create political leverage, and local communities may begin looking to these formations for protection or representation. A temporary security instrument can therefore acquire a political life well beyond the mission for which it was created.

This is the trajectory I am most concerned about. The rebel of yesterday becomes the government ally and counterinsurgent of today. If that ally is allowed to build an independent command structure, retain substantial weapons, develop a loyal constituency and accumulate political bargaining power, today’s government partner could become tomorrow’s autonomous armed actor and, under different political conditions, could eventually return to rebellion.

The logic of እሾክን በሾክ may therefore work in the short term. One thorn can indeed help remove another. The harder question is what happens when the second thorn remains deeply embedded after the first one has been removed.

The government needs to think beyond immediate battlefield effectiveness and establish safeguards while these formations are still dependent on state support.

1. Rehabilitation and reintegration:
Former rebels should undergo serious rehabilitation and reintegration processes to ensure they understand that they are no longer outlaws but lawful state actors, with an obligation to uphold the law, respect state authority and serve all citizens.

2. Professional command:
They should be placed under experienced, moderate and professional commanders who understand the complexities and sensitivities of Ethiopia’s multi-ethnic political environment.

3. Strict supervision:
These formations should remain under tight supervision by federal and regional security institutions, which must intervene swiftly whenever tensions or clashes emerge with other armed groups or communities.

4. Weapons regulation:
Their weapons and capabilities must be strictly regulated. They should not be armed to a level that enables them to believe they can independently challenge regional or federal security institutions.

5. Clear exit strategy:
There should be clear benchmarks and mechanisms for disarming, demobilizing and integrating these forces into the regular regional or federal security apparatus once their counterinsurgency objectives are fulfilled or when the risks they pose begin to outweigh their usefulness.

I find the broader contradiction difficult to ignore, given that the federal government dismantled regional special police forces partly amid concerns that heavily armed regional formations were deepening polarization and conflict, yet it is now helping organize former ethno-nationalist rebels into new armed formations rooted in many of the same regional and identity-based fault lines.

I understand the immediate military calculation, and it may even prove highly effective in weakening several insurgencies, but my concern is what happens afterward, particularly if these forces are not carefully controlled, professionalized and eventually integrated or demobilized. Ethiopia may discover that it solved one security problem by creating the foundations of another.

The former rebel who becomes today’s counterinsurgent could eventually become tomorrow’s armed political challenger.

text:
I'm very bullish on the future of Apero Advisors and the city of Charlotte. Hence why I went on the Builders of Charlotte podcast with @colin_thornton , @bitforth, and @drewhburdick. 

When people ask me about whether or not I have clients locally, I tell them that I don't yet but there's a ton of capital in Charlotte and most of it's being deployed on some very non-interesting things. Of course we work on non-interesting things at Apero but I'm excited for the future once I've integrated myself into the business landscape here.

In the future I think any PE firm worth their salt is going to have an AI partner (whether that's an internal hire or an agency) that helps them standardize AI operations across sales, marketing, and product across their entire portfolio with data and reporting all rolling back up to the fund itself in a way that doesn't really exist today for most funds.

Also we do this at Apero for growth operating partners😏 

A few things from the recording that stuck:

• GTM engineering is principles applied to sales problems, not "automate everything." Shorten the path between two outcomes. Keep a person in the loop.
• Volume is fine. Slop is not. Because everyone's blasting volume, something that clearly came from a human stands out more than ever.
• Don't write a single line of code until you've had 100 conversations with prospects. Deeply understand the problem from first principles before building anything. Too many people are putting code in and expecting money to come out when it comes to product development. 

Also, you may have noticed I'm hitting the media button hard! Here's why:

I've been running outbound email. We get replies. Converting those into real opps has been harder. Not because the channel is dead, but because consulting / implementation is not a SaaS checkout. Timelines are longer. The offer has to be clear. And people need to already know who you are when the email lands.

So we're leaning hard into content and media on purpose. Brand first, then outbound works better. Without a brand, cold OB is asking strangers to trust a generalist firm on a high-consideration buy. That's a bad bet.

I'm starting to treat GTM a little more traditionally again: lead gen, inbound funnels, podcasts, posts, being findable when someone is actually in-market. Outbound stays in the mix. It just can't be the whole motion when you're selling work, not seats. And eventually I believe it will be a highly profitable channel for us! First things first though, need to build the brand. I always want email to be on at various volumes testing messaging and angles, I just don't think it's reliable for us enough yet to rely on. 

If you're in Charlotte and want to chat about any of the above, or work in a PE firm and you're wondering how to professionalize the GTM motions for 2027 for your portcos, hmu!

text:
The factory small-block Chevy reached 400 cubic inches in 1970, using a 4.125-inch bore and 3.750-inch stroke in an architecture that had begun with the 265 in 1955. When Chevrolet discontinued the 400 after 1980, the factory's small-block displacement story appeared to be finished. The aftermarket disagreed. By combining different blocks, stroker crankshafts, and larger bores, builders pushed the basic small-block architecture far beyond anything Chevrolet offered in production. The 383 stroker became one of the most popular combinations, followed by larger combinations such as 396, 408, 421, and eventually 434 cubic inches. A modern 434 can produce power that would have been extraordinary for any small-block in the muscle-car era. Skip White Performance in Kingsport, Tennessee, has built combinations producing around 625 horsepower from a 434-cubic-inch small-block, demonstrating just how far the original architecture can be taken with purpose-built aftermarket components.

The difference is that a serious 434 is no longer simply a bored and stroked factory 350. Skip White's high-output combinations use an aftermarket racing block designed specifically for the stresses involved. The Dart block provides thicker cylinder walls, four-bolt main caps, and additional structural strength compared with a production small-block casting. A forged 4340-steel crankshaft and forged connecting rods handle the increased cylinder pressure and high-rpm loading, while forged 2618-alloy pistons provide the strength and thermal tolerance required for a serious naturally aspirated performance engine. CNC-ported AFR cylinder heads, a COMP Cams camshaft, Howards valvetrain components, Scorpion roller rockers, Cloyes timing components, and an ATI Super Damper complete a combination built around airflow and durability rather than simply increasing displacement. The oiling system is upgraded as well, with a performance Melling pump and a baffled Champ oil pan with a windage-control system.

That component list is important because 625 horsepower does not come from displacement alone. A 434-cubic-inch engine has considerably more airflow potential than a stock 350, but the cylinder heads, camshaft, compression ratio, intake, carburetor, exhaust system, and RPM range determine how effectively that displacement is used. The Dart block also changes the equation because the builder is no longer asking a decades-old production casting to tolerate loads it was never designed to handle. The combination can retain the familiar small-block Chevy dimensions and mounting points while using modern aftermarket hardware throughout the engine. That is why a 434 can make more power than a factory LS6 454 while occupying the physical footprint of a traditional small-block.

But there is an significant catch, and it is one that horsepower advertisements often leave out. A 625-hp 434 built around a large camshaft is not automatically a good street engine. The aggressive cam timing that helps the engine produce power at high RPM can reduce idle quality, manifold vacuum, and low-speed torque. The result is an engine that wants the right gearing, converter, vehicle weight, and operating range. In a relatively light car with appropriate rear gears and a converter matched to the camshaft, the combination can be brutally effective. Put the same engine in a heavy vehicle with tall gearing and a low-stall converter, and much of its theoretical power becomes irrelevant because the engine spends too much of its time below the RPM range where the camshaft and cylinder heads work efficiently.

That is the real lesson behind a serious aftermarket small-block. The original Chevrolet architecture may have started life as a compact 265-cubic-inch V8, but the aftermarket turned it into an engine platform capable of displacement and power figures Chevrolet's production engineers never offered. A 434 making 625 horsepower is impressive, but the number alone does not tell you whether the engine is usable. The right combination of block, rotating assembly, cylinder heads, camshaft, oiling system, gearing, converter, and vehicle weight matters just as much as the dyno sheet. The most credible builders understand that horsepower has consequences. A good 434 is not just an engine that makes 625 horsepower. It is an engine built for a car that can actually use it.

text:
Ethiopia–Somalia Rift Opens a Strategic Opportunity for Somaliland

The El Alamein declaration has widened the policy distance between Addis Ababa and Mogadishu. Somalia joined Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan in affirming that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states and rejecting recognition or support for Somaliland. Ethiopia, meanwhile, continues to seek reliable sea access through negotiation and mutual benefit. 

This divergence creates a consequential opening for Somaliland. Ethiopia needs dependable access to the sea; Somaliland has a strategic coastline, the port of Berbera and a direct interest in building regional trade and security ties. A partnership based on negotiated access, investment and shared economic benefits could serve both countries’ long-term interests.

For Somaliland, the opportunity is diplomatic as well as economic. Addis Ababa and Hargeisa can turn their shared interests into concrete agreements on port use, transport links, customs, energy, maritime security and cross-border commerce. Ethiopia can gain a reliable route to the sea, while Somaliland can attract investment, expand Berbera’s role and strengthen its international partnerships.

This moment calls for clear strategic choices. Ethiopia should move from general statements about sea access toward practical negotiations with Somaliland. Somaliland should present a detailed offer built on mutual benefit and respect for its sovereignty. The goal should be a durable partnership that creates prosperity and stability across the region.

The growing distance between Ethiopia and Somalia is a political reality. Somaliland has an opportunity to respond with diplomacy, preparation and a compelling proposal, positioning itself as a constructive partner in the Horn of Africa’s changing regional order.

text:
Ireland deserves to escape EU tyranny on Fishing!

Ireland’s fishing industry is right to demand the same Common Fisheries Policy opt-out Brussels was ready to offer Iceland. 
If the EU can bend the rules for one island nation to protect its fleets and coastal towns, it can stop treating Irish waters as a shared resource for everyone else.
In June 2026 the Irish Fish Producers Organisation renewed that call after reports that Fisheries and Oceans Commissioner Costas Kadis had told the Financial Times an Icelandic accession deal could include fisheries and aquaculture exemptions. Analysts suggested that might mean an administrative zone around Iceland where the CFP would not apply.

Iceland later rejected a return to membership talks, but the episode still exposed the double standard.
IFPO chief executive Aodh O’Donnell said his organisation would not oppose special treatment for Iceland but only if Ireland got the same. 

A carve-out for Reykjavík would be a tacit admission that the CFP cannot serve island nations with major marine resources. Ireland is one of those nations. 
It sits on some of Europe’s richest fishing grounds, yet Irish opportunities have shrunk for decades while other member states keep access to Irish waters.
O’Donnell’s case is straightforward. Geography, dependence on fishing and unique marine resources were enough for Brussels to find flexibility for a country not even in the EU. The same arguments apply to Ireland. Fishermen here have been told for years that the policy is fixed and quota shares cannot move through Brexit losses, further cuts, fleet decommissioning and the failure to deliver the long-standing Hague Preferences. 

Ireland also bore a disproportionate share of the Brexit settlement, contributing about 40 percent of the value of fish transferred to the UK under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

There cannot be one set of rules for Iceland and another for Ireland. The government should use this precedent and demand equivalent derogations: a review of Ireland’s place in the CFP, a fairer share of the wealth taken from Irish waters, and real national control over fisheries so coastal communities are no longer run from Brussels. If the CFP does not fit Iceland, it has already failed Irish fishing.

43By Ivan PennVisuals by Patrick JunkerIvan Penn, who has covered energy for almost 20 years, reported from the Hanwha Qcells factory in Cartersville, Ga.Oct. 5, 2026
Producers of solar panels in the United States say they are on the cusp of a technological breakthrough that could upend the industry and even threaten China’s grip on it.The manufacturers are racing to develop new kinds of panels that can generate 25 percent more energy than most such devices available today. If they are successful, the advance will allow the world to meet the rapidly rising demand for electricity with less land and roof area.The new technology, known as tandem solar, involves adding second and third layers of material, like a layer cake, to allow panels to convert more of the sun’s radiance into electricity.Researchers have been working to perfect tandem panels for many years, but now several companies, including Tandem PV, First Solar and Hanwha Qcells, say they are preparing to sell such panels commercially soon, after successfully testing the devices and obtaining certifications from technical bodies.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENT“It is the next frontier,” said Mike Carr, executive director of the Solar Energy Manufacturers for America Coalition. He acknowledged that Chinese companies were also working on tandem solar but said their technology “is not better than ours and maybe even behind us.”But the new tandem panels and their manufacturers will face many challenges. Power producers will be reluctant to buy new devices that are too expensive or until manufacturers can convince them that tandem panels will not degrade more quickly than conventional panels.U.S. politics could be another barrier. Republicans in Congress and the Trump administration have made it hard for new solar farms to obtain federal permits while trying to increase the use of fossil fuels and nuclear power plants.Then there is China, which controls about 80 percent of the solar panel market by supplying either panels or their components.China devastated the U.S. solar panel manufacturing industry by offering devices at prices far lower than companies in the United States, Germany and Japan — which dominated the industry until around 2010.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe Biden and Trump administrations have tried to revive U.S. solar manufacturing with tariffs, subsidies and other policies. Partly as a result, new factories have been built across the country in recent years. Hanwha, a South Korean company that bought the German solar manufacturer Qcells in 2012, has spent billions on production lines in Georgia, including in Cartersville, north of https://t.co/UCk79h6ziS experts say perfecting tandem panels before the Chinese do would allow the United States, Germany and other countries to reclaim a big share of the global solar industry.Qcells has been testing its tandem solar panels in its lab in Germany as well as in fields in the United States, Australia, Cyprus and South Korea to show that they are ready. Among other things, the company has been blasting panels with LED light to see how they will perform. It has also been firing balls of ice — some roughly the size of marbles, others as big as or slightly bigger than golf balls — at panels to see how they handle extreme weather.Simulating hail in a test at Qcells.
Image📷A calibrated air gun shoots the ice at high velocity to test the impact resistance of the panel’s protective safety glass.CreditCredit...
VideoThe tests are designed to reassure energy companies, investors and lenders that the new panels will last 20 to 30 years once they are installed in baking deserts or in fields subject to torrential downpours.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTThe power industry is “quite conservative in accepting new technologies,” said Fabian Fertig, head of tandem research and development for Qcells, who is based in Leipzig, Germany. “We’ve been focused on stability. We have to convince banks that this new technology can deliver.”Scientists developed early tandem panels decades ago, but it has taken time to ensure that they could withstand harsh conditions — from heat and humidity to pounding hail.“There are all these questions around how long they actually last,” said Chetan Krishna, a principal at RMI, a research organization that specializes in sustainability and was previously known as the Rocky Mountain Institute. “Are there degradation issues that we don’t know yet?”Mr. Krishna and other experts say they believe the tandem solar panels are very close to being ready.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTBut the technology remains expensive. By some estimates, these panels could cost three to three and a half times as much as conventional devices, which are typically made of one layer of silicon.The cost of buying and installing conventional panels for solar farms ranges from about 93 cents to $1.06 per watt, according to a report by the Solar Energy Industries Association.Andrés Gluski, chief executive of AES, a big utility and power company, said price would be crucial to the success of tandem panels because Chinese manufacturers sold solar panels at very low prices. China “could probably supply the world twice over,” he said.Qcells has been blasting panels with LED light to see how they will perform.The technology for modern solar panels was created at AT&T’s Bell Labs in 1954. But broad use of it didn’t take off until the 1980s as the devices became more efficient at converting sunshine into electricity. Improvements helped lower costs and have made the technology the cheapest way to generate electricity.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTIn recent years, energy companies have also figured out how to pair solar panels with batteries to supply energy hours after the sun has set. Solar and batteries accounted for 70 percent of the capacity added to U.S. grids in the first half of this year, according to Wood Mackenzie, an energy research https://t.co/AbiAwnqF8p energy made up nearly 9 percent of the electricity produced in the United States in 2025, up from 3 percent in 2020, according to the Energy Information Administration.Widespread use of tandem panels could significantly increase solar’s share of the country’s electricity, helping to satisfy the surging demand for power from data centers used to develop artificial https://t.co/nBBmPvYiRV analysts evaluate the dependability of different sources of power by measuring their capacity factors. In theory, a power source that can supply electricity 24 hours a day, 365 days a year would have a capacity factor of 100 percent. But no power plants operate at that level because they require maintenance, upgrades, refueling and so on.Nuclear plants typically offer the highest capacity factors, in the low 90s. Large natural gas power plants generally operate at about 58 percent, while U.S. solar farms average roughly 24 percent, according to the E.I.A. That is primarily because they produce electricity only when the sun is shining and cannot convert all of the light they receive into usable energy.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTSheep grazing among the solar arrays at a Qcells testing site.

VideoSolar executives assert that tandem panels could have capacity factors of more than 31 percent. As a result, energy companies would be able to generate the same electricity on less land and with fewer materials.“If you build a utility field, you need fewer cables,” said Mr. Fertig of Qcells. “If you have a rooftop, you can get the same power out of less of your rooftop.”Qcells became the first manufacturer to make a tandem panel that has been independently certified under standards established by Underwriters Laboratories and the International Electrotechnical Commission, two groups that validate and set standards for various products.AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTAnother company working on such devices — Tandem PV in Fremont, Calif. — says it has been testing panels under various conditions across the country for the last year.“We’re showing less than 1 percent degradation per year,” Scott Wharton, chief executive of Tandem PV, a name that refers to the photovoltaic technology used to convert sunlight into electricity. text:
Minnesota’s Somali settlement is a case of compassion without a standard. It is failing and we are at a critical moment. It is what happens when a low-education refugee population from a clan-based, low-trust society is settled in one metro, given immediate access to a generous welfare state, and told that maintaining a separate culture is the goal.

There are about 80,000 to 110,000 people, most already citizens, concentrated in Minneapolis, Hennepin, Ramsey, and St. Cloud with new enclaves and concentrations building in neighboring counties. There are too many to undo and that is not a legal option as well so let’s look for real solutions. We need to stop feeding the problem.

**What has failed**

Equal rules were dropped. Students see Somali classmates skip the punishments everyone else gets.

About 12 gangs, roughly 300 kids with an additional Halo of perhaps 1000 more young men and thousands that will not cross them. There are a known 14 homicides and 100-plus shootings in two years, plus incredible amounts of carjackings, ongoing fights and physical altercations, and mall robberies.

Welfare is the norm. About half the children in poverty, weak English after a decade, food stamps and Medicaid in most households. (79% are on some form of welfare.

Fraud used the same nonprofits that did the welcoming. Meal, autism, and housing cases were overwhelmingly this network.

No Western country with a dense Somali population has closed the gap. Sweden is worse.

** Send them back is not a real option.**

Most are US-born or naturalized. Citizens cannot be deported for failed integration.
Some are removable, non-citizens after serious convictions, status fraud, and the few thousand who never naturalized. That is a slice and not a realistic solution.

**What would work**

Same offense, same consequence in schools and courts. No racial suspension targets.

Federal gun charges, adult charging for carjacking, trespass bans, witness support.

English and work required for cash and food aid. Contract bans after fraud convictions.

Stop new placements and chain migration into Minnesota.
Deport the removable slice. Offer paid exit to anyone who will take it. Do not pretend the citizens are leaving.

Churches: quit the resettlement pipeline, back one standard, help individuals who will live by it. Stop the feel good compassion that is actually hurting not helping. In the Muslim community, Imams need to stop making an apology from leaders naming Somalis a condition for helping. They must stop defending the wrongdoing otherwise they are a veto to any progress. 

Electing new leaders that will not allow the corruption to continue. Holding all of our elected leaders, principles, administrators, and religious leaders accountable. Many of our current leaders are in on the grift and cover up and it’s time for this to end. Others live in fear of retribution for breaking with the ranks. 

** If there’s a model we can follow, it’s Denmark, not Sweden. ** 

Denmark already has done the version people called cruel: lower benefits, temporary status, breakup of the enclaves, mandatory early learning of Danish. They cut the inflow of Somalis. It did not remove the citizens. Minnesota has not done even the mild version of that. “Minnesota Nice” is the perfect environment for the problem to continue, we need to toughen up. If not, the neighborhoods and the schools are in huge trouble. It’s way past time to take this problem seriously and we need everyone to work together to turn things around in Minnesota.

text:
🚨 The men who ‘protect our  women’

The Guardian has published the accounts of seven women who say they were abused by key figures in Britain’s anti-immigration street patrol movement (see below).

One of the women described a former partner who once attacked her with a machete. He now organises protests outside houses of multiple occupancy and coordinates groups of men to patrol her town, ostensibly to ‘protect women’. “He’s a bully in every way,” she told the paper.

Why would men with histories of violence towards women be drawn to movements whose rallying cry is “save our women” or “protect our women”? The contradiction is clear, and it’s tempting to reach for a ready-made answer, whether hypocrisy, projection, or simple opportunism.

I offer a summary of how several theoretical perspectives might account for the pattern.

Psychoanalytic theory, the specialist domestic abuse literature, social psychology and the historical sociology of moral panics each provide a different explanation. They overlap in places and conflict in others. My argument here is that one of them, the account of abuse as entitlement and control, explains the pattern most directly, and that the others are best read as explaining elements which that account leaves untouched. Before turning to them, it’s worth being clear about what the evidence does and does not show.

The strongest evidence comes from police data on people arrested during anti-migrant disorder, obtained by the Guardian and others through FoI requests.

The largest dataset concerns the 2024 summer riots in England and Northern Ireland. The Guardian first found that 41% of 899 people arrested in the riots had been reported for domestic abuse-related crimes before they took part in the disorder. A later FoI exercise found that 21% of 949 people detained in England and Northern Ireland were subsequently reported for intimate partner violence, a group making up a majority of the 1,280 people arrested over the riots.

Smaller datasets from Northern Ireland and southern England point the same way. In Belfast, 23 of the 48 people arrested over the August 2024 disorder had previously been reported for domestic abuse. After the June 2025 Ballymena riots, The Detail found that a third of those arrested had been reported for domestic abuse beforehand, and 14 of the 100 arrested were reported in the 13 months that followed. That second figure should be read alongside the fact that a third of the Ballymena arrestees were under 18.

In Southampton, Hampshire police data obtained by the Guardian showed that 22 of the 37 people detained after the protests of 2 June, which followed the life sentence handed to Vickrum Digwa for Henry Nowak’s murder, had been reported for crimes associated with intimate partner violence. That’s 59%.

The evidence on street patrols is different in kind. The Guardian’s latest report rests on the testimony of seven women, several of whom hold restraining or non-molestation orders, together with a small number of named cases involving convictions or protection orders. It identifies at least 14 patrol groups across the UK. That establishes a pattern worth taking seriously, but it gives no figure for how many patrol members have abuse histories.

Four cautions follow. First, a report is not a conviction. The police figures count people reported for domestic abuse; some were charged or convicted, and many were not. Some coverage has blurred this, describing the 2024 cohort as “convicted” when the data does not support it.

Second, the data is incomplete, since four forces, including Merseyside and Greater Manchester, said they could not supply the figures within FoI cost limits.

Third, there is no clean baseline. Without a matched comparison with men of similar age, class and area, the overlap can fairly be called striking and repeated, but its exact size relative to the general population is unknown. 

Fourth, arrestees are a subset. Those arrested may differ from protesters, and protesters from patrol members.

None of this means that everyone who joins a patrol or attends a protest has a history of abuse. It does mean keeping two groups of men distinct.

The first group is the organisers and leading figures described in the Guardian’s testimonies. For them there is direct, if limited, evidence of abuse. The second is the much larger cohorts arrested at disorder, where police data shows a recurring overlap with domestic abuse reports.

The theories below apply most directly to the first group, as accounts of what these movements offer such men. They apply to the second group as accounts of why the same movements may draw in men already known to police for partner violence. Neither group stands for patrol members or protesters in general. My question is narrower: why men with such histories appear to find these movements so congenial, and why some of them end up near the front.

The first perspective, and the one that most readily springs to mind, is psychoanalytic. Developed by Freud and systematised by Anna Freud, psychoanalytic theory describes defence mechanisms: unconscious strategies by which the mind protects itself from thoughts and feelings it cannot tolerate. Several of them map onto the pattern with uncomfortable precision.

Projection is the attribution of one’s own unacceptable impulses to someone else. On this reading, a man who cannot acknowledge his own violence towards women relocates it in a racialised outsider. The “predatory migrant” becomes the container for what he disowns in himself. Theodor Adorno and his colleagues, in The Authoritarian Personality (1950), identified “projectivity” as a core authoritarian trait: a readiness to believe that wild and dangerous sexual impulses are rampant among other people.

Displacement is the redirection of an impulse from its original object to a substitute. In the classic formulation the substitute is safer, as when a man shouted at by his boss goes home and kicks the dog. Here the movement runs the other way. Aggression already expressed at home finds a second, sanctioned outlet in public, where intimidation and control earn applause instead of arrest.

Reaction formation is the adoption of an attitude that is the opposite of an unacceptable one. An abuser who joins such a movement can recast himself as a guardian of women. The hi-vis vests and black ‘uniforms’, often including balaclavas, seen at so many of the recent protests work as a costume of protection that inverts what such a man’s former partners actually experienced.

Splitting divides objects into the wholly good and the wholly bad. Women become either the pure, endangered “our women” or the bad woman who answers back, leaves, or calls the police. One can be avenged in the abstract while the other is punished in practice.

The richest text in this tradition is Klaus Theweleit’s Male Fantasies (1977-78), a study of the writings of the German Freikorps, the paramilitary volunteers of 1918-23 who became a recruiting ground for Nazism. Theweleit argued that these “soldier males” built an armoured, rigid self against a terror of women, desire and dissolution, and discharged that fear as violence against designated enemies. The image of uniformed men standing outside a school gate to protect children from an imagined threat sits uneasily close to his analysis.

The weakness of this approach is evidential. Projection and reaction formation are inferences about inner life, and they are hard to test. A careful therapist would also refuse to diagnose anyone they had not met. Used responsibly, these concepts describe the logic of a discourse and the self-image a movement offers its members and should not be read as clinical claims about particular men.

What this perspective explains, and the others do not, is the shape of the discourse itself: why a movement with such men among its leaders would insist that the danger to women comes from outsiders, and never from within its own ranks.

Many specialists in domestic abuse would be wary of the psychodynamic account, and their objection matters. Since the 1980s, the dominant models in the field have tended to treat abuse primarily as a matter of entitlement and control, a set of beliefs about what a man is owed, rather than as a symptom of unconscious conflict, poor impulse control, or anger.

The Duluth model’s Power and Control Wheel, developed with survivors in Minnesota, maps abuse as a pattern of tactics: isolation, intimidation, threats, economic control, and the use of children. Evan Stark’s work on coercive control, which shaped the offence created in England and Wales by the Serious Crime Act 2015, emphasises the systematic regulation of a partner’s life.

Lundy Bancroft, who spent years running programmes for abusive men, argues in Why Does He Do That? that abusers are not out of control at all. They are acting on a coherent belief that they have the right to govern a woman’s behaviour.

Seen this way, there is no hidden mechanism to uncover. An organiser who controls his partner at home and patrols “his” streets is doing the same thing at different scales. In both settings he asserts ownership over territory and over women’s bodies, and polices who may come near them. The possessive pronoun in “save our women” says this openly.

One of the women interviewed by the Guardian put it in almost exactly these terms: “He likes power, and I feel like this is giving him some sort of power. It’s all about power and control in everything he does.”

This perspective best explains the continuity of tactics. The same pattern of surveillance, intimidation and territorial control appears in the testimonies about home life and in the conduct of the patrols, which stop, question, and demand documents from men of colour.

A third perspective, from social psychology, helps explain why protectiveness and hostility towards women can live together in the same person.

Peter Glick and Susan Fiske’s theory of ambivalent sexism (1996) distinguishes two forms.

Hostile sexism views women as manipulative and seeks to punish those who challenge male authority. 

Benevolent sexism idealises women as pure and fragile, in need of male protection.

The two sound like opposites, yet across many countries the researchers found them positively correlated. They work as a carrot and a stick: women who conform are cherished and shielded, and women who ‘step out of line’ are punished. Consider the young woman with blue hair, who is so often the object of scorn, ridicule or aggression within these movements, or women and girls who adopt a ‘queer’ identity. They fall outside the protected category of “our women” and often become ‘legitimate’ targets instead.

The “protect our women” patrol is benevolent sexism made visible. It casts women as passive objects to be guarded, while the testimonies in the Guardian describe the hostile face directed at women who resist. On this account, the two sets of behaviour belong to one coherent attitude.

Leon Festinger’s theory of cognitive dissonance (1957) offers a related mechanism, and a more testable one than the psychoanalytic concepts.

When people hold two beliefs that conflict, or act against their own self-image, they feel a discomfort they are motivated to reduce, usually by justifying the behaviour rather than changing it. A man who sees himself as a protector of women, but whose partner has experienced him as anything but, has an obvious dissonance to resolve: he can blame her, minimise what happened, or redouble his commitment to the protective role.

Public, visible guardianship of “our women” may be one of the more effective ways of quieting that discomfort. The entitlement model would add that for some men the dissonance may never arise, because they simply do not regard their conduct as wrong in the first place.

The sociologist Michael Kimmel adds a further piece with the idea of aggrieved entitlement, set out in Angry White Men (2013). Men who believe they have been denied a status they were promised, whether as breadwinner, head of household, or simply as someone who matters, experience that loss as an injustice. 

Movements that name a culprit and offer a uniformed role restore a sense of standing. For a man whose authority at home has been challenged by a partner leaving, a court order, or a police caution, a patrol may offer a public stage on which that authority is reasserted.

This perspective explains something the control model takes for granted: how protective rhetoric and punitive practice coexist without being felt as a contradiction, and where the boundary between ‘our women’ and ‘legitimate targets’ is drawn.

The psychological accounts explain why particular men might be drawn in. Historical sociology helps explain why the script is there waiting for them.

The figure of the dark stranger who threatens “our” women is one of the oldest devices in racial politics. In the American South after Reconstruction, lynching was routinely justified as the protection of white womanhood. Ida B. Wells, in Southern Horrors (1892), showed that most lynchings did not even involve an allegation of rape, and that the charge served to police Black economic and social advancement.

In Britain, the 1919 seaport riots in Liverpool, Cardiff and elsewhere were fuelled in part by resentment of relationships between Black and Arab seamen and white women. The 1958 Notting Hill riots followed an attack on Majbritt Morrison, a white Swedish woman married to a Jamaican man. The comparison here is with the script and makes no claim about the scale or nature of the acts. What persists across these very different episodes is a narrative in which ‘protecting women’ licenses action against racialised men.

The sociology of moral panics, from Stan Cohen’s Folk Devils and Moral Panics (1972) to Stuart Hall and colleagues’ Policing the Crisis (1978), gives us the tools to read the current wave.

A ‘folk devil’ is constructed, typically racialised and sexualised. ‘Moral entrepreneurs’ step forward to lead the response. The term comes from Howard Becker’s Outsiders (1963), where it covers both the crusaders who campaign for new rules and the agencies that enforce them. Cohen uses it more narrowly. In Folk Devils and Moral Panics the moral entrepreneurs are the editors, politicians, clergy and campaigning groups who name the folk devils as a menace and demand that something be done. The magistrates, courts and senior police belong to what he calls the control culture, which responds with escalating measures of control. The panic offers ordinary people a role in restoring order. Street patrols are that role made literal, complete with uniforms.

A moral panic also does further kinds of work: it selects and distorts. It directs public anxiety about violence against women towards a narrow and racialised category of offender, and away from the far more common reality of harm by men women know. A panic that locates the threat in the stranger leaves the domestic abuser invisible and may even allow him to recast himself as the threat’s opponent. As Farah Nazeer of Women’s Aid told the Guardian about the 2024 placards, it is troubling that some people in the crowds carrying such slogans had themselves committed, or been accused of, domestic abuse.

What this perspective adds is the script itself: why it was available, why it attaches so readily to migrants, and what it diverts attention from.

Taken together, these explanations overlap, but they conflict at one point. Theweleit and Adorno describe a personality organised defensively against something it cannot face. Bancroft and Stark describe men who are in control and believe they are entitled to be. The two can coexist, since a man may act from conscious entitlement while taking comfort in a script that projects violence onto others, but they cannot both be the primary account of the same man.

On evidential grounds, the entitlement and control model has the stronger claim. It is more parsimonious, explaining the pattern from behaviour that can be observed and documented in testimony, protection orders and police reports, without positing inner states that cannot. It also fits the Guardian testimonies, which describe deliberate and sustained control more than eruptions of a disowned impulse, and it takes those accounts at face value rather than speculating about what was going on in the men’s heads. I find it more persuasive for a further reason, though not an evidential one: it places responsibility with the men themselves.

The other perspectives remain necessary because each explains something the control model leaves out. Ambivalent sexism explains why protection and punishment coexist, and where the boundary between them falls. The history of moral panics explains why a ready-made racial script exists for these men to step into, and why it diverts attention from where most violence against women happens. The psychodynamic concepts describe the structure of the discourse. A rhetoric that relocates male violence onto an outsider, and lets those who practise it appear as protectors, has a projective shape whatever is going on in any individual’s head.

Whether a given man is projecting, or simply acting consistently on his beliefs about women, is a question no one can settle from the outside.

Setting the theories aside, a simpler point remains for public debate: the evidence, though incomplete, shows a repeated overlap between domestic abuse and anti-migrant disorder, and the Guardian’s testimonies place men with histories of abuse among the leaders of the street patrols.

The national picture is the background against which the slogan should be read.

In the year ending March 2025, 40% of adult female homicide victims in England and Wales were killed by a partner or ex-partner and a further 16% by a family member; over half (56%) died in domestic homicides. No suspect had yet been charged in 23% of adult female cases, so these proportions will shift as investigations conclude.

For rape and assault by penetration, the Crime Survey for England and Wales, combining its 2020 and 2025 surveys, found that in their most recent incident since the age of 16, 44.5% of female victims were attacked by a partner or ex-partner and 15% by a stranger.

Individual protests have often begun with a specific crime, and those crimes are real. But a movement that casts itself as the protector of “our  women” should be judged against where the danger to women most often lies, and on the conduct of the men who lead it. If it will not confront the abusers in its own ranks, it protects them far better than it protects any woman.

text:
Before you go to bed!

We wake each day with questions, carrying plans that may never unfold the way we imagined.

The future stands behind a curtain, silent, unwilling to reveal its script, yet life has never offered guarantees.

The seed enters the soil without seeing the flower. The sailor leaves the shore without seeing the destination. The child takes a first step without knowing how far the journey will go.

Perhaps peace is not found in knowing what comes next, but in trusting ourselves to meet whatever comes.

Uncertainty is not always the enemy, sometimes it is the space where possibility lives, it is where new paths appear, where strength is discovered, where faith learns to walk without seeing the whole road.

So when tomorrow feels unclear, hold tightly to today. Do the work before you. Love the people beside you. Take the next step you can see.

text:
Chronic sleep loss accelerates aging at the cellular level. A new preprint from the Leibniz Institute on Aging identifies a molecular switch that may explain why, and shows that flipping it can rescue some of the damage in worms, mouse brain data, and human cells.

Researchers tested this in worms, mouse brain data, and human cells. The switch is a protein complex called DREAM.

First, a quick primer.

Your DNA is wrapped around proteins called histones, like thread around spools. The more histones your cells make, the tighter the DNA is packed. Tightly packed DNA is harder to damage, but it's also harder for repair machinery to reach.

DREAM is a group of proteins that sits on your DNA and controls which genes are active, including how much histone gets made. The researchers found that DREAM follows your sleep-wake cycle.

During wakefulness, DREAM is high. DNA packs tighter and the genome is better shielded. During sleep, DREAM drops. DNA loosens, and repair and cleanup genes get access to do their work.

Think of it like a building. During the day it's locked down for security. At night the doors open and the maintenance crew comes in. If the doors never open, the repairs pile up.

When sleep or the body clock is disrupted, DREAM doesn't drop on time. The repair window stays closed.

What the researchers found:

• Worms with a mildly disrupted body clock lived a normal lifespan. But if they also carried proteins that clump like those in Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease, they became paralyzed much faster

• Lowering DREAM in those worms reversed the paralysis and reduced the protein clumps

• In mouse brains, DREAM activity was lower during sleep and higher while awake. Sleep-deprived mice kept it elevated

• Those mice also failed to turn on a DNA repair gene and kept stress signals high

• In human cells with a disrupted body clock, a compound called harmine, which blocks DREAM, restored energy production and protein-making genes toward normal

• Harmine also protected clock-disrupted worms even though it didn't fix the clock itself

That last point matters. The benefit came from acting downstream of the broken clock, not from repairing it.

Why does one switch matter so much? Because it touches many systems at once. In the clock-disrupted worms, cells lost some of their defenses against oxidative damage, burned energy less efficiently, and kept making proteins at full speed while already struggling to clear damaged ones. Blocking DREAM moved many of these back toward normal.

The authors also suggest timing could matter. DREAM is meant to rise and fall daily, so a blocker might work best if used only during the sleep window.

Several caveats:

• This is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed

• Most of the hands-on evidence comes from worms, plus gene activity data in mice and cultured human cells

• Harmine is not a proven sleep substitute, and DREAM also regulates cell division, so side effects are a real concern

• The authors are listed as inventors on a patent application based on these findings

What this means for longevity:

• Sleep may be an active repair process, not just rest. If DREAM has to drop for repair genes to get access, then sleep timing and consistency matter, not only total hours

• Sleep loss and circadian disruption may speed up aging through shared machinery. Shift work, irregular schedules, and chronic short sleep could all keep the repair window closed

• Brain aging may be especially exposed. Neurons don't divide to replace damaged parts, and the worm data tie poor clock function to faster damage from Alzheimer's-like clumping proteins

• Future therapies may target the downstream switch rather than the clock itself. That could matter for people who can't easily fix their sleep, though this is a long way from the clinic

This doesn't replace sleep. It offers a mechanism: sleep loss keeps a protective program running too long, and that crowds out repair. Whether the same logic holds in whole mammals is the next test.

For longevity, the point is cumulative. Repair windows missed in your 30s, 40s, and 50s add up, and the damage that builds may shape how your brain and body hold up in your 70s and 80s.
