text:
Former Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. posted a 55% completion rate allowed in 47 games, ranking fourth-lowest among NFL corners since 2023. Given this level of on-field performance, the Steelers’ decision to trade a reliable perimeter defender and franchise cornerstone to the Dallas Cowboys for a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick early in the 2026 season is difficult to justify without context.

The trade reportedly stemmed from a contract stalemate. Negotiations appeared to unravel when it emerged the Steelers were prepared to offer a contract with minimal guarantees beyond the first year. The latest developments have drawn criticism from local sports talk circles.

Details circulating around contract talks indicated an average annual value near $28 million, with roughly $42 million guaranteed at signing but no guarantees beyond year one. This structure prompted Porter to push back, as the team was unwilling to guarantee the second year, leaving him to shoulder long-term physical risk. Pittsburgh has a history of avoiding second-year guarantees, though it did provide a three-year, $123 million extension with $108 million guaranteed to star pass rusher T.J. Watt.

Despite the contention, Porter opened 2026 strongly after the trade, recording 4.5 sacks, six tackles for loss, and an interception through Week 4. The Steelers, meanwhile, had also recently re-signed wide receiver DK Metcalf to a four-year, $132 million deal with $60 million guaranteed at signing, including second-year guarantees, following his trade from Seattle—an arrangement that drew its own share of debate given his on-field consistency.

Porter felt disrespected by the organization for what he perceived as a lack of loyalty, a sentiment echoed by some pundits who argued the Steelers prioritized tradition over rewarding rising talent. There was speculation about why Porter was listed on briefly on injured reserve with a back issue early in the 2026 season; Porter later explained that sitting out the first three games was his own decision amid the contract stalemate.

Ultimately, Porter and the Steelers moved on, trading the cornerback to Dallas. In the long run, the deal could benefit both sides: Porter gains an opportunity to showcase his abilities on a new team and potentially secure a larger contract in 2027, while Pittsburgh recoups assets and refreshes its defensive group.

Porter’s departure leaves a notable gap in the Steelers’ secondary. He had been one of the league’s more effective young corners, notably not allowing a touchdown in coverage since Week 8 of the 2023 season, underscoring the potential impact of his absence on Pittsburgh’s defense this season.

text:
Where the Heap Stands.
A plain account of an old puzzle, and of one new way of answering it.
Developed by William Wimberly, working with AI assistance.

Part one. The puzzle.

Imagine a single grain of wheat sitting on a table. Nobody would call that a heap. Now add a second grain. Still not a heap. Add a third. Still not a heap. It seems obvious that adding one grain can never turn something that is not a heap into something that is. One grain is simply too small to make that kind of difference.

Now keep going. A thousand grains. Ten thousand. A million. At some point you are looking at an enormous pile of wheat, and of course it is a heap.

But here is the trouble. If one grain can never make the difference, and you only ever added one grain at a time, then you never crossed a line. So a million grains is not a heap either. And that is absurd.

This puzzle is about two thousand four hundred years old. It was first posed by a Greek thinker named Eubulides, and it is called the sorites paradox, from the Greek word for heap. Philosophers have been arguing about it ever since, and they still do not agree on the answer.

It would be easy to dismiss this as a word game. It is not. Almost every boundary that matters in real life works the same way. When does a drizzle become rain? When does someone go from tipsy to drunk? When does a warm forehead become a fever? When is a child old enough? Each of these lines gets drawn somewhere, often with real consequences, and none of them survives the question: why there, and not one step over? The heap is simply the cleanest laboratory version of a problem we live with every day.

Part two. Why the puzzle is so stubborn.

The puzzle rests on four ideas, and each one seems impossible to give up.

First, one grain is not a heap. Nobody disputes that.

Second, adding a single grain never turns a non-heap into a heap. Philosophers call this tolerance. The word heap seems to tolerate tiny changes.

Third, a million grains is a heap. Obvious.

Fourth, ordinary logic. If each step follows from the one before, you can chain the steps together as many times as you like.

The four ideas cannot all be true at once. Give up any one of them and the contradiction disappears. The whole history of the puzzle is a history of people choosing which one to give up, and paying a price for it.

Part three. The answers people have tried.

The first family of answers says there really is an exact grain where the pile becomes a heap. We simply cannot know which grain it is. The line is real but hidden. This view is called epistemicism, and its best-known defender is the philosopher Timothy Williamson. Its strength is that it keeps ordinary logic completely intact. Its weakness is that it asks us to believe in a fact that no one could ever discover, fixed by our language in a way no one can explain.

The second family says the word heap is fuzzy at the edges. There are clear heaps, clear non-heaps, and a blurry zone in between. The trouble is that this just moves the problem. Where exactly does the blurry zone begin? If the edge of the blurry zone is sharp, we have a hidden line again. If it is blurry too, we have a second heap puzzle, one level up. The original essay behind this project called this the bump in the rug. You push the bump down in one place, and it pops up two feet away.

A third answer, which has received attention more recently, borrows an idea from engineering called hysteresis. Think of a home thermostat. It does not switch on and off at exactly seventy degrees, or it would chatter itself to death. It switches the heat on at sixty-eight and off at seventy-two. In between, what it does depends on what it was doing a moment ago. Human judgment can work similarly. Show someone colours shifting slowly from red to orange, and they switch their answer at one point. Run the colours backwards and they switch at a different point. Applied to the heap, the idea is that there is no line, only a sticky zone, and whether a pile in that zone counts as a heap depends on whether you got there by adding grains or taking them away.

The original essay argued that this idea, clever as it is, only moves the bump in the rug. How sticky is the stickiness? If the stickiness is a definite amount, there is a hidden exact line after all. If it is itself fuzzy, the puzzle starts again one level up. When the claims about hysteresis were checked against published experiments, the evidence also turned out to be weaker than the essay assumed. One careful study of colour judgments went looking for hysteresis and found the opposite effect.

There is one more answer worth knowing. The philosopher Diana Raffman argues that a vague word has many equally acceptable stopping places, and that wherever a particular speaker happens to stop is permissible, not a true boundary of the word. Keep that idea in mind, because it comes back later.

Part four. The idea behind this project.

The idea at the heart of this project starts with a simple observation about English.

You can say that one stick is longer than another even when the difference is a single millimetre, and what you say is simply true. But you cannot point to the longer of two nearly identical sticks and call it the long one. That sounds wrong. The comparison word, longer, handles tiny differences easily. The plain word, long, refuses them. It needs a real, visible gap before it makes sense to use it.

The linguist Christopher Kennedy described this effect. He called the situations where tiny differences are at stake crisp judgments, and he showed that plain words like long and tall resist crisp judgments while comparison words like longer and taller do not.

Now look again at the heap puzzle. It asks: which grain made it a heap? That is a hairline question. It asks you to separate two piles that differ by a single grain. And it asks this using exactly the kind of plain word that refuses hairline distinctions. It is like demanding the exact minute something happened when the only words you are allowed are morning, afternoon and evening.

So here is the proposal. The question which grain made it a heap may not be a hard question with a hidden answer. It may be a question that the word heap cannot answer at all, because the question does not fit the word. Think of asking what lies north of the North Pole. The answer is not hidden. The question simply does not apply.

Philosophers of language have a name for this kind of failure. When a question or a sentence takes something for granted that is not true, it is said to have a failed presupposition. The classic example is the sentence, the present king of France is bald. It is not exactly false, because there is no present king of France to be bald or not bald. The sentence has no answer to give. This project claims that which grain made it a heap fails in the same way. And that matters, because it means we can reject the idea that one grain never makes a difference, without being forced to say there is a particular grain that did. Ordinary logic usually forces that second step. A failed presupposition is one of the very few ways to avoid it.

Part five. What the computer models showed.

Before testing an idea on people, it is worth checking that the idea holds together. So three small computer models were built.

The first model used just ten piles, from one grain to ten, and assumed that neighbouring piles could not be told apart. It then checked every possible situation, every combination of piles a person might be looking at, and asked whether a sensible line between heap and non-heap could be drawn without ever separating two piles that look identical. Out of more than a thousand possible situations, only four had no sensible line at all. And those four were exactly the situations where every pile is in view at once, which is precisely the situation the puzzle needs. Everywhere else, a line could be drawn, but it always fell between piles that were noticeably different.

The same first model also tried a well-known alternative logic, called tolerant and strict logic, which blocks the chain of reasoning at a different point. It did stop the chain. But it also allowed contradictory statements to be accepted side by side, so it did not give the clean result this project was after.

The second model added realism. People do not notice differences with perfect consistency, and larger piles need larger differences before anyone notices. So the model let the threshold for noticing a difference wobble randomly from one occasion to the next. The result held up. In a genuine heap series, where neighbouring piles really do look alike, the line-drawing question had no sensible answer on the large majority of occasions. And on the occasions when a line could be drawn, it fell at a difference someone could actually notice.

The third model made the randomness shared, the way a person might be sharp one day and tired the next. The result mostly survived. But on rare occasions of unusually sharp attention, a person can notice even a one-grain difference, and then a line can be drawn. That is not a problem for the idea. On those occasions, the piles are no longer alike enough to create the puzzle in the first place.

An honest word about what these models prove. They show the idea is consistent, and that it does not fall apart when realistic noise is added. They do not show that the idea is true of real people. In fact, the main result of the first model follows almost directly from its own starting assumption. All of the real content lies in that assumption, which is that people actually treat the line-drawing question as one that has no answer. Only people can tell us whether that is so.

Part six. The thermostat, turned around.

A common objection runs like this. Real life forces sharp lines all the time. Courts, doctors and computers must decide yes or no. Doesn't that bring the puzzle straight back?

The answer is that when a decision must come out yes or no, people stop using the vague word and switch to a number. The law does not say drunk. It says a blood alcohol level of point zero eight or above. A doctor does not say feverish. A doctor says one hundred point four degrees or higher. These numbered lines are exact, and nobody finds them paradoxical. No one thinks the difference between point zero seven nine and point zero eight is a deep puzzle about the meaning of the word drunk.

The thermostat makes the point perfectly. It switches at sixty-eight and seventy-two degrees, and no one has ever looked at a thermostat and called it a paradox. That is because it runs on numbers, not on the word warm. The puzzle only appears when we ask a plain word to do a number's job.

What remains when a number is chosen is arbitrariness. Why point zero eight and not point zero seven nine? That is a fair practical question, and even a moral one, but it is not a contradiction in our language.

Part seven. What other researchers have already tested.

Before designing a study, it is important to check whether someone has already done it. A focused search of the main experimental papers turned up several useful findings.

The most striking came from the very researchers whose work this idea builds on. Kristen Syrett, Christopher Kennedy and Jeffrey Lidz ran experiments in which children and adults were shown two rods and asked to hand over the long one. Everyone handed over the longer rod. But every pair of rods they used differed clearly. Their paper even notes that calling one of two nearly identical rods the long one sounds wrong, and then deliberately sets that case aside. So the exact prediction this project depends on has been named in print, and has never been tested.

Other studies asked people about borderline cases, such as someone who is neither clearly tall nor clearly not tall. People strongly prefer to say such a person is neither tall nor not tall, rather than both tall and not tall. Even three-year-old children show this preference. That fits the idea of a gap, but a gap for one borderline case is not the same as refusing the line-drawing question itself.

An older study by Bonini and colleagues asked people where boundaries lie, and its authors read their results as evidence that there is a hidden line we cannot know. Another team, Sam Alxatib and Jeffry Pelletier, read the very same results as evidence for gaps. One set of data, two opposite conclusions. That is a warning. A study is only useful if its results cannot be read both ways.

Finally, a researcher named Jérémy Zehr found that sentences with failed presuppositions, like the one about the king of France, produce a different pattern of answers from ordinary vague sentences. That gives this project something precise to measure against.

Part eight. Problems found along the way, and how they were fixed.

Several problems were discovered while the plan was being built, some by outside reviewers and some during checking. Each one improved the design.

The first problem is that heap is a noun. Kennedy's findings are about adjectives, words like tall and long, which have comparison forms like taller and longer. There is no such word as heapier. So the project had quietly assumed that a vague noun behaves like a plain adjective. That needed to be tested, not assumed.

The second problem was hidden in the first version of the experiment. Imagine showing someone two large piles and asking them to point to the heap. If both piles are obviously heaps, the person will balk, but only because the word the in the heap implies there is exactly one. That is a different problem entirely, and it could have been mistaken for support.

The third discovery came from thinking about a pile of wheat spread flat across a floor. A million grains spread out in a single layer is not a heap. Nobody calls it one. So the word heap seems to need two things: a heaped shape, with grains resting on other grains, and enough grains to be worth naming. Call these the form axis and the size axis. The shape seems to be the sharp part. A flat layer is never a heap. The size seems to be the soft part. And the classic puzzle only ever moves along the size axis, because it always imagines a heaped pile slowly losing grains, so the shape never changes.

If that is right, then the vague part of the word heap behaves like the phrase a big enough pile. The noun carries the plain adjective big inside it. And that would mean Kennedy's findings about adjectives apply to heap after all, which would solve the first problem rather than leaving it open.

Part nine. The honest costs.

Every answer to this puzzle has a price, and this one does too.

The main cost is this. If the question which pile is the last non-heap has no answer when the whole series is in view, then the statement every pile in the series is either a heap or not a heap also has no answer in that situation. That gives up a principle of ordinary logic, called the law of excluded middle, for those particular sentences. Defenders of traditional logic will count that as a real loss.

There is also a strong objection to answer. A defender of the hidden-line view can say: fine, pick a standard. By the standard of one hundred grains, pile ninety-nine is not a heap. This project's reply is that once you add an explicit standard, you have switched from the plain word to a numbered rule, like the thermostat. But whether people actually treat it that way is a question about English that only the study can settle.

And there is a methodological caution worth stating plainly. Several reviews of this idea were produced by AI systems that were given the project's own framing. When those reviews agreed with the idea, they were echoing it, not confirming it. Agreement from a source that was handed the answer is not evidence.

Part ten. The next step: asking real people.

The plan starts small, with a short pilot test that anyone could run with a handful of photographs and ten to fifteen people who have never heard of the idea.

Each person sees real photographs of piles of wheat and hears six short requests, in a random order.

First, shown two piles that differ only slightly, they are asked: point to the big pile. This is the plain adjective, the true test of Kennedy's effect.

Second, shown the same two piles, they are asked: point to the bigger pile. This is the comparison word, which should be easy.

Third, shown the same two piles again, they are asked: point to the heap. This tests the noun. Does it behave like the first request or like the second?

Fourth, shown two obviously large piles of clearly different sizes, they are asked: point to the heap. This checks the problem with the word the. If people balk here too, any balking at the third request cannot be credited to the idea.

Fifth, shown one large pile and a few scattered grains, they are asked: point to the heap. This should be easy for everyone.

Sixth, shown the same amount of wheat twice, once heaped and once spread flat, they are asked: point to the heap. This tests the shape idea.

The predictions were written down before any data exist. The first request should cause noticeably more hesitation than the second. The sixth request should be easy, because shape is the sharp part of the word. And the third request should be hard in the same way as the first, because between two heaped piles only the soft, size part of the word is left. If all of that happens, the idea has its first real evidence. If the first request turns out to be just as easy as the second, the central claim is in trouble, and the right move is to stop and rethink before going further.

If the pilot passes, a larger study follows, with around one hundred and fifty participants. That study shows people a full row of forty piles and asks which is the last pile that is not a heap. The answer choices are designed so that each one matches exactly one competing theory. One answer is: there is one, but I cannot tell which. That matches the hidden-line view. Another is: there is one, but no particular pile is it. Another is: it is true in a way and false in a way. And another is: the question does not apply to these piles. That last answer matches this project.

The larger study also includes two comparison questions. One is a question with a known failed presupposition, such as asking which of the piles is the one made of gold. The other is an ordinary vague sentence about a single pile. The decisive test is which of those two the heap question resembles in the way people answer it.

Before that larger study begins, the plan calls for two things. The first is to find a faculty adviser in linguistics, psychology or philosophy who can check the materials. The second is to file what is called a pre-registration: a dated, locked public record of every prediction and every rule for judging the results, written before a single answer is collected. That way, no one can say the goalposts were moved after the fact.

Part eleven. Where things stand.

Here is where the project sits today.

The puzzle asks for a line that no single grain can draw. The usual answers either hide the line somewhere we can never find it, or blur it in a way that simply moves the problem. This project offers a different answer. The plain word heap, like the word big, is not built for hairline distinctions, while comparison words like bigger are. So the question which grain made it a heap may have no answer, not because the answer is hidden, but because the question does not fit the word.

That idea holds together logically, and it survives the tests a computer can run. A search of earlier research found that no one has yet asked people the key question, and that the researchers behind the grammar idea named the crucial case and chose not to test it. Along the way the idea has been sharpened: the word heap seems to need a heaped shape as well as a large enough size, and only the size part is vague.

What remains is the most important part, and only people can supply it. Show someone two nearly identical piles and ask them to point to the big pile. Then ask them to point to the bigger pile. If the first request makes people hesitate and the second does not, the idea has its first real evidence, and a larger, carefully planned study can follow. If not, the idea will need to change. Either way, the answer will come from the world, not from argument.

A note on sources.

The main works drawn on in this account are: the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on the sorites paradox, by Diana Raffman and Dominic Hyde. Christopher Kennedy's papers Vagueness and Grammar, and Vagueness and Comparison. Syrett, Kennedy and Lidz, on children's understanding of gradable adjectives. Serchuk, Hargreaves and Zach, Four Experimental Studies on Vagueness. Alxatib and Pelletier, The Psychology of Vagueness. Égré and Zehr, Are Gaps Preferred to Gluts. Weicker and Schulz, on children's interpretation of vague adjectives. Jérémy Zehr's dissertation on vagueness and presupposition. Égré, de Gardelle and Ripley, on order effects in colour categorisation. Cobreros, Égré, Ripley and van Rooij, on tolerant, classical and strict logic. Dzhafarov and Perry, on perceptual matching and the sorites. And Mark Sainsbury's discussion of Raffman's work.

The computer models, the literature search and much of the drafting were done with the help of an AI assistant. The questions, the judgment calls and the essay that started it all are William's.

End of document.

text:
The UNIVERSITY OF OREGON is Jennifer Freyd’s longtime academic home. She and Carly Smith developed the Institutional Betrayal Questionnaire there and used it with University of Oregon (UO) students; their early work showed that when a school creates conditions that make assault seem normal, or responds poorly after it occurs, trauma symptoms worsen. That frame is especially relevant to this week’s alert about five reported sexual assaults on or near campus in the first week of classes. It is a painful irony.

Freyd later sued UO over a documented pay gap with male colleagues of similar rank and seniority. The case reached the Ninth Circuit and settled in 2021 for $350,000 plus a $100,000 donation to the Center for Institutional Courage she founded. She often used her own school, UO, as an example of Institutional Betrayal.

By contrast, she has pointed to in-state rival Oregon State (OSU) under President Ed Ray as an example of the alternative: after the 1998 Brenda Tracy case involving OSU athletes came to light, Ray ordered a review, apologized publicly, and brought @brendatracy24 in as a consultant. Freyd has called that sequence institutional courage.

She made the same argument in an invited 2017 presentation to the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine workshop on sexual harassment in academia, held at UC Irvine (“Moving from Institutional Betrayal to Institutional Courage”), and has continued speaking on these issues in academic and legal settings, including work connected to family-violence initiatives.

The research she started at UO still offers the clearest measure of whether this week’s alert is followed by transparency and support, or by another round of institutional failure.

—

“[Brenda Tracy] changes the lives of the guys who hear her speak.”

—Stanford FB coach David Shaw (2017)

text:
Those are stronger claims, and a court may yet distinguish between a conceded failure to pay and an allegation of motive.
But the company’s foundational denial in its summons — that it is not in arrears at all — collides with the documentary record its chairman created. 
Employees are, in substance, being asked to apologise for describing a state of affairs their employer had already described, in writing, as a failure to meet an unconditional obligation.
The episode matters beyond one newsroom.
Ncube has spent years cultivating a public identity as a defender of independent journalism, free speech and accountability. 
His newspaper titles have, at their best, insisted that powerful institutions answer for the gap between what they say and what they do. 
That standard is not suspended when the institution belongs to Ncube. 
A publisher who tells staff their delayed salaries represent broken trust, then instructs lawyers to tell a court that talk of arrears is a knowing falsehood, invites precisely the scrutiny that Ncube has long claimed to champion.
There is also a practical cruelty in the remedy sought by Ncube through his ZimInd Publishers.
The defendants are sued jointly and severally. 
Many are journalists; some have already left. 
The claim does not merely dispute their account of a meeting. It seeks to price their speech at US$100,000 and to compel them to retract, in terms approved by the company, statements whose factual core their chairman had conceded, publicly. 
In a media market already strained by debt, currency volatility and political pressure, the message to newsrooms is hard to miss: internal complaint about unpaid wages may be treated as an attack on the proprietor’s reputation.
That is the character of the lawsuit. 
It is lawfare against a newsroom: the use of civil process not to correct a falsehood, but to raise the cost of speaking about wages, conditions and the conduct of the man who chairs the company. 
The timing makes the purpose plain. 
The statements complained of were made on the day Ncube himself put the salary failure on the public record. 
The suit arrived seven months later, after labour proceedings had already tested the arrears, and it names the targeted journalists and staff who were in the room.
And the claim may also be legally incompetent in its present form. 
Defamation protects the reputation of the person or entity actually defamed. 
The de jure plaintiff is ZimInd Publishers. 
The de facto complainant is Ncube. 
On the company’s own pleading, the sting of the alleged statements is aimed at him: that the chairman was cruel and insensitive, that arrears accumulated under his watch and thus through his negligence, that the withholding of salaries reflected malice and corruption at the top.
A company may sue for words that injure its own trading reputation. 
It cannot, by substituting its name for his, convert a personal grievance into a corporate one. Where the target of the words is the individual, the individual is the proper plaintiff. 
To the extent the lawsuit is brought to vindicate Ncube's personal standing rather than any distinct corporate injury, it is brought by the wrong party — a formal defect that goes to competence, not merely to emphasis.
All told, Ncube was right, in March, that salaries preserve dignity. 
Consistency preserves it too. 
An apology offered as leadership loses its meaning when the underlying fact is later disowned under oath, and when the instrument chosen to police the contradiction is a damages claim against the people who heard it. Organisations, Ncube wrote at the time, reveal their character under strain. 
The question this lawsuit poses is simple, and it is still unanswered. Given the public admission of 5 March 2026 — the same day the alleged defamation is said to have occurred — what, exactly, was Trevor Ncube apologising for?

text:
THE THIRTY MILE DOCTRINE

CASE SIX: THE “KEGNA” HYPOTHESIS — WHEN “OURS” BECOMES A DOCTRINE OF ENTITLEMENT

The previous five cases examined Ethiopia’s maritime argument through history, sovereignty, treaties, state conduct, population, geography, and international law. This case asks a different question. It does not concern whether Ethiopia requires access to the sea, because that need is already established. It concerns the intellectual architecture through which a legitimate national requirement may be transformed into a claim of historical entitlement. To examine that possibility, one must enter a politically sensitive area with considerable discipline, because an argument about political ideology must never become an accusation against an ethnic population.

The Afaan Oromo word “Kegna,” commonly rendered in this political context as “ours,” carries significance far beyond its ordinary linguistic meaning when incorporated into nationalist political discourse. Within strands of Oromo political thought, questions of historical dispossession, land, political domination, demographic presence, Finfinne, administrative boundaries, and restoration have occupied a central place for decades. Those ideas emerged from a particular historical experience and cannot responsibly be attributed to Oromo people collectively. Oromo political thought is diverse, often internally contested, and represented by movements that disagree profoundly about Ethiopia, federalism, nationalism, democracy, armed struggle, and the meaning of Oromo self determination. The hypothesis presented here therefore concerns a possible pattern within political ideology and statecraft, not an ethnic characteristic and certainly not an indictment of the Oromo people.

The question is whether a particular reasoning structure has migrated from domestic politics into the foreign policy of the Ethiopian state under Abiy Ahmed. That structure can be examined without accepting or rejecting every historical grievance from which it developed. It begins with historical possession, moves through an allegation of dispossession, treats the resulting legal arrangement as morally defective, and concludes that present possession cannot completely extinguish the rights supposedly created by the past. Population and historical memory then reinforce the claim, while existing legal boundaries become increasingly subordinate to an asserted historical entitlement. In its simplest political expression, something regarded as having once been “ours” remains subject to recovery because the historical process through which it ceased to be “ours” is itself considered illegitimate.

Applied inside Ethiopia, that reasoning has appeared most controversially in disputes involving land, identity, administrative boundaries, Addis Ababa or Finfinne, historical incorporation, demographic claims, and competing narratives of ownership and dispossession. Those disputes are enormously complex and cannot be adjudicated here. What matters for the present inquiry is whether a similar structure can be detected in the emerging Red Sea doctrine: Ethiopia historically possessed the coastline; Ethiopia lost it through a political process now portrayed as defective; the resulting geography is described as unnatural or unsustainable; Ethiopia’s enormous population is invoked against the much smaller populations of coastal neighbors; proximity is offered as further evidence of the absurdity of the present arrangement; and the maritime question gradually moves from the language of negotiated access toward the language of historical right.

If that pattern exists, the significance is substantial because the argument no longer concerns ports alone. It concerns the possibility that a domestic political conception of historical entitlement has been elevated into the foreign policy of a sovereign state. The international system cannot determine territorial sovereignty according to a doctrine of “ours” because nearly every border on earth intersects with somebody’s older map, displaced population, vanished kingdom, imperial frontier, colonial settlement, military defeat, federation, annexation, partition, or historical grievance. Once historical possession becomes a continuing source of territorial entitlement independent of contemporary law, there is no principled point at which history must stop.

The Horn of Africa demonstrates the danger particularly clearly. Ethiopia can reach backward to periods when political formations centered in the northern highlands extended toward or across the Red Sea. Eritrea can reach to Italian colonial boundaries, the subsequent British administration, the federal settlement, the dissolution of that federation, and a thirty year independence struggle. Somalia possesses its own historical and territorial narratives. Sudan has its own. Every community inhabiting the region can identify a period in which political authority, population, commerce, military power, or cultural influence crossed boundaries that exist today. Selecting the historical moment most favorable to one claimant cannot become a legal method for determining twenty first century sovereignty.

The hypothesis becomes more consequential when population enters the argument. Historical entitlement says the territory was once connected to us. Demographic entitlement says our present need is greater. Geographic entitlement says the territory lies extraordinarily close to us. Economic entitlement says our development is constrained without it. Strategic entitlement says our national security requires it. Individually, each proposition may explain why Ethiopia considers the Red Sea essential. Combined, however, they can create the appearance of a cumulative right that international law does not recognize. Five powerful political arguments do not automatically become one legal title.

This distinction is particularly important in evaluating Abiy Ahmed. It would be intellectually careless to conclude that every statement he makes about the Red Sea originates from Oromo nationalism, just as it would be careless to attribute his maritime policy to Oromo society generally. Ethiopia possessed Red Sea ambitions, anxieties, and historical memories long before Abiy Ahmed entered office. Ethiopian governments of different ideological traditions have understood the strategic consequences of landlocked geography. A country of Ethiopia’s size would probably seek diversified maritime access regardless of the ethnicity or political background of its prime minister. The Kegna hypothesis therefore cannot establish causation merely by observing similarities in rhetoric.

It can, however, establish a legitimate question for investigation. Does Abiy Ahmed consistently reason from historical possession toward present entitlement? Does his government treat boundaries and ownership differently when it believes earlier political processes produced an unjust result? Does demographic weight appear repeatedly as a justification for revisiting settled arrangements? Does the language surrounding the Red Sea resemble political arguments previously used around land, historical ownership, administrative geography, and the recovery of what is regarded as having been lost? If documentary evidence establishes that recurring pattern across speeches, policies, party doctrine, official statements, and territorial disputes, then the hypothesis becomes stronger. If the evidence does not establish it, the hypothesis must be rejected rather than preserved merely because it is politically attractive.

That evidentiary standard matters because this series is not strengthened by turning suspicion into fact. The strongest indictment of a political doctrine is not an accusation delivered before the evidence arrives. It is a pattern demonstrated so carefully that the conclusion becomes difficult to escape. “Kegna” should therefore be understood here as the name of a hypothesis under examination: whether the political logic of historical ownership, dispossession, demographic necessity, and recovery has migrated into Ethiopia’s contemporary Red Sea strategy and supplied an ideological vocabulary through which negotiated access can gradually be reconceived as entitlement.

International law provides the limiting principle that such a doctrine lacks. A people may remember what was once theirs. A state may mourn territory it once possessed. A nation may conclude that its predecessors made catastrophic decisions. Governments may seek through peaceful negotiation to alter arrangements they consider economically damaging. None of those rights includes the authority to make another sovereign state’s territory legally provisional merely by declaring that history, demography, geography, or necessity has restored an older entitlement. The moment “ours” crosses an international frontier, it encounters another word of considerably greater legal consequence: sovereignty.

The thirty mile doctrine has now moved through almost every layer of the Ethiopian argument. History has been heard. Meles Zenawi has been placed under examination. Eritrean independence and Ethiopia’s subsequent recognition have entered the record. The Algiers Agreement and Abiy Ahmed’s own 2018 conduct have been considered. Population, commercial necessity, access, naval ambition, and historical entitlement have been separated from one another. One major question remains before the final judgment can be approached: whether Ethiopia’s maritime campaign is being pursued by Ethiopia alone.

That question requires following aircraft, weapons, money, military relationships, ports, Gulf interests, Somaliland, and the rapidly changing security architecture surrounding the Red Sea. It requires separating documented evidence from allegation with particular care because the accusation is considerably larger than diplomatic sympathy. It asks whether an external power has helped create the material conditions under which Ethiopia can pursue ambitions that would otherwise remain political rhetoric.

THE CASE CONTINUES

text:
The simple doctrine of Jesus of Nazareth is the concentration of what he himself says the kingdom is, how a person enters it, and what he refuses to do with the sword, the judgment seat, and the titles of religious rule. What follows stays inside his words in the Gospels, as they stand in the SBL Greek New Testament, turned into close English. Where the narrative must be distinguished from a sentence of his, it is marked as narrative.

He opens with a summons, not a statute. Repent, he says, for the kingdom of the heavens has drawn near (Matt 4:17). Asked when that kingdom comes, he answers that it does not come with observation, and that no one will say, Look, here, or, There, because the kingdom of God is within you (Luke 17:20–21). To Pilate he says that his kingdom is not of this world; if it were, his servants would have been fighting so that he might not be handed over to the Jews; but now his kingdom is not from here (John 18:36). The people who have that kingdom are named before any office is named. They are the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger and thirst for justice, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for justice (Matt 5:3–10). The peacemaker is called a son of God. The persecuted are blessed. Persecution is not the instrument he blesses.

He moves the received commands inward. Anger is already liable to judgment (Matt 5:22). The gift waits on the altar until the worshipper is reconciled to his brother (Matt 5:23–24). Do not resist the evil one, he says; turn the other cheek (Matt 5:39). Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt 5:44). The law and the prophets, he says, reduce to this: whatever you wish that people would do to you, do so to them (Matt 7:12). The first word about judgment is aimed at the hearer. Do not judge, so that you may not be judged (Matt 7:1). Piety done to be seen by people is already disqualified (Matt 6:1; 23:5). Worship, he tells the Samaritan woman, is soon neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and truth (John 4:21–24). His own yoke is kind, his burden light, and he is meek and humble in heart (Matt 11:29–30). Against that he sets the scribes and Pharisees, who bind heavy burdens and lay them on people's shoulders and will not move them with a finger (Matt 23:4), and who shut the kingdom of the heavens in front of people (Matt 23:13). To his own he forbids the titles of that system. Do not be called Rabbi, call no one father on the earth, do not be called instructors, for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers (Matt 23:8–10).

When a house or a city will not receive the words, the instruction is to shake off the dust of the feet (Matt 10:14). When a Samaritan village will not receive him, James and John ask whether they should call fire down from heaven. He turns and rebukes them, and they go to another village (Luke 9:54–56). Of an outsider casting out demons in his name he says not to forbid him, for whoever is not against us is for us (Mark 9:39–40). Asked to divide a family inheritance, he answers, Man, who appointed me a judge or divider over you? (Luke 12:14). Shown the tribute coin, he says to give back the things of Caesar to Caesar, and the things of God to God (Matt 22:21). To the twelve, after a request for the seats at his right and left, he says that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them, and that it shall not be so among them (Matt 20:25–26). In Luke's form those rulers are called benefactors, and again he says, But you are not so (Luke 22:25–26). Greatness among his own is service, and the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life a ransom for many (Matt 20:28).

In the field he has the householder stop the servants who want the tares pulled now. No, lest in gathering the tares you uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest (Matt 13:29–30). The harvest is the end of the age, the reapers are angels, and the judgment is the Son of Man's (Matt 13:39–41). At the arrest he says to put the sword back into its place, for all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matt 26:52), and to put the sword into the sheath (John 18:11). In Luke he says, Let it be, thus far, and heals the ear (Luke 22:51). Of his coming he says that the Son was not sent to condemn the world (John 3:17), and that he did not come to judge the world but to save the world (John 12:47). Freedom, in his words, is this: you will know the truth, and the truth will make you free; if the Son frees you, you will be free indeed (John 8:32, 36). The last command is to make disciples, baptizing them and teaching them to keep all that he commanded (Matt 28:19–20). The authority he names is given to him, not handed to Caesar (Matt 28:18). One narrative act stands beside the speeches. When he knows they are about to seize him to make him king, he withdraws to the mountain, alone (John 6:15).

A fair statement of the doctrine does not drop the sentences that cut the other way. He did not come to abolish the law or the prophets but to fulfill them, and whoever relaxes a least commandment and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom (Matt 5:17–19). That intensifies the demand on the hearer. It does not appoint an officer to compel the neighbor's confession. In the same speech the demand moves inward, and retaliation is forbidden. He says the scribes sit on Moses' seat, and that his hearers should do and keep whatever they tell them (Matt 23:2–3). The next clause withdraws imitation of their works, and the paragraphs that follow forbid their burdens, their display, and their titles. Recognizing a seat is not a license to build a new one that binds conscience by law. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword, is followed at once by household division and by the taking of one's cross (Matt 10:34–38). That sword divides loyalties. The sword in the garden is to be put back. Compel them to come in is the householder's word to a servant, inside a parable, after the invited have refused a feast (Luke 14:23). The servant is sent for the poor, the maimed, the blind, and the lame, and then to the roads and hedges, so that the house may be filled (Luke 14:21–23). No court, oath, or penalty for unbelief is named. The same speaker, faced with a real village that will not receive him, rebukes the request for fire and goes elsewhere (Luke 9:54–56). Final separation he reserves to the end of the age and to himself. He does not say that the ruler must produce it now.

The thing opposed is definite: a government that establishes religion and by that establishment compels conscience, whether by penalty, by exclusion from common right, by a required oath, by required worship, or by required speech about God. His words already forbid that arrangement, on grounds he states.

He divides the two claims and will not let one swallow the other. The coin bears Caesar's image, and Caesar's things go back to Caesar. He does not say that the inscription reaches the things of God. A law that makes the things of God payable at Caesar's office erases the distinction he drew in the same sentence (Matt 22:21). He defines his kingdom by the absence of fighting servants. The proof offered to Pilate that the kingdom is not of this world is that his servants were not fighting to keep him from being handed over. Establishment that compels conscience is that fight by other means. Servants who fight show, by his own test, that the kingdom is of this world. He has said that it is not (John 18:36).

He names civil rule and bans it among his own. The rulers of the nations lord it over them, their great ones exercise authority over them, and they are called benefactors. It shall not be so among you (Matt 20:25–26; Luke 22:25–26). Conscience is the last place that pattern can be allowed and still leave his sentence standing. To compel the neighbor's worship, speech, or inner assent is to lord it over him in the matter Jesus marked as God's. The greatness he permits is service. A ransom is not a tax on belief (Matt 20:28). He forbids the early harvest. The servants see the tares and ask to gather them. He says no, because the wheat would be uprooted with them, and both are to grow together until the harvest (Matt 13:29–30). Compelling conscience is that forbidden gathering. It treats present agreement as the harvest and the magistrate as the reaper. He says the reapers are angels and the time is the end of the age (Matt 13:39–41).

His method with refusal is exit, not penalty. Dust is shaken off (Matt 10:14). The disciples who would call fire are rebuked, and the road leads to another village (Luke 9:54–56). Do not forbid him (Mark 9:39). Do not resist the evil one (Matt 5:39). Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt 5:44). A government that punishes the conscience it cannot persuade has replaced each of those sentences with its opposite. The good he calls blessed cannot be produced by compulsion, because he locates it in the heart. The pure in heart see God (Matt 5:8). True worship is in spirit and truth, unbound from this mountain and from Jerusalem (John 4:23–24). Freedom is knowing the truth, and the Son freeing, not a court certifying (John 8:32, 36). A compelled word may fill a roll. It cannot be the purity, the spirit and truth, or the freedom he describes. He also says that his yoke is kind and his burden light (Matt 11:30), and he condemns those who bind heavy burdens for others (Matt 23:4). Establishment that compels conscience is that kind of binding, tied on by law.

He refuses the offices by which compulsion would be done. Who appointed me a judge or divider over you? (Luke 12:14). He forbids his disciples the titles of religious rank, because one is their teacher and they are all brothers (Matt 23:8–10). He withdraws when a crowd would make him king (John 6:15). He puts the sword back (Matt 26:52). The work he gives at the end is discipling, baptizing, and teaching what he commanded: speech and baptism, not the keys of a prison (Matt 28:19–20). The one compulsion he pictures fills a house with the people the city had left out (Luke 14:23). The pressure runs toward the poor, the maimed, the blind, and the lame, after the invited have excused themselves (Luke 14:21–23). It is a servant's urgency at a feast, not a ruler's penalty against a conscience. Set beside the command not to resist the evil one (Matt 5:39), beside the rebuke of fire from heaven (Luke 9:54–56), and beside the statement that his servants would have been fighting (John 18:36), it will not carry a charter for the magistrate. The house is filled by bringing in those who were never asked. It is not filled by forcing the lips of those who will not come.

Left in his words, the doctrine is a kingdom not of this world, entered by repentance and held in the heart, taught by a meek teacher whose burden is light, extended by disciples who shake dust and do not call fire, withheld from the sword and from the judgment seat, and kept distinct from Caesar's coin. A government that establishes religion so as to compel conscience takes the coin's side of his sentence and spends it on the things of God (Matt 22:21). It makes servants fight after he said that their not fighting was the proof (John 18:36). It lords it over the persons he said were not to be lorded over (Matt 20:25–26). It pulls the tares he said to leave (Matt 13:29–30). It binds the heavy burden he condemned (Matt 23:4). His words do not ask the ruler to do any of that. They say it shall not be so.

text:
La gauche a conquis la culture occidentale avec deux armes : une idée et un réseau.

Nous avons l'idée. Il nous manque le réseau.

Depuis des mois, je parle avec des patriotes du monde entier. Américains, Brésiliens, Argentins, Polonais, Italiens. Des entrepreneurs, des intellectuels, des élus, des anonymes. Tous ont compris la même chose : le progressisme est une arnaque, et nous vivons depuis des décennies dans un empire du mensonge.

Sous mon post sur Gramsci, un Polonais m'a écrit : « En Pologne, on le savait depuis toujours. Mais personne ne voulait écouter. »

Cette phrase, je l'entends dans toutes les langues.

Le diagnostic est le même d'un pays à l'autre. Les mêmes mots, les mêmes slogans, les mêmes méthodes. Ce qu'on vit à Paris, ils le vivent à São Paulo, à Varsovie, à Rome. Je l'ai vu de mes propres yeux à San Francisco.

Tout le monde est d'accord.

Et ce ne sont plus seulement des militants. Des milliardaires l'ont compris aussi. Vincent Bolloré et Pierre-Édouard Stérin en France. Elon Musk aux États-Unis.

Mais j'ai constaté autre chose. Et c'est beaucoup plus grave.

Chacun se bat seul.

Chaque pays mène sa guerre dans son coin, avec sa langue, ses médias, ses partis, ses héros. Les Polonais ne savent pas ce que font les Argentins. Les Italiens ne lisent pas les Brésiliens. Les Français réinventent chaque matin ce que les Américains ont testé il y a trois ans.

On gagne des batailles. On ne mène pas une guerre.

Et c'est exactement là que la gauche nous a toujours battus.

Relisez l'histoire. La gauche a toujours été internationale. Première Internationale en 1864. Deuxième en 1889. En 1919, Lénine fonde à Moscou la Troisième, le Komintern : un réseau mondial de partis, de journaux, d'écoles de cadres et de mots d'ordre.

Vous savez qui a passé plus d'un an à Moscou, au Komintern, au début des années 1920 ?

Antonio Gramsci.

L'homme qui a théorisé la conquête de la culture était un homme de l'Internationale. La conquête se faisait nation par nation. Le cerveau, lui, était mondial.

Et ça n'a jamais cessé. Je vous l'ai déjà raconté : la French Theory de Foucault, Derrida et Deleuze est partie de Paris dans les années 70, a conquis les campus américains, puis nous est revenue quarante ans plus tard sous le nom de wokisme. Un aller-retour transatlantique. Un seul écosystème.

Alors voilà ce que nous allons devoir faire.

Reconstruire un réseau mondial. Pas un parti. Pas une organisation centrale avec un chef. Un réseau de femmes et d'hommes libres, chacun enraciné dans sa nation, tous reliés entre eux. Pas de centre, donc pas de point de défaillance unique.

On me dira que des patriotes qui s'organisent à l'échelle du monde, c'est une contradiction.

Non. C'est la seule réponse possible à un adversaire qui s'est toujours organisé à l'échelle du monde. Défendre sa nation n'a jamais interdit d'avoir des alliés. Ça l'a toujours exigé.

Ce réseau aura une mission : mener la contre-révolution culturelle.

La gauche a fait la longue marche à travers les institutions. Nous allons faire la marche retour.

Les écoles. Les universités. Les rédactions. L'édition. Le cinéma. La musique. Le sport, dernier temple du mérite qu'on a transformé en tribune. La justice, et les écoles qui forment ceux qui la rendent. Les administrations. Les fondations. Absolument toutes.

Pas par la force. Par la compétence, le talent et le travail. En formant ceux qui demain écriront, enseigneront, jugeront, filmeront. Exactement comme ils l'ont fait : institution par institution, génération par génération.

Sauf que nous n'avons pas cent ans devant nous. Et nous n'en aurons pas besoin.

Parce que l'IA est en train de tout accélérer.

Je passe mes journées à construire de l'IA. Laissez-moi vous dire ce que je vois.

Jusqu'ici, l'hégémonie culturelle tenait grâce à un verrou : le coût de production. Un film coûtait des millions. Il fallait un studio, un distributeur, une commission, une subvention. Celui qui tenait le guichet tenait la culture.

Ce verrou est en train de sauter. Ce qui demandait des centaines de personnes et des millions d'euros demandera bientôt une poignée de gens talentueux et déterminés.

Le deuxième verrou, c'était la langue. C'est elle qui enfermait les patriotes dans leurs frontières. Aujourd'hui, un Polonais lit ce post dans sa langue en un clic. Demain, un film tourné en France sortira le même jour en vingt langues, avec les voix d'origine.

Et il y a un nouveau champ de bataille, le plus important de tous. Gramsci l'avait compris : l'hégémonie se loge dans le sens commun, dans ce que les gens trouvent évident. Demain, le sens commun, ce sera ce que répondent les machines. La longue marche passera aussi par les modèles.

Mais les outils ne suffisent pas. Un outil sans organisation, c'est du bruit.

Les réseaux nationaux doivent se parler. Se synchroniser. Se soutenir.

Pas de ligne imposée d'en haut. Chaque nation garde sa souveraineté. Le réseau fait circuler ce qui fonctionne.

Quand une méthode marche à Buenos Aires, elle doit être testée à Paris la semaine suivante. Quand un film sort à Varsovie, il doit être vu à São Paulo le mois d'après. Quand l'un des nôtres est censuré, débancarisé ou traîné dans la boue, ce n'est pas à un pays de répondre. C'est à tous.

Partager les méthodes. Les talents. Les financements. Les canaux de diffusion. Les victoires.

La gauche a mis un siècle à construire son réseau. Avec l'IA, nous pouvons construire le nôtre en dix ans.

L'empire du mensonge est fissuré. Mais il ne tombera pas tout seul.

Sa chute totale passera par une contre-révolution. Et une contre-révolution, ce n'est pas une révolution à l'envers. Ce n'est pas remplacer un mensonge par un autre. C'est laisser le réel reprendre ses droits.

Il faut rendre justice à l'adversaire. La gauche a été brillante. Patiente. Méthodique. Elle a investi des trésors d'intelligence dans cette conquête : des penseurs, des revues, des maisons d'édition, des festivals, des prix, des carrières entières consacrées à une seule idée.

Pendant ce temps, la droite gérait. Elle construisait des usines pendant que la gauche construisait des récits.

Et ce sont les récits qui ont gagné.

Ce niveau d'intelligence, de patience et d'ambition, c'est à nous de le déployer maintenant. Nous, le camp de la raison, du mérite et du bon sens.

Et nous avons ce qu'ils n'ont jamais eu.

Ils avaient les institutions sans les peuples. Nous avons les peuples sans les institutions.

Plus pour longtemps.

La gauche a longtemps prétendu avoir le sens de l'histoire. Il a changé de camp.

Ce qui nous manque, ce sont les histoires.

Lénine aurait dit : « De tous les arts, le cinéma est pour nous le plus important. » La gauche l'a pris au mot. La droite, elle, pense encore que le cinéma, c'est du divertissement.

Girard l'a montré : on désire ce que désirent ceux qu'on admire. Et ceux qu'on admire, c'est la fiction qui les fabrique. Pendant cinquante ans, les héros de nos enfants ont été écrits par l'autre camp.

Il nous faut les nôtres. Des films. Des séries. Des dessins animés. Des documentaires. Des jeux vidéo.

Pour raconter comment la gauche a tout capturé, institution par institution. Comment le wokisme est devenu la phase terminale d'une longue entreprise de démolition de l'Occident. Comment on a appris à toute une génération à avoir honte de ce qu'elle est.

Et surtout, pour raconter ce que nous aimons. On ne gagne pas une guerre culturelle en expliquant ce qu'on combat. On la gagne en faisant aimer ce qu'on défend.

La beauté. L'ambition. La science. Le mérite. La civilisation qui nous a fait naître.

Ce combat ne se gagnera pas avec des commentateurs. Il se gagnera avec des bâtisseurs. Des scénaristes, des réalisateurs, des animateurs, des ingénieurs, des producteurs. Des gens qui fabriquent au lieu de s'indigner.

En prison, Gramsci a écrit que la crise, c'est quand « l'ancien meurt et que le nouveau ne peut pas naître ».

Près d'un siècle plus tard, l'ancien monde qui meurt, c'est le sien.

Le nouveau peut naître. Mais il ne naîtra pas tout seul. Il naîtra si nous le construisons. Ensemble. Partout. En même temps.

Patriotes de tous les pays, unissez-vous.

text:
Dans 50 ans, les livres d'histoire diront qu'Elon Musk a gagné une guerre que personne ne savait qu'on était en train de perdre.

Une guerre commencée il y a 100 ans, dans une cellule de prison italienne.

En 1926, Mussolini fait arrêter un intellectuel sarde de 35 ans. Au procès, le procureur aurait dit : « Nous devons empêcher ce cerveau de fonctionner pendant vingt ans. »

Il s'appelait Antonio Gramsci.

Son cerveau n'a jamais cessé de fonctionner. En prison, il a rempli des milliers de pages qui sont devenues l'un des textes politiques les plus influents du XXe siècle. Je pense qu'on est en train de vivre le moment où sa théorie s'effondre.

Laissez-moi vous expliquer.

Gramsci se posait une question simple. Pourquoi la révolution communiste a-t-elle réussi en Russie mais échoué partout en Occident ?

Sa réponse : en Occident, le pouvoir ne tient pas seulement par l'État, la police et l'armée. Il tient par la culture. Par ce que les gens trouvent normal, évident, « de bon sens ». Il appelle ça l'hégémonie culturelle.

Donc, pour prendre le pouvoir, il ne faut pas d'abord prendre le palais. Il faut d'abord prendre les esprits. Les écoles. Les universités. Les journaux. Le théâtre. L'édition. Les tribunaux. C'est la « guerre de position » : une conquête lente, institution par institution. Quand la culture a basculé, la politique suit toute seule.

Quarante ans plus tard, l'activiste allemand Rudi Dutschke en fera un slogan : la longue marche à travers les institutions.

Pendant des décennies, on a vécu avec une énigme que personne n'arrivait vraiment à expliquer.

Pourquoi presque tous les artistes sont-ils de gauche ? Les acteurs, les chanteurs, les profs, les journalistes, une bonne partie de la magistrature. Pourquoi un pays pouvait voter à droite élection après élection et voir quand même sa culture parler d'une seule voix ?

On nous répondait : « c'est parce que les gens éduqués sont de gauche. »

Je crois que la réponse est plus simple. Gramsci avait écrit la recette, et elle a été appliquée. Quand tu contrôles qui obtient la subvention, le poste, la bonne critique, le prix, l'invitation sur le plateau, tu contrôles ce qui devient « la culture ».

La même énigme existait à l'échelle du monde.

Pourquoi tant de pays en développement, notamment en Amérique latine, revotaient-ils encore et encore pour des gouvernements socialistes ou de gauche radicale ? Venezuela, Bolivie, Nicaragua, l'Argentine des Kirchner, la Colombie de Petro. L'économie s'effondrait, les cartels prospéraient, le chaos s'installait. Et pourtant le même vote revenait.

Ma conviction : la pauvreté n'était pas un accident du système. C'était un électorat. Et autour, il y avait tout un écosystème d'ONG, de médias « indépendants » et de programmes de « société civile », financé en grande partie par l'argent occidental.

Puis, début 2025, il s'est passé quelque chose que personne n'avait jamais osé faire.

Elon et DOGE ont ouvert les livres de USAID. Une agence quasi intouchable depuis 1961, des dizaines de milliards de dollars par an. La grande majorité des programmes ont été coupés, et l'agence a été absorbée par le Département d'État.

Le robinet a été fermé.

Et regardez ce qui s'est passé depuis.

Bolivie : le MAS perd le pouvoir après presque vingt ans. Équateur : Noboa réélu. Honduras : la droite reprend le pays. Chili : Kast élu. Argentine : Milei remporte largement les élections de mi-mandat.

Et il y a deux jours, le Brésil.

Jair Bolsonaro est inéligible, condamné à 27 ans de prison. La gauche pensait avoir refermé le chapitre. Lula, 80 ans, briguait un quatrième mandat face à un pays qu'on disait acquis.

Dimanche, son fils Flávio est arrivé en tête du premier tour. Plus de 47 % contre près de 45 % pour Lula. Lula lui-même a reconnu un résultat « inattendu ».

Le plus grand pays d'Amérique latine est à un second tour de basculer.

Le plus grand virage à droite du continent depuis des décennies.

Coïncidence ? Je ne crois pas. Quand le financement disparaît, le récit perd ses haut-parleurs.

Il reste un dernier vrai bastion. L'Europe.

Bruxelles finance ses propres réseaux d'ONG, avec une opacité que même la Cour des comptes européenne a pointée. Les grandes fondations comme l'Open Society de Soros. Les entités supranationales qui produisent de la norme sans jamais passer devant un électeur.

C'est la dernière forteresse de l'hégémonie culturelle. Et elle commence à se fissurer.

Je suis convaincu que tout ça va s'effondrer, et plus vite qu'on ne le pense.

Gramsci avait raison sur un point essentiel : la culture précède la politique. Mais il avait oublié que ça marche dans les deux sens. Quand une culture artificielle perd ses perfusions, ce qu'il y a de vrai en dessous remonte à la surface.

Ce qui vient après, je crois que c'est une renaissance. Une culture qui recommence à aimer la beauté, l'ambition, la science, la civilisation qui l'a fait naître.

Et dans les livres d'histoire, on se souviendra que tout a commencé quand un homme a décidé de regarder les comptes.

Il fallait quelqu'un d'assez riche pour ne dépendre de personne, d'assez fou pour s'y attaquer et d'assez libre pour encaisser la haine qui allait suivre.

Merci Elon.

📷NO HUDDLE FEATURE📷

Carter MacDonald 
@cartermacd2027
 Fremd High School 
@Fremd_Football 
WR 6'3 190 Lbs. 
C/O 2027 

The combination of frame and movement ability gives this young man several ways to challenge coverage. He has the size to present a substantial target, yet carries that frame with the quickness and ease of a smaller receiver. What catches my attention is how he applies that movement within his routes. He varies his releases, changes pace to sell his intentions and uses his body language to influence a defender before committing to his path. His speed gives him the ability to get on top of coverage, while his footwork and body control allow him to work underneath and adjust to the football. He shows receiving value from both the X position and the slot, with the route range to attack different areas of the field. That blend of size, speed and technical detail is where his mismatch potential begins.

The opening go route provides a good look at his approach against press coverage from the X position. He uses a hesitation release to interrupt the corner’s timing, avoiding the early jam before immediately getting on top of him. I like that the vertical advantage starts with his work at the line. Keeping the corner from establishing contact allows him to get into the stem cleanly and put his acceleration to work. He finishes with soft hands, showing receiving touch to accompany the release and speed. He consistently catches the football away from his frame, showing reliable hands and the ability to secure it without relying on his body to complete the catch. Immediately after that, his work over the middle in the red zone highlights a different part of his route ability. With less space available, he uses body language to sell the route and influence the defender’s positioning. That manipulation helps him create an opening within a condensed area. These two plays show how he can use release timing to access space downfield and route deception to get open closer to the goal line.

At :23, the stop-and-go from the slot shows how effectively he can change the pace of a route. His initial explosiveness off the line establishes the vertical threat before he briefly settles and looks back at the quarterback. That combination of deceleration and head movement gives the underneath route a convincing presentation. He then accelerates vertically again, using the change in tempo to set up the second phase of the route. The detail I appreciate is how his body language supports what his feet are selling. His release variety extends beyond the hesitation, with a foot-fire release also appearing on the tape. That gives him another way to challenge a defender’s timing at the line. He also shows an understanding of when to settle against zone coverage, finding an available spot rather than continuing through open space. His willingness to work underneath and across the middle adds substance to that coverage awareness. His speed also translates after the catch on drag routes. Once he secures the football, he accelerates into space and separates from pursuit, giving his work across the middle value beyond the completion. At :49, the fourth-and-short catch highlights his concentration and adjustment ability. He goes down to secure the low throw and completes the catch for a critical first down. Finishing a delivery outside an easy catch position when the offense needs a conversion is a meaningful example of his situational value.

His ability to work a full route tree receives further support at 1:17 on the out route from the slot. I love the deceleration into the break and acceleration coming out. He controls his speed to change direction, then quickly builds it back as he works outside. That footwork helps him create separation at the top of the stem and carry it through the break. At 1:28, the hard jab release gives us another look at how he influences press coverage. He gets the corner to commit to the initial action before accelerating in the opposite direction and getting upfield. Compared with the opening hesitation, this release asks the defender to respond to a more decisive directional sell. Having both approaches available adds depth to his work at the line. He follows the release with strong body control while adjusting to the football and late hands to finish the catch. Delaying the presentation of his hands limits the early cue a corner can use to locate the arriving ball. The rep brings together release deception, acceleration and catch-point detail, showing the technical work involved from the start of the route through the finish.

FINAL THOUGHTS

I’m impressed with how comfortably he combines his size with the movement demands of the position. He has the frame to offer a substantial target and the speed to threaten vertically, but his ability to control that speed gives his route running much of its value. He can slow down to sell an opportunity or change direction, then accelerate again to create separation. His release variety helps him access his routes against press, while his awareness against zone allows him to find space and make himself available. Those qualities give him value outside and from the slot, with the ability to work underneath, across the middle and downfield.

His consistent hands provide a dependable finish to that route work. He catches away from his frame and shows the body control and concentration to adjust when the delivery requires it. Once the football is secured, his acceleration can create additional separation from pursuit, adding yardage to his underneath opportunities. What stands out to me is the number of ways he can be useful within the passing game. He brings size without sacrificing movement, speed with the control to set up defenders, and receiving skill that holds value in critical situations. His mismatch potential comes from that combination, giving the offense a receiver who can create and finish opportunities at different depths and from multiple alignments.

text:
Artificial intelligence is coming for Israel’s voters

Israel’s 2026 election is the clearest warning yet that AI isn’t just “changing politics” — it’s weaponizing it. What’s happening right now in Israel should terrify every democracy on Earth.

It starts with a deepfake: a perfectly realistic video of Gadi Eisenkot meeting Mahmoud Abbas. A meeting that never happened. A hard‑right party pushed it to paint Eisenkot as a secret appeaser. It became the first AI campaign ad ever forced offline under Israel’s new disclosure law. But here’s the part nobody wants to hear:

The deepfake is NOT the real threat.

The real danger is everything happening under the surface — invisible, automated, and already influencing millions.

This article lays out the toolkit:

🔥 Bot swarms posing as real voters, hijacking conversations and poll results that journalists treat as public sentiment. 
🔥 AI avatars with phone numbers and credit cards infiltrating WhatsApp groups. 
🔥 Chatbots talking to voters, extracting psychological profiles, feeding persuasion engines. 
🔥 Hyper‑targeted messaging built from browsing history, purchases, geolocation, music habits. 
🔥 AI robocalls mimicking party leaders so convincingly you only realize it’s fake after a few sentences. 
🔥 Content flooding designed to manipulate chatbot outputs — activists literally uploading old material to Reddit because “ChatGPT uses it.”

This isn’t campaigning. It’s behavioral engineering.
And the imbalance is brutal.

Netanyahu’s bloc has spent years building unified voter databases and AI‑driven influence systems originally designed for foreign psychological operations. 

Now those tools are being used domestically. The opposition is fragmented — but backed by a furious, highly technical protest movement ready to escalate.

Meanwhile, regulators are outmatched.

The Shin Bet only looks for foreign interference. The National Cyber Directorate doesn’t want the responsibility. The police and the election committee have almost no tools — mostly begging tech companies to take things down.
On election day, enforcement collapses entirely.

Parties are preparing to use illicitly collected data to target supporters with reminders — and opponents with distractions, misinformation, or time‑wasting offers designed to suppress turnout. The Supreme Court even banned observers from reporting who has voted, removing a key transparency mechanism.
And global tech companies are watching Israel like a laboratory. Whatever works there will be exported.

This election is not just a national event. It’s a stress test for democracy under AI pressure.

Israel is showing the world what happens when political actors gain access to tools that can reshape perception, distort reality, and manipulate behavior at scale.

The warning lights aren’t blinking. They’re blazing.

#attention...
#alert...
An Instagram account posted offers to sell tickets to a concert by the artist Ghostly Kisses in Baghdad, claiming they were “gift tickets from TicketZone,” in an attempt to mislead users into believing they were issued by the official platform.

#The_Truth:
The tickets being sold are fake and fraudulent. An Instagram account is promoting the sale of tickets for Ghostly Kisses’ concert in Baghdad, claiming they are “gift tickets from TicketZone,” whereas “TicketZone” does not issue tickets in this format and does not offer a service by that name.

We investigated the matter and found that the scam operates as follows:

The scammer asks the victim to transfer phone credit in exchange for the ticket, then asks for her phone number and logs into the genuine “TicketZone” website using that number.

The victim then receives a genuine one-time password (OTP) via WhatsApp from Digital Zone’s verified account, leading them to believe the ticket was issued by “TicketZone.”

The scammer then sends an image of a fake ticket—created using artificial intelligence—via a link on the “https://t.co/eV2pfvOjsC” website, accompanied by a message titled "Ticket Gift Notification," claiming that "TicketZone" has gifted the victim a ticket worth 60,000 dinars.

According to available information, the ticket is fake, as “TicketZone” does not issue tickets with this design, nor does it have any service or campaign called “Gift Ticket from TicketZone.”

Furthermore, the QR code does not appear on “TicketZone” tickets at the time of purchase; rather, it appears 6 hours before the concert starts. Furthermore, tickets for the Ghostly Kisses concert on the “TicketZone” platform are completely sold out, which means that anyone currently offering a ticket for this concert is not selling a ticket issued by the platform.

It was also found that there are two versions of the counterfeit ticket bearing the same order number, “TZ-78456322,” However, the first copy is a SILVER ticket priced at 60,000 dinars and dated Friday, December 11, while the second copy is a GOLD ticket priced at 85,000 dinars and dated Saturday, December 12, which confirms that the tickets are counterfeit.

For its part, the “TicketZone” platform issued a warning via a “Story” on its official Instagram account about fraud attempts involving the sale of counterfeit tickets and claims that they are “gift tickets” from the platform, It confirmed that no tickets for the concert are currently on sale, stressing that any ticket sold in this manner is unofficial and its authenticity is not guaranteed, It also clarified that the QR code for entry appears only 6 hours before the concert and that its official design is completely different from the counterfeit one, urging the public not to transfer any funds to individuals or entities outside of its platform. 

#it_ends_with_us

text:
Why was Flash Player discontinued?

Answer: Adobe killed it through years of mismanagement and neglect, but it was already bad.

During the 2000s, Flash was THE vector for computer viruses. It was the most insecure thing on your computer, and because back then people still browsed more than 3 websites, that meant CONSTANTLY being exposed to the worst shit the internet had to offer. It was used for ads that would take over your entire browser, show you horrible distracting shit and other things. It was so bad that just blocking Flash removed 90% of the garbage on the web. “Flashblock” was a thing alongside Adblock.

Flash also murdered your computer. It used insane amounts of CPU, more than the rest of your browser combined. It slowed web pages to a crawl, and made everything worse. Every Flash-based website sucked and was miserable to use. It was SLOW. It was often janky and shitty looking even on powerful PCs.

Adobe was to blame for this after they bought Macromedia in 2005. They had billions to make it not suck, but then they just kept on sucking. Google had to ship its own version of Flash with Chrome just to make it halfway secure. Apple issued patches for it THROUGH THE OS just to make it not an active vector for the latest virus or scam. And even then the exploits came so fast that Snow Leopard in 09 ended up shipping with an active Flash vulnerability on its golden master on release day.

Flash didn’t run on the iPhone at the time and the original iPad had 256MB of RAM. Flash did not run well on systems like that and Adobe refused to make it work in time for launch. They’d already screwed with Apple too many times in the 2000s (esp around Intel transition). Apple wasn’t in a mood to keep carrying their dead weight.

When the iPad came out it was the hottest thing in tech and none of the fancy Flash websites ran on it at all. This embarrassed the CEOs of those companies who suddenly looked like old farts who couldn’t keep up. They abandoned Flash immediately and that was it.

This coincided with HTML/JS getting actually really good again, so a lot of people realized that they didn’t need Flash (which cost big money!) at all.

Apart from people who still wanted it for games or some small handful of things that Flash still did well, it was dead.

Newgrounds was fun. To the rest of it, good riddance.
