text:
Let me give you the honest version of the AI portfolio question everyone is dancing around.

Duration is the enemy of stories and the friend of assets.

Right now bonds are yielding enough to make you think twice before allocating to anything that cannot show you cash conversion within a visible time horizon.

That is a regime change. Not a blip.

The last time fixed income offered this kind of real return competition to equities, the entire tech multiple expansion trade required a reset.

We are in that reset. It is just happening slowly enough that the momentum crowd has not fully registered it.

Here is where it gets interesting though.

Not all AI exposure is created equal and the bond cushion argument actually reinforces selectivity rather than wholesale retreat.

Physical AI infrastructure, power generation, liquid cooling, GPU clusters with contracted utilization, these are assets with identifiable yield profiles.

They borrow the language of tech but they behave like infrastructure.

That is exactly what you want when bonds are competing hard for capital allocation.

On the other side, legacy SaaS companies bolting AI onto stagnant ARR growth and asking you to pay 15x revenue for the privilege.

Those are the names that get re-rated when the discount rate is no longer theoretical.

The bond cushion gives disciplined allocators a genuine edge here.

You can afford to wait. You can afford to be wrong on timing.

You cannot afford to be wrong on asset quality when the cycle turns.

< Be Earl Warren
< Born 1891, Los Angeles, son of a Norwegian immigrant railroad worker
< Your father is murdered in 1938. The case is never solved.
< You work your way through UC Berkeley, then Boalt Hall law school
< Pass the bar in 1914, clerk for an oil company, draft notice comes
< First Lieutenant, U.S. Army, but the war ends before you ship out
< Back to California. You become a deputy district attorney in Alameda County
< 1925, you're the DA. You hold the job for thirteen years.
< You prosecute bootleggers, crooked sheriffs, corrupt officials
< Clean government, law and order. The newspapers love you.
< 1942, you're California's Attorney General. Japan bombs Pearl Harbor.
< You push for Japanese American internment. Loudly. Publicly. Relentlessly.
< 120,000 people, most of them citizens, sent to camps
< You call it military necessity. You warn of sabotage, fifth columns, racial treachery.
< There is no sabotage. There are no fifth columns.
< 1943, Governor of California. You win three terms.
< Republican, but you expand healthcare, prisons, highways, the state university system
< 1948, you're Dewey's running mate. You lose.
< 1952, you want the presidency. Eisenhower wants it more.
< He offers you the Supreme Court instead. You take it.
< October 1953, Chief Justice of the United States
< Your first major case: Brown v. Board of Education
< Segregated schools, seventeen states, sixty years of precedent
< The court is fractured. You need unanimity.
< You get it. 9-0. "Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal."
< The man who interned Japanese Americans now desegregates American schools
< You keep going. Miranda v. Arizona. Gideon v. Wainwright. Reynolds v. Sims.
< Criminal defendants get lawyers. Suspects get rights read. Legislatures get redrawn.
< Conservatives put up billboards: "Impeach Earl Warren"
< You retire in 1969. Nixon replaces you with Warren Burger.
< You die in 1974, still convinced the Court was the conscience of the nation

The architect of American internment became the architect of American civil rights. Same man, same career, same instinct for power deployed through law.

He never apologized for the camps.

History remembers the decisions, not the deportations.

text:
What I Saw on Oct. 7: Leadership and Israel’s Greatest Generation
‘We are going to change the map of the Mideast,’ Netanyahu said two days after the Hamas massacre.
ByOphir FalkOct. 6, 2026 12:02 pm ET

Every Jew and Israeli remembers where he was on Oct. 7, 2023. My day started shortly after 6:30 a.m., when Tzachi Braverman, the prime minister’s chief of staff, called me and said, “Get up! Come to the Kirya immediately,” referring to our military headquarters. I got dressed within minutes and rushed downstairs to wake my 19- and 21-year-old sons. I told them, “We’re at war. Get to your units.” My eldest asked, “Hezbollah or Hamas?” “Hamas,” I said. “OK,” he replied in what sounded like a sigh of relief. As I walked out the door, I passed my younger son, who was sitting in the living room waiting to be called up. “Don’t worry, it’s going to be a long war. You’ll get your chance,” I told him. He did get his chance and much more.I got in my car at about 7 a.m. I drove past my neighbor, an Air Force squadron commander, who was getting into his car. “Avner, are all your pilots coming?” I asked.“They will all come,” he said.“This isn’t another round. This time we need to go all the way,” I warned.“Absolutely,” Avner shouted in agreement.I arrived at the Kirya shortly after 8 a.m. when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was receiving updates on the unfolding attack. Horrific photos and videos of wounded and dead Israelis overwhelmed WhatsApp. Some showed Israeli civilians being slaughtered in their kibbutz homes and on the streets of Sderot.Shortly after 9:30 a.m., Mr. Netanyahu entered the situation room to receive a briefing from the military chiefs. “It’s going to be a long war,” the prime minister told me on the way to the meeting. Mr. Netanyahu, the Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, several other officials and I huddled around a small table. You could have heard a pin drop. In the room, the prime minister was briefed that “we were somewhat surprised” that “there are still a number of skirmishes and a large number of casualties.” He was told that “the situation should be under control before nightfall,” but that “we need to call up 100,000 reservists.” Mr. Netanyahu interjected: “Call up 300,000 troops immediately.” After intense questioning, he summarized, “Verify that, as I instructed this morning, a division was sent to the North and is holding a strong defense. Prevent the crossing of anyone back to Gaza. This is not another round of fighting. This is war.”At about 11:30 a.m., the prime minister addressed the public. “We are at war. Not an operation, not another round—at war.” He soon formalized the declaration of war and the war’s objectives in a meeting with the security cabinet.France’s President Emmanuel Macron was the first foreign leader to call. He urged diplomacy and offered to mediate. “Hamas is ISIS,” Mr. Netanyahu replied. “If it is not dismantled in Gaza, you will meet it in Paris.” The prime minister also emphasized that he didn’t want Mr. Macron to convey any message from him to anyone. “Hamas will soon get the message,” Mr. Netanyahu said.The next call came from then-President Joe Biden. “How can I help, Bibi?” he asked. Mr. Netanyahu said, “Hamas is worse than ISIS. They need to be dismantled.” He asked Mr. Biden to send two U.S. aircraft carriers toward Lebanon’s shores and to warn Iran and its Hezbollah proxy not to join the war. Mr. Biden promised he would. He gave the “Don’t” speech several days later, warning Iran and its proxies against escalation. As that fateful day ended, Israel’s enemies thought the Jewish state would collapse. Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals believed he was finished. Both were mistaken.On Oct. 9, the prime minister met with community leaders in southern Israel. “I ask that you stand steadfast because we are going to change the map of the Middle East,” he told the group.Three years later, Mr. Netanyahu has been proved right. Hamas has been decimated in Gaza, Palestinian terror infrastructure has been uprooted in Judea and Samaria, Hezbollah is on its knees, and Yemen’s Houthis have been hit like never before. Bashar al-Assad’s army in Syria is gone and, most important, the weakened Iranian regime will never assert the same power.After 1,096 days of fighting a war of redemption across seven fronts, Israel and its American ally are stronger than ever. Mr. Netanyahu has emerged as our greatest wartime leader, and the young soldiers of Oct. 7 are proving to be Israel’s Greatest Generation. Mr. Falk is foreign-policy adviser to Prime Minister Netanyahu.

text:
Corporate environments are not designed for true high performers.

They eventually become a nightmare for them because high performers are naturally inclined to identify problems and fix them.

You will want to address issues directly, without sugarcoating anything or tolerating nonsense. You will see the problem, call out the truth, and suggest different ways to fix it.

However, that is not what corporate organizations want. At the end of the day, they still prefer yes-men, people they can turn into a small army of obedient minions.

They need those pointless problems to exist. That is how they keep people running in circles and trapped in an endless cycle.

So, if you are a high performer, my advice is to take a step back and keep your head down. Do the bare minimum required to fulfill your responsibilities and stay off the blacklist.

It is not your responsibility and, in fact, it never has been, to fix problems you inherited from a broken system.

That is precisely why I believe Network Marketing can be a better fit than a corporate management position for competitive people who dislike stagnation and are constantly looking to grow, improve, and move forward in their careers. It offers a different environment, one where initiative, ambition, personal development, and results can play a more significant role than simply fitting into an existing hierarchy.

Of course, it is not for everyone. But if you recognize yourself in this description, it may be worth exploring whether this type of path aligns better with the way you think and work.

text:
Scott Wu runs a $48 billion company. He is also the least wealthy of its three founders.

Who he is:

- Born in Louisiana to chemical engineers who emigrated from Shanghai
- Won three International Olympiad in Informatics gold medals, and placed first overall in 2014
- Dropped out of Harvard, then co-founded Lunchclub
- In 2023 he started Cognition in a New York apartment with Steven Hao and Walden Yan
- All three are competitive programmers. Between them they hold five IOI golds
- Cognition began as a crypto project before pivoting to AI coding

What Cognition is:

- It calls itself an "agent lab." Its product, Devin, works as an autonomous software engineer
- It hands Devin long, tedious engineering work: migrations, maintenance, cleanup
- It works across several model providers, so customers can choose on cost and performance
- It bought Windsurf in 2025, days after Google hired away that company's CEO
- It is now training its own model on open-source foundations
- Customers include Mercedes-Benz, NASA, Goldman Sachs and Citi
- Cognition says Devin writes 89% of the code in its own repositories

The climb:

- $350M valuation when Devin launched in March 2024
- $10.2B in September 2025
- $26B in May 2026
- $48B on September 8, with $2B led by a16z, Accel, Founders Fund, General Catalyst and Avenir
- Run-rate revenue rose from $492M in May to $900M in September
- The Information expects $4B to $5B by year end
- In August, SpaceX approached Cognition about an acquisition. Wu said it was not for sale

Now the wealth:

- In February, Forbes put Hao at $1.3B, Yan at $830M, and Wu at $600M
- That was based on the $10.2B valuation
- Scale those stakes to $48B, after two rounds of dilution
- Hao lands near $5.6B. Yan near $3.6B. Wu near $2.6B
- So the CEO holds the smallest stake of the three founders

On secondaries:

- There is no public record of Wu selling shares
- He has called Cognition "the big one" and "the one for life"
- His stake has roughly quadrupled on paper since February, and remains almost entirely illiquid

The frame: SpaceX offered Wu an exit. He turned it down.

Instead, he raised at $48B and kept every share, as far as anyone can tell.

At 53 times run-rate revenue, Cognition is priced above Cursor's spring multiple. Wu is betting the gap closes in his favor.

text:
Let's see if I can pull this off.

My first time arriving in Florida, I knew not the language they spoke.

I saw a rather friendly person outside the airport. I knew he would offer me insights into this new country I was in, as he wore a cowboy hat.

I politely walked up to the towering figure, who represented everything I knew about America. Strong. Confident.

I bowed respectfully. I knew we would not speak the same language with words. Instead, I made a motion with my hand to my mouth, indicating I was hungry.

At first, he looked at me confused. But then he started to see the fatigue in my eyes after my long trip and knew I sought a succulent meal. He turned and pointed down the road, where stood a large sign with a pig on it.

I knew this must be where Americans consumed pork. I bowed again, offering him my warmest thanks for pointing me toward where one's stomach can be filled with the delights of this great country I was now in.

I scurried across the road. As one vehicle almost struck me, I stopped in the middle of the street, bowing for his forgiveness. He offered me a few words, which he spoke loudly, and gave me a gesture with one finger on his hand. I assumed this meant he forgave me, as he quickly drove by.

As I made my way closer to the large, pink-glowing sign of the pig, I could begin to smell the aroma of pork. My mouth watered, having not eaten anything for 17 hours.

Then I was there. A large wooden structure, which resembled one of those marvelous cabins you see in all American westerns. Alas, I would soon taste the meat which had already captured my sense of smell.

I walked inside to find a blonde woman standing at a podium. She commanded the respect of everyone waiting to enter and of those working inside.

I approached the podium, bowing to this blonde heroine, motioning again to my mouth as I sought sustenance. She said nothing, only handing me a square black box and pointing me toward a bench.

I did not know what it meant. But as she was in charge, I obeyed. I sat down on the bench, looking at others who held similar devices. One of them started to beep and light up. The family stood up and walked to the podium, where they were ushered in toward a table.

Ah! Americans use these devices to maintain order! How clever. I sat there, watching others earn their chance to enter. I knew I would soon be rewarded with such a reward.

I nearly jumped when the black box began to vibrate in my hand, the lights flickering and the sound beeping. I instantly raised my hand, informing the lady at the podium she had chosen me. I walked up to her, returning the device, and she led me inside toward a table.

After I sat down, she handed me a menu. I opened it, only to see it was all in English. But alas, many photographs depicting the meals.

A man came over and introduced himself. I stood up, bowing in appreciation and thanking him for taking the time to attend to me. I sat back down and pointed to the item on the menu I sought. He nodded and took my menu. He walked away, undoubtedly to inform the chef of my selection.

I remained seated, looking around at the others enjoying their meals. Within a moment, the man returned with a large plate, filled with the delicacies of this great country I was now in. I thanked him for this feast.

Once he departed, I wasted no time consuming the delicate American pork. There were also several different sauces to choose from. Oh, Americans! You truly have such variety!

I tasted each sauce before settling on one that was a mix of sweetness and spiciness. A truly American taste!

My eyes were not bigger than my stomach. After a few minutes of ravenous eating, my plate was clean.

To my surprise, the man returned with ANOTHER plate, filled with the exact same things I had just enjoyed! As I was still hungry, and I did not want to show disrespect, I ate all that was offered on that plate.

By then, I could feel my stomach churning, for I had eaten too much. Nevertheless, I finished all that was on my plate so as not to show any disrespect to this noble host.

But there he was, coming to my table with another plate! I looked up at him, shocked, confused. What was going on? Why were they feeding me until I exploded?

Only later did I learn the meal I had selected was an "All You Can Eat." My goodness! Americans really show hospitality!

However, at that moment I had to decline. I bowed my head in shame, having to refuse the host's warm plate of food. He did not think much of it and returned with the check for today's feast. I provided him with my credit card, which he scanned, and he printed the receipt right there at the table for me.

As my meal was complete, I tidied up the table, leaving it in the same condition as I found it. And I walked out, graciously thanking all those who worked there for the warm hospitality and fulfilling meal.

Yes, America. You truly are amazing!

Five supervised inmates working on a road crew used a wire coat hanger to unlock the car and safely rescue the 1-year-old toddler in less than two minutes... 

In 2019, a Florida family faced a frightening situation when their 1-year-old daughter was accidentally locked inside their car. The keys had been left inside, and the parents were unable to open the door.

Nearby, five prisoners were working on a supervised roadside detail with deputies when they noticed what was happening. Instead of standing by, the men offered to help. One of them used a coat hanger and carefully worked it through the door frame while the others watched and guided him.

After several attempts, they managed to unlock the car and free the little girl. The rescue was captured on video by the child’s mother, who could be heard reacting with relief as the door finally opened.

The unusual rescue quickly attracted attention because of who had stepped in to help. The men were prisoners, but in that moment they became the ones the family needed most. The mother later joked, “Thank God for the criminals in the world,” a line that helped the story spread even further.

The prisoners were praised for their quick thinking and for using their skills to help someone in trouble. Deputies overseeing the work crew allowed them to assist, turning what could have become a dangerous situation into a surprisingly heartwarming story.

text:
For well over a year, the twin problems of rising utility bills and soaring electric demand spurred by the AI boom have consumed the energy policy debate in Virginia, the data center capital of the world.

Clean energy foes — mostly Republicans — say the state’s landmark zero-carbon mandate should be scaled back or scrapped to lower costs and meet electricity needs. Many environmental advocates, meanwhile, are calling for a moratorium on new data centers, a step taken recently by governors in both red Texas and blue New York.

But a new clean energy plan crafted by Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger offers a different solution: Leverage the growth of data centers to go carbon-free.

Unveiled Oct. 1, the document doubles down on the Virginia Clean Economy Act (VCEA), which requires utilities to produce all carbon-free energy by midcentury; and participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, a multistate compact to curtail carbon pollution.

At the same time, the blueprint lays out how investor-owned utilities Dominion Energy and Appalachian Power can comply with those laws while feeding power-hungry data centers and getting them to foot the bill.

“There’s been a lot of speculation that our clean energy laws are too ambitious or out of reach,” said Josephus Allmond, Spanberger’s chief energy officer, at a news conference to announce the plan. ​“This modeling should put that notion to bed.”

State law requires the energy plan to be updated every four years. This year’s version uses advanced planning software to model a range of energy-supply scenarios, which is a first for a Virginia governor, and uncommon for governors’ offices across the U.S., experts say.

“I can’t think of other governors’ energy plans — high-level policy documents — where they’ve actually done their homework to show that the math works, the engineering works,” said Brandon Smithwood, a vice president for renewable developer Dimension Energy, which is active across the country.

The plan outlines four utility pathways to net-zero carbon by 2050, all while meeting ​“moderate” growth in electricity demand of 85%. That projection assumes most but not all proposed data centers will come to fruition. @CanaryMediaInc https://t.co/ENkVW7EH1y

text:
7. The Lamb Was Manifested to Israel and Revealed to the World

John’s Gospel places Christ’s baptism beside the announcement, “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). The wording gathers centuries of sacrifice into one Person. Abel offered of the firstlings of his flock (Genesis 4:4). Abraham told Isaac, “God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering” (Genesis 22:8). Israel sheltered beneath the blood of the Passover lamb in Egypt (Exodus 12:1–13). Isaiah wrote of One who would be “brought as a lamb to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7). Yet the blood of animals could not take away sins, for “it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). Then John points to a living man and declares that this is God’s Lamb. Jordan manifests the One who will provide the sacrifice that every earlier lamb could only picture.

John explained, “that he should be made manifest to Israel, therefore am I come baptizing with water” (John 1:31). That statement fixes the historical purpose of his ministry. John was not starting a Christian denomination, providing a sacramental machine for dispensing eternal life, or creating an initiation ceremony for the Body of Christ. He was preparing Israel and manifesting Israel’s Messiah. God gave John a specific identifying sign: the Spirit would descend and remain upon the One who baptizes with the Holy Ghost. John saw the sign and bore record, “this is the Son of God” (John 1:34). John baptized with water; Christ baptizes with the Holy Ghost. Those two baptisms must not be stirred together into religious soup. Neither should the baptism with the Holy Ghost be confused with the baptism of fire. In Matthew 3:10–12, the fire burns fruitless trees and consumes chaff with “unquenchable fire.” The Holy Ghost is God’s gift to believers; the unquenchable fire is judgment upon Christ rejecters. Anyone asking for the baptism of fire has failed to read the verses surrounding the phrase.

From Jordan, the road leads toward Calvary. The beloved Son will be rejected by men though approved by the Father. The One upon whom the Spirit rests will be accused of working by the power of devils. The Lamb publicly manifested to Israel will be handed to Gentiles and nailed to a cross. Yet there He will accomplish the work announced by John: He will bear sin, shed His blood, die, be buried, and rise again. Salvation is not found in admiring the dove, standing in the Jordan, copying John’s diet, or arguing about the water while ignoring the Lamb. Salvation is found in the crucified and risen Son of God. “Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The baptismal scene identifies the Saviour; the cross accomplishes the payment; the resurrection declares the victory; and the gospel offers that finished work freely to every sinner who believes.

text:
THE THIRTY MILE DOCTRINE

CASE FIVE: 130 MILLION PEOPLE — WHEN DOES THE NEED FOR SEA ACCESS BECOME A CLAIM TO SOMEONE ELSE’S SOVEREIGNTY?

Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has repeatedly placed Ethiopia’s population at the center of his maritime argument. The proposition carries undeniable political force: a nation of roughly 130 million people, one of Africa’s largest populations and economies, should not remain permanently dependent upon neighboring states for access to international shipping. Ethiopia’s government has described access to the Red Sea as an existential matter, emphasized the economic burden of dependence upon foreign ports, and argued that future generations cannot simply inherit the geographic condition created in 1993. Stated fairly, the argument asks whether the international community can reasonably expect an enormous and growing country, situated remarkably close to one of the world’s most important maritime corridors, to accept permanent strategic dependence upon others.

That question deserves an answer, but the answer begins with a distinction that has become increasingly obscured in Ethiopia’s public maritime debate. Ethiopia is landlocked, but Ethiopia is not cut off from the sea. Those are not synonymous conditions. Ethiopia conducts international commerce overwhelmingly through Djibouti, whose ports handle the vast majority of Ethiopian imports and exports. Ethiopia also continued using Eritrea’s Assab port after Eritrean independence until relations between the two governments deteriorated before the 1998 war. The historical record therefore establishes something important: Eritrean independence did not itself make Ethiopian commercial use of an Eritrean port legally impossible. Sovereignty remained Eritrean while Ethiopian commerce passed through Assab. The arrangement eventually collapsed because relations between the two states collapsed, not because international law required Eritrea to choose between sovereignty and Ethiopian access.

That fact changes the question before the court of international opinion. If Ethiopia already reaches the sea commercially through Djibouti, has historically reached it through Eritrea, and can negotiate additional access with neighboring coastal states, then the central dispute is no longer whether 130 million Ethiopians are being denied the ability to reach international markets. The harder question is what kind of maritime position the Ethiopian government now seeks. Commercial access, diversified port access, preferential tariffs, dedicated terminals, long term leases, transit corridors, railway connections, and guaranteed logistical arrangements all fall within the ordinary realm of interstate negotiation. Sovereign coastline, permanent territorial control, or a naval presence capable of projecting Ethiopian military power into the Red Sea belongs to an entirely different strategic and legal category.

This distinction is particularly important when Eritrea is accused, explicitly or implicitly, of imprisoning Ethiopia behind its coastline. The available historical record does not support such a simple proposition. Eritrea permitted Ethiopia to use Assab after independence. Whatever disputes subsequently arose over the operation of the port, currency, trade, and the deterioration of bilateral relations, the basic historical fact remains that an independent Eritrea and a landlocked Ethiopia once coexisted with Ethiopia using an Eritrean Red Sea port. The proposition that Eritrean sovereignty and Ethiopian maritime commerce are inherently incompatible is therefore contradicted by the history of the two states themselves.

A more difficult hypothesis must consequently be considered. Eritrea’s present hostility toward Ethiopian maritime ambitions may not represent a permanent doctrine that Ethiopia must never use Eritrean ports. It may instead reflect Eritrea’s profound distrust of the present Ethiopian government, the deterioration of relations with Abiy Ahmed, and Eritrean fears that the language of commercial access is evolving into something more consequential. No responsible legal argument should claim without evidence that Eritrea would grant Ethiopia Assab under another Ethiopian government, much less predict the terms or duration of any future lease. The narrower proposition is sufficient: nothing in Eritrean sovereignty prevents Eritrea, at any future point and entirely by consent, from negotiating commercial access, port facilities, leases, transit arrangements, or other agreements with Ethiopia. Refusing a particular arrangement with a particular government is not equivalent to denying Ethiopia an inherent right to conduct commerce through the Red Sea.

Abiy Ahmed’s own public language makes this distinction increasingly important. He has repeatedly said that Ethiopia seeks a negotiated solution and has denied intending to invade its neighbors. Those assurances belong in the record and should not be erased merely because critics distrust his intentions. Yet his broader maritime campaign has also elevated the issue far beyond the ordinary commercial question of moving containers through a neighboring port. Ethiopia has revived its navy despite having no coastline, has pursued arrangements involving maritime access and naval facilities, and has repeatedly presented the Red Sea as a matter of national survival, strategic destiny, and future power. When commercial access becomes intertwined with naval basing and sovereign access, neighboring states are entitled to ask whether they are being approached as commercial partners or being asked to facilitate a fundamental change in the regional military balance.

That is precisely why the population argument must be subjected to legal discipline. One hundred and thirty million people create enormous economic requirements, but population does not create territorial title. If Ethiopia’s demographic size entitles it to sovereign coastline because neighboring coastal states possess smaller populations, the principle cannot logically stop at the Red Sea. It would mean that the territorial rights of smaller states become progressively weaker as neighboring populations grow. Under such a doctrine, sovereignty would no longer depend upon recognized boundaries and international law. It would depend upon comparative population, strategic necessity, and the ability of larger states to demonstrate that they could make more economically productive use of territory controlled by smaller ones.

The implications would be destructive far beyond Eritrea. Small states exist throughout the international system beside vastly larger neighbors. Their territory is not held conditionally until demographic imbalance becomes sufficiently dramatic. Djibouti does not lose sovereign authority over its coastline because Ethiopia has more than one hundred times its population. Eritrea does not acquire fewer territorial rights because Ethiopia adds millions of citizens. Somalia’s coastline does not become proportionately negotiable according to Ethiopia’s economic growth. Sovereign equality means precisely that the legal personality and territorial integrity of a state do not expand or contract according to its population.

Ethiopia’s economic argument is stronger, but it leads to negotiation rather than territorial entitlement. Dependence upon Djibouti creates genuine strategic vulnerability. Excessive reliance upon a single maritime corridor exposes Ethiopia to commercial costs, political pressure, logistical disruption, and regional instability. Any competent Ethiopian government would seek diversification. Assab is geographically attractive. Berbera is attractive. Djibouti remains indispensable. Other regional corridors may become increasingly important. Ethiopia has every reason to negotiate aggressively for favorable terms and every reason to construct a maritime strategy capable of supporting a country of its scale. International law does not require Ethiopia to remain economically complacent merely because it is landlocked.

What international law does require is consent where another state’s sovereignty begins. Ethiopia may seek access. Eritrea may negotiate it or refuse the particular terms proposed. Somalia may offer access through territory under Somali sovereignty. Djibouti may continue providing access under arrangements negotiated with Ethiopia. Kenya may become part of Ethiopia’s diversification strategy if mutually acceptable arrangements are reached. In every case, the governing principle remains the same: access is obtained through agreement with the sovereign state concerned. Ethiopia’s need strengthens its negotiating interest; it does not weaken its neighbor’s title.

The naval dimension makes that principle even more consequential. A commercial Ethiopian presence at a port and a permanent Ethiopian naval base on the Red Sea cannot reasonably be treated as strategically equivalent. A naval installation would introduce Ethiopian military power directly into one of the most contested maritime theaters in the world. Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea, Somalia, Turkey, the Gulf states, Israel, and other powers with interests around the Red Sea and the Horn would assess such a development through the lens of their own security. Their positions are not identical and should not be artificially merged, but the regional consequences explain why a coastal state may regard a request for naval facilities very differently from a request to unload Ethiopian cargo.

This is also why rhetoric surrounding Assab deserves particularly careful scrutiny. There is a profound legal difference between saying that Ethiopia historically used Assab, that Ethiopia would benefit enormously from renewed access to Assab, and that Assab somehow remains Ethiopia’s by historical right. The first proposition is historical fact. The second is a legitimate strategic objective that could be pursued through negotiation. The third requires a legal title capable of overcoming Eritrea’s internationally recognized sovereignty, and neither Ethiopia’s population nor the proximity of Assab supplies that title. Political slogans about recovering what was once Ethiopian cannot perform the work of international law.

The case therefore reaches a revealing point. Ethiopia’s predicament is real, but the evidence does not establish a country being physically denied the sea by hostile geography. It establishes a landlocked country seeking better, cheaper, more diversified, and increasingly strategic forms of maritime access. That is a legitimate national objective. The legal problem begins when the vocabulary of access starts carrying the implications of ownership, sovereign entitlement, territorial recovery, or military projection. Once that boundary is crossed, the argument is no longer simply about the commercial requirements of 130 million people. It becomes an argument about whether national necessity can create rights over another sovereign state.

That transformation leads to a deeper question that international law alone cannot answer. Why has the language surrounding Ethiopia’s maritime predicament increasingly taken the form of historical entitlement? Why do population, former possession, proximity, national greatness, and the idea of recovering what was once “ours” repeatedly appear in the same political architecture? The answer may require examining an ideological concept that predates the present Red Sea campaign and asking whether a doctrine developed within Ethiopia’s domestic politics has begun to migrate beyond Ethiopia’s borders.

THE CASE CONTINUES

CASE SIX: THE “KEGNA” HYPOTHESIS — WHEN “OURS” BECOMES A DOCTRINE OF ENTITLEMENT.

Another Country Singer Betrays: Built Career on Decent Fans, Now Zach Bryan Trades Them for Terror Apologists: Either Zach Bryan is indifferent to human suffering and murder, or he just cares about his streaming numbers.

I’m not sure that the two are mutually exclusive, mind you, and I can’t tell you if one is worse than the other. What I can tell you is that Bryan, a country star who built his reputation on decency and kinship with blue-collar fans, is now parading around Gillette Stadium — where Macklemore got himself banned from due to his anti-Semitic, pro-Palestine rhetoric, kicking off one of the dumber woke controversies of recent years — wearing a “Free Palestine” T-shirt.

From Billboard, which reported that Bryan’s Saturday concert broke the record for attendance at the Foxborough, Massachusetts venue: Bryan drew headlines after his opening night at the Kraft Group-owned venue on Friday (Oct. 2), when he wore a black T-shirt reading “Free Palestine.”

Members of Bryan’s band were also spotted wearing matching shirts, according to TMZ. The “I Remember Everything” singer did not address the shirts during the performances. Bryan’s decision to wear the “Free Palestine” shirt comes weeks after Macklemore was removed from the remaining U.S. dates of Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian remarks he made during his Sept. 4 and 5 concerts at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.

It’s worth noting what this proves: Macklemore wasn’t banned for saying “Free Palestine,” but instead for openly anti-Semitic antics like imagery of a U.S. hundred-dollar bill intertwined with the Israeli flag in a jigsaw puzzle and appearing on stage wearing a keffiyeh.

That being said, Bryan’s fanbase is different from that of Macklemore or other artists loudly banging on about the necessity of freeing an entity that was effectively free before it attacked, murdered, and raped thousands of innocent people in the nation that had left it alone, for the most part, since 2005.

Macklemore’s fans — such as they may have still existed before this kerfuffle; the rapper was, before the controversy, about as relevant as the Commodore Amiga or a Studebaker — were privileged wokeistas, and proud of it. Meanwhile, Bryan relies on red-state voters, who aren’t precisely as eager to take up keffiyeh-wearing or Jew-baiting.

And that’s effectively what Bryan is signing them up for. Over two-thirds of Gazans — 68 percent — support armed terrorism against Israel, according to an Australia/Israel Review of the polling between 2014 and 2026. Over half of them still supported the Oct. 7 attacks, according to a November 2025 survey by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research.

Bryan is also much more relevant than Macklemore is. Unlike the rapper, who has seen better days profile-wise, Bryan is effectively at the apex of his fame. His three most recent albums have reached Nos. 1 or 2 on the Billboard 200 charts, and his self-titled 2023 album has spent 162 weeks on the chart.

But then, perhaps we should have expected this from Bryan. Consider that his most recent album included “Bad News,” which disparages the enforcement of immigration law. Consider, too, the fact that he’s been accused of “emotional abuse” by ex-girlfriend Brianna LaPaglia of Barstool Sports.

According to the U.K. Independent, she alleges that Bryan offered her $12 million to sign a non-disclosure agreement about their relationship.

“The last year of my life has been the hardest year of my life dealing with the abuse from this dude,” she said on her podcast. “I’m still scared right now because I’m scared of him. My brain’s rewired and I’m scared to make him mad.”

Is that true? Perhaps. I’m inclined to believe that someone who’ll casually don a T-shirt advocating for the cause of a terror-ridden society will also inflict terror upon others. Whatever the case, this is someone who’s deeply afraid of losing the spotlight and knows what exactly the liberal media would do if he played Gillette Stadium and didn’t offer a rejoinder to the Macklemore situation. His label would be proud. His fans, not so much. But then again, with the antics of fellow country star Jelly Roll and his anti-Trump wokeness, they’re probably used to boycotting these fools by now.

The surrounding remarks place the “let them take out” line in a comparison of costs, not an instruction to Iran.

At the October 5 Nebraska rally, Trump was defending temporary higher gas and other prices tied to the Iran conflict. The sequence reported across outlets runs roughly: the war’s effects are “just artificial,” “a little bit high,” and “a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe.” He then said, “They can take out a city. Let ’em take out Los Angeles, let ’em take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.” Nearby lines also stressed that the conflict would end soon, prices would fall, and Iran would not obtain a nuclear weapon.

The White House has stated that this was not a call for an attack. Communications Director Steven Cheung said the comments have been misrepresented and that Trump “was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” adding that Iran currently has “no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” The White House rapid-response account made the same point: the U.S. action was framed as stopping Iran from gaining the ability to strike those cities.

California Democratic officials and some local leaders read the same phrasing as encouraging or treating the cities as an acceptable loss, which is the framing in the CA_Dem graphic. The wording “let them take out” is colloquial and open to that reading in isolation; the White House and the immediate cost-comparison context are the basis for the claim that it referred to the avoided maximum cost of a nuclear-capable Iran rather than an invitation for an attack.

The first was Adapa. Or was it?

Way way before Adam appears in Genesis, Mesopotamia already had a story about a human who was given the wisdom of the gods but was denied immortality.

Adapa served Ea at Eridu. 

He was summoned into the presence of Anu. 

He was offered food and drink connected with life, but he refused them because Ea told him to.

Humanity stayed mortal.

Then the same basic issue shows up again.

Adam gains knowledge that makes him “like one of us,” and suddenly immortality becomes the issue. 

The Tree of Life is blocked and humanity keeps the knowledge and loses eternal life.

Gilgamesh repeats it again. He goes searching for the secret of immortality. He gets close enough to touch it, and it slips through his hands.

Enoch as well. A human crosses into the divine realm, receives heavenly knowledge and becomes something more than an ordinary man.

Same with Apkallu. The sages connected to Ea who bring knowledge to humanity before the Flood. 

Later traditions preserve Oannes doing the same thing. He comes from the water and teaches humans how to live like civilized people.

The names and shit change, but the core story stays intact.

A being or extraordinary human receives knowledge from somewhere beyond ordinary humanity. 

That knowledge changes civilization. 

The boundary between human and divine gets dangerously thin. 
Immortality appears. 
Then the door closes.

This is why I keep looking at it.

Ancient cultures repeated this fucking story for thousands of years.

People dont keep carrying a story across centuries, languages and empires unless something inside it is real.

Adapa is simply the oldest version we can currently read.

Sumerian civilization didn't wake up and their toast was ready and a civ with fully developed mythology, priesthoods, temples and stories. 

Those traditions came from somewhere. 

There could have been earlier Adapas.
Earlier sages.

These clay tablets only show us the moment humans finally started writing the story down.

I don't think Adapa is the first.

text:
I've made 100+ hours of content about building a magnetic personal brand.

If I had to condense what I've learned into one post, I'd give founders these 10 rules:

1. Pick a buyer, not an audience.

People only stop scrolling for content that describes their exact situation, so the narrower the person you write for, the more each post feels personal to the buyers who actually matter.

Example: "Founder" is too broad. A technical B2B founder with a proven product and no market visibility has a problem you can actually speak to.

2. Start with what they want.

Buyers pay attention to outcomes they already want, so if your content opens with some mumbo jumbo, technical lingo, they have no reason to keep reading.

Example: Founders don't wake up wanting "thought leadership." They want customers and money in the bank. Talk about the money in the bank, not the thought leadership part.

3. Say what you believe, firmly.

People remember a clear position because it gives them one idea to file you under and repeat to others when you're not in the room.

Example: Mine is that founder-led marketing is the highest ROI marketing strategy in 2026. This thesis is why my company name is FounderFunnel. 

4. Show where that belief came from through stories.

An opinion with no visible source sounds random, and people trust a belief once they can see the experience that produced it.

Example: Share the life events, moments, and stories that led you to develop the strong belief you have today.

Allow people to see the backstory behind the opinion.

5. Teach with examples.

The brain holds onto specific, concrete details far better than general advice, so the example does the persuading a broad claim can't.

6. Repeat your best ideas.

A personal brand is built through repetition. 

People need to hear an idea many times before it sticks, and most of your audience only ever sees a small slice of what you post.

You will get bored of talking about the same things long before the market gets bored of hearing it.

7. Choose a marketing channel for its job.

Every platform rewards a different kind of content and attention, so matching the channel to the job keeps you from doing great work in the wrong place.

Example: YouTube lets you demonstrate depth. X lets you test ideas and join conversations. LinkedIn rewards deep well thought out content. Pick based on your buyer and what you can sustain.

8. Give a stranger somewhere to go next.

Curiosity fades minutes after someone finishes a post, so you should capture that attention while you still have it.

Send people to a longer piece of content, a video, or your website.

Example: After a post, can they find a deeper explanation, see your work, understand your offer, and contact you? If not, attention is leaking.

9. Build a system to keep publishing.

Content is hard to make consistently. You won't feel like it many days. Willpower alone won't do, so you need a system that hands you ideas and helps you create content at scale.

Example: Capture interesting conversations you've had from calls. Repurpose them into content across channels. Turn the best moments into posts and videos.

10. Measure downstream results, not just reach.

Reach tells you how many people saw something, downstream results like DMs, bookmarks, and booked calls tell you whether the right people are seeing your content.

Example: UTM track each channel you publish on. I use Datafast, you can also vibecode a tool that does the same. This will allow you to see where traffic comes from.

Also pay close attention to what people say on calls when they hop on. If they say they read your content, ask what exactly they like most.

That's your signal to do more of it.
